title: What incoming inspection protects: defect cost by stage

goals.text: Specify the documents that must accompany a received lot of components, paste or bare PCB and state what each one proves.
Classify incoming-material findings as accept, quarantine or reject and write a record a supplier can act on.

p: Incoming inspection protects the line by confirming three things before a lot is released: that it matches the purchase order, that it is in the condition the process requires, and that the supplier controlled the characteristics that affect yield. It is a gate, not a visual check. Material that is wrong, wet, expired or counterfeit has to be stopped here, because every later stage — placement, reflow, wave, cleaning, ICT, functional test, field service — is a more expensive place to find it.

The cost of the same defect rises as it moves downstream. At incoming it costs inspection time, quarantine space and a supplier conversation. After reflow it costs rework, scrap and a stopped line. In the field it costs a complaint, a warranty claim and the credibility of the plant. The exact figures come from your own accounts; the shape does not change.

A working plan also protects process stability. Released without evidence, marginal paste or a marginal bare board makes operators compensate with printer, placement or reflow changes — and those changes hide the material problem, move the defect to another stage, and make root cause analysis harder than it needs to be. That is why the record has to say what was checked, what was found and what was released: so a yield problem three weeks later can be traced back to a material condition.

p: A component lot should arrive with a packing list, a certificate of conformance, a material declaration, a restricted-substances declaration, a lot or date code, a traceability label, and any test report the purchase order calls for. Each document answers a different question. The packing list fixes quantity and shipment identity. The certificate of conformance is the supplier's declaration that the part, revision and acceptance criteria are as specified; the material declaration names the base material and the plating or termination finish. The restricted-substances declaration shows the lot was screened against the customer and regulatory requirements that apply, and the lot or date code, together with the traceability label, ties the reels on the floor to the supplier batch.

Moisture-sensitive parts add packaging to that list: a moisture barrier bag, desiccant, a humidity indicator card, and a label carrying the floor life or storage condition from the applicable JEDEC moisture sensitivity standard. Compare the label, the packing list and the purchase order before the bag is opened. Where they disagree, the lot waits in quarantine until the supplier explains the difference — a mismatch is not a typo to be resolved by the person holding the box.

Solder paste is a process material, so its paperwork has to prove identity and condition, not only composition. Expect a certificate of analysis, a safety data sheet, the lot code, the expiration date, a storage temperature record in °C, alloy composition, metal content, flux chemistry, halogen content, and rheology or printability data where the purchase order requires it. The certificate of analysis ties the lot to the specified formulation; the safety data sheet covers hazard communication. Expiration date and storage record together answer the only question that matters at the printer: was this paste kept the way the supplier says it must be kept.

Paste also arrives with handling history that the documents do not capture. Note the carton condition, any temperature excursion indicator, and whether the lot shipped under the supplier's stated temperature control. If it is outside the stated storage or shelf-life condition, quarantine it and ask the supplier for a disposition before anyone prints with it. Operator experience is not a release criterion for aged paste: a lot that looks and smells right can still be out of its window.

A bare PCB lot should carry a certificate of conformance, a material declaration, a copper thickness report in µm, a surface finish report, and — where the purchase order requires them — an impedance report and a cleanliness or solderability report. Together they cover the four things a fabricator can get wrong silently: the laminate system and flame rating, the copper that the current and impedance calculations assume, the finish type and thickness range, and the assembly readiness of the surface.

The physical package is part of the evidence too. Boards with moisture sensitivity or fine pitch should arrive in a barrier bag with desiccant, a humidity indicator and sound edges. Check those before opening, then check the boards. Warping, scratches, oxidation, delamination or exposed copper beyond the drawing limit all mean quarantine, with the location and extent recorded precisely enough that the supplier can inspect the same area and decide whether the cause is fabrication, packaging or transport.

Three dispositions, and the line between them is evidence rather than schedule pressure. Accept when the documents are complete, the packaging is intact, the environmental indicators are inside the supplier's stated limits, and the sampled material conforms to the purchase order and the applicable IPC acceptance standard. Quarantine when the evidence is incomplete or uncertain — a missing certificate, damaged packaging, a suspect humidity indicator, an unclear lot code, or a measurement sitting right at the limit in mm or °C — and when a supplier review, retest or approved rework could still disposition the lot.

Reject when the defect cannot be dispositioned safely: wrong part, counterfeit suspicion, a prohibited substance, expired paste, a wet or delaminated board, severe mechanical damage, or any safety hazard. Sample size and acceptance criteria come from your sampling plan and your process qualification, not from what is convenient today.

A deviation is a fourth path, and it has to be limited, time-bound and approved by the engineering and quality owners who carry the risk. Write down the affected quantity, the exposure of each downstream process, the extra checks the deviation requires and the date it expires. An open deviation is not an acceptance: if it is not closed on time, the lot is quarantined or rejected.

theory.h: Writing a record the supplier can act on
p: A finding record the supplier can act on names the part, the supplier lot and the internal lot, the quantities received, inspected and affected, the requirement, the observed result, the method, the location, the date, the inspector, the disposition and the action requested. Quote the purchase order, drawing or standard by reference rather than copying its text, and state what was seen or measured — not what you think of it. Photographs, label images, document copies and test data make the difference between a finding the supplier can reproduce and one it can only dispute.

Ask for a corrective action that addresses the cause and for evidence that it worked. To make that possible, give the internal part identifier, the customer part identifier, the revision, the package type, the quantity affected, and the stage at which the defect would have been caught had it escaped. A document gap needs the missing document named and the requirement that makes it mandatory. A physical defect needs the criterion, the sample size, the number of affected units and the disposition. Keep the tone factual: the supplier needs facts to change a process, and blame gives it something else to argue about.

Incoming inspection earns its cost on the defects that are hard to see later: oxidised pads, wet PCB, expired paste, the wrong alloy, the wrong plating, damaged terminations, counterfeit parts, and moisture-sensitive devices packed incorrectly. Each of them can pass a visual check and still produce poor wetting, voids, insufficient solder, tombstoning, opens, shorts, thermal stress, ICT or functional failures, and field escapes.

The cost drivers are inspection labour, quarantine space, rework labour, scrap, line stoppage, expedited replacement, complaint handling and warranty. Build the plan against your own stage costs, aim it at the characteristics with the highest downstream cost and the lowest chance of detection later, and link every finding to the stage where it would have surfaced. A wrong surface finish on a bare PCB passes visual inspection and fails at reflow. The wrong metal content in a paste prints normally and shows up as voids. A compromised barrier bag survives placement and cracks in the oven. Naming that stage is what lets you compare the cost of prevention with the cost of escape in the same units.

calc.task: Use your plant cost table. Let N be lot quantity, f be incoming escape fraction, C_in be cost per defect found at incoming, C_reflow be cost per defect found after reflow, and C_field be cost per defect found in the field. Calculate expected cost for the same defect if it is caught at incoming, if it escapes to reflow, and if it escapes to the field. State the stage cost ratio that justifies incoming inspection.
calc.solution: Start by obtaining N, f, C_in, C_reflow, and C_field from your accounting, scrap, rework, warranty, and line stoppage records. Compute incoming cost as N times f times C_in. Compute reflow cost as N times f times C_reflow. Compute field cost as N times f times C_field. Compare the results by dividing reflow cost by incoming cost and field cost by incoming cost. Use the ratios to decide whether incoming inspection resources are justified for the part family. If the ratio is high, document the avoided cost in the incoming inspection plan and review the plan when part family, supplier, or process changes.

defect.symptom: Incoming moisture barrier bag is punctured, humidity indicator card shows exceedance, and bare PCB pads show discoloration.
defect.cause: Packaging damage or storage excursion allowed moisture ingress, and the lot was not quarantined before release.
defect.action: Quarantine the lot, record lot code, quantity, packaging condition, indicator status, and pad appearance; notify supplier; request corrective action for packaging and storage; do not release until bake or replacement is approved by the applicable moisture sensitivity standard and your process qualification.

takeaways: Incoming inspection is the cheapest place to stop a material defect; every stage after it adds rework, scrap or field exposure.
A document package proves identity, condition and traceability, and each certificate answers a different question rather than repeating the others.
Dispositions follow evidence: accept, quarantine or reject on what the documents and measurements show, and time-bound any deviation.

mistakes.mistake: A certificate of conformance is treated as proof that the lot was physically inspected and is good.
mistakes.instead: Treat it as the supplier's declaration of conformity and verify the lot physically against the purchase order and the applicable acceptance standard.

mistakes.mistake: A lot is released because the line needs it, with the missing certificate promised for later.
mistakes.instead: Quarantine until the document arrives; a release without evidence is a deviation and needs a time-bound approval, not a promise.

mistakes.mistake: The incoming record says "damaged packaging" and nothing else, so the supplier cannot investigate.
mistakes.instead: Record lot, quantity, location, photographs and the requirement breached, and ask for a cause-level corrective action with evidence.

terms.def: Supplier declaration that a lot meets the purchase order and the referenced acceptance criteria; it is evidence of declared conformity, not of inspection by the buyer.
Supplier report of measured or tested values for named characteristics of a specific lot — alloy, metal content, flux chemistry, plating thickness and similar.
Controlled hold on a lot whose conformity is uncertain, preserved until evidence, retest, supplier review or an approved disposition closes it.
A limited, time-bound and approved acceptance of a lot outside a requirement, with the exposure and the additional checks recorded.

title: The documentation package: CoC/CoA, packing list, MSL label, declarations

goals.text: Specify the documents that must accompany a received lot of components, paste or bare PCB and state what each one proves.

blocks.alt: Receiving desk with a stack of controlled documents, each marked present, and one flagged as missing
blocks.caption: The documentation package: certificate of conformance, certificate of analysis, packing list, MSL label and declarations checked at receiving

p: Every lot arrives as a document-controlled object first and a physical object second. To release it, receiving needs a packing list, a certificate of conformance or certificate of analysis, and any declaration the purchase order names; moisture-sensitive parts add a sealed dry pack with an MSL label and a humidity indicator card. The exact set follows the supplier agreement, the customer specification and the risk of the lot, but the purpose never changes: identity and quantity, conformity or measured properties, moisture history, and regulatory claims each need their own evidence.

A familiar carton and a known supplier are not evidence. The package is what proves the lot is the lot the process was planned around, and it is what a later defect gets traced back to. It also tells the inspector whether to open the pack, sample it, or hold it.

The packing list records what the supplier says it shipped and how it labelled it: purchase order, part number, revision, quantity, lot or batch code, date code, package type and handling notes. Against it, receiving matches cartons to the expected quantity and traceability code. For paste it names the type, container size and lot; for bare boards, the part number, revision, panel or array count and packaging requirements.

A packing list settles what left the supplier's dock, not what it passed. When it disagrees with the purchase order, the carton labels or the certificate, the lot waits until the discrepancy is explained, and the packing-list number and the mismatch go into the incoming record.

theory.h: CoC and CoA: what they prove
p: The certificate of conformance says the delivered lot conforms to the purchase order and the referenced acceptance criteria. The certificate of analysis gives measured or tested values for named characteristics: electrical parameters, plating thickness or package integrity for components; metal content or viscosity for paste, often against IPC J-STD-004; laminate, copper weight, plating type and thickness, judged against IPC-A-600 or IPC-6012 for bare boards.

Either certificate is only evidence for the lot it names. One that covers a different lot proves nothing about the received lot, however well the part number matches, so check the lot or date code, the certificate date, the supplier name and the referenced specification before accepting it.

A sealed dry pack carries an MSL label and a humidity indicator card. The label gives the moisture sensitivity level and the floor life assigned under IPC/JEDEC J-STD-033; the card shows whether the pack's environment went past the supplier's humidity threshold. Neither one declares the parts fit to place. What they record is handling: how the lot was protected, and how much of its floor life is left once the bag is opened.

Opening the pack starts the clock, and the remainder is tracked against the label value and your own schedule. A damaged pack, a broken seal or a card showing an exceedance sends the lot to quarantine for evaluation. Record the MSL value, the floor-life value, the card status and the seal condition as part of the incoming evidence.

Paste paperwork has to cover identity and process suitability at once. The packing list names type, container size and lot code. The CoA or CoC shows the lot was manufactured and tested against the agreed specification, often IPC J-STD-004, with shelf-life information, and the container label has to agree with both. Storage and handling conditions belong to the process: 2 °C to 10 °C is a common range, and your facility controls decide the rest.

Paste that comes back into storage should carry its handling history — how many times it was opened, how long it sat outside — because both affect printability and may force mixing or discard. A certificate proves the paste was acceptable at the supplier, not that it survived transport, storage and handling. Record lot code, expiry date, storage condition and handling notes.

Bare boards arrive with evidence that they were built to the purchased design and acceptance level. The packing list fixes part number, revision, quantity and lot code. The CoC or CoA covers the laminate material, copper weight, plating finish and the dimensional or electrical results the purchase order asks for; acceptance may reference IPC-A-600 for visual and dimensional criteria and IPC-6012 for qualification and performance. Plated through holes need a plating type and thickness range, and the board needs a lot or panel mark that matches the documents.

Controlled-impedance boards add coupon results or a statement that the coupons were tested; special finishes add the finish type and any storage limits. Where the revision, material class or finish does not match the purchase order, the lot is quarantined even if it looks right. Record the revision, the lot code and the certificate reference.

Declarations sit beside the quality certificates and cover regulatory and contractual claims: restricted substances under RoHS or REACH where the purchase order invokes them, counterfeit avoidance for authorised-channel control on high-reliability or safety parts, conflict minerals where reporting applies. None of them says the lot will process well on your line. They say the supplier has made a specific claim about origin, composition or compliance.

Tie the declaration to the lot or a defined lot range and keep it with the incoming record. A missing declaration does not make the boards unusable, but it blocks the compliance claim until the document arrives. Record the declaration type, its revision and the range it covers.

theory.h: Disposition based on the document package
p: Disposition follows the evidence, and a document gap is still a stop. Matching part numbers, revisions, lot codes, quantities and certificates mean release is possible. A missing CoC, a mismatched lot code, a damaged dry pack or an expired shelf life is a document or handling defect rather than a physical one, and it holds the lot until the evidence is corrected.

Write down the document numbers, certificate dates, MSL values, indicator status and any deviation. A quarantined lot records which document or condition failed and what has to happen before release; a released lot records that the package was complete and that its handling limits passed to the process. That record is what makes a defect traceable months later, and what turns a repeated document failure into a supplier corrective action.

The package does not stop at the receiving door. Paste type, shelf-life status, MSL floor-life start and board revision go onto the work order or MES record. Component lot codes are linked to the feeder or magazine, paste open time, storage time and open count are visible to the printer operator, and the board revision and lot code are linked to the panel or array actually assembled.

The handoff is what keeps a released lot from being run with the wrong parameters, and it is what makes containment possible: when a suspect condition appears, the process can say which lots saw it. Record it in the same traceability system that holds the inspection result.

calc.task: A dry pack label states a floor life of 168 h per IPC/JEDEC J-STD-033. The pack is opened at the start of the shift. Placement is scheduled 170 h after opening. Determine whether the floor life is exceeded.
calc.solution: First, identify the floor-life value from the label: 168 h. Next, identify the elapsed time from opening to placement: 170 h. Then compare elapsed time with floor life: 170 h is greater than 168 h. Then calculate the exceedance: 170 h minus 168 h equals 2 h. Finally, disposition: do not place the components without a qualified re-bake or other approved action under IPC/JEDEC J-STD-033; quarantine and record the exceedance.

defect.symptom: Incoming dry pack has an MSL label, but the humidity indicator card shows the supplier exceedance color and the pack seal is creased.
defect.cause: The dry pack was damaged or opened before receipt, so the humidity indicator card reflects exposure outside the controlled dry-pack environment.
defect.action: Quarantine the lot, record the label and card status, inspect for oxidation or coplanarity issues, and follow IPC/JEDEC J-STD-033 bake and re-bag requirements if the lot is to be used; notify the supplier with photos and lot traceability.

takeaways: A lot is only released when its documents prove identity, conformity and handling history, so the paperwork is evidence rather than an attachment.
Check every certificate against the lot code it names, because a certificate for a different lot proves nothing about the material you received.
Record the document values that drive the process — paste type, MSL floor life, board revision — and pass them on to the work order, not just to the file.

mistakes.mistake: Accepting a lot because the part number on the certificate matches
mistakes.instead: Verify the lot or date code, the certificate date and the referenced specification, and quarantine any lot the certificate does not name.

mistakes.mistake: Recording the MSL level but not the floor-life start time
mistakes.instead: Record the bag-open time and the cumulative exposure so the remaining floor life is known before placement, per IPC/JEDEC J-STD-033.

mistakes.mistake: Filing the certificate in a quality folder and stopping there
mistakes.instead: Transfer paste type, shelf-life status, MSL start and board revision to the work order or MES record so the process runs on the same values.

terms.def: A supplier statement that the delivered lot conforms to the purchase order and the acceptance criteria it references.
A supplier report of measured or tested values for named characteristics of a specific lot.
The time a moisture-sensitive component may spend out of its dry pack at a stated ambient condition before reflow, assigned by moisture sensitivity level.
A card in a dry pack that changes colour to show whether the pack exceeded a stated humidity threshold.

skills: Lesson m01l01: What incoming inspection protects: defect cost by stage

title: Sampling a lot: lot definition, sample size, inspection level, AQL concept

goals.text: Build a sampling plan for a stated lot and inspection level, and explain what the plan does and does not protect against.

theory.p: A lot is the smallest quantity of incoming material you can treat as one population for inspection: same part number, revision, supplier, manufacturing lot or date code, packaging and process route. Mixed revisions, date codes or supplier plants are separate lots unless your quality plan says the differences cannot affect the characteristics being inspected. For SMT and THT material, a lot may be a reel, a tray stack, a bag of through-hole parts or a shipment of bare boards, depending on how the supplier controls traceability.

theory.h: Choose the inspection level from risk and cost
theory.p: The inspection level sets how many units you inspect relative to lot size. ISO 2859-1 offers general levels and special levels for destructive or expensive tests, and its normal general level is the usual starting point for incoming inspection when nothing argues for another. Drop to a lower general level when lots are stable and defects are expensive to find; raise it when the supplier is new, the part is critical or recent data show variability. Special levels need a documented rationale, and your incoming inspection procedure should confirm the choice.

theory.h: Treat AQL as a supplier quality target
theory.p: AQL, the acceptable quality level, is the quality level a plan is designed to accept with high probability while the supplier's process runs at that average. It is not a maximum defect rate for every lot, and it never means an accepted lot is defect-free. ISO 2859-1 lists preferred AQL values; incoming inspection commonly uses 0.65 %, 1.0 % and 2.5 % defective, chosen by defect class and risk. Critical defects justify a much tighter plan or full inspection, while minor cosmetic defects tolerate a looser one.

Counting critical, major and minor defects together lets a single AQL hide risk. For incoming material, define what makes a unit defective in each class: a wrong part number or damaged pads is critical, a small cosmetic mark outside a functional area is minor. Where you inspect several characteristics, decide whether one sample serves all classes or whether each needs its own sample and AQL. Record the defect class in the inspection record so the plan can be reviewed against supplier data.

theory.h: Build the plan from lot size, level and AQL
p: Building a plan means turning lot size and inspection level into a sample size code letter, then reading the accept and reject numbers for the chosen AQL. In ISO 2859-1, a lot of 1201 to 3200 units at general inspection level II gives code letter K, which means n = 125. At AQL 1.0 % defective under normal single sampling, Ac = 3 and Re = 4: inspect 125 units, accept on 3 or fewer defective units, reject on 4 or more.

Read the level and the lot band together, never one without the other. The same lot band gives code letter H (n = 50, Ac = 1, Re = 2 at AQL 1.0 %) at level I and code letter L (n = 200, Ac = 5, Re = 6 at AQL 1.0 %) at level III. The 3000-unit lot in the worked example sits inside 1201 to 3200, which is why it resolves to K; 5,000 units would fall into the next band, 3201 to 10000, and give L with n = 200.

theory.h: Know what the plan protects against
theory.p: A sound plan makes rejection increasingly likely as the supplier's average quality falls below the AQL, so bad lots tend not to be accepted. It also gives a repeatable basis for normal, tightened and reduced inspection when the standard's switching rules apply. What it cannot do is certify an individual accepted lot as defect-free, catch defects outside the inspected characteristics, or replace supplier process control, incoming test coverage and line containment when something escapes.

theory.h: Plan disposition and feedback up front
theory.p: Define the disposition before inspection starts — return, sort, use-as-is with concession, or rework — with traceability to the sample results. When an accepted lot then fails on the line, work out whether the lot definition was wrong, the sample missed a localised defect, the characteristic was outside the plan, or the supplier changed material or process. Feed the answer into the next review of inspection level and AQL, and change them by revising the quality plan rather than by adjusting them case by case.

calc.task: An incoming lot of 3000 SMT boards is defined as a lot. Use ISO 2859-1 general inspection level II and an AQL of 1.0% defective. Build a single sampling plan and state the accept/reject rule.
calc.solution: 1. Confirm lot definition: 3000 boards, same part number, revision, supplier lot, and packaging. 2. Select standard: ISO 2859-1 normal single sampling. 3. Find sample size code letter: lot size 1201 to 3200 at general inspection level II gives code letter K. 4. Find sample size: code letter K corresponds to n = 125 boards. 5. Select AQL: 1.0% defective. 6. Read accept/reject numbers for n = 125 and AQL 1.0%: Ac = 3, Re = 4. 7. Rule: inspect 125 boards; accept if defective boards <= 3; reject if defective boards >= 4. 8. If rejected, quarantine the lot and apply the documented disposition; if accepted, record the sample result and continue normal inspection unless switching rules indicate a change.

defect.symptom: Incoming SMT boards pass the AQL plan, but the first boards after reflow show tombstoned small chip resistors at a feeder position.
defect.cause: The incoming plan sampled for visible damage and part identity but did not test solderability, coplanarity in millimetres, or moisture sensitivity under the line reflow profile; the lot may have contained a localized tape/reel or storage issue that the sample missed.
defect.action: Quarantine the lot, increase sample size for solderability and coplanarity checks, verify moisture sensitivity level and floor life against J-STD-033, review the feeder setup and reflow profile against your paste/equipment datasheet, and revise the incoming inspection plan if the characteristic should be included.

takeaways: Define the lot from part number, revision, supplier, lot code and packaging, because sampling a mixed population tells you nothing about any of its parts.
Read inspection level and lot band together to get the code letter, then take the sample size and the accept and reject numbers for the chosen AQL.
Treat AQL as a target the plan is built around, not as permission to ship defects, and keep critical, major and minor classes apart.

mistakes.mistake: Choosing the sample size straight from the lot size
mistakes.instead: Convert lot size and inspection level into a code letter first, then read the sample size; the same lot gives 50, 125 or 200 units depending on the level.

mistakes.mistake: Applying one AQL to critical and cosmetic defects together
mistakes.instead: Give critical defects their own plan or full inspection, and record the defect class so the split survives the next review.

mistakes.mistake: Treating an accepted lot as proof of zero defects
mistakes.instead: Judge the plan by what it protects against, and investigate the lot definition, the sample and the characteristic list when an accepted lot fails on the line.

terms.def: The quality level at which a sampling plan accepts a lot with high probability when the supplier's process runs at that average.
The ISO 2859-1 letter derived from lot size and inspection level that fixes the sample size for the plan.
The largest number of defective units in the sample that still allows the lot to be accepted.
The standard's rules for moving between normal, tightened and reduced inspection according to recent inspection results.

skills: Lesson m01l02: The documentation package: CoC/CoA, packing list, MSL label, declarations

title: Component verification: part number, date code, package, counterfeit red flags

goals.text: Specify the documents that must accompany a received lot of components, paste or bare PCB and state what each one proves.
Classify incoming-material findings as accept, quarantine or reject and write a record a supplier can act on.

blocks.alt: Magnified reel and chip package showing markings and date code, with red callouts for resurfaced bodies, mismatched lead finish and sanded markings
blocks.caption: Component verification: part number, date code, package and the counterfeit red flags

p: Incoming verification is the first engineering control that keeps wrong, damaged, expired, mixed or suspect material out of production. Before release, the receiving engineer has to prove four things for components, paste and bare boards alike: the item is the correct part, it traces to a manufacturer or supplier lot, it was handled inside its storage and process limits, and it meets the contractual quality and compliance requirements.

The output is a record, not a stamp. Purchasing, quality, engineering and the supplier all read it, so it names the purchase order, part number, lot or date code, quantity, documents reviewed, physical findings, disposition and any supplier action.

A component lot normally arrives with a packing list, a delivery note or invoice, a certificate of conformance, manufacturer lot traceability and the special handling labels the part needs. The packing list fixes what was shipped and how much; the certificate of conformance states conformity to the purchase order and specification without replacing physical verification; lot traceability ties reels, trays, tubes or waffle packs to one manufacturer lot, which is what recall, failure analysis and counterfeit investigation depend on.

Moisture-sensitive devices come in a moisture barrier bag with desiccant, a humidity indicator card and an MSL label consistent with IPC/JEDEC J-STD-033. Where the contract calls for them, declarations such as RoHS or REACH prove the supplier's declared compliance status, not the composition of every piece in the lot.

Paste is a process material, so its record has to prove chemistry, condition and usable life. The certificate of analysis or conformance identifies alloy, powder type, flux chemistry, metal content, lot number, manufacture date, expiration date, storage temperature and any mixing or warming instruction. That makes it evidence of the specified formulation and of shelf life, nothing more.

A safety data sheet, shipped or available through the supplier's controlled portal, covers hazard classification and handling requirements rather than process quality. Check the lot number on the jar or cartridge against the certificate, inspect the seal, and confirm the paste never left the conditions in its datasheet. A missing certificate holds the lot in quarantine until traceable documentation arrives.

Bare boards need documentation that proves material, construction and acceptability: a packing list, a certificate of conformance and, where the contract requires it, qualification or performance evidence against IPC-6012. The certificate identifies part number, revision, layer count, material, copper weight, finish, panel dimensions, lot number and any special requirement such as controlled impedance, plating thickness or flammability.

Material declarations may reference IPC-4101, and flammability may reference UL 94. Visual and dimensional features are commonly judged against IPC-A-600, though the purchase order can impose tighter limits. Before release, match revision, material, finish and panel size to the drawing and the purchase order.

theory.h: Verify part number, package and date code
p: Physical verification runs outside in: carton, then inner packaging, then component marking. Supplier label, purchase order and certificate must agree on part number, manufacturer, package type, quantity and lot or date code. On tape and reel, check tape width, cover tape, reel size and orientation against the placement equipment and the datasheet; on trays, tubes and waffle packs, check for mixed cavities and cracked carriers.

Read date codes against the manufacturer's own convention, and ask when the convention is unknown rather than guessing. Altered, laser-etched, re-marked or inconsistent marking makes the lot suspect, so quarantine it. Where counterfeit risk is high, add X-ray, decapsulation, electrical test or authorised-distributor traceability.

Counterfeit avoidance is an incoming engineering control, not only a purchasing question. Red flags include an unusually low price, an unusually short lead time, missing manufacturer traceability, an unknown or unauthorised distributor, mixed date codes, mixed manufacturers, altered labels, bulk repackaging, old date codes, inconsistent tape or reel packaging and markings unlike the manufacturer's normal style.

None of these proves fraud, but any of them justifies quarantine and further verification. For high-risk parts, buy from authorised distributors, demand manufacturer traceability and apply controls consistent with SAE AS6081. Isolate a suspected lot, photograph the packaging and markings, record lot and date codes and ask the supplier for evidence; if traceability never arrives or verification fails, reject the lot and update the approved supplier list or risk assessment.

Acceptance needs complete documentation, correct identity, acceptable condition and no unresolved red flag. Quarantine covers the lot that may be usable but whose evidence is incomplete or suspect: missing traceability, mixed date codes, damaged moisture barrier packaging, or an age that needs engineering review. Reject applies to the wrong, expired or damaged lot, to one that fails verification, and to one whose authenticity cannot be proven.

Disposition follows the quality management system — ISO 9001, or ANSI/AS9100 where the contract invokes it — which requires nonconforming output to be controlled and documented. A record the supplier can act on carries the purchase order, part number, lot or date code, quantities received, accepted, quarantined and rejected, the objective evidence, required containment, a corrective action request and a response due date. Say what was observed and where, not that the packaging was bad.

calc.task: A lot of 12,000 surface-mount ICs arrives under a purchase order that requires a single manufacturer lot, package type matching the purchase order, and a date-code age no greater than 12 months at receipt. The packing list shows 12,000 pieces. The certificate of conformance is present, but the manufacturer lot traceability sheet is missing. The reel labels show date code 2401, except a reel shows date code 2301. The receipt date code is 2504. The date-code format is assumed to be YYMM; verify the supplier convention. Counted quantity is 11,980 pieces. Classify the lot and write the supplier-facing finding.
calc.solution: Step A: compare purchase order, packing list, and certificate of conformance; part number and package type match, so identity is not the primary finding. Step B: note missing manufacturer lot traceability; without it, the lot cannot be proven to be a single manufacturer lot, so the finding is quarantine pending traceability. Step C: calculate date-code age for the main lot: 2401 to 2504 is 15 months, which exceeds the 12-month purchase-order limit by 3 months. Step D: calculate date-code age for the mixed reel: 2301 to 2504 is 27 months, which also exceeds the limit and shows mixed date codes. Step E: compare counted quantity 11,980 with packing list 12,000; shortage is 20 pieces. Step F: disposition is quarantine the entire lot, not accept, because missing traceability, mixed date codes, and date-code age exceedance are counterfeit and process-risk red flags; reject if the supplier cannot provide manufacturer traceability, authorized-distributor evidence, or an approved concession. Step G: supplier record should state purchase order number, part number, lot number, receipt date, quantity received, quantity counted, missing documents, date-code findings, mixed-lot finding, shortage, disposition, containment, required corrective action, and response due date.

defect.symptom: A reel of resistors is opened at the placement machine, and the tape contains parts with two different date codes and slightly different marking styles. The outer label shows a single lot number, but the inner reel label is partially covered by a second label.
defect.cause: The supplier or distributor likely repackaged mixed stock, relabeled the reel, or shipped an unauthorized substitute lot. The incoming inspection did not verify inner labels, date-code consistency, or manufacturer traceability before release.
defect.action: Stop the machine, quarantine the reel and the remaining lot, photograph the outer label, inner label, tape, and markings, and record the lot number, date codes, quantity, and purchase order. Quarantine the lot pending supplier traceability and counterfeit assessment. If traceability cannot be proven or the parts fail verification, reject the lot, issue a corrective action request to the supplier, and review the approved supplier list and incoming inspection plan.

takeaways: Prove identity, traceability, handling and compliance before release, and write the result as a record the supplier and the line can both act on.
Check lot traceability and date-code consistency as carefully as the certificate, because repackaged or mixed stock is what counterfeiting looks like at receiving.
Use accept, quarantine and reject deliberately: incomplete evidence is a quarantine, not an acceptance with a note.

mistakes.mistake: Accepting a lot on a certificate of conformance alone
mistakes.instead: Verify the physical marking, the lot code and the inner labels against the certificate before release.

mistakes.mistake: Reading date codes with an assumed convention
mistakes.instead: Confirm the manufacturer's date-code format, then compute the age against the purchase-order limit.

mistakes.mistake: Recording a vague finding such as bad packaging
mistakes.instead: State what was observed, where, on which lot, and what containment and corrective action you require.

terms.def: Evidence linking the packaged parts to a specific manufacturing lot at the original manufacturer.
A part whose identity, grade or origin is misrepresented, including re-marked, refurbished or unauthorised copies.
The controlled holding of material whose disposition is not yet established.
The manufacturer's code for the production date of a lot, read against that manufacturer's convention.

title: Solder paste, flux and adhesive receipt: alloy, powder, expiry, cold chain

goals.text: Specify the documents that must accompany a received lot of components, paste or bare PCB and state what each one proves.
Classify incoming-material findings as accept, quarantine or reject and write a record a supplier can act on.

blocks.alt: Cold-storage cabinet with paste jars and a temperature log, a magnified label with alloy code and expiry, and a powder particle size distribution curve
blocks.caption: Solder paste, flux and adhesive receipt: alloy, powder, expiry and the cold chain

theory.h: Receipt is a records check first
theory.p: Match a received lot to the purchase order and the supplier's shipping documents before opening it or moving it to stores. The minimum set is a packing list, a certificate of conformance or test report, lot traceability and any special handling label. The packing list fixes what was shipped and how many units; the certificate records what the supplier tested or inspected against the purchase order; traceability links the material to a manufacturing batch, a date and a test result; the handling label shows the lot was intended for moisture, electrostatic, temperature or shelf-life control.

p: For components, ask for the packing list, the certificate of conformance, the lot or date code, the manufacturer's test report where required, the moisture-sensitive device label with desiccant and humidity indicator card where applicable, and electrostatic discharge packaging. Quantity and part number come from the packing list, conformity from the certificate, and lot age from the date code, which also drives first-in, first-out control.

Under J-STD-033 the MSD label and the humidity indicator card show whether the lot was packed for moisture control and whether the indicator has changed state. The ESD packaging shows the lot was protected in transit.

A paste certificate of conformance should state lot number, manufacture date, expiry date, alloy composition, powder type, flux classification, viscosity or printability data, halogen or residue classification and storage instructions. The lot number ties the paste to the supplier's batch test, and the two dates show whether it is inside the stated shelf life.

Alloy and powder type prove the paste matches the process, using the classifications of IPC J-STD-005 for paste, IPC J-STD-006 for powder and IPC J-STD-004 for flux. Viscosity or printability data show the supplier measured a property the stencil actually depends on, and the safety data sheet covers handling hazards.

For bare boards, ask for the packing list, the certificate of conformance, the IPC-A-600 class or the purchase-order class, the bare-board test report, the finish type and thickness report, an impedance report where impedance is controlled, the material declaration, and moisture barrier packaging with a humidity indicator card where required. Quantity and panel type come from the packing list; inspection and test against the purchase order come from the certificate.

The class statement fixes the visual and dimensional acceptance level. The test report proves continuity and isolation were checked, the finish report proves the surface finish suits soldering or wire bonding, and the indicator card shows whether the moisture barrier package was compromised.

Accept when purchase order, documents, packaging, lot identity, expiry and physical condition all match the receiving specification. Quarantine when the material may be usable but the evidence is incomplete or a limit was exceeded: a missing certificate, an activated humidity indicator card, a temperature excursion past the supplier's shipping limit, or an expiry that needs supplier retest. Reject when the material cannot be used safely or cannot be traced — wrong alloy, wrong powder type, wrong board finish, severe mechanical damage, contamination, counterfeit suspicion, or an expired lot without a valid retest.
Record the decision with its evidence. A verdict alone tells the next person nothing.

theory.h: Write a record the supplier can act on
p: A useful record carries the purchase order, part number, supplier lot, quantity received, quantity affected, the requirement or drawing clause, the observed condition, the measurement or photo reference, the disposition, the containment action and the requested corrective action. Objective wording states the lot, the requirement, the deviation and the impact.

Ask the supplier to confirm test data, shipping temperature and packaging condition, and whether the lot can be retested or reconditioned. "Bad paste" and "damaged boards" name no requirement and no lot.

Paste and moisture-sensitive material need a time and temperature record, not just a date. For paste, compare manufacture date, expiry date, storage temperature and any time above the supplier's storage limit; many datasheets specify 2 °C to 10 °C, and your own datasheet decides. For components, check packaging, humidity indicator card and the floor-life clock under J-STD-033.

Exceed a control limit and the lot goes to quarantine pending supplier data. Accept it and mark it for use-first, then recheck expiry and packaging before opening. Storage temperature, shelf life and excursion limits vary by supplier, so read them from the datasheet rather than from habit.

calc.task: A solder paste lot has manufacture date 2025-01-01 and expiry 2025-07-01. It is received 2025-04-01. The shipping temperature logger shows 36 h above 10 °C. The supplier datasheet says the lot may be accepted without retest if cumulative time above 10 °C is less than 48 h. Determine the remaining shelf life and the incoming disposition.
calc.solution: First, confirm the lot number, manufacture date, expiry date, and storage instructions on the certificate of conformance. Second, calculate lot age at receipt: 2025-01-01 to 2025-04-01 is 90 days. Third, calculate remaining calendar shelf life: 2025-04-01 to 2025-07-01 is 91 days. Fourth, compare the temperature excursion to the supplier limit: 36 h is less than 48 h. Fifth, because the documents are complete, the lot is within expiry, and the excursion is below the supplier limit, accept the lot with use-first control and recheck the expiry and packaging before opening. If the excursion had been 48 h or more, or if the certificate of conformance were missing, quarantine the lot and request supplier retest data.

defect.symptom: Stencil printing shows paste balls, inconsistent deposit volume, and poor release from the stencil after a new paste lot is opened.
defect.cause: The lot was stored above the supplier's recommended temperature range for an extended period, causing flux separation or viscosity drift, and the incoming record did not capture the storage temperature or expiry status.
defect.action: Quarantine the lot, retain the container and shipping record, measure viscosity and printability against the supplier datasheet, and issue a supplier corrective action request with the lot number, storage temperature record, observed print defects, and request for batch test data and retest or replacement.

takeaways: Match the lot to its documents before opening it, because a lot that cannot be traced cannot be released however good it looks.
Read paste and moisture-sensitive records as time and temperature evidence, not as a date on a label.
Record the requirement, the observation and the evidence, so the supplier can answer with data instead of an apology.

mistakes.mistake: Releasing a lot on a complete-looking certificate without checking the lot number
mistakes.instead: Compare the certificate lot number with the jar, reel or panel label, and hold the lot while they disagree.

mistakes.mistake: Ignoring a temperature excursion because the paste is still within expiry
mistakes.instead: Compare the excursion hours with the supplier's limit and quarantine anything at or above it.

mistakes.mistake: Writing the disposition without the supporting measurement
mistakes.instead: Attach the observed value, the photo reference and the clause it failed, so the record stands on its own.

terms.def: The controlled temperature path a material follows from manufacture through storage and transport to use.
A period in which a material left its specified storage or transport temperature range.
Consuming the oldest acceptable lot first so material does not expire in stores.
The supplier's report of measured values for named properties of a specific lot.

title: Bare PCB receipt: surface finish, planarity and warpage, packaging, shelf life

goals.text: Specify the documents that must accompany a received lot of components, paste or bare PCB and state what each one proves.
Classify incoming-material findings as accept, quarantine or reject and write a record a supplier can act on.

blocks.alt: A PCB with exaggerated warp, a planarity measurement setup with a height gauge, a surface finish cross-section and a sealed barrier package with desiccant
blocks.caption: Bare PCB receipt: surface finish, planarity and warpage, packaging and shelf life

theory.p: A bare board lot arrives with a packing list, a purchase order reference, a lot or batch identifier and, where the purchase order requires it, a certificate of conformance or certificate of analysis. The packing list fixes what was shipped and how many; the purchase order reference fixes part number, revision, quantity and delivery condition; the lot identifier ties the panels to fabrication date and process records; the certificate records the supplier's verification against the purchase order and the acceptance criteria.

p: State the finish unambiguously — immersion silver, immersion tin, organic solderability preservative, electroless nickel immersion gold, or hard gold on selected pads — and ask for the type, the thickness or coating class, and the supporting test report. Plated finishes may cite IPC-4101 for base material and finish requirements and IPC-6012 for qualified product performance.

Solderability splits in two: IPC/JEDEC J-STD-002 covers component solderability, while bare board solderability is commonly specified against IPC-6012 and the customer drawing. Check the finish against the assembly process, the reflow profile and the paste chemistry before release.

theory.p: The board drawing or IPC-6012 usually carries the planarity and warpage limits, with different acceptance for rectangular and irregular boards and for each class. Incoming inspection records the method it used: a flat reference surface, a feeler gauge, an optical flatness gauge or a coordinate measuring machine. Fine-pitch components, press-fit connectors and large area arrays may need tighter limits than IPC-6012 gives generically. Confirm the requirement against the placement machine datasheet, the stencil release behaviour and the reflow support method.

Package bare boards against mechanical damage, contamination, oxidation and moisture absorption: sealed moisture barrier bags with desiccant and a humidity indicator card, or rigid trays for fragile and high-value boards. The packaging should carry the seal date, the lot identifier and any moisture sensitivity level the supplier assigned. IPC/JEDEC J-STD-033 is written for moisture-sensitive devices and is commonly referenced for this practice even when the item is a bare board. At receipt, check bag integrity, desiccant condition and the indicator card reading.

Shelf life is how long a material may stay in its original sealed packaging under stated storage conditions before requalification. Floor life is how long a moisture-sensitive item may stay out in factory ambient before it must be reconditioned or soldered. On bare boards the surface finish, the packaging integrity and the storage environment drive shelf life, while IPC/JEDEC J-STD-033 provides the framework for level, floor life and reconditioning of moisture-sensitive parts. Compare the supplier's shelf life and storage temperature with your own stores and your assembly schedule.

p: Classify every finding as accept, quarantine or reject. Accept releases the lot to stores or production because it meets the purchase order and the documented acceptance criteria. Quarantine holds a lot with a nonconformance that engineering, quality or the supplier may disposition — a missing report, questionable packaging, a borderline measurement. Reject applies to a failed critical requirement: wrong finish, a damaged moisture barrier with a failed indicator, warpage past the assembly limit.
Write the disposition so the supplier can fix the cause rather than only read the symptom.

theory.p: A useful record names the purchase order, the lot identifier, the quantity inspected, the quantity affected, the requirement violated, the measured result, the acceptance limit, the standard or drawing reference and the requested action. Instead of "boards are bent", write: "Lot 4471, 12 of 250 boards measured with twist above the drawing limit of IPC-6012 Class 3; requested action: return affected boards, provide root cause, and submit corrected flatness data for the next three lots." The supplier can then trace the lot, reproduce the measurement and prevent recurrence.

calc.task: A lot of 500 bare PCBs is received with a drawing requirement that the surface finish be organic solderability preservative and that flatness meet IPC-6012 Class 3. Incoming inspection finds 18 boards with twist above the drawing limit, 1 moisture barrier bag with a failed humidity indicator, and a missing supplier certificate of conformance. Classify the lot and write the disposition.
calc.solution: Step 1: Identify the requirements. The purchase order requires organic solderability preservative finish, IPC-6012 Class 3 flatness, intact moisture barrier packaging, and a certificate of conformance. Step 2: Compare findings to requirements. The finish type is correct. Flatness fails on 18 boards. Packaging fails on 1 bag. Documentation fails because the certificate of conformance is missing. Step 3: Determine severity. Flatness failure affects assembly placement and reflow seating, so it is a product conformance issue. Packaging failure affects moisture control and shelf life, so it is a storage and reliability issue. Missing certificate of conformance affects traceability and acceptance evidence, so it is a documentation issue. Step 4: Classify the lot. The lot cannot be accepted as received. Quarantine the lot pending disposition. If the flatness failure is outside the drawing limit and cannot be dispositioned by engineering, reject the affected boards. If the packaging failure is isolated and the boards are otherwise within moisture limits, quarantine only the affected bag. Step 5: Write the supplier-actionable record. State purchase order, lot identifier, quantity received, quantity affected, measured result, IPC-6012 Class 3 reference, packaging failure, missing certificate of conformance, and requested actions: return or disposition the 18 boards, provide root cause for flatness, provide corrected flatness data for the next lots, replace the damaged bag or provide requalification evidence, and submit the missing certificate of conformance.

defect.symptom: A received lot of bare PCBs has a sealed moisture barrier bag, but the humidity indicator card shows a failed state and several boards show dull, discolored immersion silver pads.
defect.cause: The lot may have exceeded its sealed shelf life, the bag seal may have leaked, the desiccant may have been insufficient or saturated, or the boards may have been exposed to factory ambient conditions beyond the supplier-stated floor life. Discoloration can indicate oxidation or contamination of the immersion silver surface.
defect.action: Quarantine the lot. Record the lot identifier, seal date, humidity indicator reading, storage temperature, and number of affected boards. Verify the supplier-stated shelf life and storage conditions. If the boards are within the supplier requalification window and the surface finish is still solderable by your incoming test, request engineering disposition. If the surface finish fails solderability or the moisture exposure cannot be traced, reject the lot and ask the supplier for root cause, corrected packaging, and updated shelf-life documentation.

takeaways: Identify the surface finish and its thickness from the certificate, because the finish decides whether the reflow profile and paste chemistry will work.
Measure planarity and record the method, since a twist number means nothing without the surface and technique behind it.
Write the disposition against the requirement and the measured value, so the supplier can trace the lot and correct the cause.

mistakes.mistake: Releasing boards whose moisture barrier bag failed the humidity indicator
mistakes.instead: Quarantine the affected bag and evaluate finish condition before any board reaches the line.

mistakes.mistake: Quoting warpage without the method behind it
mistakes.instead: Record the reference surface and gauge, so the supplier can reproduce the measurement.

mistakes.mistake: Accepting a finish change that matches the purchase order text but not the drawing
mistakes.instead: Compare finish type and thickness against the drawing, and quarantine on any mismatch.

terms.def: Departure of a board from flatness, measured as bow or twist against a reference surface.
The time a sealed material remains usable under stated storage conditions before requalification.
The time a moisture-sensitive item may stay exposed to factory ambient before reconditioning or soldering.
An organic coating on copper that protects solderability and is displaced during soldering.

title: Nonconforming material at dock: quarantine, MRB, supplier notification

goals.text: Classify incoming-material findings as accept, quarantine or reject and write a record a supplier can act on.

blocks.alt: Reference sheet: a locked quarantine cage with red hold tags, the MRB decision flow with use as is, rework, return to supplier and scrap branches feeding supplier notification, and a hold tag
blocks.caption: Nonconforming material at the dock: quarantine, MRB and supplier notification

theory.p: Classify incoming material against the purchase order, the drawing, the specification and the incoming inspection plan. ISO 9001:2015 requires control of externally provided processes, products and services, so the dock record has to show the evidence behind an accept, a quarantine or a reject.

Quarantine is a controlled hold on material that is suspect, incomplete or awaiting review. Segregate it physically or hold it in the system, label it with part number, lot, quantity, date and hold reason, and keep it traceable to the receiving transaction. The hold is what keeps the material out of production while the material review board or the quality function assesses risk.

A material review board reviews the nonconformance report, drawings, measurement data, photos, supplier lot history and downstream process risk. It may accept, rework, sort, use as-is with concession, return or scrap. The disposition names who approved it and what verification is required before release.

Notification works when it is specific: part number, lot, purchase order, quantity received, quantity inspected, finding, specification requirement, measured result and evidence. Ask for containment, root cause, corrective action, and replacement or return authorisation according to the contract. "Bad parts" gives the supplier nothing to correct.

Accept when the evidence shows conformance to the specified requirements. Quarantine when documentation, packaging, moisture, ESD, shelf life or measurement uncertainty leaves the status unclear. Reject when a confirmed finding affects fit, form, function, safety or a regulatory requirement, or when the quarantine cannot be resolved inside the planned disposition window.

A usable record ties the finding to the lot and to any downstream use: inspector, date, location, measurement method, calibration status, sample size, observed defects, disposition, approvals and closure evidence. For electronic components, record moisture-sensitive device status and verify it against the device datasheet and IPC/JEDEC J-STD-033, because the level drives the bake and floor-life decision.

theory.h: Closing the loop with the line
theory.p: Dock dispositions move the assembly schedule. A released lot goes to the line with its approved status and any special handling notes; a rejected lot triggers substitutes or a schedule change. Close the supplier corrective action only after containment, root cause and an effectiveness check are documented.

calc.task: A lot of 1,000 chip resistors arrives on 20 reels. The incoming plan samples 4 reels and 100 units. Findings: 5 units are outside the specified resistance tolerance, 2 reels have damaged tape pockets, and 1 reel has a moisture indicator above the limit. The internal acceptance limit for electrical nonconformance is 2%. Classify each finding and the lot, then write a supplier record.
calc.solution: Step 1: Verify the purchase order, part number, lot code, quantity, packaging, labels, and calibration status of measuring equipment. Step 2: Record the sample basis: 4 reels sampled from 20 reels, and 100 units inspected. Step 3: Calculate the electrical defect rate: 5 units outside tolerance divided by 100 units inspected equals 5%. Step 4: Compare the electrical defect rate with the internal acceptance limit: 5% is greater than 2%, so the electrical finding is classified as reject unless the MRB accepts it based on documented risk. Step 5: Classify the damaged tape pockets on 2 reels as quarantine pending MRB because damaged pockets can cause dropped components, feeder jams, or misalignment. Step 6: Classify the moisture indicator exceedance on 1 reel as quarantine pending MRB; verify the device datasheet and IPC/JEDEC J-STD-033 before any bake, reflow, or release decision. Step 7: Classify the lot as reject for the confirmed electrical nonconformance, with the full lot held under quarantine until MRB disposition. Step 8: Write the supplier record with part number, lot, purchase order, quantity received, quantity inspected, sample size, measured result, specification requirement, defect rate, photos of damaged tape and moisture indicator, affected reel numbers, requested containment, requested root cause, requested corrective action, and return or replacement authorization status.

defect.symptom: Small chip components tombstone on one side after reflow, and the feeder occasionally stalls on the same reel.
defect.cause: Incoming tape pockets are damaged and allow components to shift or fall, and the reel may have been exposed to handling damage before delivery.
defect.action: Quarantine the reel and lot, notify the supplier with photos and reel traceability, request packaging containment, and have the MRB decide whether to return, sort, or accept only after verified inspection.

takeaways: Hold suspect material under a labelled, traceable quarantine, because a verbal hold nobody can audit protects nothing.
Send the supplier the requirement, the measured result and the evidence, so the corrective action can address the cause.
Record who inspected, with which method and calibration, so the dock decision can be reproduced later.

mistakes.mistake: Leaving quarantined material in the stores location with only a paper note
mistakes.instead: Segregate it physically or hold it in the system, and label part number, lot, quantity and reason.

mistakes.mistake: Notifying the supplier with a symptom only
mistakes.instead: State the requirement, the measurement and the affected reels or units, and ask for the specific action the contract allows.

mistakes.mistake: Closing a corrective action when the replacement arrives
mistakes.instead: Keep it open until containment, root cause and an effectiveness check are all documented.

terms.def: The cross-functional group that dispositions nonconforming material and records the basis for its decision.
The controlled holding of suspect or incomplete material until a disposition is approved.
A written approval to use material that does not meet the stated requirement.
Immediate action to stop nonconforming material from moving further into the process or to the customer.

title: Moisture inside a package: what happens during reflow and why

goals.text: Determine the MSL rating and remaining floor life of a device from its markings, bag data and reflow history.

theory.h: Why moisture inside a package matters
p: Most plastic packages are built from hygroscopic materials: mold compound, die attach, underfill and polymer substrates. All of them take up water vapour from the air around them, and how much depends on package size, material composition, storage temperature, relative humidity and exposure time. Reflow then vaporises that water fast, raises internal pressure and loads weak interfaces.
The damage shows up as delamination, package cracking, die attach voiding, wire lift or intermittent electrical failures that surface long after the board passed test.

blocks.alt: Reference sheet: package cross-section with moisture ingress, vapour pressure, delamination and popcorn crack through storage, preheat, reflow and cooling; a moisture barrier bag with desiccant and humidity indicator card; a floor-life clock
blocks.caption: Moisture inside a package: ingress, vapour pressure at reflow, delamination and cracking; the barrier bag and the floor-life clock

p: Water enters through the package body and through seams, exposed die surfaces and porous interfaces. Diffusion is slow at room temperature and quickens as temperature rises. A device in a dry cabinet or a sealed moisture barrier bag with desiccant stays below a critical internal moisture level; once the bag opens, absorption starts from the factory environment.
Packages do not absorb at the same rate. Thin, large or strongly hygroscopic packages react faster than thick, small ones.

Reflow heats the package body and its interfaces quickly. Water that has diffused in vaporises and expands, and where the vapour pressure exceeds the strength of an interface, the interface separates. The industry calls it the popcorn effect.

Visible damage may be a crack or a lifted lead, but the same event can leave delamination at the die attach, the mold compound or the substrate interface with nothing to see. An electrical test can pass at that point and fail later under thermal cycling or humidity stress.

The moisture sensitivity level classifies how quickly a device absorbs moisture under defined ambient conditions. Floor life is the total ambient exposure a device may take before it must be baked before reflow. Under IPC/JEDEC J-STD-033 the typical floor lives are MSL 1 unlimited, MSL 2 12 months, MSL 3 168 h, MSL 4 72 h, MSL 5 48 h, MSL 5a 24 h, and MSL 6 with no floor life, which makes the bake mandatory before use with the post-bake reflow window taken from the label.
These are package-level control limits, not predictions that a specific device will fail past them. They exist to stop moisture-related reflow damage before it starts.

blocks.caption: J-STD-033 floor life at <=30 °C / 60% RH
head: MSL level
Floor life
Typical use
rows: No floor life: bake before use, reflow within the label limit

p: The MSL rating may sit on the device label, the moisture barrier bag, the tape and reel label or the package datasheet. A missing or unclear marking means you use the datasheet or treat the device as the most restrictive applicable level until someone verifies it.

Bag data should carry the MSL, the humidity indicator card status, the desiccant condition and the bag opening date. Card thresholds are card-specific, so check the card datasheet and IPC/JEDEC J-STD-033. A card past its threshold says the internal environment is no longer acceptable for direct reflow, even when the calculated floor life has time left.

Floor life is cumulative ambient exposure, not time since the last bag opening. Under IPC/JEDEC J-STD-033 a qualifying reflow completed inside the remaining floor life resets it. Floor life that expired before reflow means baking before reflow, and a humidity indicator card past its threshold means baking regardless of the remaining floor life.
Some programs also cap the number of reflows or require special handling after several passes. Check the package qualification, the customer procedure and IPC/JEDEC J-STD-033 rather than assuming.

Control starts with dry storage, sealed moisture barrier bags, desiccant and humidity indicator cards. A dry cabinet often runs at 5 % to 10 % RH, but only the 5 % RH or less band suspends the floor-life clock under J-STD-033 — a 10 % cabinet is comfortable and earns no credit. Confirm the setpoint against your equipment datasheet.

Check bake conditions, cabinet setpoints and reflow profiles against IPC/JEDEC J-STD-033, the package datasheet and your paste and equipment datasheets. Track bag opening time, card status, reflow time, bake time and any reflow count limit. When the next reflow will not happen inside the remaining floor life, bake first; visual inspection and electrical test will not tell you whether the package is dry.

calc.task: A device label says MSL 3. The moisture barrier bag was opened 100 h ago. The humidity indicator card has not exceeded its threshold. The device was reflowed 70 h after bag opening, and 40 h have elapsed since that reflow. Determine the MSL rating and remaining floor life.
calc.solution: 1. Read the MSL rating from the marking: MSL 3. 2. Use the IPC/JEDEC J-STD-033 floor life for MSL 3: 168 h. 3. Check the humidity indicator card: it has not exceeded its threshold, so the card does not force bake. 4. Check reflow history: the device was reflowed at 70 h after bag opening, which is within the 168 h floor life. 5. Under IPC/JEDEC J-STD-033, a qualifying reflow within the floor life resets the floor life. 6. Calculate remaining floor life after reflow: 168 h minus 40 h elapsed since reflow equals 128 h. 7. Result: MSL 3, remaining floor life 128 h, provided the reflow met the applicable profile and no reflow count limit applies.

defect.symptom: After reflow, some packages show package cracking, lifted leads, or popcorn-like deformation, while others pass electrical test but later fail with intermittent opens or delamination found by X-ray or acoustic microscopy.
defect.cause: MSL devices were exposed to ambient conditions beyond their floor life, or the humidity indicator card exceeded its threshold before reflow. Common line causes include bags left open too long, missing floor-life tracking, reflow scheduling delays, incorrect bake, or failure to reset floor life after a qualifying reflow.
defect.action: Quarantine affected lots. Verify MSL markings, bag opening time, humidity indicator card status, desiccant condition, reflow time, and bake records against IPC/JEDEC J-STD-033. Bake devices that exceeded floor life or humidity indicator card threshold before reflow. Review storage, bag opening, floor-life tracking, and reflow scheduling controls. Inspect suspect packages with X-ray or acoustic microscopy and update the process control plan to prevent recurrence.

takeaways: Absorbed moisture turns to vapour in reflow, so the failure mechanism is internal and often invisible to electrical test.
Treat floor life as cumulative ambient exposure, and reset it only through a qualifying reflow or an accepted bake.
A humidity indicator card past its threshold forces a bake even when the calculated floor life still has hours left.

mistakes.mistake: Counting floor life from receipt or from the last reflow without checking the procedure
mistakes.instead: Count from the bag opening, and treat a reflow as a reset only where IPC/JEDEC J-STD-033 and your procedure allow it.

mistakes.mistake: Relying on a 10 % RH dry cabinet to suspend floor life
mistakes.instead: Use the 5 % RH or less band for suspension, and record the setpoint you actually ran.

mistakes.mistake: Releasing a device that passed electrical test after moisture exposure
mistakes.instead: Inspect for delamination and bake the lot, because the electrical result does not show internal separation.

terms.def: Package cracking or interface separation caused by moisture vaporising during reflow.
The J-STD-020 classification of how much ambient exposure a non-hermetic package tolerates before reflow.
The ambient exposure a moisture-sensitive device may accumulate before it must be baked.
Separation between layers inside a package, such as mold compound and die or substrate.
