title: Reading MSL reality: J-STD-033 / J-STD-020 markings, barrier bag, HIC

goals.text: Determine the MSL rating and remaining floor life of a device from its markings, bag data and reflow history.

blocks.alt: A magnified MSL label with a caution symbol, a barrier bag shown as a translucent panel with a humidity indicator card and desiccant inside
blocks.caption: Reading moisture sensitivity markings: MSL label, barrier bag, humidity indicator card and desiccant

p: J-STD-020 sorts non-hermetic surface mount devices into moisture sensitivity levels. The rating says how much ambient exposure a device tolerates before a reflow cycle is likely to damage the package. It says nothing about shelf life, ESD class or solderability.
Read the MSL code from the supplier label, the bag or the device marking, then apply the floor-life rule that J-STD-020 and the label give for that level.

J-STD-033 handling practice expects a moisture barrier bag labelled with the MSL, floor life, date and, where they apply, bake or exposure information. In practice the MSL may appear on the outer box, the reel label, the bag label or the package marking.

A missing or unreadable marking is a stop, not a guess. Check the purchase record, the supplier datasheet or your internal material specification, and treat the part as unknown until someone verifies it.

IPC/JEDEC J-STD-033 defines floor life at reference conditions of 30 °C and 60 % RH for the common MSL ratings, while J-STD-020 assigns the level itself. Typical values are MSL 1 unlimited, MSL 2 1 year, MSL 2a 4 weeks, MSL 3 168 h, MSL 4 72 h, MSL 5 48 h and MSL 5a 24 h; MSL 6 is special and normally requires bake before use.
Use the label value whenever it is more restrictive than the table, and check the current revision of J-STD-020, because the tables are updated.

A moisture barrier bag slows moisture ingress; it does not create a permanent dry environment. J-STD-033 practice adds desiccant and a humidity indicator card to show whether the interior is still inside the intended humidity range. Read the card against the card manufacturer's scale.
A spot past its threshold, a punctured bag or a compromised seal means the contents count as exposed, so evaluate bake or quarantine before reflow.

theory.p: The clock starts when the moisture barrier bag opens, not when the device arrives. Time on the line, in a dry cabinet or on a feeder counts as ambient exposure unless your controlled storage procedure explicitly grants credit. A completed bake per J-STD-033 can restart the clock where your procedure accepts the bake record; otherwise keep counting from the original open time.

p: Reflow after the floor life has expired drives moisture into package interfaces and causes damage. A reflow completed while floor life remained is acceptable from a moisture standpoint, but the device can reabsorb moisture afterwards.

Before a second reflow, check the exposure since the last dry event — bag opening or an accepted bake, and confirm whether your procedure treats a completed reflow as a dry event too. Verify the profile against your paste and equipment datasheets for peak temperature and time above liquidus rather than assuming a universal value. Where exposure passed the floor life before any reflow, bake first and record bake temperature, time and device count.

Determine remaining floor life by combining the MSL rating, the floor-life value from J-STD-020 or the label, the bag open date and time, the HIC condition and the reflow or bake records. When the sources conflict, take the most restrictive value and quarantine the material until the discrepancy is resolved.
That keeps the decision traceable and stops it resting on one marking or one indicator.

calc.task: A bag label states MSL 3 with a floor life of 168 h per J-STD-020. The bag was opened E hours ago. One reflow was completed at R hours after opening. Determine the remaining floor life and whether a bake is required before a second reflow.
calc.solution: Confirm the floor life F from the label or J-STD-020; here F = 168 h. Calculate remaining floor life before the next reflow: remaining = F - E. Check the first reflow: if R was less than F, the reflow occurred within floor life and no bake was required for that reflow. If E has reached or passed F, the floor life expired before the second reflow; bake per J-STD-033 or your approved procedure before reflow. If the HIC shows an exceeded threshold or the bag was damaged, treat the device as exposed even if E is less than F, and bake or quarantine per your procedure. Record the bake, reflow profile, and exposure time so the next decision starts from a known dry event.

defect.symptom: After reflow, boards show intermittent opens, lifted leads, or package cracks on a few MSL devices, while nearby parts look normal.
defect.cause: The affected devices exceeded their floor life before reflow, or the barrier bag/HIC condition was not checked, so moisture remained in the package and expanded during reflow.
defect.action: Quarantine the lot, verify the MSL label, bag open time, HIC, and reflow records, bake per J-STD-033 or the manufacturer's limits, then reflow a sample and inspect. Correct the storage control by adding a bag-open timestamp and HIC check before kitting.

takeaways: Read the MSL from the label and the floor life from J-STD-020 or the label, and apply the more restrictive of the two.
Start the floor-life clock at bag opening, and count line time, cabinet time and feeder time as ambient exposure unless your procedure grants credit.
Combine MSL, open time, HIC condition and reflow history into one record, because any single indicator can mislead.

mistakes.mistake: Treating the MSL rating as a shelf-life statement
mistakes.instead: Read it as a reflow-risk class and take shelf life from the material specification.

mistakes.mistake: Using a barrier bag as proof the parts are dry after a seal failure
mistakes.instead: Treat contents as exposed and bake or quarantine before reflow.

mistakes.mistake: Taking the label value when the standard table is stricter
mistakes.instead: Use the most restrictive value and record which source you followed.

terms.def: A card that shows the humidity reached inside a barrier bag by a colour change at defined thresholds.
A foil-laminate bag that slows moisture ingress and carries the MSL and exposure data.
The 30 °C and 60 % RH ambient at which J-STD-033 floor lives are defined.
Controlled heating that drives absorbed moisture out of a package so the floor-life clock can restart.

title: Floor-life accounting: clock start, accumulation, reset rules

goals.text: Determine the MSL rating and remaining floor life of a device from its markings, bag data and reflow history.

blocks.alt: Reference sheet: a timeline where exposure accumulates across three bag openings, pauses in a dry cabinet and resets to zero at a bake, a reel with a handwritten exposure log, and a start / accumulate / pause / reset rules table
blocks.caption: Floor-life accounting: clock start, accumulation across exposure events, the dry-cabinet pause and the bake reset

theory.h: Floor life is an exposure budget
p: Floor life is the cumulative time a moisture-sensitive device may stay outside its moisture barrier bag in factory conditions that J-STD-033 treats as no more than 30 °C and no more than 60 % RH. It is not shelf life, not a reflow count, not solderability life and not a quality rating. The budget exists to limit moisture uptake before reflow.

The clock starts at the first exposure to ambient air, which usually means bag opening, but it also starts when a device leaves a sealed bag, when the bag is punctured, or when the device otherwise meets uncontrolled air. From there it accumulates through storage, kitting, feeder loading, placement, reflow, inspection, test and any other open-air handling until a qualifying reset is performed.

theory.h: Where the MSL rating comes from
p: The moisture sensitivity level normally shows on the device marking, the tape-and-reel label, the moisture barrier bag label or the datasheet. Where sources disagree, account with the most restrictive valid source and then resolve the discrepancy with the supplier or the device owner.

J-STD-033 assigns floor life by level: MSL 1 unlimited under the standard's storage condition, MSL 2 12 months, MSL 2a 4 weeks, MSL 3 168 h, MSL 4 72 h, MSL 5 48 h, MSL 5a 24 h, and MSL 6 bake before use. Those values start the arithmetic; they never replace tracking the actual exposure.

theory.h: Clock start is exposure, not discovery
p: In storage the practical clock start is the recorded bag-open time or the first verified exposure. A missing bag-open time leaves the exposure uncertain, so treat the device conservatively until the exposure can be bounded.

An intact-looking bag can still hide a compromised seal, a puncture, or desiccant that has been exposed for an unknown period. The humidity indicator card and desiccant condition support the assessment but do not replace a time record. Prior exposure before the device reached storage belongs in the cumulative total; where it cannot be bounded, use the nonconforming material process rather than assuming a full MSL floor life remains.

Floor life accumulates whenever the device sits outside a compliant moisture barrier bag in conditions covered by J-STD-033: on the floor, in a feeder, on the placement machine, in the reflow oven, on the conveyor, in inspection, and waiting between operations. Reflow is not a separate charge; the open-air time around it is what counts.

Multiple reflow passes add the open-air time of each pass, so the cumulative exposure has to be tracked pass by pass. Where the storage environment is hotter or more humid than the J-STD-033 reference condition, the simple table may not be enough — use the device datasheet, supplier guidance and your facility's controlled storage limits.

Putting a device back in a bag does not reset anything. J-STD-033 allows a reset after a qualifying bake performed to the applicable bake table for the package and MSL, followed by repacking with desiccant and a humidity indicator card where required.

Record the bake with start time, end time, temperature and the responsible person or system record. A bake that did not follow the applicable J-STD-033 condition resets nothing, and neither does one on a package already exposed past the point where evaluation is required. MSL 6 devices need a bake before use, so a recent bag opening gives them no usable floor life.

The minimum useful record is part number, lot or date code, MSL, bag-open time, cumulative open-air time, storage temperature and humidity, desiccant status, humidity indicator card status, any bake records, and the reflow or other handling history. A spreadsheet suits a small operation; an MES or WMS record is better because it cuts manual error and preserves traceability.

Whatever the tool, keep one time unit and show the calculation method on the record. Where storage is not controlled to the J-STD-033 reference condition, record the actual conditions and the basis for any adjustment or quarantine.

theory.p: Remaining floor life equals the MSL floor life from J-STD-033 minus the cumulative open-air time already used. A positive result allows continued use only if the remainder covers the planned process and the environment stays inside the applicable limits. A non-positive result means bake before reflow, or disposition under your own procedure. After a valid bake and reset, recalculate from the reset point with the full MSL floor life.

p: In storage the job is to stop unknown exposure from becoming an uncontrolled reflow risk. With incomplete records, bound the exposure, quarantine the material and decide between bake, supplier evaluation and scrap. Appearance, a fresh desiccant packet or a new humidity indicator card prove nothing on their own.

A short reflow pass is not negligible when the device has already used most of its floor life. Check the applicable J-STD-033 revision, the device datasheet and your facility's controlled storage limits, because handling times and conditions vary by site and product.

calc.task: A tape-and-reel is marked MSL 3. The bag label shows the bag was opened 100 h ago. The MES shows 6 h of open-air reflow handling. Storage remained within the J-STD-033 reference condition of no more than 30°C and no more than 60%RH. Determine the MSL rating and remaining floor life.
calc.solution: Step 1: Identify the MSL from the marking and bag label. Both sources indicate MSL 3. Step 2: Look up the floor life for MSL 3. J-STD-033 gives 168 h for MSL 3. Step 3: Add the recorded open-air exposure. Bag-open storage exposure is 100 h. Open-air reflow handling is 6 h. Total cumulative open-air time is 100 h + 6 h = 106 h. Step 4: Subtract cumulative exposure from the MSL floor life. Remaining floor life is 168 h - 106 h = 62 h. Step 5: Interpret the result. The device has 62 h of remaining floor life under the stated conditions. If the planned process cannot be completed within that time, or if the exposure record is later found to be incomplete, the device should be evaluated for bake or quarantine before reflow.

defect.symptom: After reflow, multiple units from the same lot show package cracking, delamination, or popcorn-like damage, while units from another lot with the same part number and reflow profile pass inspection.
defect.cause: The failed lot had its floor-life clock started when the moisture barrier bag was opened, but the open-air time was not fully recorded. Storage time, feeder time, and reflow handling time were not added to the cumulative exposure, so the lot was reflowed after its J-STD-033 floor life had already been consumed.
defect.action: Quarantine the remaining lot and any related lots with incomplete exposure records. Verify the bag-open time, storage conditions, reflow handling time, and any bake records. If the cumulative exposure cannot be bounded, treat the material as requiring bake or supplier evaluation before reflow. Correct the storage record so that bag-open time, cumulative open-air time, and reset events are captured in the MES or WMS.

takeaways: Budget floor life as cumulative open-air time from the first exposure, not as shelf life and not as time since the last bag.
Reset the clock only with a qualifying bake to the J-STD-033 table for that package and MSL, followed by repacking.
Record bag opening, cumulative exposure and every reset in one traceable system, so the next shift inherits a number instead of an assumption.

mistakes.mistake: Restarting the clock because the device went back into a sealed bag
mistakes.instead: Reset only after a qualifying bake, and record the bake temperature, time and operator.

mistakes.mistake: Adding bag-open hours but forgetting feeder, placement and reflow handling
mistakes.instead: Track every open-air interval, because the sum is what the floor-life table is compared against.

mistakes.mistake: Assuming a fresh desiccant packet restores the budget
mistakes.instead: Bound or evaluate the prior exposure; desiccant protects the future, not the past.

terms.def: The total time a device has spent outside a compliant moisture barrier bag since its last valid reset.
A bake performed to the J-STD-033 condition for the package and MSL, recorded and followed by proper repacking.
The bake completion or dry-event moment from which floor life is counted again.
The sealed, desiccant-filled bag that suspends floor-life accumulation while the device stays inside it.

title: Baking and dry cabinets: when required, conditions by package, records

goals.text: Decide whether a batch must be baked, specify the bake/dry-storage condition and justify it by package type.

blocks.alt: Reference sheet: a nitrogen dry cabinet with reels, a bake oven with a ramp-hold-cool curve, thin, medium and thick package outlines, and a blank bake log
blocks.caption: Baking and dry cabinets: when required, conditions by package thickness, and the records

theory.h: The bake decision starts with package and exposure
p: Bake or not is not a question about the part name. Take the moisture sensitivity level, the package type, whether the moisture barrier bag was opened, dry pack integrity, humidity indicator card status, desiccant condition and the planned time to reflow together.

A batch that will be consumed inside the remaining floor life in qualified dry storage may not need baking at all. Where exposure, cabinet performance or bag condition cannot be proven, treat the batch as exposed and bake or quarantine it. The person who controls the lot record makes the call; the line operator alone does not.

For plastic packages, IPC/JEDEC J-STD-033D assigns moisture sensitivity levels and floor life. Under typical ambient conditions MSL 3 has 168 h, MSL 4 has 72 h, MSL 5 has 48 h and MSL 5a has 24 h; higher levels follow supplier-specified conditions. Floor life begins when the dry pack opens or when the package meets ambient air.
Check the controlled revision and any supplier limit, because some suppliers shorten floor life for large packages, high moisture content or long reflow profiles.

theory.h: Dry storage suspends or extends exposure
p: IPC/JEDEC J-STD-033D recognises dry storage at 5 % RH or less as the condition that suspends the floor-life clock: below that humidity the device gains no moisture, so exposure stops accumulating. A common 10 % RH cabinet is not equivalent. It slows the clock instead of stopping it and leaves parts on a shortened budget, which makes 10 % RH a cheaper mitigation for devices with budget to spare and never a substitute for the 5 % RH requirement.

Calibrate, alarm and log the dry cabinet, and treat the qualified limit as the one written in your procedure. A cabinet out of range means the time inside it counts as floor life. Keep reels in sealed bags or dry cabinets after opening, and for trays and tubes use sealed containers with desiccant and a humidity indicator card when no cabinet is available.

Read the bake table in IPC/JEDEC J-STD-033D for the package type, then the component or tape datasheet. Bake time in J-STD-033 Table 4-1 is indexed to package body thickness and to the moisture sensitivity level, with separate columns for floor life exceeded by more than 72 h and by 72 h or less, so all three variables come off the table before anyone quotes a time.

Tape and reel must not be baked above 40 °C, because carrier tape and cover tape soften and deform. The 40 °C column is therefore long: for bodies up to 1.4 mm it runs 8 days at MSL 2 up to 22 days at MSL 5a, and for 1.4 to 2.0 mm 25 to 79 days. A 48 h or 168 h bake at 40 °C will not dry a reel.

Loose parts in trays or tubes can use the 125 °C column, again by thickness and MSL: 5 to 16 h up to 1.4 mm, 18 to 48 h at 1.4 to 2.0 mm and 48 h at 2.0 to 4.5 mm, and only where the tray, tube and component materials are rated for it.

Table 4-2 is a different table. It covers the supplier dry-pack bake before packing at a fixed 24 h maximum exposure time, and its 125 °C figures — 7 to 28 h up to 1.4 mm and 18 to 48 h above that — must never be quoted as a user rebake recipe.

Above 90 °C the cumulative bake time is limited to 96 h unless the supplier states otherwise, because intermetallic growth and solderability loss accumulate. Check the tape, tray, tube and equipment datasheets: tape can soften, trays can warp and some coatings blister.

Bare boards and THT components absorb moisture too, but the bake rule follows laminate, coating and package. Use the board supplier's bake condition; common practice is 105 °C to 125 °C for 2 h to 24 h, longer for thick boards or high moisture.

Apply the same MSL logic to THT plastic packages as to SMT. Bake before assembly when the board or component passed its qualified exposure or shows moisture indicators, and confirm that the bake temperature will not damage solder mask, silkscreen or plated features.

theory.h: Records that make the decision auditable
p: Record lot or reel ID, MSL, package type, dry pack open date and time, humidity indicator card reading, desiccant status, dry cabinet RH, bake start and end, bake temperature, controlled bake humidity, operator and disposition.

A batch released without bake records its remaining floor life and the planned reflow window. A baked batch records the recipe and any reflow qualification result. Keep the record with the lot so the next shift can see whether the floor life still holds.

Bake when the batch passed floor life, when the dry pack or desiccant failed, when the humidity indicator card is above its threshold, or when the dry cabinet ran out of range. Quarantine when the MSL is unknown, the package is damaged, the bake recipe is not qualified for the package, or the device has already been reflowed and the supplier requires requalification.

Never bake a package that cannot take the temperature or the time; use qualified lower-temperature dry storage or return the material to the supplier. The purpose is to stop moisture flashing in reflow, not to add a handling step.

calc.task: A batch of IPC/JEDEC J-STD-033D MSL 4 ICs in tape and reel was opened 50 h ago. The dry cabinet is not qualified for floor-life suspension, so all storage time counts. The planned reflow window starts in 30 h. Decide whether bake is required and specify a tape-and-reel bake condition.
calc.solution: 1. Use IPC/JEDEC J-STD-033D floor life for MSL 4: 72 h. 2. Counted exposure = 50 h. 3. Remaining floor life = 72 h - 50 h = 22 h. 4. Planned delay = 30 h. Since 30 h exceeds 22 h, bake is required before reflow. 5. A tape-and-reel bake cannot exceed 40°C, and at 40°C the J-STD-033 Table 4-1 time for a body up to 1.4 mm is about 9 days, which does not fit a 30 h window. Either move the reflow inside the remaining floor life, suspend the clock in a qualified dry cabinet at 5% RH or less, or de-reel, bake loose parts at 125°C for 7 h and re-reel; verify the chosen route against the J-STD-033D bake table, the tape datasheet and the reflow window. 6. Record lot ID, bake start and end, temperature, operator, and reflow qualification if required.

defect.symptom: After reflow, several QFN packages show lifted leads, voided solder joints, and one package has a visible crack; the lot had been stored in a dry cabinet with a logged RH of 12% while the setpoint was 5%.
defect.cause: The IPC/JEDEC J-STD-033D MSL 4 floor life was exceeded because the dry cabinet excursion was not treated as exposure; moisture in the package flashed during reflow.
defect.action: Quarantine the lot, verify MSL and open date, bake per a qualified tape-and-reel recipe, requalify reflow, repair the cabinet, and add alarm and log review.

takeaways: Read bake time from J-STD-033 Table 4-1 by package thickness, MSL and how far floor life was exceeded, never from memory.
Respect the 40 °C ceiling for tape and reel, and expect days rather than hours at that temperature.
Suspend floor life only at 5 % RH or less; a 10 % RH cabinet slows the clock without earning any credit.

mistakes.mistake: Applying a tray bake recipe to a tape-and-reel lot
mistakes.instead: Keep reels at or below 40 °C, and use de-reeling or a qualified dry cabinet when the bake window is too long.

mistakes.mistake: Quoting Table 4-2 as a user rebake recipe
mistakes.instead: Table 4-2 is the supplier dry-pack bake before packing; take the user recipe from Table 4-1.

mistakes.mistake: Treating a 12 % RH cabinet excursion as suspended floor life
mistakes.instead: Count the excursion as exposure and bake or quarantine the lot.

terms.def: The moisture barrier bag, desiccant and humidity indicator card that protect a moisture-sensitive device before use.
The stop of floor-life accumulation that J-STD-033 grants at 5 % RH or less in qualified dry storage.
The total time a package has spent above 90 °C, limited because solderability degrades with it.
A card whose colour spots show the peak humidity inside a dry pack.

title: The ESD control program: EPA, grounding, straps, mats, ionizers, packaging

goals.text: Audit an ESD protected area against a control checklist and rank the gaps by risk.

blocks.alt: Reference sheet: plan view of an EPA bench with dissipative work surface, wrist strap, floor mat, common ground point, ionizer, shielding bag, conductive tote and signage; an operator at the bench; a daily checks table
blocks.caption: The ESD control program: protected area boundary, grounding, straps, mats, ionizers and packaging

p: An ESD control program is a management system, not a bag of gadgets. In storage the protected area is defined by the materials handled, the sensitivity of the parts, the packaging in use, and the people and equipment that move them. ANSI/ESD S20.20 and IEC 61340-5-1 both demand a documented program with written procedures, training, qualification and periodic audit.

Start the storage audit with the control plan, then check that the physical area matches it: EPA boundaries, entry controls, grounding provisions, packaging inventory, ionizer coverage where needed, and records. A missing or stale plan is the first gap, and it is programmatic rather than hardware.

Grounding in an EPA removes charge and holds conductive items at a common potential. The reference must trace to a building electrical ground or another qualified point, and the bonding network must be continuous and inspectable. ANSI/ESD S6.1 covers grounding and equipotential bonding; use it to confirm that racks, carts, shelving, tables and floor systems are bonded as the control plan requires.

Storage failures are usually the subtle ones: a cart or rack grounded at one point but isolated by casters, plastic feet, painted contact surfaces or a broken bonding jumper. Measure or inspect by the program method, and check the result against the equipment datasheet and site electrical safety requirements.

Personnel grounding works through wrist straps, footwear and floor systems, or a combination, depending on the task and the control plan. ANSI/ESD S1.1 governs wrist straps, which suit static controlled workstations; footwear and floor systems are qualified under ANSI/ESD STM97.1 and ANSI/ESD STM97.2.

Wrist straps are impractical while moving pallets, but they still belong at receiving inspection, kitting and rework benches. Check that the chosen method suits the task, that the strap or footwear is worn correctly, that the floor is qualified for that footwear, and that the system is tested at the required interval. Where the plan allows an exception, document the risk basis and the compensating controls.

Static dissipative or conductive mats cover benches and staging surfaces where people handle sensitive items. ANSI/ESD STM4.1 covers static dissipative worksurfaces, having superseded S4.1, and ANSI/ESD STM11.11 characterises surface resistance or resistivity.

In storage, mats get misused: laid on insulating shelves, grounded through a damaged cord, or treated as general work surfaces with no defined ground path. Verify that the mat connects to the EPA ground reference through the required resistor or bonding method, that the connection is intact, and that insulating packaging, tape or plastic trays do not bypass it. Check resistance limits against the mat datasheet and the site control plan.

Ionizers neutralise charge on isolated conductors and insulators that cannot be grounded. ANSI/ESD STM3.1 covers ionization, and performance qualification and periodic verification are judged against its offset-voltage and discharge-time limits; it is the ESDA counterpart of IEC 61340-4-7. Footwear and flooring, by contrast, are qualified under ANSI/ESD STM97.1 and STM97.2.

In storage, ionizers usually sit at unpacking, kitting or inspection stations where plastic bags, foam, labels and tape generate charge. Check placement, airflow, balance and maintenance: ionization does nothing if the ion stream is blocked, the emitter points are dirty, or the unit is out of balance. Verify balance and discharge time against the ionizer datasheet and the program acceptance criteria.

Packaging is a primary storage control, because parts may sit in a container for hours or days. ANSI/ESD S541 covers ESD packaging, including shielding bags, conductive containers and closure methods.

Confirm that the packaging class matches part sensitivity and the storage environment, that shielding bags are closed and undamaged, and that containers suit the EPA grounding scheme. Storage frequently gets this wrong by putting a shielding bag on an insulating shelf and trusting it against every field. Shielding reduces field exposure; the package still has to be handled and stored as it was qualified. Check package type, closure and storage configuration against the packaging datasheet and the control plan.
A useful audit follows a checklist tied to the control plan and records evidence: photos, serial numbers, test dates, operator observations. Rank each gap by exposure, sensitivity and detectability.

High risk means many sensitive parts affected, repeated daily, undetected downstream. Medium risk is a local gap with limited exposure or partial detection. Low risk is documentation or housekeeping with little direct charge-transfer path. Deliver a corrective action list with owner, due date and verification method rather than a list of nonconformances.

calc.task: Audit a storage EPA with 12 checklist items. Each item is scored 0 to 3 for control strength, where 0 is absent, 1 is present but unverified, 2 is verified but has a minor gap, and 3 is fully compliant. Exposure is scored 1 to 5 based on daily part movement through the control. Sensitivity is scored 1 to 5 based on the most sensitive part family stored in the area. Calculate a risk score for each gap as (3 - control strength) x exposure x sensitivity, then rank the top three gaps.
calc.solution: Step 1: Record the control strength, exposure, and sensitivity for each gap. Example gap A: grounding jumper on rack missing, control strength 0, exposure 5, sensitivity 4. Risk score = (3 - 0) x 5 x 4 = 60. Example gap B: wrist strap tester not used for one shift, control strength 1, exposure 3, sensitivity 4. Risk score = (3 - 1) x 3 x 4 = 24. Example gap C: ionizer balance record missing, control strength 1, exposure 4, sensitivity 3. Risk score = (3 - 1) x 4 x 3 = 24. Example gap D: shielding bag closure not inspected at receiving, control strength 2, exposure 5, sensitivity 5. Risk score = (3 - 2) x 5 x 5 = 25. Example gap E: mat ground cord damaged at one bench, control strength 0, exposure 2, sensitivity 5. Risk score = (3 - 0) x 2 x 5 = 30. Step 2: Rank by risk score. Gap A is highest at 60. Gap E is next at 30. Gap D is next at 25. Gaps B and C tie at 24 and can be ranked by exposure or sensitivity; if exposure is prioritized, Gap C ranks above Gap B. Step 3: Convert to actions. Gap A requires immediate bonding repair and retest. Gap E requires bench isolation and mat ground repair. Gap D requires receiving inspection update and package closure check. Step 4: Verify closure by re-audit or test record, not only by visual confirmation.

defect.symptom: Incoming inspection finds intermittent ESD damage on a small number of connectors from a storage rack, while the same part family is acceptable when staged on a grounded bench.
defect.cause: The rack is bonded at one corner, but the shelf surface is painted or coated, and parts are placed in shielding bags that are not closed. The rack appears grounded, but the bags and shelf create an isolated charge path, and the open bags allow field exposure during movement.
defect.action: Isolate the rack, verify the bonding path to the EPA ground reference, clean or replace the shelf contact surfaces, require closed shielding bags for stored parts, and requalify the rack storage configuration against the control plan. Add a rack bonding check to the shift audit and verify closure with a follow-up inspection of the affected part family.

takeaways: Audit the storage EPA against its own control plan first, because a stale plan makes every downstream check meaningless.
Verify grounding by measurement to the reference, since a rack that looks bonded can be isolated by paint, casters or a broken jumper.
Rank gaps by exposure, sensitivity and detectability, and hand back actions with owners rather than a list of findings.

mistakes.mistake: Treating a grounded-looking rack as bonded
mistakes.instead: Measure the bonding path to the EPA reference and inspect contact surfaces for paint or insulation.

mistakes.mistake: Treating a dry cabinet or an unmonitored ionizer as a substitute for grounding
mistakes.instead: Qualify each control to its own standard and keep the test records with the equipment.

mistakes.mistake: Closing an audit finding on a visual check
mistakes.instead: Verify closure with a repeat test or re-audit record.

terms.def: A defined space in which all conductive items and personnel are bonded and sensitive items are handled under documented controls.
Connecting conductive items so they sit at the same potential and cannot discharge into each other.
Equipment that neutralises static charge by delivering balanced positive and negative ions to the air.
Packaging that limits electrostatic field exposure to the parts inside it.

skills: Lesson m02l04: Baking and dry cabinets: when required, conditions by package, records

title: Case: expired floor life found mid-lot

goals.text: Decide whether a batch must be baked, specify the bake/dry-storage condition and justify it by package type.
Contain a moisture or ESD exposure breach and define the traceability range.

blocks.alt: Reference sheet: a partially used reel on a feeder with a floor-life expired tag, a clock past its limit, the stop / quarantine / bake / MRB / scrap decision flow and a containment checklist
blocks.caption: Case: expired floor life found mid-lot — stop the feeder, quarantine, then bake / MRB / scrap

theory.h: Floor life is a clock, not a label
p: A moisture-sensitive device starts consuming floor life when its moisture barrier bag opens and the device meets ambient air. The clock runs under the moisture sensitivity level assigned by IPC/JEDEC J-STD-020 and the handling rules of IPC/JEDEC J-STD-033, which defines floor life at reference conditions of 30 °C and 60 % RH — so a hot, humid stores area burns the clock faster than a controlled dry cabinet.

An expired clock does not make the batch scrap. It makes it a process deviation that has to be contained before reflow. The first questions are whether the exposure history is known, whether the remaining floor life covers the planned reflow, and whether the package type can be baked safely.

theory.h: Deciding whether the batch must be baked
theory.p: Compare elapsed floor life with the floor life for the device level in IPC/JEDEC J-STD-033. If elapsed time exceeds the allowed floor life and reflow is planned, bake before reflow unless the component manufacturer provides a documented exception. If dry storage is used, IPC/JEDEC J-STD-033 uses a dry storage target of 5% RH or less; if the cabinet runs above that, treat the devices as exposed and recalculate floor life. If the device is classified as the lowest moisture sensitivity level under IPC/JEDEC J-STD-020, baking is usually not required unless contamination, handling damage, or a customer requirement says otherwise. If floor life has not been exceeded and dry storage is compliant, the batch can normally proceed, but the storage record must be complete.

p: IPC/JEDEC J-STD-033 indexes bake conditions to the carrier, the package body thickness, the moisture sensitivity level and the maximum temperature the component allows.

For loose parts in trays, tubes or waffle packs whose carriers and components are rated for it, the 125 °C column of Table 4-1 applies: 5 to 16 h for a body up to 1.4 mm, 18 to 48 h for 1.4 to 2.0 mm and 48 h for 2.0 to 4.5 mm, with the longer times at higher MSL and when floor life was exceeded by more than 72 h.

The 24 h figure sometimes quoted for a 125 °C bake is the supplier dry-pack condition from Table 4-2, not a user bake, so it must not become a production recipe. For tape and reel, J-STD-033 provides the lower-temperature long bake at 40 °C — 8 to 22 days for a body up to 1.4 mm and 25 to 79 days for 1.4 to 2.0 mm, by MSL — because the tape, reel, labels and cover tape cannot take more heat. Cumulative bake time above 90 °C is limited to 96 h unless the supplier states otherwise.

Justify the condition by package type: polymer tape and reels deform, labels lift and cover tape shifts at high temperature. Check the chosen condition against the component datasheet, the carrier datasheet and the oven capability.

theory.p: After baking, store the batch in a dry cabinet at 5% RH or less under IPC/JEDEC J-STD-033, or repackage it in a moisture barrier bag with desiccant and a humidity indicator card. The floor-life clock is reset only when the bake, dry storage, and packaging conditions are met and documented; otherwise the original exposure remains part of the batch history. Dry cabinets need calibrated humidity sensors and logged RH, not just a setpoint. If the cabinet RH rises above the target, the exposure clock may resume or the prior exposure may remain unresolved. For practice-based dry cabinet setpoints, alarm limits, and bake durations, verify against your equipment datasheet and your moisture control procedure.

p: When expired floor life turns up mid-lot, stop feeding the affected reels, trays or tubes and quarantine every device from the same lot, date code, vacuum bag, dry cabinet and handling window. Nothing from that batch reflows until the bake decision is made and documented.

Record the MSL, lot code, date code, reel or serial identifiers, open time, elapsed floor life, dry cabinet RH, temperature, storage location and the planned reflow time. Where some devices already reflowed, isolate the boards and assess them by electrical test, X-ray, cross-section or failure analysis. Keep containment wide enough to cover commingled lots and incomplete records.

Where an ESD control failure turns up in storage or staging, quarantine the devices and boards in the EPA for the breach window. ANSI/ESD S20.20 and IEC 61340-5-1 require an EPA with grounded personnel, ESD protective packaging, verified work surfaces and controlled handling.

Check wrist strap logs, floor and surface resistance records, ionizer status, packaging type and operator training. ESD damage is often latent, so visual inspection may show nothing. If the breach surfaces after assembly, trace every board handled in the EPA from the last verified control check to the moment of discovery, and widen the range where records are incomplete.

The range covers all units sharing the lot or date code, storage location, dry cabinet, vacuum bag, shift, feeder, work order, reflow oven and reflow profile. For an ESD breach, add every board handled in the EPA during the breach window, plus feeders, magazines, conveyors, bins, packaging and any adjacent lots that may have been commingled.

Where the storage system uses bins without full serial control, widen the range to the whole bin, lot or shift. The aim is a population bounded by evidence, not the smallest population you can argue for.

Three outcomes cover most cases: bake and repack where the package type allows, scrap where baking is not allowed or the package is damaged, or release only after the bake record, dry storage record and traceability disposition are complete.

Document the deviation, containment, bake condition, dry storage RH, reflow qualification and final disposition. Check practice-based values such as cabinet alarm limits, bake loading density and reflow scheduling windows against your equipment datasheet and process control plan. The decision should stand on the exposure record, the package type and the reflow plan.

calc.task: A lot of MSL3 QFN devices in tape and reel is found mid-lot with expired floor life. The lot has 12 reels, each with 500 units. The vacuum bag was opened 200 h before the planned reflow. The dry cabinet RH was 7% RH at 28 °C. Two reels were placed on feeders and 180 boards were populated. An ESD wrist strap alarm was also found disabled for 4 h in the same storage area. Decide whether the batch must be baked, specify the bake and dry-storage condition by package type, and define the traceability range.
calc.solution: Step 1: Identify the moisture sensitivity level. The devices are MSL3 under IPC/JEDEC J-STD-020, and the floor-life rules come from IPC/JEDEC J-STD-033. Step 2: Compare elapsed floor life with IPC/JEDEC J-STD-033. MSL3 floor life is 168 h at 30 °C and 60% RH. Elapsed time is 200 h, so the floor life is exceeded by 32 h. Step 3: Check dry storage. IPC/JEDEC J-STD-033 uses a dry storage target of 5% RH or less. The cabinet was at 7% RH, so the storage condition is not compliant and the exposure cannot be treated as controlled dry storage. Step 4: Decide whether to bake. Because floor life is exceeded and reflow is planned, bake before reflow unless the component manufacturer provides a documented exception. Step 5: Select bake condition by package type. The package is tape and reel, which contains polymer tape, reel, cover tape, and labels. If the carrier cannot withstand 125 °C, use the IPC/JEDEC J-STD-033 lower-temperature long bake at 40 °C, which for an MSL 3 body up to 1.4 mm is 9 days and therefore does not fit a short reflow window. If the component and carrier datasheets allow 125 °C, the IPC/JEDEC J-STD-033 125 °C column applies only to loose parts in trays or tubes and is indexed to both body thickness and MSL level: for this MSL 3 lot with floor life exceeded by 32 h, 7 h up to 1.4 mm, 17 h at 1.4 to 2.0 mm and 48 h at 2.0 to 4.5 mm, with longer times at higher MSL levels and when the exceedance is greater than 72 h. For this case, choose the 40 °C long bake as the conservative tape-and-reel condition, or de-reel, bake the loose parts at 125 °C for the thickness-indexed time and re-reel; verify the chosen route against the J-STD-033 bake table, the tape datasheet and the reflow window. Step 6: Define post-bake storage. Store at 5% RH or less under IPC/JEDEC J-STD-033, or repackage in a moisture barrier bag with desiccant and a humidity indicator card. Step 7: Calculate affected device count. 12 reels x 500 units per reel = 6000 units. Step 8: Define moisture traceability range. Include all 12 reels, the same lot and date code, the same vacuum bag, the same dry cabinet, the same storage location, the same shift, the two reels on feeders, the 180 populated boards, the feeders, the placement program, the reflow oven, the reflow profile, the work order, the incoming lot, the operator, and the storage RH records. Step 9: Define ESD traceability range. Because the wrist strap alarm was disabled for 4 h, include all devices and boards handled in the EPA during those 4 h, plus the same lot, storage location, feeders, magazines, conveyors, bins, packaging, and work orders. If records are incomplete, widen to the full shift or full lot. Step 10: Disposition. Quarantine the 6000 units, bake the unreflowed units under the selected condition, repackage or store under compliant dry storage, and disposition the 180 boards through electrical test and failure analysis as needed.

defect.symptom: After reflow, several boards show intermittent opens and lifted leads, and X-ray shows voiding or cracking near the QFN package body on boards that used the expired-floor-life reels.
defect.cause: MSL3 tape and reel devices exceeded IPC/JEDEC J-STD-033 floor life, the dry cabinet ran above the 5% RH target, and the batch was fed to placement without a bake decision or traceability containment.
defect.action: Stop the line, quarantine all reels from the same lot, date code, vacuum bag, and dry cabinet, and isolate the affected boards. Do not reflow the remaining batch. Bake the unreflowed devices using an IPC/JEDEC J-STD-033 condition allowed by the tape and reel carrier, then store at 5% RH or less or repackage with desiccant and a humidity indicator card. Trace all boards from the affected reels, feeders, work order, reflow oven, and shift, and disposition them through electrical test, X-ray, and failure analysis.

takeaways: Treat an expired floor life as a contained deviation, not as scrap and not as a label problem.
Check the carrier before choosing the bake, because tape and reel caps the bake at 40 °C and turns hours into days.
Bound the traceability range by evidence — lot, bag, cabinet, shift, feeder, oven — and widen it whenever records are incomplete.

mistakes.mistake: Baking a tape-and-reel lot at 125 °C to save time
mistakes.instead: Keep reels at or below 40 °C or de-reel and bake loose parts to a qualified recipe.

mistakes.mistake: Releasing the batch after a 7 % RH cabinet reading
mistakes.instead: Treat anything above 5 % RH as exposure and recalculate floor life before reflow.

mistakes.mistake: Limiting containment to the two reels on the feeder
mistakes.instead: Include the whole lot, bag, cabinet and shift, and widen further where records cannot prove otherwise.

terms.def: A batch whose recorded exposure exceeds the allowed floor life before reflow.
Action that stops suspect material from moving further into the process while the disposition is decided.
Damage that leaves a part working at test and failing later in service.
The set of units, lots and handling records that the evidence shows to be affected by an exposure.

title: The paste volume budget: what the joint needs before the aperture is drawn

goals.text: Calculate area ratio, aspect ratio and expected deposit volume for an aperture and state whether it will release paste adequately.

theory.h: Paste volume is a joint requirement
p: Define the joint before drawing the aperture: pad geometry, component termination, target standoff, acceptable fillet, and the paste volume needed to wet the termination and form a reliable joint. The aperture then has to deliver that volume while staying inside the pad, so reflow creates no bridge.

Stencil thickness, paste rheology, print speed, squeegee pressure, separation speed and cleaning cycle all decide how much paste actually transfers. Treat the aperture as a volume source and the print process as the transfer mechanism between them.

set the joint volume target first, then size the aperture.</text> <text x='20' y='304' font-size='11' class='d'>Fixes: thinner foil, step-down pocket, larger or rounded aperture, polished or nano-coated walls, other paste.</text> </svg>
blocks.caption: Aperture geometry and paste release: area ratio ≥ 0.66 and aspect ratio ≥ 1.5; a thick foil with a narrow aperture gives low ratios and a short deposit

blocks.alt: Reference sheet: stencil macro photograph, release geometry cross-section, good release versus poor release comparison, and the joint target to SPI workflow
blocks.caption: Paste volume budget: joint target first, then deposit volume, aperture and SPI verification

theory.h: Area ratio compares contact area with wall adhesion
p: Area ratio is the aperture area divided by the sidewall area of the stencil wall. For a rectangular aperture the sidewall area is the perimeter times the stencil thickness, so area ratio equals length times width divided by perimeter times thickness.

A higher ratio gives the paste a larger bottom contact area against the wall that holds it in the aperture. IPC-7525 stencil design guidelines are the common reference for release indicators, with a working target of about 0.66 or above; confirm that against your paste and equipment datasheet.

theory.h: Aspect ratio describes depth against width
p: Aspect ratio is aperture width divided by stencil thickness, and for rectangular apertures you take the smaller dimension, because that dimension controls the narrowest release path. A low ratio means a deep, narrow hole where paste clings to the sidewalls and fails to release cleanly.
IPC-7525 again supplies the release indicator, with a common working target above about 1.5. Fine-pitch designs often fall below it and need a process or paste change rather than a longer argument.

theory.h: Deposit volume is nominal volume times transfer efficiency
p: Nominal deposit volume is aperture area multiplied by stencil thickness. Expected deposit volume multiplies that by transfer efficiency, which absorbs paste left in the aperture, paste smeared during separation, and paste never released at all.

Transfer efficiency depends on the process, so measure it or take it from paste and equipment data. Where planning needs a single number, use a conservative value from the paste datasheet or a recent print trial.

theory.h: Set the joint volume target first
p: Estimate the required paste volume from pad area, desired deposit height, component termination geometry and paste manufacturer guidance. On chip components the deposit has to wet the termination and form a fillet without giving adjacent pads enough paste to bridge in reflow.

Larger pads leave more room: adjust volume through aperture area, stencil thickness or a step stencil. Compare the calculated expected deposit volume with the required volume before committing to the aperture.

When area ratio or aspect ratio comes out low, reduce stencil thickness, enlarge the aperture within the pad, choose a paste with better release, or change the print parameters. Electropolished walls, laser-cut shape, wall taper and step stencils also help.
Every one of those trades volume against release and bridging risk, so judge them on print trials and inspection data rather than on a single ratio.

Calculate area ratio, aspect ratio, nominal volume and expected deposit volume. Ratios that meet the release indicators from your applicable design guideline, together with an expected volume that meets the joint requirement, make adequate release likely.

A low ratio means the aperture may release badly even when nominal volume looks generous. A low volume means the joint may be underfilled even when release is good. Document the assumptions and confirm with paste deposit measurement.

calc.task: A small chip resistor has a 0.50 mm by 0.40 mm pad. Stencil thickness is 0.12 mm. Use a transfer efficiency of 0.90. Calculate area ratio, aspect ratio, nominal deposit volume, and expected deposit volume. State whether release is adequate using the IPC-7525 release indicators.
calc.solution: Aperture area = 0.50 mm x 0.40 mm = 0.20 mm^2. Perimeter = 0.50 mm + 0.40 mm + 0.50 mm + 0.40 mm = 1.80 mm. Sidewall area = 1.80 mm x 0.12 mm = 0.216 mm^2. Area ratio = 0.20 mm^2 / 0.216 mm^2 = 0.926. Aspect ratio = smaller aperture dimension / stencil thickness = 0.40 mm / 0.12 mm = 3.33. Nominal deposit volume = 0.20 mm^2 x 0.12 mm = 0.024 mm^3. Expected deposit volume = 0.024 mm^3 x 0.90 = 0.0216 mm^3. Release adequacy: area ratio 0.926 is above about 0.66 and aspect ratio 3.33 is above about 1.5, so release is likely adequate. Compare 0.0216 mm^3 with the required joint volume from paste and component data; if it is lower, increase aperture area, reduce stencil thickness, or improve transfer efficiency.

defect.symptom: After reflow, several small chip components show insufficient solder fillet or opens on one side, while adjacent larger pads look normal.
defect.cause: The small aperture had low area ratio or aspect ratio, or transfer efficiency was lower than assumed, so the expected deposit volume was not delivered.
defect.action: Measure paste deposit volume, compare with required joint volume, reduce stencil thickness or enlarge aperture within pad, adjust paste and print parameters, and re-run a print trial with inspection.

takeaways: Set the joint volume target before the aperture exists, then check that the aperture can deliver it inside the pad.
Judge release on both area ratio and aspect ratio, because a deep narrow aperture can pass one and fail the other.
Take transfer efficiency from measurement or the paste datasheet, since a generic factor hides the process you actually run.

mistakes.mistake: Designing the aperture and checking the volume afterwards
mistakes.instead: Fix the joint volume first and size the aperture against it.

mistakes.mistake: Using a single release ratio as a pass or fail verdict
mistakes.instead: Combine both ratios with SPI data and the paste datasheet before releasing the design.

mistakes.mistake: Assuming nominal volume equals deposit volume
mistakes.instead: Multiply by a measured transfer efficiency and compare with the joint requirement.

terms.def: Aperture opening area divided by the stencil sidewall area, the usual indicator of paste release.
Aperture width divided by stencil thickness, taken on the narrowest dimension of a rectangular aperture.
The share of nominal aperture volume that reaches the pad as a printed deposit.
A stencil with locally reduced thickness that lowers paste volume in selected areas.

title: Area ratio and aspect ratio: definitions, calculation, fine-pitch consequences

goals.text: Calculate area ratio, aspect ratio and expected deposit volume for an aperture and state whether it will release paste adequately.

blocks.caption: Worked example: 0.25 × 0.25 mm aperture in 0.10 mm foil — area ratio 0.625 (below 0.66), aspect ratio 2.5

blocks.alt: Reference sheet: isometric aperture with opening and wall areas, a width versus foil thickness section, the two ratio definitions, a macro photograph of complete and short fine-pitch deposits, and the fine-pitch consequence
blocks.caption: Area ratio and aspect ratio: definitions, the fine-pitch consequence, and what short deposits look like

p: Area ratio is the aperture opening area divided by the sidewall area of the stencil aperture. On a rectangular aperture the opening is width times length, and the sidewall is the perimeter times the foil thickness.
IPC-7525C treats area ratio as a key indicator of paste release, because the paste has to separate from those walls and transfer to the pad.

A higher area ratio gives the paste more opening area against the wall it must leave, and transfer tends to improve with it. A low ratio means the wall contact area is large next to the opening, so paste sticks in the aperture and the pad gets an inadequate deposit.

IPC-7525C gives area-ratio guidance for stencil design, but the practical release limit also depends on paste rheology, wall finish, print speed, snap-off distance and squeegee pressure. Check all of it against your paste and equipment datasheet.

theory.p: Aspect ratio is the aperture dimension divided by foil thickness. On a rectangular aperture you use the smallest dimension, because it controls the narrowest paste channel. IPC-7525C discusses aspect ratio as a stencil geometry parameter tied to paste release and aperture wall effects.

p: As pitch falls, apertures shrink while foil thickness often stays where it was, so aspect ratio rises and area ratio drops. High aspect ratio apertures make release more sensitive to print parameters and wall condition.
On fine-pitch designs, review aspect ratio together with area ratio, paste type and SPI results. A single pass or fail number cannot carry a fine-pitch decision.

The theoretical maximum deposit is aperture area multiplied by foil thickness. The expected deposit is lower, because paste never transfers perfectly, and it is commonly estimated by multiplying the theoretical volume by a transfer efficiency factor.
Take that factor from your paste, stencil, printer and SPI data. A generic assumption hides the process you are actually running.

theory.p: Fine-pitch apertures can produce low area ratio, high aspect ratio and small deposit volume at the same time. The joint then risks insufficient paste, voids, opens or inconsistent transfer, and the process becomes sensitive to paste slump, stencil wear, wall roughness and print parameter drift.

p: Combine area ratio, aspect ratio, expected deposit volume and process data. Where area ratio sits near or below the IPC-7525C guidance range, or the expected volume is close to the minimum the component and pad need, review the design.
The review covers foil thickness, aperture size within the pad, wall finish, paste selection and print parameters.

calc.task: A rectangular stencil aperture is 0.25 mm by 0.25 mm, and the foil thickness is 0.10 mm. Calculate the area ratio, aspect ratio, theoretical deposit volume, and expected deposit volume using an assumed transfer efficiency of 0.85. State whether the aperture is expected to release paste adequately according to common IPC-7525C area-ratio guidance.
calc.solution: 1. Aperture area = width × length = 0.25 mm × 0.25 mm = 0.0625 mm². 2. Aperture perimeter = 2 × (width + length) = 2 × (0.25 mm + 0.25 mm) = 1.00 mm. 3. Sidewall area = perimeter × foil thickness = 1.00 mm × 0.10 mm = 0.10 mm². 4. Area ratio = aperture area / sidewall area = 0.0625 mm² / 0.10 mm² = 0.625. 5. Aspect ratio = smallest aperture dimension / foil thickness = 0.25 mm / 0.10 mm = 2.5. 6. Theoretical deposit volume = aperture area × foil thickness = 0.0625 mm² × 0.10 mm = 0.00625 mm³. 7. Expected deposit volume = theoretical volume × transfer efficiency = 0.00625 mm³ × 0.85 = 0.0053125 mm³. 8. In nanoliters, 0.0053125 mm³ × 1000 nL/mm³ = 5.3125 nL. 9. The area ratio is 0.625, which is below the commonly cited IPC-7525C area-ratio guidance value of 0.66. Therefore, paste release is expected to be marginal to inadequate for robust production unless supported by SPI data, paste datasheet, and print parameter validation. 10. Possible actions include reducing foil thickness, increasing aperture dimensions within the pad boundary, improving stencil wall finish, selecting a paste with better release characteristics, or optimizing print speed, pressure, and snap-off distance.

defect.symptom: After reflow, fine-pitch components show intermittent opens, voids, or insufficient solder joints, and stencil apertures retain paste residue after printing.
defect.cause: The aperture area ratio is too low for reliable paste release, often because the aperture is small relative to foil thickness and sidewall area. Rough or worn stencil walls, inappropriate paste rheology, or print parameters that do not support release can worsen the problem.
defect.action: Review the aperture area ratio and aspect ratio against IPC-7525C guidance and your paste/equipment datasheet. Reduce foil thickness or increase aperture size within the pad if allowed, improve stencil wall finish, verify paste selection, and optimize print parameters. Confirm the result with SPI and reflow inspection.

takeaways: Calculate area ratio and aspect ratio from the same three numbers — aperture dimensions and foil thickness — before the stencil is ordered.
Compare the expected deposit with the joint requirement, because a good area ratio can still leave too little paste.
Treat a low area ratio as a design review trigger supported by SPI data, not as an automatic rejection.

mistakes.mistake: Increasing foil thickness to raise paste volume
mistakes.instead: Thicker foil lowers area ratio and costs release; raise aperture area or use a step stencil instead.

mistakes.mistake: Judging a fine-pitch aperture on area ratio alone
mistakes.instead: Read aspect ratio and the SPI deposit data with it, since both drive transfer.

mistakes.mistake: Using a textbook transfer efficiency in the design review
mistakes.instead: Take the factor from your own printer, paste and SPI results.

terms.def: Aperture opening area divided by sidewall area, the standard indicator of paste release in stencil design.
Aperture width divided by foil thickness on the narrowest aperture dimension.
The fraction of theoretical aperture volume that reaches the pad as a deposit.
Component lead spacing small enough that aperture dimensions approach the limits of paste release.

title: Foil, thickness, step stencils, laser cut and wall finish

goals.text: Select foil thickness and aperture geometry for a given pad stack and pitch, and justify each choice by the defect it prevents.

blocks.alt: Cross-sections of a plain foil, a step stencil with two thicknesses, a rough laser-cut wall and a smooth electropolished wall
blocks.caption: Foil, thickness, step stencils, laser cut and wall finish — how the foil and its walls set the deposit

theory.h: Foil thickness sets volume and release risk
p: Foil thickness is the primary control on deposited paste volume: for a given aperture, volume is roughly aperture area times foil thickness. Thicker foil helps large pads, thermal relief and high-volume joints, and it raises the chance of slump, bridging and poor release on fine pitch.
Choose from the supplier's available range, commonly 0.075 mm to 0.200 mm, and check the choice against your paste rheology, your printer and your SPI capability.

Two release checks carry most of the work. Area ratio is aperture area divided by the product of aperture perimeter and foil thickness, and IPC-7525 commonly uses a minimum of 0.66 for reliable release. Aspect ratio is aperture width divided by foil thickness, with a common minimum of 1.5.
Both are design guidelines rather than guarantees, because paste type, wall finish and print speed decide the outcome too.

theory.h: Pad stack and pitch drive the thickness
p: Start from the tightest pitch on the board. Fine-pitch QFP, QFN and BGA pads usually need thinner foil or a local thin step so the aperture walls sit close enough to control paste shape. Larger pads and thermal pads may need more volume, which a thicker local step can supply where pitch is generous.
Where a board mixes both, decide up front whether one foil thickness can satisfy every feature or whether the design needs a step stencil.

theory.h: Aperture size is usually reduced from the pad
p: A full-pad aperture can overfill closely spaced pads and bridge, while a small one starves the joint and opens. Many processes reduce the aperture a few percent to tens of percent of the pad dimension, depending on paste slump, reflow profile and pad finish; your paste and equipment datasheet settles the number.
On rectangular pads keep the reduction balanced, so the deposit stays centred and favours no lead.

A step stencil changes foil thickness locally: thin where the fine-pitch apertures are, thicker over large pads and thermal pads. Place the step where it does not disturb the support of nearby fine-pitch apertures, and keep the transition far enough from sensitive features to avoid paste leakage or uneven squeegee support.
Confirm the stencil maker's minimum step size, transition method and maximum step height. Those are process limits of that supplier, not universal values.

Laser cutting controls wall taper and finish. Rough or irregular walls hold paste, increase residue and make release less repeatable, while an aggressive taper changes the effective aperture at the top and the bottom of the foil.

Ask for the wall finish and taper the stencil maker can actually hold, such as electropolished or coated walls, and verify the result with SPI and print inspection. A finish does not fix a geometry problem.

A practical order is: find the tightest pitch and the paste-volume requirements, choose a base foil thickness, size apertures to meet the IPC-7525 area-ratio and aspect-ratio guidelines while controlling volume, add a step only when one thickness cannot serve both ends of the board, then run a print trial with SPI.
Adjust aperture size before changing foil thickness where you can, because aperture changes iterate faster and cost less.

calc.task: A board has 0.40 mm x 0.40 mm QFP pads on 0.50 mm pitch and a 1.00 mm x 1.00 mm thermal pad. Select a base foil thickness and aperture size for the fine-pitch pads, select a local step thickness for the thermal pad, and check the IPC-7525 area-ratio and aspect-ratio guidelines.
calc.solution: Start with the tightest pitch: 0.50 mm pitch QFP pads. Choose a base foil thickness of 0.100 mm to limit paste volume and reduce bridging risk; verify that the paste datasheet supports this thickness for the chosen aperture. Reduce the 0.40 mm pad to a 0.38 mm x 0.38 mm aperture to lower bridging risk while retaining paste volume. Calculate area ratio for the fine-pitch aperture: area = 0.38 mm x 0.38 mm = 0.1444 mm^2; perimeter = 1.52 mm; area ratio = 0.1444 mm^2 / (1.52 mm x 0.100 mm) = 0.95. This is above the IPC-7525 guideline of 0.66. Calculate aspect ratio: 0.38 mm / 0.100 mm = 3.8. This is above the IPC-7525 guideline of 1.5. For the 1.00 mm x 1.00 mm thermal pad, choose a local step thickness of 0.150 mm to increase paste volume without thickening the entire stencil. Use a 0.95 mm x 0.95 mm aperture. Check the thermal pad area ratio: area = 0.95 mm x 0.95 mm = 0.9025 mm^2; perimeter = 3.80 mm; area ratio = 0.9025 mm^2 / (3.80 mm x 0.150 mm) = 1.58, above the IPC-7525 guideline of 0.66. Aspect ratio = 0.95 mm / 0.150 mm = 6.33, above the IPC-7525 guideline of 1.5. Place the step transition away from the 0.50 mm pitch QFP apertures and confirm the stencil maker can hold the step and wall finish. Run SPI to verify paste volume, bridging, and release before production.

defect.symptom: Bridging appears between adjacent fine-pitch QFP leads after reflow, with excess paste visible between leads on SPI.
defect.cause: The foil thickness or aperture size was selected for larger pads and is too aggressive for the fine-pitch area; rough or poorly controlled laser-cut walls can also reduce paste release and leave paste residue between apertures.
defect.action: Reduce the fine-pitch aperture size, then reduce local foil thickness or add a thin step if volume is still too high. Recheck area ratio and aspect ratio against IPC-7525, request a smoother wall finish or verified taper from the stencil maker, and rerun SPI to confirm the change.

takeaways: Set foil thickness from the tightest pitch first, then check the larger pads against it, because paste volume scales directly with thickness.
Read area ratio and aspect ratio against IPC-7525 before the stencil is cut, and treat either one failing as a design change, not a print tweak.
Add a step stencil only where a single thickness genuinely cannot serve both fine pitch and large thermal pads.

mistakes.mistake: Thickening the whole foil to feed one thermal pad
mistakes.instead: Use a local step and keep the fine-pitch area thin.

mistakes.mistake: Assuming an electropolished wall rescues a failing area ratio
mistakes.instead: Fix the aperture geometry first, then verify the finish with SPI.

mistakes.mistake: Placing a step transition next to fine-pitch apertures
mistakes.instead: Keep the transition clear of features that depend on even squeegee support.

terms.def: A stencil whose foil thickness changes in defined areas to give different paste volumes on one board.
Aperture area divided by aperture perimeter times foil thickness.
Aperture width divided by foil thickness on the narrowest dimension.
The change in aperture size between the top and bottom of the laser-cut wall.

title: Aperture geometry by component: chip, QFP fine pitch, QFN/LGA, BGA

goals.text: Select foil thickness and aperture geometry for a given pad stack and pitch, and justify each choice by the defect it prevents.

blocks.alt: Four aperture shapes side by side with a label for each component family and the deposit each produces
blocks.caption: Aperture geometry by component: chip, fine-pitch QFP, QFN/LGA and BGA

theory.h: Pad stack and stencil thickness trade-off
p: Foil thickness sets paste volume per aperture. For a given pad stack, pick a thickness that delivers enough paste for fillet and standoff without the excess that bridges or the shortage that opens.

Selection usually starts from the smallest pitch and the smallest aperture in the assembly, then gets checked against the larger components. Common thicknesses are 0.10 mm to 0.15 mm for fine-pitch work and 0.12 mm to 0.18 mm for mixed boards, subject to the stencil supplier's capability and the paste datasheet. IPC-7525 covers thickness, aperture area and sidewall finish.

theory.h: Chip components: aperture area and paste balance
p: For chip resistors and capacitors the aperture should match pad size while still allowing paste to form a wettable fillet. A common starting point is aperture area at 80 % to 100 % of pad area, with less area on the smallest parts to prevent tombstoning and bridging.

On the smallest chips the aperture width may be 0.10 mm to 0.15 mm and the length 0.20 mm to 0.30 mm, but the final values come from IPC-7525, the IPC-7351 land pattern and the observed release. Where the pad sits on a large copper area, reduce aperture area so the extra heat does not turn into excess paste and solder balling.

theory.h: QFP fine pitch: area ratio and sidewall control
p: Gull-wing fine-pitch packages need enough paste to wet the lead foot while keeping solder mask clearance between adjacent pads. Area ratio — aperture opening area divided by aperture wall area — is the useful control, and IPC-7525 discusses how it drives release.

A practical target is 0.66 or higher for small apertures, with sidewall polish and paste viscosity adjusted when the ratio falls below. Below 0.5 mm pitch, narrow the aperture relative to the pad, use trapezoidal or rounded shapes, and check the result against IPC-7525 and the paste datasheet to keep bridges out.

theory.h: QFN and LGA: peripheral pads and thermal escape
p: QFN and LGA packages usually carry peripheral pads plus a central thermal pad. Peripheral apertures should be sized to avoid coplanarity defects and bridging, while the centre aperture is segmented or reduced to control volume and let gas escape.

A common approach divides the thermal pad into several small apertures with 0.10 mm to 0.20 mm between segments, or uses a reduced-area pattern; check it against IPC-7525 and the IPC-7351 land pattern guidance. An oversized centre pad traps paste and causes voiding, non-wetting or package lift, while an undersized one costs thermal performance and joint reliability.

theory.h: BGA: pitch, aperture area and collapse
p: On BGA the geometry follows ball pitch, ball diameter and paste collapse during reflow. IPC-7095 covers BGA design and assembly, including paste deposition and land pattern considerations.

Apertures are usually smaller than the ball diameter to limit paste volume and bridging, especially at 0.5 mm pitch and below. At larger pitches the aperture may approach the land area, but paste rheology and the reflow profile still have to be verified. Where BGA pads share a board with fine-pitch parts, a step stencil or local thickness change can serve both.

theory.h: Foil thickness for mixed component sets
p: Find the smallest pitch and smallest aperture that must release paste reliably, then choose thickness against them. A thinner foil cuts volume and keeps bridges off fine-pitch QFP, QFN and BGA pads, but it can starve larger components and open joints when the paste fails to wet the pad. A thicker foil feeds the large parts and coplanarity, and raises the bridging risk on fine pitch.
On a board with both, consider a step stencil or local thickness change, and check the transition location against IPC-7525 and what the stencil fabricator can hold.

Aperture shape, wall finish and aperture reduction are process controls, not drawing decoration. Rounded corners, trapezoidal apertures and reduced-area patterns can improve release and cut bridging, but they have to be tested with the actual paste, squeegee pressure and print speed.

Judge joints against IPC-A-610 and confirm the printed deposit with paste volume measurement or two- and three-dimensional inspection. Values such as area-ratio targets, reduction percentages and thickness ranges are practice-based, so check them against your paste and equipment datasheet and your first-article results.

Tie every geometry choice to a defect it prevents. Adequate area ratio with clean sidewalls prevents insufficient paste and opens; reduced aperture area with thinner foil prevents fine-pitch bridging; segmented centre pads prevent voiding and lift on QFN and LGA; controlled BGA aperture area prevents collapse and bridging.
The choice is a balance. The thickness that prevents opens on a large pad can bridge a 0.4 mm pitch QFP, so justify the final value by the dominant defect risk and confirm it by inspection.

calc.task: A 0.4 mm pitch QFP has land width 0.25 mm and land length 0.60 mm. The board also has 0.5 mm pitch BGA pads. Select foil thickness and aperture geometry for the QFP, and justify each choice by the defect it prevents.
calc.solution: 1. Identify the smallest pitch: 0.4 mm. Use IPC-7525 area-ratio guidance and choose a thin foil, 0.10 mm, to reduce paste volume and bridging risk. 2. Reduce aperture width to 0.22 mm and length to 0.55 mm to leave solder mask clearance and control volume. 3. Calculate area ratio: aperture area = 0.22 mm x 0.55 mm = 0.121 mm^2. Sidewall area = 2 x (0.22 mm + 0.55 mm) x 0.10 mm = 0.154 mm^2. Area ratio = 0.121 / 0.154 = 0.79. This is above the practical target of 0.66 associated with IPC-7525 area-ratio guidance, so release should be acceptable if sidewall finish and paste viscosity are verified. 4. Check paste volume: aperture area 0.121 mm^2 multiplied by foil thickness 0.10 mm gives 0.0121 mm^3 per aperture. For the 0.5 mm pitch BGA, verify that the same foil does not create insufficient paste; if needed, use a step stencil or local thickness change, and verify against IPC-7095 and paste datasheet. 5. Justify: thinner foil and reduced aperture prevent bridging between 0.4 mm pitch leads; adequate area ratio prevents opens from poor release; rounded corners reduce paste trapping and solder balls. 6. Inspect first article per IPC-A-610 and measure printed volume; adjust if bridges or opens appear.

defect.symptom: Solder bridges between adjacent QFP leads at 0.4 mm pitch after reflow; X-ray shows excess paste between leads.
defect.cause: Foil thickness 0.15 mm and aperture width equal to pad width produced high paste volume and poor release control; area ratio may be adequate but volume excessive.
defect.action: Reduce foil to 0.10 mm, reduce aperture width to 0.22 mm, use rounded or trapezoidal apertures, verify area ratio of at least 0.66 against IPC-7525, adjust paste viscosity and squeegee pressure, re-run first article and inspect per IPC-A-610.

takeaways: Start thickness selection at the smallest pitch and smallest aperture, then check that the large components still get their volume.
Segment the QFN thermal pad so gas can escape, because a solid centre aperture traps paste and voids the joint.
Justify each geometry choice by the defect it prevents, and confirm the result with SPI and IPC-A-610 inspection.

mistakes.mistake: Using one foil thickness for a board with 0.4 mm QFP and large thermal pads
mistakes.instead: Step the stencil or accept a compromise on the dominant defect risk, and verify both areas.

mistakes.mistake: Filling the QFN centre pad with one large aperture
mistakes.instead: Segment it into small apertures with 0.10 mm to 0.20 mm gaps so volatiles escape.

mistakes.mistake: Sizing chip apertures at full pad area on the smallest parts
mistakes.instead: Reduce area to prevent tombstoning and bridging, then verify with SPI.

terms.def: The large central land under a QFN or LGA that carries heat and needs a controlled paste volume.
One end of a chip component lifting during reflow because the two joints wet at different rates.
Deliberately making the stencil opening smaller than the land to control paste volume and bridging.
The copper geometry on the board that the aperture and the component termination must match.
