title: Aperture calculator and drawing review

goals.text: Calculate area ratio, aspect ratio and expected deposit volume for an aperture and state whether it will release paste adequately.
Accept or reject a delivered stencil from its measurement report against the issued specification.

blocks.alt: A calculator panel taking pad geometry, foil thickness and wall condition and outputting area ratio, aspect ratio and volume, beside a stencil drawing review checklist
blocks.caption: Aperture calculator and drawing review — inputs, release metrics and the review checklist

theory.h: What the aperture calculator is for
theory.p: An aperture calculator turns pad geometry, foil thickness and wall condition into release metrics you can review before fabrication: area ratio, aspect ratio and expected deposit volume. Those numbers let the process engineer decide whether the stencil will release paste and whether the drawing needs revision before anyone buys the foil.

p: Area ratio is aperture opening area divided by the wall area the paste must leave. IPC-7525C recommends an area ratio above 0.66 for reliable release.
Values below that still work with some paste types, print speeds, squeegee pressures and foil finishes, but only after qualification against your paste and equipment datasheet.

theory.p: Aspect ratio is aperture width divided by foil thickness, taken on the smaller dimension of a rectangular aperture because that dimension controls the release path. IPC-7525C recommends above 1.5. Thick foil on a small aperture pulls the ratio down and leaves paste sticking in the hole.

Wall taper affects how easily paste leaves the aperture. IPC-7525C recommends a wall taper in the range of 85 to 90 degrees, measured from the horizontal plane, because a slight taper reduces the effective wall area. Electropolishing, laser-drill condition, burrs, and clogging also affect release and should be reviewed on the drawing and measurement report.

Expected deposit volume starts at aperture area times foil thickness, with a taper correction when the bottom opening is smaller than the top. What actually transfers depends on transfer efficiency, which moves with paste rheology, print speed, squeegee pressure and foil finish — check it against your paste and equipment datasheet.

Drawing review confirms aperture dimensions, tolerances, foil thickness, wall taper, fiducials, aperture-to-pad alignment, step features and the paste assumptions. It also confirms that the supplier's measurement method and sample size can actually verify the delivered stencil.

theory.h: Accept or reject from the measurement report
p: Accept against the issued specification, not against general guidance. A measured value outside the issued tolerance means the stencil is rejected or dispositioned by engineering, unless a qualified deviation exists.
Area ratio or aspect ratio below the qualified release limit triggers review even when every aperture dimension sits inside tolerance, because dimensions alone do not guarantee release.

calc.task: A drawing specifies a square aperture 0.30 mm by 0.30 mm in a 0.120 mm thick foil. The issued specification requires area ratio at least 0.66, aspect ratio at least 1.5, foil thickness 0.120 mm plus or minus 0.010 mm, aperture size 0.30 mm plus or minus 0.02 mm, wall taper 85 to 90 degrees, and flatness no greater than 0.10 mm. A delivered stencil report gives measured aperture 0.295 mm by 0.298 mm, thickness 0.118 mm, area ratio 0.63, aspect ratio 2.5, wall taper 86 degrees, and flatness 0.08 mm. Calculate area ratio, aspect ratio, expected deposit volume, and accept or reject.
calc.solution: Step 1: Calculate nominal aperture area. Area = 0.30 mm x 0.30 mm = 0.090 mm2. Step 2: Calculate nominal perimeter. Perimeter = 4 x 0.30 mm = 1.20 mm. Step 3: Calculate nominal area ratio. Area ratio = aperture area / (perimeter x foil thickness) = 0.090 / (1.20 x 0.120) = 0.625. Step 4: Calculate nominal aspect ratio. Aspect ratio = aperture width / foil thickness = 0.30 / 0.120 = 2.5. Step 5: Calculate nominal deposit volume. Nominal volume = aperture area x foil thickness = 0.090 x 0.120 = 0.0108 mm3. Step 6: Apply a taper correction. For an 85 degree wall taper from horizontal, the wall angle from vertical is 5 degrees. Bottom side = 0.30 - 2 x 0.120 x tan(5 degrees) = 0.279 mm. Bottom area = 0.279 x 0.279 = 0.0778 mm2. Average area = (0.090 + 0.0778) / 2 = 0.0839 mm2. Tapered volume = 0.0839 x 0.120 = 0.0101 mm3. Step 7: Estimate expected paste deposit. Using an example transfer efficiency of 80 percent, expected deposit = 0.0101 x 0.80 = 0.0081 mm3. Verify transfer efficiency against your paste and equipment datasheet. Step 8: State release adequacy. The nominal area ratio 0.625 is below the IPC-7525C recommended value of 0.66, so paste release may be inadequate unless qualified by paste and equipment testing. Step 9: Review the delivered report. Thickness 0.118 mm is within 0.120 mm plus or minus 0.010 mm. Aperture 0.295 mm by 0.298 mm is within 0.30 mm plus or minus 0.02 mm. Aspect ratio 2.5 is above 1.5. Wall taper 86 degrees is within 85 to 90 degrees. Flatness 0.08 mm is within 0.10 mm. Step 10: Accept or reject. Reject the stencil against the issued specification because the measured area ratio 0.63 is below the required 0.66. Quarantine the stencil and disposition it through engineering, rework, or replacement.

defect.symptom: Fine-pitch QFN pads show low paste height, opens, or insufficient solder joints after a new stencil is introduced.
defect.cause: The aperture area ratio is below the qualified release limit because the aperture is small relative to the foil thickness, and the wall taper or wall finish is not adequate for the paste being used.
defect.action: Stop printing with the stencil, quarantine it, and verify aperture dimensions, foil thickness, wall taper, area ratio, and cleanliness. Reject or rework the stencil if it is outside the issued specification, then qualify the corrected design with SPI and cross-section before release.

takeaways: Calculate area ratio, aspect ratio and expected volume before the stencil is ordered, and reject the drawing if either ratio misses its limit.
Judge a delivered stencil against the issued specification, including measured area ratio, not only the aperture dimensions.
Put wall taper, wall finish and cleanliness on the drawing and report, because release depends on them as much as on geometry.

mistakes.mistake: Accepting a stencil because every dimension is in tolerance
mistakes.instead: Check the measured area ratio against the issued release limit as well.

mistakes.mistake: Comparing measured values to IPC-7525 general guidance instead of the drawing
mistakes.instead: Use the issued specification, and document any limit the drawing leaves silent.

mistakes.mistake: Skipping the taper correction in the volume estimate
mistakes.instead: Apply it whenever the bottom opening is smaller, or the expected volume comes out optimistic.

terms.def: The angle of the aperture wall from the horizontal; IPC-7525 allows the taper to be specified, and 85 to 90 degrees is common practice.
Aperture volume corrected for taper and multiplied by transfer efficiency.
The supplier's record of measured stencil characteristics against the issued drawing.
A documented engineering approval to use a value outside the issued specification.

title: Stencil acceptance, cleaning regime and lifetime tracking

goals.text: Accept or reject a delivered stencil from its measurement report against the issued specification.

blocks.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 960 330' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='Stencil acceptance checklist with the issued specification values: foil 0.120 mm, aperture 0.400 mm, area ratio at least 0.66, wall taper at least 85 degrees, tension 25-35 N/cm, step depth 0.050 mm; plus cleaning and lifetime tracking'><style>text{font-family:'IBM Plex Mono',monospace;fill:#e2e8f0}.d{fill:#94a3b8}.t{fill:#53d1cc}.r{fill:#f44336}.o{fill:#ff9800}</style> <text x='20' y='24' font-size='13' class='t'>INCOMING STENCIL — check reported value AND tolerance band against the issued spec</text> <rect x='20' y='46' width='14' height='14' fill='none' stroke='#53d1cc'/><text x='44' y='58' font-size='11' class='d'>foil thickness</text><text x='230' y='58' font-size='11'>0.120 ± 0.010 mm</text> <rect x='20' y='70' width='14' height='14' fill='none' stroke='#53d1cc'/><text x='44' y='82' font-size='11' class='d'>aperture width</text><text x='230' y='82' font-size='11'>0.400 ± 0.025 mm</text> <rect x='20' y='94' width='14' height='14' fill='none' stroke='#53d1cc'/><text x='44' y='106' font-size='11' class='d'>area ratio</text><text x='230' y='106' font-size='11'>≥ 0.66 (issued spec, IPC-7525C guidance)</text> <rect x='20' y='118' width='14' height='14' fill='none' stroke='#53d1cc'/><text x='44' y='130' font-size='11' class='d'>wall taper</text><text x='230' y='130' font-size='11'>≥ 85°</text> <rect x='20' y='142' width='14' height='14' fill='none' stroke='#53d1cc'/><text x='44' y='154' font-size='11' class='d'>tension</text><text x='230' y='154' font-size='11'>25-35 N/cm</text> <rect x='20' y='166' width='14' height='14' fill='none' stroke='#53d1cc'/><text x='44' y='178' font-size='11' class='d'>step depth</text><text x='230' y='178' font-size='11'>0.050 ± 0.010 mm</text> <rect x='20' y='190' width='14' height='14' fill='none' stroke='#53d1cc'/><text x='44' y='202' font-size='11' class='d'>registration, flatness</text><text x='230' y='202' font-size='11'>per drawing</text> <rect x='520' y='40' width='360' height='1' fill='#334155'/> <text x='520' y='64' font-size='12' class='t'>CLEANING REGIME</text> <text x='520' y='84' font-size='11'>underside wipe: dry / wet / vacuum cycle per SPI trend</text> <text x='520' y='102' font-size='11'>off-line wash after the run; inspect apertures</text> <text x='520' y='120' font-size='11' class='d'>never scrape apertures; log every wash</text> <text x='520' y='154' font-size='12' class='t'>LIFETIME TRACKING</text> <text x='520' y='174' font-size='11'>print count · wash count · tension re-check · damage log</text> <text x='520' y='192' font-size='11'>retire on tension loss, aperture wear, frame damage</text> <text x='520' y='210' font-size='11' class='d'>release decision documented before use on the line</text> <rect x='20' y='240' width='860' height='1' fill='#334155'/> <text x='20' y='266' font-size='11'>Where the spec is silent: design reference from IPC-7525C and the paste/equipment datasheet, then record the accepted limit.</text> <text x='20' y='290' font-size='11' class='d'>Acceptance = measurement report + tolerance band + area ratio recomputed from the measured foil and aperture, not the nominal.</text> </svg>
blocks.caption: Stencil acceptance checklist from the issued specification, plus the cleaning regime and lifetime tracking

blocks.alt: Reference sheet: a framed stencil under a thickness gauge, an acceptance checklist with blank value lines, the understencil wipe and off-line wash sequence, and a lifetime usage log
blocks.caption: Stencil acceptance, cleaning regime and lifetime tracking; specification values in the figure above

p: Treat the delivered stencil as a controlled part. Acceptance starts with a traceable measurement report naming the drawing revision, measurement method, operator, date and serial number.

Compare each reported value to the issued specification, not to a generic guideline. A report that omits a required characteristic, gives no tolerance band, or shows an unapproved deviation is held or rejected until the supplier supplies corrected data.

theory.p: Review foil thickness, aperture width and length, wall taper, area ratio, step depth, registration, tension and flatness, confirming both the reported value and the tolerance band for each. Where the specification is silent, take the design reference from IPC-7525C and the paste or equipment datasheet, then document the accepted limit before release.

p: Area ratio and wall taper control release. A low area ratio, a poor taper or a damaged wall leaves paste in the aperture or smears it across the pad.
On small apertures, check the supplier's measured values against the paste datasheet and the printer capability. A nominal design value means little once the measured geometry is marginal.

Foil thickness sets paste volume, and step features give different volumes on one stencil. Confirm that thickness sits inside the issued tolerance and that step depth, location and transition angle match the drawing.
An error in either one produces too much or too little paste even when every aperture looks correct.
Tension holds registration and board contact steady, so measure it after fabrication and periodically through service. Flatness governs contact across the print area.

Use the supplier's measurement method and the issued limit. Where the specification defines no limit, set a range from printer capability and paste process data, then verify it against your paste and equipment datasheet.

Write the cleaning method, chemistry, temperature, cycle time, rinse and drying sequence into a controlled document. Ultrasonic, spray, immersion and wipe methods differ in aggressiveness and in what residue they remove.
Verify the regime against your paste and equipment datasheet, and inspect the apertures after cleaning before the stencil returns to service.
Track each stencil by serial number and log print cycles, paste exposure, cleaning cycles, cleaning method, inspection findings, tension, thickness, aperture wear and step condition.
Retire on measured drift, repeat defects or a failed inspection, not on a fixed cycle count alone. Use the trend data to set warning and reject limits for your own process.

calc.task: Issued specification: foil thickness 0.120 mm +/-0.010 mm; aperture width 0.400 mm +/-0.025 mm; area ratio minimum 0.66 (issued spec, based on IPC-7525C guidance); wall taper minimum 85 deg; tension 25-35 N/cm; step depth 0.050 mm +/-0.010 mm. Measurement report: thickness 0.128 mm; aperture width 0.418 mm; area ratio 0.64; wall taper 87 deg; tension 28 N/cm; step depth 0.055 mm. Accept or reject and state reason.
calc.solution: Calculate foil thickness limits: 0.120 mm - 0.010 mm = 0.110 mm and 0.120 mm + 0.010 mm = 0.130 mm. Reported 0.128 mm is within 0.110-0.130 mm, so pass. Calculate aperture width limits: 0.400 mm - 0.025 mm = 0.375 mm and 0.400 mm + 0.025 mm = 0.425 mm. Reported 0.418 mm is within 0.375-0.425 mm, so pass. Compare area ratio: reported 0.64 is below the minimum 0.66, so fail. Compare wall taper: reported 87 deg is above the minimum 85 deg, so pass. Compare tension: reported 28 N/cm is within 25-35 N/cm, so pass. Calculate step depth limits: 0.050 mm - 0.010 mm = 0.040 mm and 0.050 mm + 0.010 mm = 0.060 mm. Reported 0.055 mm is within 0.040-0.060 mm, so pass. Overall result: reject or hold because area ratio fails. Request rework, replacement, or an engineering deviation only if process validation shows acceptable paste release.

defect.symptom: After a cleaning cycle, small apertures print thin or missing paste, and adjacent pads show smearing.
defect.cause: Cleaning regime left paste residue or damaged aperture walls; ultrasonic power, time, chemistry, or cleaning frequency was not qualified for the stencil and paste.
defect.action: Quarantine the stencil, inspect apertures under magnification, clean with a qualified method, re-measure area ratio and wall condition, and requalify cleaning frequency and dryness before release; if wall damage is found, retire or rework.

takeaways: Accept against the issued specification, including the measured area ratio, because dimensions in tolerance can still hide a release failure.
Record tension, flatness and step condition at acceptance and through life, since these drift before the apertures do.
Retire a stencil on measured trend, not on a cycle count someone picked before the program started.

mistakes.mistake: Passing a report that omits the area ratio
mistakes.instead: Require the characteristic on the report and hold the stencil until it is measured.

mistakes.mistake: Treating a cleaning cycle as validated because it looks clean
mistakes.instead: Inspect apertures under magnification and requalify the cycle after any chemistry or power change.

mistakes.mistake: Retiring the tip on the cycle count alone
mistakes.instead: Retire on tension, thickness and repeat-defect trend, and keep the records that show the drift.

terms.def: How accurately the aperture pattern aligns with the board pads during printing.
The stretching force on the stencil mesh or foil, expressed in N/cm, that keeps the print area flat.
The local thickness difference built into a step stencil.
The unique identifier that ties a stencil to its measurement report and lifetime history.

title: From aperture to deposit: how stencil geometry becomes paste volume

goals.text: Calculate the paste deposit volume from aperture geometry and evaluate SPI volume results against the joint requirement.

p: Aperture design decides how much paste reaches each pad and how cleanly it leaves the foil. The aperture has to be large enough to feed the joint and small enough to keep adjacent pads apart, which puts pad geometry, paste rheology, foil thickness, print speed, squeegee pressure and reflow behaviour into one balance.
For the process engineer the objective is narrower: an aperture that repeats its deposit and produces a predictable joint.

blocks.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 900 200' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='Screen printing cycle phases'><style>text{font-family:'IBM Plex Mono',monospace}</style><rect x='40' y='80' width='180' height='48' rx='10' fill='rgba(83,209,204,.06)' stroke='rgba(83,209,204,.35)' stroke-width='1.5'/><rect x='260' y='80' width='180' height='48' rx='10' fill='rgba(83,209,204,.06)' stroke='rgba(83,209,204,.35)' stroke-width='1.5'/><rect x='480' y='80' width='180' height='48' rx='10' fill='rgba(83,209,204,.06)' stroke='rgba(83,209,204,.35)' stroke-width='1.5'/><rect x='700' y='80' width='160' height='48' rx='10' fill='rgba(76,175,80,.1)' stroke='#4caf50' stroke-width='1.5'/><line x1='220' y1='104' x2='260' y2='104' stroke='#53d1cc' stroke-width='1.5'/><line x1='440' y1='104' x2='480' y2='104' stroke='#53d1cc' stroke-width='1.5'/><line x1='660' y1='104' x2='700' y2='104' stroke='#53d1cc' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='130' y='109' fill='#cbd5e1' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle'>1 FILL APERTURES</text><text x='350' y='109' fill='#cbd5e1' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle'>2 PRINT / SHEAR</text><text x='570' y='109' fill='#cbd5e1' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle'>3 SNAP-OFF</text><text x='780' y='109' fill='#4caf50' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle'>4 SPI CHECK</text><text x='130' y='150' fill='#94a3b8' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle'>paste on stencil</text><text x='350' y='150' fill='#94a3b8' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle'>squeegee + pressure</text><text x='570' y='150' fill='#94a3b8' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle'>separation speed</text><text x='780' y='150' fill='#94a3b8' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle'>volume / height / area</text><text x='40' y='30' fill='#edf2f7' font-size='14' font-weight='600'>SCREEN PRINTING CYCLE</text><text x='40' y='50' fill='#94a3b8' font-size='12'>EVERY PARAMETER YOU SET ACTS ON ONE OF THESE PHASES</text></svg>
blocks.caption: The four phases of a screen print cycle

blocks.alt: Screen printer cycle showing squeegee print, stencil snap-off gap, paste release and a deposit inspection scan
blocks.caption: Print cycle: squeegee, snap-off, paste release, then inspection of the deposit

blocks.title: Print parameters map to phases
blocks.text: Squeegee pressure and speed act on the print phase; separation speed acts on snap-off; aperture design acts on fill. When a defect appears, first decide which phase of the cycle it was born in, then change one parameter of that phase.

p: Area reduction compares aperture area with pad area. A full-area aperture matches the pad; a reduced one is smaller, and fine-pitch designs reduce area to keep paste from bridging where slump or smear is likely. Too much reduction starves the joint and leaves insufficient solder.
A common starting point is 10 % to 20 %, verified against the paste datasheet, print inspection and reflow results.

Area ratio is aperture opening area divided by sidewall area, and the sidewall is the aperture perimeter times the foil thickness. A low ratio puts more paste in contact with the wall than with the pad, and release suffers.
IPC-7525 stencil design guidelines commonly use 0.66 or higher as the target. It is a guideline, because paste type, foil finish and print settings move the real limit.

Aspect ratio is the smaller aperture dimension divided by foil thickness, which describes how narrow the hole is relative to its depth. Low aspect ratio makes release hard on small apertures, and IPC-7525 commonly targets 1.5 or higher.
Check both ratios together. An aperture can pass one target and fail the other, and the failed parameter usually names the print defect.

theory.h: Foil thickness from volume and aperture
p: Foil thickness follows from the paste volume required and the aperture area available, since approximate volume is aperture area times thickness before losses. Thicker foil adds volume and lowers both ratios, so release gets harder; thinner foil releases better from small apertures and may not feed larger joints.
Common thicknesses run about 0.08 mm to 0.15 mm for fine pitch and 0.10 mm to 0.20 mm for larger components, with the final choice verified against the paste and equipment datasheets.

Pitch class decides how much area reduction is needed and how exposed the print is to smear. In the 0.5 mm class a typical pad is around 0.30 mm square, where a small reduction controls bridging without killing release. Finer pitch means smaller apertures, thinner foil or tighter paste control; coarser pitch tolerates thicker foil and less reduction.
Check area ratio, aspect ratio, paste volume and print inspection rather than leaning on a single rule.

Geometry creates its own failure modes. Low area ratio gives incomplete release, so pads come up thin or empty; low aspect ratio leaves paste in the hole or smears it during lift-off. An aperture too large for the pitch bridges after print or in reflow, and one too small opens, weakens or tombstones the joint.
Thin foil cuts volume, and thick foil worsens release and raises smearing.

Start from the pad drawing, pick an initial area reduction from pitch and paste behaviour, select the foil thickness that can deliver the volume, then calculate both ratios. If either falls below the IPC-7525 guideline, shrink the aperture within the pad boundary or reduce the foil.
Then verify with print inspection, release testing and reflow cross-sections, and document the aperture dimensions, foil thickness, both ratios, and the paste and equipment used.

calc.task: For a 0.5 mm pitch QFP with 0.30 mm square pads, choose a 10% aperture area reduction and check area ratio and aspect ratio for 0.12 mm foil. If the area ratio is low, specify a foil thickness that meets IPC-7525 release targets while keeping paste volume practical.
calc.solution: Step one: calculate pad area. Pad area = 0.30 mm x 0.30 mm = 0.09 mm2. Step two: apply 10% area reduction. Aperture area = 0.081 mm2. Step three: for a square aperture, calculate side length. Side length = square root of 0.081 mm2 = 0.285 mm. Step four: calculate perimeter. Perimeter = four times 0.285 mm = 1.14 mm. Step five: calculate sidewall area for 0.12 mm foil. Sidewall area = 1.14 mm x 0.12 mm = 0.1368 mm2. Step six: calculate area ratio. Area ratio = 0.081 mm2 / 0.1368 mm2 = 0.592. Step seven: calculate aspect ratio. Aspect ratio = 0.285 mm / 0.12 mm = 2.38. Step eight: compare with IPC-7525 stencil design guidelines. The aspect ratio is above 1.5, but the area ratio is below 0.66, so paste release may be poor. Step nine: reduce foil thickness to 0.10 mm and recalculate. Sidewall area = 1.14 mm x 0.10 mm = 0.114 mm2. Area ratio = 0.081 mm2 / 0.114 mm2 = 0.711. Aspect ratio = 0.285 mm / 0.10 mm = 2.85. Step ten: check approximate paste volume. Paste volume = 0.081 mm2 x 0.10 mm = 0.0081 mm3. Step eleven: verify the 0.10 mm foil choice against paste datasheet, stencil manufacturer capability, print inspection, and reflow results.

defect.symptom: After printing, 0.5 mm pitch QFP pads show thin paste or missing paste on some pads, and reflow produces opens or weak joints.
defect.cause: The aperture area reduction combined with 0.12 mm foil produced an area ratio below the IPC-7525 guideline of 0.66, reducing paste release from the aperture.
defect.action: Reduce foil thickness to 0.10 mm or increase the aperture within the pad boundary while keeping the area reduction controlled. Recalculate area ratio and aspect ratio, confirm they meet IPC-7525 targets of 0.66 and 1.5, and verify with paste inspection and reflow cross-sections.

takeaways: Check area ratio and aspect ratio together before releasing a stencil, because an aperture can pass one and fail the other.
Trade foil thickness against release, since every millimetre of foil that adds volume also lowers both ratios.
Verify a new aperture with print inspection and reflow cross-sections, and record the numbers that produced the result.

mistakes.mistake: Reducing aperture area to stop bridging without recalculating the ratios
mistakes.instead: Recalculate area ratio and aspect ratio after every area change, and reduce foil if the ratio falls below 0.66.

mistakes.mistake: Choosing foil thickness from habit rather than from the joint
mistakes.instead: Derive the thickness from the volume the joint needs and the area the aperture has.

mistakes.mistake: Documenting only the aperture dimensions on the drawing
mistakes.instead: Record the foil thickness, both ratios and the paste used, or the design cannot be reproduced.

terms.def: The percentage by which the aperture area is made smaller than the pad area.
Aperture opening area divided by the sidewall area of the aperture.
The smaller aperture dimension divided by the foil thickness.
The component lead spacing band that governs aperture and foil choices.

skills: Lesson m03l06: Stencil acceptance, cleaning regime and lifetime tracking

title: Reading SPI data: measurement principle, volume/height/area/offset, artifacts

goals.text: Interpret an SPI report — volume %, height, area, offset, histograms, trend — and name the dominant defect mode with its likely cause.
Separate a real print defect from an SPI artifact and correct the inspection setup.

blocks.alt: A three-dimensional laser scan of a deposit producing a height map, with volume, height, area and offset readouts and a scan-artifact callout
blocks.caption: Reading SPI data: measurement principle, volume, height, area, offset, and the artifacts that look like defects

p: Solder paste inspection reports the deposit on each pad, usually as volume, height and area. Volume is the primary process metric because it tracks how much solder will be available after reflow. Height is the deposit thickness above the board surface, and area is the printed footprint once the paste has released and spread.

The three are related, since volume is roughly height times area, but not exactly: SPI algorithms, lighting, board surface and paste texture all move the measurement. Judge sufficiency on volume, transfer and stencil fill on height, and release, smear and bridging risk on area.

Treat SPI as a monitor of the print step, not as a final acceptance test for the assembly. When the process is new or changed, confirm the SPI-to-joint relationship with reflow, X-ray, cross-section or functional data on your own paste, stencil, board and component mix.

A defensible target starts at the stencil geometry: for a simple rectangular aperture, nominal volume is aperture area times stencil thickness. Printed volume usually comes out lower because paste does not release perfectly, and the loss follows paste rheology, wall condition, squeegee pressure, print speed, cleaning cycle and board support.

Group apertures into classes, because release changes with geometry. Small chip apertures, fine-pitch connectors, BGA pads and large thermal pads often need different windows. IPC-7525 gives the design guidance for area ratio and related behaviour, and low area ratio apertures may need modified paste, stencil or printer settings. One global volume limit across all pads ignores that the aperture classes fail for different reasons.

A process window is the range of SPI metrics that yields acceptable joints for a product and process. Control limits describe the stable variation of your printing process and come from your own data after special causes are removed. Spec limits may come from customer drawings, the IPC-A-610 acceptability requirements, or a validated product window.

Control limits are not spec limits and spec limits are not control limits. For each aperture class, set a target volume, lower and upper volume limits, and the height and area limits that support them. Verify the window against the paste datasheet, the stencil design, the SPI calibration and the reflow profile.

The same volume can be acceptable on one pad geometry and marginal on another, because wetting, component mass, pad size and thermal mass differ. Document the basis for each limit so it can be reviewed when paste, stencil, board or SPI software changes.

Common-cause spread is the repeatable variation you see when printer, paste, stencil, board and environment behave as expected: a stable band around target with no isolated outliers and no sustained shift.

Normal paste viscosity variation, slight board warp, squeegee wear inside its life, stencil tension variation and humidity changes all produce it. Common-cause spread is not automatically a defect, but a band too wide for the product means the process is not capable.

Stabilise paste temperature, paste lot handling, cleaning cycles, stencil tension, board support and squeegee condition. Then collect new data and re-establish the window. If the band stays wide, check measurement repeatability, SPI calibration and the correlation between SPI readings and reflowed joints.

Special-cause spikes are isolated readings or short runs outside the stable band, and they usually mark a process change: a single high-volume pad after a stencil wipe, a cluster of low-volume pads on one board, a step change after a paste lot change.

Confirm the reading is real before touching a limit, using the image, the measurement confidence and the pad location. Then inspect the stencil underside, the squeegee blade, the paste condition, board seating, alignment and the cleaning cycle.

A spike that repeats at one pad location points to stencil damage, pad geometry, local coplanarity or a measurement artefact rather than a global printer fault. A spike that moves randomly points to paste contamination, unstable board support or intermittent stencil contact. Record the response so the next alarm can be triaged in minutes.

theory.h: Reading height and area with volume
p: Height and area explain why volume moved. Low height with normal area suggests incomplete fill or poor release. Low height with low area suggests a clogged aperture, insufficient squeegee pressure, poor transfer or lost coplanarity. High height with normal area suggests overfill from stencil flex, excess pressure or paste that is too stiff.
High area with normal height suggests bleed, smear, stencil lift or a poor wall condition. High area with low height suggests spread without volume, which brings bridging risk without enough solder.
Read all three together, because volume alone hides compensating errors: low height with high area can land on target volume while still printing a defective pattern.

Collect SPI data from stable production, separate the aperture classes, and remove known special causes. Calculate mean and spread per class, then apply a margin that reflects measurement repeatability, paste lot variation, stencil wear and the reflow or X-ray results that define an acceptable joint.

A common starting point is a window around the validated nominal volume, with height and area limits checked against stencil thickness and aperture area. Verify the final limits against your paste and equipment datasheet and against IPC-A-610 for the product class.

Review the limits whenever stencil thickness, paste type, aperture design, SPI calibration or printer hardware changes, and keep the rationale with the process documentation so quality, manufacturing and engineering can defend the window in an audit or a customer review.

calc.task: A small chip aperture has an area of 0.080 mm^2 and the stencil thickness is 0.120 mm. The validated nominal printed volume is 0.0096 mm^3. Set volume, height, and area limits using 80% to 120% of nominal for each metric. An SPI reading shows volume 0.0072 mm^3, height 0.096 mm, and area 0.075 mm^2. Determine whether the reading passes and identify the likely metric driving the failure.
calc.solution: Step 1: Calculate nominal volume from stencil geometry. Nominal volume = aperture area x stencil thickness = 0.080 mm^2 x 0.120 mm = 0.0096 mm^3. Step 2: Set volume limits using 80% to 120% of nominal. Lower volume limit = 0.8 x 0.0096 mm^3 = 0.00768 mm^3. Upper volume limit = 1.2 x 0.0096 mm^3 = 0.01152 mm^3. Step 3: Set height limits using 80% to 120% of stencil thickness. Nominal height = 0.120 mm. Lower height limit = 0.8 x 0.120 mm = 0.096 mm. Upper height limit = 1.2 x 0.120 mm = 0.144 mm. Step 4: Set area limits using 80% to 120% of aperture area. Nominal area = 0.080 mm^2. Lower area limit = 0.8 x 0.080 mm^2 = 0.064 mm^2. Upper area limit = 1.2 x 0.080 mm^2 = 0.096 mm^2. Step 5: Compare the SPI reading to the limits. Volume = 0.0072 mm^3, which is below 0.00768 mm^3, so volume fails. Height = 0.096 mm, which is at the lower height limit. Area = 0.075 mm^2, which is within 0.064 mm^2 to 0.096 mm^2. Step 6: Interpret the result. The low volume is driven mainly by low height, not by low area. This suggests incomplete paste transfer or insufficient aperture fill rather than excessive paste spread. Check stencil underside condition, paste viscosity, squeegee pressure, cleaning cycle, board coplanarity, and SPI measurement confidence. Verify the limits against your paste and equipment datasheet before making permanent changes.

defect.symptom: SPI shows isolated high-volume spikes on fine-pitch QFP pads, with high area and normal height, occurring after the stencil wipe cycle.
defect.cause: Paste smear or stencil underside contamination from a worn squeegee blade or insufficient wipe, causing paste to spread into adjacent apertures.
defect.action: Stop the line, inspect the squeegee blade and stencil underside, clean or replace the blade, verify wipe pressure and cleaning cycle, run a verification board, and review the SPI limits for the affected aperture class against the paste and equipment datasheet.

takeaways: Judge sufficiency on volume, but diagnose with height and area, because a target volume can hide a compensating defect.
Keep control limits from your own stable data and spec limits from the drawing or IPC-A-610, and never substitute one for the other.
Confirm the reading is real before adjusting a limit: check the image, the confidence and the pad location first.

mistakes.mistake: Applying one volume window to every aperture class
mistakes.instead: Set separate windows for chip, fine-pitch, BGA and thermal pad classes, and justify each.

mistakes.mistake: Tightening the limits after a special-cause spike
mistakes.instead: Correct the cause first, then rebuild limits from data with the special cause removed.

mistakes.mistake: Reading volume without height and area
mistakes.instead: Read all three, since low height with high area can hit target volume and still print badly.

terms.def: The stable, ordinary variation of a process that is running as designed.
A variation that comes from an identifiable change rather than from ordinary process noise.
The range of print metrics that produces acceptable joints for a product.
The SPI system's own rating of how reliable a given reading is.

title: Printer setup: squeegee pressure and speed, snap-off, separation, wipe cycle

goals.text: Tune squeegee, snap-off, separation and wipe settings for a stated defect and predict the direction of each change.

blocks.alt: Side view of a printer showing the squeegee, the paste roll, the snap-off gap between stencil and board, the separation motion and the wipe cycle
blocks.caption: Printer setup: squeegee pressure and speed, snap-off, separation and wipe cycle

theory.h: Printer setup is a coupled process
p: Squeegee pressure, squeegee speed, snap-off, separation and wipe cycle are not independent knobs. Together they govern paste roll movement, aperture fill, paste release and residue management.
For a stated defect, change one variable at a time, inspect the deposit, and predict the direction of the next change from the paste and equipment datasheet.

Squeegee pressure is force per unit of blade length, never a bare force, because 100 N is a light touch on a 400 mm blade and a crushing load on a 100 mm blade. Low pressure leaves apertures underfilled, especially small ones or high aspect ratio stencils. High pressure drives paste under the stencil, wears the blade, deforms the stencil and disturbs the paste roll.

Industry guidance clusters around 0.5 to 1.5 kg per 25 mm of blade, which is 0.2 to 0.6 N/mm; work in N/mm and state the blade length with every setting, because 0.2 N/mm on a 250 mm blade is 50 N and 0.6 N/mm is 150 N. Start at the lower end and raise it until the stencil wipes clean, then verify against the paste and equipment datasheet and the printed deposit.

Speed sets how long paste has to fill the apertures and how much paste roll is dragged ahead of the blade. Too slow and the roll sits longer, inviting bleed and smearing; too fast and fill time drops, air gets trapped and transfer falls short.
A common starting range is 20 to 80 mm/s, adjusted for fine pitch, paste viscosity and stencil thickness, and verified against your paste and equipment datasheet.
Snap-off is the controlled lift-off after the print stroke. It helps paste leave the aperture walls and keeps the stencil from dragging paste across the board.

A fast snap-off pulls paste out of the apertures or leaves tails; a slow one lets paste smear as the board or stencil moves. A common lift-off speed range is 5 to 30 mm/s, confirmed against the paste and equipment datasheet.

Separation is the stencil-to-board gap at the start of the print stroke. Too small and the stencil contacts the board, bleeding paste and contaminating the roll; too large and transfer falls, the roll is pushed ahead and the stencil flexes more.
A common starting range is 0.5 to 1.5 mm, verified against your paste and equipment datasheet and the board support condition.

The wipe manages residue on the stencil underside and the condition of the paste roll. Dry, wet and vacuum wipes behave differently. Too frequent wiping strips paste from apertures, disturbs the roll or pushes solvent into the paste; too infrequent wiping lets paste dry, clog apertures and reduce release.
A common dry wipe interval is every 1 to 5 prints, checked against your paste and equipment datasheet and solvent compatibility.

theory.h: Tuning method and direction of change
p: For insufficient paste, raise pressure within its band, slow the stroke if fill time is the limit, reduce separation if the gap is too large, and wipe more often if apertures are clogging.

For bleed or bridging, lower pressure, slow down if roll drag is suspected, increase separation if the gap is too small, and adjust snap-off for clean release. Confirm the result with deposit height and volume, 2D or 3D inspection, and the applicable IPC workmanship standard.

calc.task: A 0.4 mm pitch QFP with 0.35 mm apertures shows insufficient paste. Current settings are 125 N on a 250 mm blade, 45 mm/s print speed, 12 mm/s snap-off, 1.0 mm separation, and dry wipe every 3 prints. The paste datasheet recommends 0.2 to 0.6 N/mm of blade length. Calculate the current pressure per blade length, decide whether it is in range, and state the first predicted adjustment.
calc.solution: Step 1: Calculate pressure per blade length: 125 N / 250 mm = 0.5 N/mm. Step 2: Compare with the recommended range: 0.5 N/mm is inside 0.2 to 0.6 N/mm, at the upper end, so pressure is not the limiting factor and the diagnosis moves on. Step 3: Keep the force at 125 N and note the band for this blade — 0.2 N/mm is 50 N and 0.6 N/mm is 150 N — so the setting has room in both directions if a later experiment calls for it. Step 4: Since aperture fill is the symptom and pressure is already high in its band, the first predicted adjustment is a slower print stroke: reduce speed from 45 mm/s to 30 mm/s to give the paste more time to fill 0.35 mm apertures. Step 5: Check other settings: snap-off 12 mm/s is within 5 to 30 mm/s, separation 1.0 mm is within 0.5 to 1.5 mm, and wipe every 3 prints is within 1 to 5 prints. Step 6: Verify the corrected settings against your paste/equipment datasheet and inspect deposit height and volume.

defect.symptom: Insufficient paste volume on 0.4 mm pitch QFP pads, leading to open joints after reflow.
defect.cause: Print speed is too high for the aperture fill time at 0.35 mm apertures, while squeegee pressure at 0.5 N/mm already sits in the upper half of its band, so pressure is not the first lever; separation may also be too large for stable paste transfer.
defect.action: Reduce print speed to 30 mm/s first, keep squeegee pressure inside 0.2 to 0.6 N/mm of blade length (50 to 150 N on this 250 mm blade) and move it only if the slower stroke does not close the gap, reduce separation to 1.0 mm if it is above the recommended range, and verify against your paste/equipment datasheet.

takeaways: Express squeegee pressure per blade length in N/mm, because a bare force says nothing without the blade it acts on.
Change one setting at a time and predict the direction from the defect, so the next print tells you whether the model was right.
Verify every starting range against the paste and equipment datasheet before it becomes a production setting.

mistakes.mistake: Raising squeegee pressure first for every low-volume defect
mistakes.instead: Check fill time and separation first when pressure already sits mid-band.

mistakes.mistake: Quoting pressure as a bare force
mistakes.instead: Convert to N/mm and record the blade length, or the setting cannot be transferred to another machine.

mistakes.mistake: Wiping more often to fix bleed
mistakes.instead: Excess wiping strips paste and dries the stencil edge; fix the underside contamination instead.

terms.def: The controlled separation of the board from the stencil after the print stroke.
The stencil-to-board gap set at the start of the print stroke.
The bead of paste that rolls ahead of the squeegee and feeds the apertures.
The interval and method used to clean the stencil underside between prints.

corrections.why: 0.45 kg per 25 mm is 0.18 N/mm, not 0.2 N/mm; the kilogram band is restated as the exact equivalent of the 0.2 to 0.6 N/mm band the lesson, its calculation and m04l07 all use.
0.70 kg per 25 mm is 0.27 N/mm, not 0.6 N/mm; 0.6 N/mm on 25 mm is 15 N, which is 1.5 kg.

title: Paste behaviour: viscosity, thixotropy, metal load, slump, handling and life

goals.text: Interpret an SPI report — volume %, height, area, offset, histograms, trend — and name the dominant defect mode with its likely cause.
Tune squeegee, snap-off, separation and wipe settings for a stated defect and predict the direction of each change.

blocks.alt: A viscosity versus shear-rate curve showing thixotropic hysteresis, a slump test, a metal load readout and a paste life clock
blocks.caption: Paste behaviour: viscosity, thixotropy, metal load, slump, handling and life

theory.h: What SPI measures and how to read it
p: SPI compares the printed deposit with the stencil aperture volume. Volume percent is usually measured deposit volume divided by nominal aperture volume, so 100 % means the aperture filled to stencil thickness and released without loss.

Height is the mean or maximum deposit thickness, area is the footprint of paste on the board, and offset is the centre-to-centre displacement between aperture and deposit. Histograms show the spread around the mean: a narrow one means repeatable release, a bimodal one usually means two release states, clean stencil against partially blocked apertures. Trends expose paste ageing, stencil fouling, squeegee wear and temperature drift. Judge the print against the IPC acceptance criteria for the product class.

Viscosity controls how much shear it takes to push paste through the aperture and how much it resists flowing afterwards. Thixotropy is the recovery of viscosity after shear: adequate recovery holds the deposit's shape, slow recovery lets it slump.

Metal load, the powder fraction, drives density, volume and rheology. A higher metal load can raise deposit height for the same stencil thickness, and it may also raise viscosity and hurt wetting when the flux balance does not match. Read the paste datasheet for metal load, viscosity at the relevant shear rates and recommended stencil thickness.
Slump is lateral flow after release, seen as more area and less height. It comes from low viscosity, excessive paste temperature, too much squeegee shear or a slow snap-off.

Bleed is paste sitting on the board between apertures, usually from underside contamination, insufficient wiping or paste that is too fluid. Bridging joins adjacent apertures and is likelier when paste is too stiff, the underside is dirty, or separation is too high. Read area and height together: high area with low height suggests slump, high area with normal height suggests bleed or offset.

theory.h: Handling and paste life on the stencil
p: Paste life is how long the paste stays printable after it reaches the stencil. Solvent evaporation, temperature rise and repeated rolling all raise viscosity and cut slump resistance.

Paste that prints well at the start of a shift can print low volume later if the underside dries or the paste stiffens. Keep the stencil clean, control paste temperature and check open time against the datasheet. When the SPI trend shows gradual volume loss, look at paste handling before touching the squeegee settings.
Pressure and speed control shear and fill. More pressure improves fill and can smear paste or damage the stencil; less speed improves fill and costs throughput.

Snap-off speed decides how fast the board leaves the stencil: too fast pulls paste and drops height, too slow smears. Separation is the distance the board moves before snap-off: too much stretches the paste and lowers height, too little smears. Wipe length and pressure clean the underside; too little leaves paste that bleeds, too much strips apertures or dries the stencil edge.

Typical starting points are stencil thickness 0.10-0.15 mm, squeegee speed 25-40 mm/s, squeegee pressure 5-15 N, separation 0.5-1.5 mm and wipe length 1-3 mm, all verified against your paste and equipment datasheet.

theory.h: Reading SPI for the dominant defect mode
p: Low volume percent with low height and normal area usually means incomplete fill or poor release. Low volume percent with high area suggests slump or bleed. Normal volume percent with high offset means alignment or registration. High volume percent with high area and low height can mean excessive wipe pressure or paste that is too fluid.

Histograms separate random variation from drift: a broad one points to unstable snap-off or paste rheology, a shifted mean points to a setting or the paste condition. Typical handling is 20-30 °C and 40-60 % RH with open time often 4-8 h, verified against the paste and equipment datasheet.

theory.h: Tuning direction for a stated defect
p: Low volume and low height with a clean SPI area call for slightly more squeegee pressure, less squeegee speed, slower snap-off, less separation, and less wipe pressure or length if either is excessive.

Low volume with high area calls for less squeegee pressure, less speed, faster snap-off and less separation. Bleed at normal volume calls for a longer or harder wipe and a clean stencil. Bridging calls for less separation, a more effective wipe and a viscosity check. Change one setting at a time and verify against the datasheet.

calc.task: An SPI report for a 0.40 mm x 0.40 mm aperture in a 0.12 mm stencil shows mean height 0.085 mm, mean area 0.145 mm^2, volume 62%, offset 0.02 mm, a broad histogram, and a downward volume trend over 4 h. Calculate the measured volume and nominal aperture volume, then name the dominant defect mode and likely cause.
calc.solution: Nominal aperture area = 0.40 mm x 0.40 mm = 0.16 mm^2. Nominal aperture volume = 0.16 mm^2 x 0.12 mm = 0.0192 mm^3. Measured deposit volume = 0.145 mm^2 x 0.085 mm = 0.012325 mm^3. Volume percent = 0.012325 mm^3 / 0.0192 mm^3 x 100% = 64.2%, close to the reported 62% within measurement rounding. Height is below stencil thickness and area is below nominal area, so the dominant defect mode is incomplete aperture fill and poor paste release, not slump. The broad histogram and downward trend suggest paste stiffening on the stencil or squeegee pressure/speed drifting away from the fill window. Likely cause: paste viscosity/thixotropy drift combined with insufficient squeegee pressure or too high squeegee speed. Predicted tuning: increase squeegee pressure slightly, reduce squeegee speed, reduce snap-off speed, reduce separation, reduce wipe pressure or length if excessive, and verify paste temperature and stencil cleanliness.

defect.symptom: SPI shows volume percent falling from 95% to 70% over 4 h, mean height dropping from 0.11 mm to 0.08 mm, area near nominal, offset below 0.02 mm, and a histogram shifting left without an additional peak.
defect.cause: Paste on the stencil has aged and increased in viscosity, while squeegee pressure and speed remained fixed, so apertures are not fully filled and release becomes incomplete.
defect.action: Reduce squeegee speed, increase squeegee pressure slightly, reduce snap-off speed, reduce separation, reduce wipe pressure or length if excessive, clean the stencil underside, and verify paste temperature and open time against the paste datasheet. Re-run SPI after each change.

takeaways: Read volume percent with height and area, because the same volume percentage means different defects at different heights.
Treat a broad histogram and a drifting mean as two different messages: instability against a real change.
Check paste age, temperature and open time before changing printer settings when volume falls slowly over a shift.

mistakes.mistake: Chasing a falling volume trend with squeegee pressure
mistakes.instead: Check paste temperature, open time and stencil cleanliness first.

mistakes.mistake: Reading the paste volume percent alone
mistakes.instead: Confirm height and area, since slump and incomplete fill both lower volume but need opposite responses.

mistakes.mistake: Changing several settings in one trial
mistakes.instead: Change one variable per trial, or the result tells you nothing about which setting mattered.

terms.def: Measured deposit volume divided by nominal aperture volume, expressed as a percentage.
The recovery of paste viscosity after shear, which lets a printed deposit hold its shape.
Lateral flow of the deposit after release, showing as larger area and lower height.
The percentage of metal powder by weight in the solder paste.

title: SPI as process evidence: mean, spread, capability, stop/adjust decisions

goals.text: Interpret an SPI report — volume %, height, area, offset, histograms, trend — and name the dominant defect mode with its likely cause.

blocks.alt: A control chart of deposit volume showing the mean, the spread and the limits, with a decision flow for stop, adjust and continue
blocks.caption: SPI as process evidence: mean, spread, capability, and the stop / adjust decision

theory.h: What SPI evidence means on the print stage
p: Solder paste inspection is process evidence for the print step, not final joint acceptance. It reports what the stencil deposited before reflow: volume, height, area, offset, histogram shape and trend over time.

Use it to confirm the print process is stable and centred, and to name the dominant defect mode before boards move downstream. A good SPI result does not guarantee good soldering; a poor or drifting one is a strong early signal that the print step needs attention.

Volume is the most useful single metric because it combines area and height. Low volume with normal height points to reduced paste area: incomplete aperture fill, partial clogging, a weak squeegee roll, or paste that does not release cleanly.

Low volume with normal area points to reduced height: collapse, excessive wipe, low viscosity, or insufficient transfer. High volume at normal height points to area expansion, bleed or underside contamination.

Area says whether the footprint matches the aperture. Low area points to incomplete fill, paste dry-out, clogging or poor snap-off. High area points to bleed, underside paste, excessive pressure, or a separation fast enough to smear the deposit.

Offset is positional error. A consistent direction suggests alignment, vision, conveyor, stencil tension or board support. A random one suggests board handling, fiducial quality, camera focus or unstable seating.
A histogram counts how many prints fall at each value. A narrow peak near target is what you want.

A wide distribution means an inconsistent process, often from unstable paste temperature, cleaning variation, squeegee wear or board-to-board support differences. A low-skewed histogram suggests paste depletion, aperture clogging, insufficient pressure or paste too viscous. A high-skewed one suggests overfill, bleed or underside paste. A bimodal shape means two populations are being mixed: two stencil zones, two board types, two squeegee passes or two SPI calibration regions.

Trend charts beat isolated measurements. A step change means something changed suddenly: paste lot, stencil, squeegee blade, tension adjustment, SPI calibration or a maintenance action. A gradual drift means something is changing slowly: viscosity, ambient temperature, stencil wear, cleaning effectiveness or blade wear.
Establish whether the trend is stable, drifting or stepped before adjusting anything, because adjusting an unstable process hides the real cause.

Capability compares the process spread with the specification limits. Cp describes spread alone — whether the process could fit inside the limits if centred. Cpk adds centring — whether it actually is centred enough to meet them.

For paste printing, use the control plan limits for the product and paste system, not only the SPI machine tolerance. Capability means something only while the process is stable: with a step, a drift or repeated out-of-limit points, correct the process first, then recalculate.

A stable, centred, capable process against the control plan continues and gets monitored. A stable but off-centre process is adjusted through the levers that move transfer: paste temperature, squeegee pressure, squeegee speed, snap-off speed, cleaning frequency and underside wipe.

An unstable process stops for investigation before any small parameter change. Repeated out-of-limit prints, a systematic offset, or capability that will not come back after a controlled adjustment stops the line, quarantines suspect boards, and gets verified against SPI maps, stencil inspection and cross-section or pull-back evidence.

calc.task: A SPI report for a fine-pitch QFN paste print shows target paste volume = 100%, measured mean = 92%, standard deviation = 6%, lower specification limit = 85%, and upper specification limit = 115%. The histogram is skewed low, offset is within tolerance, and the trend is stable. Calculate Cp and Cpk, identify the dominant defect mode, and decide whether to adjust or stop.
calc.solution: First, confirm that the process is stable. The trend is stable, so capability can be evaluated. Second, calculate the process spread. For a normal capability calculation, the spread is six standard deviations: 6 x 6 = 36 percentage points. Third, calculate Cp using the specification width divided by the process spread: Cp = (115 - 85) / 36 = 30 / 36 = 0.83. This means the process spread is too wide for the specification window. Fourth, calculate Cpk by checking the distance from the mean to each specification limit and dividing by three standard deviations. Three standard deviations = 3 x 6 = 18 percentage points. Upper side: (115 - 92) / 18 = 23 / 18 = 1.28. Lower side: (92 - 85) / 18 = 7 / 18 = 0.39. Cpk is the smaller value, so Cpk = 0.39. Fifth, interpret the result. The low Cpk is dominated by the lower side, meaning the process is centered too low. The low Cp also shows the spread is too wide. The dominant defect mode is low paste volume, likely from incomplete aperture fill, paste depletion, insufficient squeegee pressure, poor snap-off, or paste rheology that is not transferring well. Sixth, decide the action. Because the trend is stable and the defect mode is clear, adjust first: verify paste temperature and viscosity, inspect stencil apertures and underside, review squeegee pressure and speed, review snap-off speed, and review stencil cleaning frequency. Run verification prints and recalculate capability. If out-of-limit prints persist, if the histogram remains low-skewed, or if capability remains below the control plan limit, stop the line and quarantine suspect boards.

defect.symptom: SPI shows low paste volume concentrated on one side of the board, with normal height and reduced area. The trend shows a step change after a stencil change.
defect.cause: Stencil alignment or tension is causing incomplete aperture fill on that side, possibly combined with a squeegee pressure gradient across the board.
defect.action: Stop the line, verify stencil tension and alignment, inspect aperture fill using SPI area and height maps, adjust squeegee pressure and speed according to the paste and stencil datasheet, run verification prints, and quarantine boards printed after the step change until the cause is confirmed.

takeaways: Judge capability only on a stable process, because Cp and Cpk on a drifting trend describe a process that no longer exists.
Read volume with height and area before naming a defect, since volume alone confuses under-fill with spreading.
Distinguish a step change from a gradual drift, because the first points to an event and the second to wear.

mistakes.mistake: Recalculating capability after every process adjustment
mistakes.instead: Establish stability on a control chart first, then compute capability from that data.

mistakes.mistake: Adjusting print parameters during a drift before checking paste age
mistakes.instead: Check paste temperature, open time and stencil cleanliness first, then touch the machine.

mistakes.mistake: Reading a bimodal histogram as random variation
mistakes.instead: Find the two populations — panel side, stencil zone, board type — before changing limits.

terms.def: The specification width divided by six standard deviations, a measure of spread alone.
The distance from the mean to the nearer specification limit in standard deviations, a measure of spread and centring.
A distribution with two peaks, showing that two different populations are being measured together.
An abrupt shift in a trend chart caused by a single event in the process.

Lesson m04l02: Reading SPI data: measurement principle, volume/height/area/offset, artifacts

title: Print defect atlas: under-fill, excess, bridging, skew, smearing, slumping

goals.text: Interpret an SPI report — volume %, height, area, offset, histograms, trend — and name the dominant defect mode with its likely cause.

blocks.alt: Six small deposit cross-sections labelled with each print defect, shown beside a correct deposit for comparison
blocks.caption: Print defect atlas: under-fill, excess, bridging, skew, smearing and slumping

theory.h: What an SPI report is trying to answer
p: A solder paste inspection report is a measurement, not only a screen. It shows how much paste was deposited, where, and how consistently: volume percentage against nominal, paste height, paste area, placement offset, histograms, and trend over time.

The engineer reads those metrics to infer the dominant print defect and trace it to a process cause. Take the acceptability limits from the product specification and the relevant IPC-A-610 class, then check them against the paste, stencil and printer datasheets.

theory.h: Volume percentage as the first clue
p: Volume percentage compares measured paste volume with the nominal volume expected from aperture area, stencil thickness and paste density. Low volume usually means under-fill, incomplete transfer or paste lost during release. High volume means excess paste, overfilling or accumulation from poor cleaning.
Volume alone misleads, because a pad can carry the right volume in the wrong shape, height or place. Read it with height, area and offset.

theory.h: Height and area separate under-fill from spreading
p: Low height with low area supports under-fill or incomplete transfer. Low height with high area suggests smearing or slumping, where paste spread sideways and lost height. High height with high area points to excess paste and bridging risk, and high height with low area to poor release, paste buildup or a local stencil problem.
Process windows vary with paste and stencil design, so check them against your own paste datasheet and design rules.
Offset measures how far the paste centroid sits from the pad centre. Skew is a pattern of consistent directional displacement across pads, components or panel locations.

A random offset pattern points to board support, conveyor handling or vision instability. A consistent direction points to stencil alignment, board seating, support pin interference or a systematic vision offset. Where offset is small but area and height are normal, the dominant issue is registration rather than deposition.
A histogram counts measurements in each range of volume, height, area or offset. Narrow and near target means stable printing.

A broad histogram means instability: viscosity drift, cleaning variation, inconsistent squeegee pressure. Shifted low means under-fill or incomplete transfer; shifted high means excess paste or accumulation. A bimodal shape means two populations are being measured together, such as one panel side printing differently from the other, or one stencil area behaving differently.

theory.h: Trend data: stable defect or drift
p: Trends distinguish stable, drifting, stepping and oscillating behaviour. A stable low-volume trend suggests a design or setup issue — aperture size, stencil thickness, paste rheology. A gradual drift toward low volume suggests paste drying, stencil clogging or degrading cleaning. A step change follows an event such as a paste lot, stencil, squeegee or program change. Oscillation points to cleaning frequency, board support variation or conveyor handling.
Trend data decides whether you face a fixed defect mode or a process drift, and the two need different responses.

The dominant mode is the one that explains the combined pattern. Under-fill shows low volume, low height and low area. Excess shows high volume, high height and high area. Bridging shows high volume or area between adjacent pads, especially at fine pitch. Skew shows normal volume and shape with a consistent offset. Smearing shows low height with an elongated or irregular area, and slumping shows low height with a widened area and poor edge definition.
The likely cause then follows from whether the pattern is uniform, localised, directional, drifting or step-like.

calc.task: A SPI report for a fine-pitch QFP area shows mean volume at 82% of nominal, mean height at 0.11 mm versus nominal 0.12 mm, mean area at 95% of nominal, mean offset at 0.04 mm, a histogram shifted low with a long tail toward low volume, and a trend that has drifted downward over the last several boards. Identify the dominant defect mode and the most likely cause.
calc.solution: Step 1: Check volume percentage. The mean volume is 82% of nominal, which is below target and suggests insufficient paste transfer. Step 2: Check height. The mean height is 0.11 mm versus nominal 0.12 mm, confirming that the paste is thinner than intended. Step 3: Check area. The mean area is 95% of nominal, which is close to target and argues against major smearing or slumping. Step 4: Check offset. The mean offset is 0.04 mm, which is small and does not explain the low volume. Step 5: Check histogram. The histogram is shifted low with a tail toward low volume, indicating a population of pads receiving too little paste. Step 6: Check trend. The downward drift suggests a process change over time rather than a fixed design error. Step 7: Combine the evidence. Low volume, low height, near-normal area, small offset, low-shifted histogram, and downward trend point to under-fill as the dominant defect mode. Step 8: Infer likely cause. A gradual downward drift with under-fill is commonly associated with paste viscosity increase, stencil clogging, reduced transfer efficiency, or insufficient cleaning. Verify against paste datasheet, stencil condition, cleaning frequency, and printer settings.

defect.symptom: SPI shows high volume and high area between adjacent QFP leads, with a histogram shifted high and a trend that worsens after cleaning intervals are extended.
defect.cause: Excess paste remains on the stencil surface or between apertures because cleaning is not removing paste residue effectively, allowing paste to accumulate and bridge adjacent pads during print.
defect.action: Increase cleaning frequency, verify cleaning solvent condition and wipe quality, inspect stencil underside for residue, and confirm paste release behavior against the paste datasheet. Re-run SPI after adjustment and monitor the high-volume trend.

takeaways: Read the whole report before naming a defect, because volume, height, area and offset each rule alternative causes in or out.
Use the histogram to see whether one population or two are printing, and split by panel side or stencil zone when it is bimodal.
Separate a stable defect from a drift in the trend, since a design fix does not cure a degrading stencil.

mistakes.mistake: Diagnosing smearing from a low volume percentage alone
mistakes.instead: Confirm height and area, since smearing shows low height with widened area rather than low area.

mistakes.mistake: Ignoring offset because volume is acceptable
mistakes.instead: Check the offset trend, because registration drift produces defects the volume screen cannot see.

mistakes.mistake: Treating an oscillating trend as random
mistakes.instead: Look for cleaning frequency and board support variation before changing print parameters.

terms.def: Measured deposit volume as a percentage of the nominal aperture volume.
A consistent directional displacement of deposits across pads or panel locations.
A deposit that is short in volume, height and area because the aperture did not fill or release.
Lateral flow of the deposit after release, producing a wider, flatter print.

title: Print troubleshooting logic and one-variable-at-a-time experiments

goals.text: Tune squeegee, snap-off, separation and wipe settings for a stated defect and predict the direction of each change.
Separate a real print defect from an SPI artifact and correct the inspection setup.

blocks.alt: A troubleshooting flow that first rules out inspection artifacts, then changes one print parameter at a time while recording the others
blocks.caption: Print troubleshooting logic and one-variable-at-a-time experiments

p: Confirm the defect repeats and is not an SPI artefact first. Record the component, panel location, stencil age, paste lot, squeegee pressure, speed, snap-off distance and speed, wipe frequency and SPI threshold.

A defect that exists only in the SPI report gets verified by manual inspection, paste weight or cross-section before anyone touches the printer. Change one setting at a time so the response can be attributed to it.

Pressure pushes paste into the apertures and keeps the underside clean. Low pressure leaves paste in the aperture, so volume drops or deposits vanish; high pressure smears paste, bleeds it and wears the stencil faster.

Set pressure per unit of blade length, around 0.2 to 0.6 N/mm (0.5 to 1.5 kg per 25 mm), which is 50 to 150 N on a 250 mm blade. A bare force figure cannot be checked without the blade length, and a 5 to 15 N setting would be far too light for any production blade. Verify against your paste and equipment datasheet.
Speed controls shear thinning and fill time, typically 10 mm/s to 50 mm/s. Higher speed fills small apertures less; lower speed fills better and may bleed more.

Snap-off distance sets how far the stencil separates from the board after printing. Too little and the stencil drags paste, smears apertures or holds paste, giving low volume and tails. More distance often improves release from small apertures, and too much stretches the paste, makes tails and costs registration.
Typical distances are 0.5 mm to 2.0 mm, confirmed against the stencil and equipment datasheet. A faster snap-off can improve release; a slower one reduces stringing.
Wiping clears the stencil underside. Infrequent wiping leaves paste that smears, bridges and creates false SPI shorts. Excessive wiping dries paste, clogs apertures and cuts transfer volume.

Typical frequency is every 1 to 5 prints, checked against paste open time and the equipment datasheet. Wipe more often when underside paste causes smears, less often when paste drying or clogging appears.

Print quality follows aperture area ratio, sidewall finish, stencil thickness, paste viscosity and thixotropy. Small apertures with a low area ratio or rough sidewalls release poorly however sensible the printer settings are.

When a single-variable experiment produces no response, evaluate the stencil design or paste rheology instead of stacking printer changes. Keep the stencil clean and inspect for residue, damaged apertures and wear.

theory.h: Separating SPI artefacts from real defects
p: SPI can report missing paste, low volume or shorts from threshold settings, lighting, focus, fiducial errors, board warp, paste colour, solder mask variation or stencil residue.

Confirm a real defect by manual inspection, paste weight, cross-section, repeatability across panels and downstream assembly results. Fix the inspection setup by cleaning the stencil, recalibrating the SPI, adjusting threshold and lighting, refocusing, re-teaching fiducials and using a known good board. When the artefact disappears after that correction, leave the printer alone.
Define the defect, the baseline settings and the acceptance metric before testing. Hold a stable paste lot, a clean stencil and consistent board condition.

Run enough boards to see the effect, for example 10 boards and 30 measured deposits per condition, and record volume, height, area and any visual tails or smears. Change only the selected setting, run the same measurement set, and compare. Lock the change when it improves the metric without new defects; otherwise revert and test the next setting separately.

calc.task: A 0402 resistor print shows low paste volume on SPI. The stencil thickness is 0.10 mm and the aperture is 1.0 mm x 0.5 mm. Baseline SPI average volume is 0.035 mm^3. The target is 0.045 mm^3. Baseline settings are squeegee pressure 100 N on the 250 mm blade (0.4 N/mm), squeegee speed 25 mm/s, snap-off distance 1.5 mm, and wipe every 3 prints. Design a single-variable experiment using snap-off distance.
calc.solution: Calculate aperture area: 1.0 mm x 0.5 mm = 0.50 mm^2. Calculate theoretical stencil volume: 0.50 mm^2 x 0.10 mm = 0.050 mm^3. Calculate current fill factor: 0.035 mm^3 / 0.050 mm^3 = 0.70, or 70%. Calculate target fill factor: 0.045 mm^3 / 0.050 mm^3 = 0.90, or 90%. Keep pressure, speed, and wipe frequency unchanged. Change only snap-off distance from 1.5 mm to 2.0 mm. Run 10 boards and measure 30 deposits. Record mean volume, height, area, and tails. If mean volume reaches 0.043 mm^3 to 0.047 mm^3 with no tails or smearing, accept the change. If tails appear, reduce snap-off distance to 1.75 mm and repeat. If volume does not change, revert to 1.5 mm and test a single next variable, such as reducing squeegee speed to 20 mm/s or raising pressure by 0.1 N/mm (25 N on this blade), recording each result separately.

defect.symptom: SPI reports low paste volume on 0402 deposits on the left panel side. Manual inspection shows short deposits and paste residue in the stencil apertures.
defect.cause: Snap-off distance is too low for the small apertures, so paste release is incomplete. The wipe frequency is not the primary cause because underside smearing is not dominant.
defect.action: Increase snap-off distance from 1.5 mm to 2.0 mm while holding pressure, speed, and wipe frequency constant. Run 10 boards, measure 30 deposits, and verify volume, tails, and smearing. If tails appear, reduce snap-off distance to 1.75 mm. If volume remains low, test squeegee speed separately.

takeaways: Verify a defect exists before tuning, because an SPI threshold or lighting error sends you adjusting a printer that is already correct.
Design the experiment before the trial: defect, baseline, metric, sample size and the one setting you will change.
Revert a change that fails and test the next variable alone, so each result belongs to one cause.

mistakes.mistake: Changing pressure, speed and snap-off distance in one trial
mistakes.instead: Change one variable per trial, or the result cannot be attributed.

mistakes.mistake: Setting squeegee pressure as a bare force in newtons
mistakes.instead: State N/mm with the blade length, so the setting transfers to another machine.

mistakes.mistake: Tuning the printer against an unrepeated SPI reading
mistakes.instead: Confirm repeatability by manual inspection or paste weight first.

terms.def: The gap the board and stencil reach during separation after the print stroke.
Measured deposit volume divided by the theoretical aperture volume.
A trial that changes one process setting and holds every other condition constant.
A reading caused by the inspection setup rather than by the printed deposit.
