title: Machine types and what accuracy, repeatability and throughput really mean

goals.text: Select nozzle, pick height and placement force for a component within its mechanical limits.
Verify a placement program and setup before production and identify a missing or expired calibration.

p: Placement moves components from feeders, trays or rails onto the board and fixes their starting position before reflow or insertion. Accuracy is how close the commanded position is to the true board location, repeatability is how tightly repeated placements cluster, and throughput is the rate of valid placements.
The three interact. Faster motion, weak vacuum, worn feeders or an unverified program all turn a repeatable machine into a systematic defect source.

blocks.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 900 200' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='Pick and place cycle'><style>text{font-family:'IBM Plex Mono',monospace}</style><rect x='40' y='80' width='170' height='48' rx='10' fill='rgba(83,209,204,.06)' stroke='rgba(83,209,204,.35)' stroke-width='1.5'/><rect x='250' y='80' width='170' height='48' rx='10' fill='rgba(83,209,204,.06)' stroke='rgba(83,209,204,.35)' stroke-width='1.5'/><rect x='460' y='80' width='170' height='48' rx='10' fill='rgba(83,209,204,.06)' stroke='rgba(83,209,204,.35)' stroke-width='1.5'/><rect x='670' y='80' width='190' height='48' rx='10' fill='rgba(83,209,204,.06)' stroke='rgba(83,209,204,.35)' stroke-width='1.5'/><line x1='210' y1='104' x2='250' y2='104' stroke='#53d1cc' stroke-width='1.5'/><line x1='420' y1='104' x2='460' y2='104' stroke='#53d1cc' stroke-width='1.5'/><line x1='630' y1='104' x2='670' y2='104' stroke='#53d1cc' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='125' y='109' fill='#cbd5e1' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle'>PICK FROM FEEDER</text><text x='335' y='109' fill='#cbd5e1' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle'>VISION / CHECK</text><text x='545' y='109' fill='#cbd5e1' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle'>ALIGN</text><text x='765' y='109' fill='#cbd5e1' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle'>PLACE + FORCE</text><text x='125' y='150' fill='#94a3b8' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle'>nozzle, vacuum</text><text x='335' y='150' fill='#94a3b8' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle'>missing / tilt / size</text><text x='545' y='150' fill='#94a3b8' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle'>theta correction</text><text x='765' y='150' fill='#94a3b8' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle'>placement accuracy</text><text x='40' y='30' fill='#edf2f7' font-size='14' font-weight='600'>PLACEMENT CYCLE</text><text x='40' y='50' fill='#94a3b8' font-size='12'>DEFECTS ARE BORN IN ONE OF THESE FOUR MOMENTS</text></svg>
blocks.caption: Pick-and-place cycle and where its defects originate

blocks.alt: Pick-and-place machine with gantry, placement head and nozzles, feeder bank, fiducial marks on a board and an axes travel diagram
blocks.caption: Pick-and-place machine overview: placement accuracy and repeatability, feeder bank, fiducials, axes travel

p: Pick a nozzle that reaches the component without touching adjacent parts, feeder walls or the board. For SMT, match the tip diameter to the component top area and mass; for THT, match the gripper or insertion nozzle to the lead diameter and body clearance.
Check nozzle ID, vacuum port size, tip length and clearance against the component drawing, the feeder datasheet and the machine nozzle map.

Pick height is the nozzle Z position where it contacts the component. Too high and the pick is missed or the feeder wears; too low and the component is pushed into its pocket, the tape distorts, or a brittle part cracks.
Set the initial value from component height, feeder pocket depth, tape thickness and nozzle tip length, then confirm it with a dry run and microscope inspection.

Placement force has to seat the component in paste, or hold a THT lead, without crushing the part, displacing paste or bending leads. On SMT it is usually a small controlled value above component weight and paste resistance; on THT it follows lead diameter, hole size, plating and insertion speed.
Verify the value against the component maximum force, the nozzle contact area and the machine's force capability.

A machine can be repeatable and still inaccurate when axes, vision or nozzle offsets are uncalibrated. Calibration and compensation fix accuracy; stable feeders, clean nozzles and a steady air supply protect repeatability.
Throughput counts only while the first-article placement stays inside the process window, because speed that adds mispicks or misalignment buys rework and scrap.
Before production, verify the BOM, component library, nozzle map, feeder setup, pick and place coordinates, rotation, skip logic, vision settings, stencil alignment and panel support.

Run a low-speed dry cycle or first article, inspect the first board, and compare measured placement offsets with the program. Record the result so a later defect can be traced to setup, program or machine condition.
Confirm that machine axes, the vision system, the nozzle changer, feeder alignment and any force or torque sensor hold current calibration under the equipment OEM and the plant quality system.

A missing or expired certificate produces consistent offsets, rotation errors, mispicks or force drift. If the certificate is absent, expired or outside its scope, stop the setup and escalate before production.

calc.task: A chip resistor has a body of 1.0 mm x 0.5 mm x 0.35 mm and a mass of 0.001 g. The component datasheet gives a maximum placement force of 0.30 N. The feeder pocket depth is 0.20 mm, and the component top is therefore 0.15 mm below the feeder top datum. Available nozzles are 0.20 mm, 0.30 mm, and 0.40 mm diameter. The machine vacuum can provide 40 kPa at the nozzle tip. Select a nozzle, set an initial pick height, and choose a placement force that stays within the mechanical limits.
calc.solution: Component top area = 1.0 mm x 0.5 mm = 0.50 mm^2. The 0.40 mm nozzle is too large for the 0.50 mm width because it leaves little clearance; the 0.20 mm nozzle may be acceptable but gives less vacuum area. Select the 0.30 mm nozzle. Its tip area = pi x (0.30 mm / 2)^2 = 0.0707 mm^2 = 0.0707 x 10^-6 m^2. Vacuum force = pressure x area = 40000 Pa x 0.0707 x 10^-6 m^2 = 0.00283 N. Component weight = 0.001 g = 1 x 10^-6 kg; weight = 1 x 10^-6 kg x 9.81 m/s^2 = 9.81 x 10^-6 N. The vacuum force is much larger than the weight, so the pick can be stable if the nozzle seals cleanly. Pick height: component top is 0.15 mm below the feeder top datum. Set the initial contact point at -0.15 mm relative to the feeder top datum, then verify with a dry run. Placement force: use a verified range such as 0.05-0.15 N for small chip components, then confirm against the paste and equipment datasheet. Choose 0.10 N. This is below the 0.30 N component limit and above the weight, so it can seat the part without excessive force. Check nozzle contact pressure = 0.10 N / 0.0707 x 10^-6 m^2 = 1.41 MPa. Verify this against the component and nozzle datasheet; if the component limit is lower, reduce the force or use a larger nozzle only if clearance allows. Before production, verify the nozzle map, feeder setup, pick height, placement force, and calibration certificate. If the certificate is missing or expired, stop and recalibrate.

defect.symptom: A first-article board shows chip components with a consistent offset toward one edge, and some small parts are tombstoned after the feeder was changed.
defect.cause: The placement program used an old nozzle offset or feeder calibration, and the machine calibration certificate was missing or expired, so the commanded coordinates did not match the true machine position.
defect.action: Stop the setup, verify the calibration certificate and scope, recalibrate the affected axes and nozzle changer, reload the correct nozzle map and feeder setup, run a low-speed dry cycle, inspect the first article, and release for production only after measured offsets are within the verified process window.

takeaways: Set pick height from the component, pocket and nozzle geometry, then confirm it on a dry run rather than trusting the program.
Keep placement force above the seating need and below the component's stated maximum, and verify the nozzle contact area behind that number.
Check calibration scope before the setup, because an expired certificate explains offsets that no programming change will fix.

mistakes.mistake: Choosing a nozzle that fits the component body but not its clearances
mistakes.instead: Check adjacent parts, feeder walls and board clearance, not just the tip diameter.

mistakes.mistake: Correcting an offset with program coordinates when calibration has expired
mistakes.instead: Verify and renew calibration first, then measure the offset again.

mistakes.mistake: Running at full speed straight from a new program
mistakes.instead: Prove the first article at low speed and compare measured offsets before releasing production.

terms.def: How close the commanded placement position is to the true board location.
How tightly repeated placements cluster around their own mean.
The nozzle Z position at which it contacts the component in the feeder or tray.
The machine table that pairs each component with its nozzle and vacuum setting.

title: Feeders, nozzles, pick height and placement force limits by component

goals.text: Select nozzle, pick height and placement force for a component within its mechanical limits.

blocks.alt: A placement head with interchangeable nozzles, a feeder bank, and a pick-height measurement with a placement force gauge
blocks.caption: Feeders, nozzles, pick height and placement force limits by component

theory.h: Why nozzle, pick height and force control matter
p: On SMT and THT placement, the nozzle, the pick height and the placement force decide whether a component is picked cleanly, placed accurately and seated without mechanical damage.

The nozzle must match component geometry and mass. Pick height sets the vertical distance between nozzle tip and component or board surface. Placement force controls how firmly the part is pressed into paste, a socket, a hole or a seating surface. The three are interdependent: an undersized nozzle slips or crushes a corner, and excessive force cracks ceramic bodies, deforms leads or squeezes paste where it does not belong.

Start from the component supplier's mechanical limits and the machine's nozzle and force capability, then tune inside a narrow window while checking first-article samples and in-process inspection data.

Base nozzle choice on the component top surface, mass, height and tolerance. Chip resistors, capacitors and inductors usually take a vacuum nozzle with a flat or slightly rounded tip that contacts the top surface without covering the terminals.

Larger or heavier parts may need more contact area or a mechanical gripper to stop tipping and slipping. Packages with exposed metal lids, such as some power devices, benefit from a compliant tip or a bigger vacuum area that spreads the point load. THT leads, sockets and connectors may need grippers, push-down tools or guide pins instead of vacuum.
Check nozzle dimensions, vacuum flow and tip material against the placement machine datasheet and the component drawing.

Pick height is the vertical position where the nozzle meets the component in the feeder or tray. Too high and the vacuum fails to seal, so the part is missed or picked at an angle. Too low and the nozzle pushes the component into its pocket, damages the feeder or strikes the carrier.

On tape and reel, set pick height so the nozzle just touches the component top with enough travel to establish vacuum without compressing it. On trays, allow for tray thickness, pocket depth and component height variation. A practical starting point is contact plus a small overtravel, often 0.05 mm to 0.20 mm, verified against the machine manual and the feeder supplier's guidance.

Force must be enough to seat the component and establish paste contact, and low enough to protect component and board. Small passives need little force, because their mass and the paste viscosity do the seating; larger parts may need more to overcome lead springback, connector retention or paste resistance.

Ceramic capacitors, brittle packages and thin leads are damaged by point loads and excess force. The component datasheet should state a maximum placement force or allowable mechanical load; where it does not, use a conservative value and validate it by destructive or non-destructive inspection. Many small SMT components start in the 0.1 N to 1.0 N range, verified against the supplier and the machine.

Failure modes differ by component. Small ceramic capacitors crack under point loading, especially with a worn or misaligned tip. Large MLCCs are sensitive to bending stress during placement and reflow, so force and support area both matter.

Connectors and sockets need enough force to clear retention features and not enough to bend terminals or damage housings. THT parts need insertion force without bending leads, damaging plating or cracking the board. Exposed die, glass or brittle packages forbid narrow nozzles and high point loads, and compliant leads take enough force to seat without flattening them past the supplier's limit.
Nozzle condition is a major defect source. A worn, chipped or contaminated nozzle loses vacuum seal, shifts the pick centre or loads the component unevenly.

Check nozzle alignment on the machine maintenance schedule and inspect tips for wear, residue and diameter change. Trend vacuum pressure and, where available, force feedback to catch drift. On high-reliability products, track nozzle life and replace on measured wear or a validated cycle count, using the machine manual and the nozzle supplier's recommendations.

Validate the nozzle, pick height and force with a controlled trial. Start from the component supplier's limits, run a small sample set, and inspect for missed picks, tilted components, tombstoning, paste squeeze-out, lead deformation and component damage.

On critical parts, add cross-sectioning or dye-and-pry to expose hidden cracks. Record nozzle number, pick height, force, vacuum level and any alarms, then lock the recipe and control changes through change management. If the process drifts, check nozzle wear, feeder alignment, tape peel force and board support before touching placement force.

calc.task: Select a nozzle, pick height, and placement force for a 0402 MLCC with a maximum supplier placement force of 0.5 N, a component height of 0.5 mm, and a tape pocket depth of 0.8 mm. The placement machine has a nozzle with a 0.25 mm tip diameter and a force control range of 0.05 N to 2.0 N. Determine a reasonable starting setup and the checks needed before production.
calc.solution: 1. Confirm the component limit: the supplier states a maximum placement force of 0.5 N, so the machine force must be set below this value with margin. 2. Select the nozzle: a 0.25 mm tip is small enough for an 0402 body but should be checked for vacuum coverage and tip wear; verify against the machine nozzle chart. 3. Set pick height: with a component height of 0.5 mm and pocket depth of 0.8 mm, the nozzle should contact the top surface with a small overtravel, for example 0.05 mm to 0.10 mm, then verify that the feeder does not deform and the component does not tilt. 4. Set placement force: start at 0.15 N to 0.25 N, which is below the 0.5 N limit and above the machine minimum of 0.05 N. 5. Run a trial: inspect for missed picks, tilted components, tombstoning, paste squeeze-out, and nozzle marks. 6. If paste contact is insufficient, increase force in small steps, for example 0.05 N increments, while staying below 0.5 N. 7. If cracks or nozzle marks appear, reduce force, check nozzle alignment, and consider a softer or larger contact area if the machine and component geometry allow. 8. Lock the recipe after first-article inspection and record the nozzle number, pick height, force, vacuum level, and inspection results.

defect.symptom: Small ceramic capacitors show corner cracks after reflow, and some units have visible nozzle marks on the top surface.
defect.cause: The nozzle tip is too small or worn, causing point loading, and the placement force is too high for the component's mechanical limit.
defect.action: Stop the line, verify the component supplier's maximum placement force, reduce force to a validated lower value, replace or realign the nozzle, and run a controlled trial with inspection for cracks, nozzle marks, and paste contact. If cracks persist, escalate to the component supplier and review nozzle geometry and board support.

takeaways: Derive pick height from component height, pocket depth and tip length, then prove it on a dry run before production.
Keep placement force between the seating requirement and the component's stated maximum, with the nozzle contact area checked.
Track nozzle wear and vacuum trend, because a degrading tip changes both the pick and the load without any program change.

mistakes.mistake: Choosing a nozzle by body size alone
mistakes.instead: Check vacuum coverage, tip wear and clearance to neighbouring parts as well.

mistakes.mistake: Raising force to fix a missed paste contact
mistakes.instead: Inspect nozzle alignment, paste deposit and board support first, since force is rarely the real limit.

mistakes.mistake: Replacing nozzles on a fixed calendar count
mistakes.instead: Replace on measured wear or a validated cycle count, and record the evidence.

terms.def: The vertical position where the nozzle contacts the component in the feeder or tray.
The extra downward travel after first contact, which establishes vacuum without compressing the part.
A destructive test that reveals cracks by forcing dye into them and separating the part.
Force concentrated on a small area, which is what causes cracks in brittle components.

title: Fiducials, board recognition, vision calibration, measuring placement offset

goals.text: Diagnose offset, skew, rotation, missing, wrong-part and polarity defects from measured data and name the mechanism.
Verify a placement program and setup before production and identify a missing or expired calibration.

blocks.alt: A board with global and local fiducials inside a camera view, a calibration target, and a placement offset measurement crosshair
blocks.caption: Fiducials, board recognition, vision calibration and measuring placement offset

p: A fiducial is the reference feature the vision system uses to locate the board and, at component level, to locate the part relative to the nozzle. Global fiducials usually sit on board edges or panel rails and establish origin, scale and rotation.

Local fiducials sit near dense or fine-pitch components and compensate local warpage, panel bow or thermal expansion. Fiducial quality usually matters more than nominal position: a clean, high-contrast circular or cross fiducial with a stable edge measures better than a poorly defined shape. Check diameter, contrast and placement tolerance against the placement equipment datasheet and the fabrication drawing.

theory.h: Board recognition combines support, vision and geometry
p: Recognition starts when the conveyor or pallet presents the board. The machine may use edge sensors, clamps, pins or vision to find it, and vision-based recognition typically measures two or more fiducials and computes a transformation from machine to board coordinates.

Poor support lets the measured fiducial positions move during placement. A program with the wrong fiducial type, wrong coordinates or wrong panel origin places components consistently in the wrong place. Before production, confirm that support height, clamp force, conveyor speed and fiducial search window match the board type and the machine setup sheet.

theory.h: Vision calibration links pixels to coordinates
p: Vision calibration converts an image measurement into a machine coordinate measurement. Camera calibration fixes the relationship between pixel distance and physical distance, including scale, centre offset and, on some systems, lens distortion. Nozzle or placement calibration fixes the relationship between nozzle centre and measured component centre.

Calibration that is missing, expired or done with the wrong camera, lens, nozzle or lighting lets the machine report a coordinate the component never reached. Check calibration status as part of setup verification, not after a defect appears, and verify interval and pass criteria against the equipment datasheet and the plant calibration procedure.

theory.h: Offset is a vector, not a distance
p: Placement offset usually arrives as X and Y displacement from target, and a single magnitude hides direction: 0.05 mm in X and 0.05 mm in Y is not the same as a 0.07 mm diagonal.

Diagnose with the sign and magnitude of X, Y and rotation. A constant offset across many boards points to board coordinates or calibration. An offset that changes with board position points to support, conveyor or fiducial recognition. An offset that changes with component type points to nozzle, feeder or component vision.

theory.h: Skew and rotation are not offset
p: Skew is angular misalignment against the board coordinate system. Rotation error can appear as a component angle error or as an asymmetric offset between opposite ends of the part, and a component can be centred yet rotated, or displaced because it rotated about a point away from its centre.

Small passives, odd-form parts and parts near board edges, where the vision field of view is limited, rotate most often. Check the acceptable rotation limit against the assembly drawing, the IPC-A-610 class requirements and the footprint geometry.

theory.h: Missing, wrong-part and polarity are detected differently
p: Component vision reports a missing part when it finds nothing at the expected location after placement, and post-placement inspection reports it when it finds an empty footprint.

Wrong-part defects surface through component height, body size, terminal count, marking or feeder configuration. Polarity surfaces through orientation-sensitive features: a dot, chamfer, notch, asymmetric terminal or marking. Feeder setup and program verification prevent some of these, and vision catches others. A missing component can also come from a failed pick, a feeder that did not advance, or a part dropped in transfer.

theory.h: Verify program geometry, not only part numbers
p: A placement program carries part numbers, coordinates, rotation, pick height, place height, nozzle selection, feeder assignment and vision parameters. Verification confirms that the coordinate origin matches the fiducial scheme, that rotation matches the footprint, and that the selected nozzle and feeder are physically installed.

A program can pass a part-number check and still cause defects through wrong fiducial coordinates, a wrong component centre offset, or a vision search window too small. Prove the placement with a dry run or test board before production, especially after a program revision, nozzle change, feeder change or calibration event.

theory.h: Calibration status is part of setup
p: Before production, confirm that camera calibration, nozzle calibration and any component-specific vision calibration are current and inside tolerance. A record that is missing, expired or tied to a different nozzle, camera, lens or feeder leaves the setup unverified.

Missing calibration produces symptoms that look like mechanical drift: a constant X or Y offset, inconsistent rotation, poor repeatability. Stop the setup, perform or confirm the calibration, and re-run a verification board before releasing production.

calc.task: A placement program targets a 0402 resistor at X = 120.000 mm, Y = 80.000 mm, rotation = 0 degrees. A measured placement result is X = 120.045 mm, Y = 79.985 mm, rotation = 0.6 degrees. The assembly drawing allows a maximum placement offset of 0.050 mm and a maximum rotation of 0.5 degrees. Calculate the X offset, Y offset, total offset, and determine whether the placement passes or fails.
calc.solution: 1. Calculate X offset: measured X minus target X = 120.045 mm - 120.000 mm = +0.045 mm. 2. Calculate Y offset: measured Y minus target Y = 79.985 mm - 80.000 mm = -0.015 mm. 3. Calculate total offset using the vector magnitude: sqrt(0.045^2 + 0.015^2) = sqrt(0.002025 + 0.000225) = sqrt(0.002250) = 0.0474 mm. 4. Compare total offset to the drawing limit: 0.0474 mm is less than 0.050 mm, so the offset passes. 5. Compare rotation to the drawing limit: 0.6 degrees is greater than 0.5 degrees, so the rotation fails. 6. Overall result: the placement fails because rotation exceeds the allowed limit, even though the total offset is within the allowed limit.

defect.symptom: A 0.5 mm pitch QFP is placed with a consistent +0.08 mm X offset on the first three boards after a program revision. The component is centered in Y and has no rotation error. The first board also shows one missing 0402 resistor near the board edge.
defect.cause: The program revision changed the global fiducial coordinates or the fiducial search window, causing the vision system to calculate the board origin incorrectly. The missing 0402 near the board edge may be related to an incorrect pick position, feeder misalignment, or a nozzle that failed to pick the part after the program change.
defect.action: Stop the setup. Verify the fiducial coordinates, fiducial type, and search window against the board drawing and the approved program. Re-run a dry run or test board with fiducial measurement and component vision enabled. Check the 0402 feeder pitch, pick position, nozzle condition, and vacuum. If the offset remains, verify camera and nozzle calibration status and perform the required calibration before releasing production.

takeaways: Measure at least two fiducials and verify their coordinates against the drawing, because a board origin error looks exactly like a calibration fault.
Record offset as a signed X and Y vector with rotation, since a magnitude and a direction demand different fixes.
Check calibration scope before the run, because an expired certificate produces offsets no coordinate edit will cure.

mistakes.mistake: Editing program coordinates to remove a constant offset
mistakes.instead: Verify fiducial coordinates and calibration first, then decide whether the program or the machine is wrong.

mistakes.mistake: Judging placement from a total offset number alone
mistakes.instead: Read X, Y and rotation separately, because a passing magnitude can hide a failing rotation.

mistakes.mistake: Accepting a part-number check as program verification
mistakes.instead: Verify fiducial origin, rotation and installed nozzle against the board, not only the BOM.

terms.def: A board or panel reference mark used to establish origin, scale and rotation for the whole board.
A reference mark near a fine-pitch area that compensates local distortion or warpage.
The established relationship between camera pixel measurements and machine coordinates.
Angular misalignment of a placed component against the board coordinate system.

skills: Lesson m05l02: Feeders, nozzles, pick height and placement force limits by component

title: Placement defect atlas: tombstone, skew, tilt, missing, wrong part, polarity

goals.text: Diagnose offset, skew, rotation, missing, wrong-part and polarity defects from measured data and name the mechanism.
Attribute a defect to placement rather than to printing or reflow using the evidence sequence.

blocks.alt: Six small board views labelled with each placement defect, shown beside a correctly placed component
blocks.caption: Placement defect atlas: tombstone, skew, tilt, missing, wrong part and polarity

theory.h: Evidence sequence before naming a mechanism
p: Start from measured data, not from a visual guess. For each defect, collect SPI volume and pad location, pre-reflow AOI position and orientation, placement head logs, feeder slot and nozzle ID, the reflow profile, and post-reflow AOI or X-ray.

A component misplaced before reflow over centred paste of correct volume points to placement. Paste offset, volume error or a bridge before placement points to printing. Correct pre-reflow placement that shifts, lifts or rotates only after reflow points to wetting or the thermal profile.

Tombstone is usually a reflow wetting imbalance, though pre-reflow tilt or paste imbalance makes placement or printing contributory. Patterns by feeder, nozzle, board location and time separate systematic placement faults from random handling faults.
Offset is the displacement of the component centre from the land centre. Read X and Y from AOI, then compute magnitude and direction.

Feeder pickup offset, tape pocket deformation, nozzle wear, vision calibration drift, board support sag and tape peel force all produce it. A consistent vector from one feeder slot points to feeder pickup or the tape pocket. A consistent direction by board location points to fiducial recognition, vision calibration or support. Random offset across feeders and nozzles points to vacuum, component drop or pocket release. Set action limits from your AOI limits, land geometry and equipment datasheet, because the acceptable offset depends on pad size, component tolerance and wetting.
Skew is angular misalignment of the body against the land edges. Measure the angle from AOI and correlate it with nozzle ID, feeder slot and component orientation.

Rotation during pick, nozzle spin, a component sitting crooked in its pocket, tape pocket geometry, vision angle error and head rotation error all cause it. Skew with offset points to pick or pocket; skew without offset points to nozzle rotation or vision angle. Skew present in pre-reflow AOI belongs to placement; a component that rotates only in reflow belongs to wetting imbalance or the profile. Check angle limits against the AOI program and the equipment datasheet.
Tilt is a non-coplanar body, and tombstone is severe tilt where one end lifts while the other stays wetted. Measure Z height, shadow, focus and, where needed, X-ray.

Nozzle height, component thickness variation, feeder pocket, board warp, paste height and reflow surface tension all play a part. Pre-reflow tilt points to placement, nozzle, feeder or board support; pre-reflow paste imbalance points to printing. Correct placement and paste followed by lift in reflow points to wetting imbalance, profile or board warp. Tombstone is often filed as a reflow defect, yet placement contributes whenever the part sits tilted, skewed or on uneven paste.
A missing part can come from an empty feeder, a failed pick, vacuum loss, a dropped component, a vision reject, a program skip or a pocket failure.

Diagnose in order: pick and place logs, feeder count, pre-reflow AOI, post-reflow AOI. No pick in the log points to an empty feeder, pocket or feeder count. A pick with no place points to vacuum, a drop or nozzle height. A logged place confirmed by pre-reflow AOI but absent after reflow points to reflow, transport or handling.

Wrong part means the placed component does not match the BOM, the program or the expected value. Feeder misload, wrong reel, wrong program, manual substitution, a tape splice and feeder slot mismatch all produce it.

Compare the BOM with the feeder map, scan the reel barcode, review AOI component recognition, and use X-ray or electrical test where the marking is not visible. A wrong part in pre-reflow AOI belongs to feeder loading or the program; a correct part with a wrong value usually means a misload or a wrong reel. On THT, tray or tube loading and the insertion program enter the same way.

Polarity defects reverse a diode, IC, tantalum, electrolytic or another polarised part. Feeder orientation, pocket orientation, manual loading, a disabled vision polarity check, nozzle rotation and program angle all cause them.

Inspect the polarity mark or pin 1, review the pre-reflow AOI polarity check, and correlate with the feeder slot. A reversed part in pre-reflow AOI belongs to feeder orientation or the program; correct polarity that reverses later points to reflow rotation, handling or a manual step. On THT, insertion direction and tray orientation dominate.
Attribution rests on the evidence sequence, not on one image: SPI, pre-reflow AOI, the reflow profile, post-reflow AOI or X-ray, and feeder and nozzle logs.

Systematic defects by feeder slot point to loading, pickup or pocket. Systematic defects by board location point to vision, fiducials or support. Random defects across feeders and nozzles point to vacuum, drop or pocket release. Defects that appear only after reflow point to wetting or the profile, and paste defects before placement point to printing.

Use your acceptance standard for disposition, but set action limits from process capability, land geometry and the equipment datasheet, and document containment, root cause, corrective action and verification data.

calc.task: During a 5000-board run, pre-reflow AOI reports 12 components with center offset greater than 0.15 mm, 8 components with skew greater than 1.5 deg, 3 missing components, 2 wrong-part components, and 1 reversed polarity component. Offset data: 10 of 12 offsets are +X 0.18 mm and Y 0.02 mm, all from feeder slot 14. Skew data: 7 of 8 skews are 2.0 deg clockwise, all from nozzle 3. Missing: 3 all from feeder slot 22. Wrong part: 2 boards have a capacitor from feeder slot 31 measured 100 nF instead of 10 nF. Polarity: 1 board has a diode reversed from feeder slot 41. SPI shows paste centered and in volume. Calculate defect rates, ppm, offset vector, and attribute each defect to placement, printing, or reflow using the evidence sequence.
calc.solution: Rate calculation: offset = 12/5000 = 2400 ppm; skew = 8/5000 = 1600 ppm; missing = 3/5000 = 600 ppm; wrong part = 2/5000 = 400 ppm; polarity = 1/5000 = 200 ppm; total = 26/5000 = 5200 ppm. Offset vector: magnitude = sqrt(0.18^2 + 0.02^2) = 0.181 mm; direction = atan2(0.02, 0.18) = 6.3 deg from +X. Offset attribution: 10 of 12 offsets are from feeder slot 14, SPI paste is centered, and the defect is present in pre-reflow AOI. Attribute to placement feeder pickup or tape pocket, not printing or reflow. Skew attribution: 7 of 8 skews are from nozzle 3 and are present in pre-reflow AOI. Attribute to placement nozzle rotation or pick rotation, not printing or reflow. Missing attribution: 3 missing components are all from feeder slot 22. Check pick/place logs; if no pick, feeder or tape pocket; if pick but no place, nozzle vacuum. Attribute to placement. Wrong part attribution: measured capacitance is 100 nF instead of 10 nF from feeder slot 31. Attribute to placement feeder misload or wrong reel, not printing or reflow. Polarity attribution: reversed diode from feeder slot 41 is present in pre-reflow AOI. Attribute to placement feeder orientation or program, not printing or reflow. Evidence rule: because SPI is normal and defects are present before reflow, printing and reflow are not primary causes; if a defect appears only after reflow, reflow would be primary.

defect.symptom: Pre-reflow AOI shows a systematic +X offset on one feeder slot, while SPI shows centered paste and post-reflow AOI shows the same offset without additional rotation or lift.
defect.cause: Feeder pickup position or tape pocket geometry is shifting the component before placement, producing a repeatable offset vector from that feeder slot.
defect.action: Contain the affected feeder slot, re-teach feeder pickup position, inspect tape peel and pocket, verify nozzle vacuum, then run a verification lot and confirm offset distribution against your AOI limits and equipment datasheet.

takeaways: Capture SPI and pre-reflow AOI before reflow, because the position of the part before and after reflow is what separates placement from wetting.
Group defects by feeder slot, nozzle and board location, since a pattern names the mechanism faster than any single image.
Set placement action limits from pad geometry and component tolerance, not from a round number that ignores both.

mistakes.mistake: Calling tombstone a reflow defect without checking pre-reflow tilt
mistakes.instead: Read pre-reflow AOI first, because a tilted part tombstone even on a good profile.

mistakes.mistake: Diagnosing a missing part from a post-reflow image alone
mistakes.instead: Check the pick and place logs to see whether the machine ever picked it.

mistakes.mistake: Treating a single offset sample as a direction
mistakes.instead: Measure across boards, since scatter and a consistent vector need different fixes.

terms.def: Angular misalignment of a placed component against its land pattern.
A chip component standing on one end after reflow because one joint wetted before the other.
A polarised component placed in the reverse orientation.
The measured value at which the process is stopped or investigated, set from capability and geometry.

title: Component library setup, program verification and first-article check

goals.text: Verify a placement program and setup before production and identify a missing or expired calibration.

blocks.alt: A component library entry with package, nozzle and vision settings, beside a program verification screen and a first-article board under inspection
blocks.caption: Component library setup, program verification and first-article check

p: Before production, verify that the placement program, component library, feeder setup, nozzle selection and machine calibration represent the approved design and process.

The check has to prove the machine can place the right components, in the right orientation, at the right coordinates, with acceptable accuracy. Run a dry run or offline simulation first, then a pre-production sample under controlled conditions.

The component library holds package geometry, body size, pin or pad pitch, polarity, rotation, pick point, nozzle, feeder type, vision settings and placement tolerance. Verify each field against the component datasheet and a physical sample.

On polarised parts, confirm the library polarity matches the silkscreen and the feeder orientation. On fine-pitch packages, confirm that tape, reel or feeder geometry does not obscure the pick point and the vision reference.
Check the coordinate origin, fiducial pattern, panel offsets, mirror settings, units, component side and layer assignment.

Confirm the feeder map matches the physical feeders, that nozzles suit component size and clearance, and that the program commands no collision with panel edges, connectors or tall components. Review the sequence for pickup order, nozzle changes and vision cycles.
Placement accuracy depends on machine calibration, vision calibration, feeder calibration, nozzle condition and conveyance alignment.

Before release, confirm that required calibration certificates exist, are traceable, sit inside the interval set by the equipment manufacturer or your calibration plan, and are supported by verification results. A certificate that is missing, expired or outside the required environmental or usage conditions leaves the setup unverified until calibration is complete and recorded.
Run a sample and inspect for missing components, wrong components, polarity and rotation errors, tombstoning and poor seating, using AOI, X-ray or manual inspection as the case needs.

Measure placement coordinates against the program and compare the deviation with the tolerance from the equipment datasheet or the process capability study. Record the measured values, the method, the operator and the disposition.

Define pass and fail before the sample runs. Criteria cover placement coordinate tolerance, polarity, rotation, missing or wrong components, and calibration status, taken from the paste, feeder, nozzle and placement equipment datasheets and confirmed against your own capability.
Release production only when program, setup, calibration and sample inspection all meet the defined criteria.
Any change to the program, component library, feeder, nozzle, panel, fiducial or calibration status repeats the relevant verification steps.

Store the program version, library version, calibration records, sample results and approval with the production record, so the setup stays traceable and containment is possible when a defect turns up later.

calc.task: A placement program specifies a tolerance of 0.05 mm for a component center. The pre-production sample shows a measured deviation of 0.03 mm. The machine calibration certificate is missing. Determine whether the setup can be released.
calc.solution: Compare the measured deviation with the tolerance. The deviation is within tolerance. Check the calibration certificate. The certificate is missing, so the setup is not verified. Reject release, complete calibration, then repeat the pre-production sample.

defect.symptom: AOI reports repeated polarity errors on polarized components after a feeder change.
defect.cause: The component library polarity or feeder orientation did not match the physical part, and the program was not reverified after the change.
defect.action: Stop the line, quarantine affected boards, correct the library and feeder orientation, run a pre-production sample, inspect polarity and rotation, update the change record, and release only after verification.

takeaways: Verify the library against a physical sample, because a polarity or rotation field copied from a datasheet can still disagree with the reel.
Treat a missing or expired calibration as a failed setup, whatever the sample deviation shows.
Record program and library versions with the sample result, so a later defect can be traced to the configuration that made it.

mistakes.mistake: Releasing on a good sample while calibration has expired
mistakes.instead: Confirm the certificate first, since the sample may pass today and fail after an axis drift tomorrow.

mistakes.mistake: Checking part numbers without checking pick point and vision reference
mistakes.instead: Confirm both for fine-pitch parts, because tape or feeder geometry can obstruct them.

mistakes.mistake: Skipping reverification after a feeder change
mistakes.instead: Repeat the polarity and rotation checks, which is exactly where a feeder change goes wrong.

terms.def: The stored geometry, orientation and handling data the machine uses for each part number.
The table that assigns each part number to a physical feeder slot.
A controlled first run inspected before the line is released.
The period within which an instrument or axis must be recalibrated.

skills: Lesson m05l04: Placement defect atlas: tombstone, skew, tilt, missing, wrong part, polarity

title: Case: shift and skew on a fine-pitch QFP

goals.text: Diagnose offset, skew, rotation, missing, wrong-part and polarity defects from measured data and name the mechanism.
Attribute a defect to placement rather than to printing or reflow using the evidence sequence.

blocks.alt: A fine-pitch QFP with measured shift and skew against a crosshair overlay, and the lead pitch tolerance band marked
blocks.caption: Case: shift and skew on a fine-pitch QFP

theory.h: Why fine-pitch QFP placement is a data problem
p: A fine-pitch QFP exposes placement error because the positional margin is small next to the lead pitch. On a 0.5 mm pitch part, a lateral shift of 0.10 mm already eats 20 % of the pitch, and 0.5 degrees of rotation moves an outer lead by tens of micrometres depending on body size.

The practical aim is to separate true placement error from measurement noise, paste print variation and reflow-induced movement, using placement verification, AOI, SPI and reflow inspection in sequence rather than one end-of-line image.

Offset is translation of the component centre from the intended centre, reported as X and Y error. Skew is a positional mismatch between opposite sides, seen as one side closer to its pads than the other. Rotation is angular error about the centre.

On a QFP a small rotation looks like skew when measured at one corner, so measure two opposite corners or use fiducial-based centre and angle data. For fine-pitch QFPs, placement targets usually sit around ±0.05 mm to ±0.10 mm for centre position and ±0.5° to ±1.0° for angle, verified against the placement machine datasheet, the component datasheet and the IPC-A-610 class requirements.

theory.h: Missing, wrong-part and polarity are a different family
p: A missing QFP is usually a feeder, vision or placement-cycle failure rather than a subtle drift. Wrong-part defects come from feeder misload, wrong program selection or gaps in barcode and serialisation control.

Polarity defects on QFPs show at the pin 1 marking, chamfer, dot or bevel, and the program can miss them with the wrong part orientation or a backwards tape. These defects are binary — present or absent, correct or reversed — and belong apart from the dimensional errors of offset, skew and rotation.

theory.h: Attributing defects with the evidence sequence
p: The strongest sequence is SPI before placement, placement verification during placement, AOI after placement, and final inspection after reflow.

Acceptable paste with a component placed outside tolerance makes placement the likely cause. Paste offset, bridging or volume variation that the component follows makes printing the likely cause. An acceptable part after placement that moves during reflow makes reflow the cause, through wetting imbalance, paste collapse or thermal effects. Do not blame placement when the pre-placement evidence already shows the same pattern.

theory.h: Common placement mechanisms on fine-pitch QFP
p: Poor fiducial recognition, camera calibration drift, nozzle wear, vacuum loss, feeder repeatability, tape peel variation and program coordinate errors all appear on this package.

Nozzle choice matters: a nozzle that presses the body too hard tilts the part, and poor vacuum lets it shift in transfer. Feeder problems often produce repeatable skew or rotation on one board side, because the part is presented at a slightly inconsistent angle. Program errors give a consistent offset across many boards, while mechanical wear gives gradual drift or intermittent outliers.

theory.h: Separating placement from printing and reflow
p: Printing defects show as paste offset, volume variation or shape distortion at pad level. A component that follows the paste points to printing.

Placement defects show as position or angle error while the paste stays acceptable. Reflow defects show as movement after the paste melted: acceptable post-placement AOI but shifted post-reflow AOI, tombstoning or coplanarity problems. Surface tension can correct small errors on a fine-pitch QFP only where paste volume and pad geometry are balanced, so partial self-centring points at reflow.
Confirm the defect type first: missing, wrong part, polarity, offset, skew or rotation. Then establish whether it is random, dependent on board position, or repeatable across boards.

Random missing parts point to feeder or vacuum. Repeatable offset or rotation points to program, fiducial or calibration. Board-position-dependent skew points to table flatness, support or nozzle transfer. A defect that appears only after reflow needs pre- and post-reflow measurements compared, and a defect that appears at SPI needs printing investigated before placement.

IPC-A-610 gives the acceptability criteria for placement and soldering without replacing machine capability targets or design-specific limits. IPC-7351 supplies land pattern and package data for pad-to-lead relationships, and IPC-7525 and the related stencil guidance help evaluate paste print capability, with exact aperture and volume targets verified against your paste, stencil and printer datasheets.
Keep internal limits tighter than the final acceptability limit, so placement can be corrected before a solder defect appears.

calc.task: A 0.50 mm pitch QFP has a body diagonal of 14.0 mm. Placement verification reports centre offset X = +0.08 mm, Y = -0.06 mm, and rotation = +0.8°. The placement machine specification for this part is ±0.10 mm centre and ±0.5° angle. Calculate the resultant centre offset, the outer-lead displacement caused by rotation, and the approximate worst-case lead displacement if centre offset and rotation act in the same direction. State whether the defect is placement-related if SPI shows acceptable paste print and post-placement AOI shows the same offset pattern.
calc.solution: 1. Calculate resultant centre offset: sqrt(0.08^2 + 0.06^2) = sqrt(0.0064 + 0.0036) = sqrt(0.0100) = 0.10 mm. 2. Compare centre offset to machine limit: 0.10 mm is at the ±0.10 mm limit, so it is borderline and should be investigated. 3. Calculate rotation displacement at the outer lead. The distance from centre to corner is half the body diagonal: 14.0 mm / 2 = 7.0 mm. 4. Convert rotation to radians: 0.8° × π / 180 = 0.01396 rad. 5. Calculate arc displacement: 7.0 mm × 0.01396 = 0.098 mm. 6. Compare rotation displacement to angle limit: 0.8° exceeds the ±0.5° machine limit, so rotation is out of specification. 7. Estimate worst-case combined lead displacement if centre offset and rotation act in the same direction: 0.10 mm + 0.098 mm = 0.198 mm, approximately 0.20 mm. 8. Compare to pitch: 0.20 mm is 40% of the 0.50 mm pitch, which is a significant risk for lead misalignment, bridging, or insufficient solder joint formation. 9. Attribution: because SPI shows acceptable paste print and the same offset pattern is present at post-placement AOI, the defect is most likely placement-related rather than printing-related. If the part were acceptable after placement but shifted after reflow, reflow would be the more likely cause.

defect.symptom: A fine-pitch QFP is consistently shifted toward one side of the board, with one row of leads closer to the paste than the opposite row. Post-placement AOI reports centre offset of about 0.12 mm and rotation of about 0.7°. SPI shows acceptable paste print. The defect repeats at the same board location and is worse on the side of the board nearest the feeder.
defect.cause: The repeatable pattern points to a placement presentation or transfer issue rather than random reflow movement. Likely mechanisms include feeder tape peel variation, nozzle wear, vacuum inconsistency, or a slightly misaligned feeder causing the part to be picked up at an angle. Because the defect is board-location dependent and appears before reflow, printing and reflow are less likely primary causes.
defect.action: Stop the line if the defect exceeds the internal placement limit. Verify the feeder for the QFP, inspect the tape peel force and cover tape alignment, and check the nozzle for wear, vacuum, and centring. Re-run a placement verification test with a known-good feeder and nozzle. If the defect moves with the feeder, replace or recalibrate the feeder. If the defect remains, check placement camera calibration, fiducial recognition, and nozzle transfer settings. After correction, confirm with SPI, placement verification, and post-placement AOI before releasing production.

takeaways: Measure centre offset and rotation on two opposite corners, because a small rotation at one corner reads as skew.
Attribute with the evidence sequence — SPI, placement, AOI, reflow — and do not blame placement when the paste already shows the pattern.
Set internal placement limits tighter than IPC-A-610 acceptance, so correction happens before a solder defect exists.

mistakes.mistake: Judging a QFP from a single end-of-line image
mistakes.instead: Compare pre-placement, post-placement and post-reflow data before naming the mechanism.

mistakes.mistake: Treating a repeatable offset as reflow self-centring
mistakes.instead: Check whether the offset exists at post-placement AOI, which settles the question.

mistakes.mistake: Blaming the program for drift that repeats by board location
mistakes.instead: Check table flatness, support and feeder presentation, which produce location-dependent patterns.

terms.def: The translation of a component centre from its intended position, reported as X and Y.
Angular displacement of the component about its centre after placement.
Uneven solder wetting that pulls a component out of position during reflow.
How well the leads or terminations of a component lie in one plane.

title: Heat transfer in the oven: convection, conduction, radiation, zone structure

goals.text: Run a thermal survey and read the profile at the coolest and hottest locations, not at the oven setpoints.

p: A reflow profile is the temperature history the board and its components actually see, not the oven setpoints. Ramp, soak, time above liquidus, peak and cooling describe it, and between them they govern flux activation, flux removal, wetting, intermetallic formation, voiding and thermal stress.

Because thermal mass differs, the same oven recipe produces different results on a different assembly, so measure the profile on the board. The best profile is not the hottest or the fastest: it is the exposure that makes reliable joints while keeping board and components inside their qualified limits.

blocks.alt: Reference sheet: side view of a convection reflow oven with preheat, soak, reflow and cooling zones, convection, conduction and radiation icons, a profiling board with thermocouples, and a profile shape with ramp, soak, TAL, peak and cooling
blocks.caption: Reflow oven zones, heat-transfer paths and the profile shape; numeric targets come from the paste datasheet and the figure above
Typical SAC305 profile envelope — paste TDS always wins
head: Zone
Typical target
What it controls
rows: Soak 60-120 s (ts); TAL 30-90 s above liquidus

p: The ramp carries the assembly to the temperature where flux activates and solvents leave without violent boiling. Typical soak ranges are 140-180 °C for 90-120 s, checked against the paste and equipment datasheet.

A heavy board with large copper planes may need a longer soak to narrow the gap between small components and large connectors. Too short a soak leaves flux active too late, which raises solder balls and voiding; too long dries the paste and reduces wetting. Judge the soak from measured board temperature, never from oven air temperature.
Time above liquidus is how long the alloy stays molten. It has to be long enough for wetting and flux removal and short enough to limit intermetallic growth and component exposure.

J-STD-020 bounds it: its classification profile sets tL, the time at liquidus, at 60-150 s for both alloy families. IPC-7530 and the paste datasheet narrow that into a working window — IPC-7530 typically calls for 30-90 s above liquidus, and the paste datasheet is the authority for the board being run. J-STD-020's own time figure, tp, is the time within 5 °C of the classification temperature, limited to 30 s on the Pb-free profile and 20 s for SnPb; it is a package qualification parameter, not the paste window for running a board.

Production profiles may use a different window if qualified. Take the liquidus temperature from the paste or alloy datasheet, because it depends on alloy and formulation, and check the measured time above liquidus at the worst-case thermocouple rather than at a convenient point.
Peak temperature is the highest measured temperature at the solder joint or component body, depending on where the thermocouple sits.

For SAC305, J-STD-020 gives no single peak: it gives classification temperatures by package size — 260 °C for small packages, 250 °C for large and 245 °C for very large at 1.6-2.5 mm thickness — and the full table is thickness times volume, where below 1.6 mm every volume allows 260 °C and above 2.5 mm the limits fall to 250 °C small and 245 °C large and very large. Each comes with tp, the time within 5 °C of that temperature, limited to 30 s.

Production peaks usually sit below the classification temperature with margin and are verified with thermocouples on the actual board. Exceeding the classification temperature damages components, delaminates packages or grows excessive intermetallic, and the peak must be judged together with time above liquidus, because a short peak and a long peak are not the same thermal exposure.
Cooling solidifies the joint and sets grain size, residual stress and warpage. Typical rates are 1-4 °C/s, verified against the paste and equipment datasheet.

Very fast cooling raises thermal shock and warpage, especially on thin boards and large BGAs. Very slow cooling produces a coarse solder structure and lets components move while the joint is still soft. Measure cooling with the same board thermocouples used for peak and time above liquidus, because the cooling curve reveals lag and gradients that the oven profile hides.

theory.h: Why thermocouples go on the board
p: Oven air temperature is not solder joint temperature. Board thickness, copper area, component mass, shielding and mounting method all create lag and gradients, so attach calibrated thermocouples with high-temperature adhesive or tape and minimal added mass.

Representative points are the centre of a large BGA, a small passive near a heavy connector, and a location near the board edge or panel rail. A thermocouple on a bare board rather than a populated one measures a profile production will never run.

Compare the measured peak with the J-STD-020 classification temperature for the package size, and the measured time above liquidus with the J-STD-020 window of 60-150 s, narrowed by IPC-7530 guidance of 30-90 s and by the paste datasheet.

Use the worst-case measured point, not the oven profile or a single thermocouple. A peak above the classification temperature, or a time above liquidus outside the datasheet window, leaves the assembly non-compliant unless a separate qualification supports the exposure. Moisture sensitivity level, floor life and bake requirements from J-STD-020 also decide whether the component tolerates the exposure at all.

Start from the paste supplier's recommended profile and the component qualification limits. Run a dummy board with thermocouples at the expected worst-case locations, then adjust zones to move the measured soak, peak and cooling toward target while keeping the curve smooth.

Repeat the measurements after any change to stackup, panelisation, component placement or oven loading. Record the profile with board type, oven model, conveyor speed, zone setpoints and thermocouple locations so the result can be reproduced.

calc.task: A SAC305 paste datasheet gives a solidus of 217 °C and a liquidus of 219 °C. A 1.6 mm board with 70 µm copper and a 12 mm BGA is reflowed. The target is to stay within the J-STD-020 classification temperature for the package size and a time above liquidus of 60-150 s, the J-STD-020 classification window. A measured profile shows ramp 1.5 °C/s, soak 165 °C for 90 s, peak 242 °C, time above liquidus 75 s, and cooling 2.5 °C/s. Build and judge the profile.
calc.solution: 1. Confirm alloy liquidus from the paste datasheet: SAC305 has a solidus of 217 °C and a liquidus of 219 °C, so time above liquidus is measured from the 219 °C crossing. 2. Set soak target from the paste datasheet, e.g. 140-180 °C for 90-120 s; choose 165 °C for 90 s for this board. 3. Ramp to liquidus; measured ramp 1.5 °C/s is within typical practice, verify against the paste and oven datasheet. 4. Calculate time above liquidus from measured data: time when temperature exceeds 219 °C until it falls below 219 °C = 75 s. 5. Compare peak 242 °C with the J-STD-020 classification temperature for the package size: 242 °C passes for a small package (260 °C) or a large package (250 °C) and would fail for a very large package (245 °C), so confirm the package size before disposition. 6. Compare time above liquidus 75 s with the J-STD-020 classification window of 60-150 s: pass. IPC-7530 typical guidance is 30-90 s, so 75 s also sits inside the usual process window; the paste datasheet remains the authority for this board. 7. Check cooling 2.5 °C/s against the paste and equipment datasheet; if warpage or cracking is observed, slow cooling. The J-STD-020 classification ramp-down limit is 6 °C/s or less. 8. Conclusion: the measured profile passes the peak ceiling and the paste time-above-liquidus window for this board, but the package size must be confirmed for the peak ceiling, and production limits should be qualified and monitored.

defect.symptom: Solder balls on paste deposit edges after reflow
defect.cause: Soak too short or ramp too fast, causing flux and solvent boiling and paste spatter; thermocouple on board showed actual soak below paste target
defect.action: Measure with board thermocouples, increase soak time or lower ramp rate to reach paste soak range, verify paste datasheet, check stencil and paste viscosity

takeaways: Measure on a populated board at the worst-case locations, because oven setpoints and bare-board runs both understate the real exposure.
Read the peak against the J-STD-020 classification for the package thickness and volume, not against a single remembered number.
Keep the paste time-above-liquidus window separate from the J-STD-020 tL classification window, since one runs the process and the other qualifies the package.

mistakes.mistake: Quoting one peak temperature for every package on the board
mistakes.instead: Read the classification temperature by thickness and volume, and check the largest part against it.

mistakes.mistake: Judging time above liquidus from the oven display
mistakes.instead: Take it from the measured curve crossing the alloy liquidus, at the worst-case thermocouple.

mistakes.mistake: Slowing cooling without checking warpage and grain structure
mistakes.instead: Verify the cooling rate against the paste datasheet and inspect the joints afterwards.

The peak temperature J-STD-020 allows for a package, set by thickness and volume.
The spreading of molten solder over a metal surface to form a metallurgical bond.
A temperature sensor attached to the board to record the actual thermal history.

title: Profile anatomy: ramp, soak, time above liquidus, peak, cooling — what each controls

goals.text: Build a profile for a given board thermal mass and alloy and check ramp, time above liquidus and peak against limits taken from the cited source.

blocks.alt: A thermal profile curve with the five zones labelled and a callout under each naming what it controls
blocks.caption: Profile anatomy: what ramp, soak, time above liquidus, peak and cooling each control

theory.h: The profile as a thermal budget
p: A reflow profile records temperature against time at a defined measurement point, usually a thermocouple on the package body or near a joint. It is never one number.

The shape of the curve decides how flux activates, how solder melts, how intermetallics form, and how the board and its components experience thermal stress. For the working engineer the useful question is which segment of the curve controls which risk.
The ramp from room temperature to the liquidus region is where solvents leave the paste and the flux starts reducing oxides.

A ramp that is too steep boils trapped solvent violently, which shows up as solder balling or tombstoning, and large boards develop gradients that warp. A ramp that is too slow dries the flux out before reflow and leaves poor wetting. Typical practice runs 1 to 3 °C/s up to about 150 °C, with the exact limit set by paste chemistry and board mass and checked against the paste and oven datasheet.
IPC J-STD-020 gives moisture sensitivity level preheat guidance for components, not a universal ramp rate for the whole profile.

The soak region, often roughly 150 to 190 °C, brings the whole assembly toward thermal equilibrium. It narrows the temperature difference between heavy ground planes and small pads, and gives the flux chemistry time to work before the solder melts.

Too short a soak leaves cold spots that refuse to wet; too long a soak over-cures the flux binder or exhausts the active agents. Many paste datasheets specify a soak window, for example 60 to 120 seconds in a defined band. Treat those numbers as starting points and confirm them with wetting tests on your own boards.

Time above liquidus is the interval in which the solder is molten and able to flow and form intermetallic compounds. SAC305 has a solidus of 217 °C and a liquidus of 219 °C; SnPb eutectic has a liquidus of 183 °C.

Too short a time produces thin intermetallic and weak joints. Too long promotes excessive intermetallic growth and grain coarsening and can damage component finishes. The window is process guidance from IPC-7530 and the paste datasheet, typically 60-120 s or 60-150 s.

J-STD-020 sets no board-assembly time-above-liquidus limit: its own time parameter is tp, the time within 5 °C of the classification temperature, limited to 30 s, and its peak figures are classification temperatures by package thickness and volume rather than by size alone — 260 °C for a thin package at any volume, 260/250/245 °C across small, large and very large at 1.6-2.5 mm thickness, and 250/245/245 °C above 2.5 mm. Check the classification temperature for your component's body size and MSL before comparing a measured peak.
The peak is the highest temperature reached. It must be high enough for complete melting and wetting and low enough to protect board and components.

Peak is usually set 10 to 25 °C above liquidus for common alloys, but the governing limit is the component's rated peak from its datasheet or from IPC J-STD-020. Exceeding the rated peak delaminates packages, cracks ceramic capacitors and damages heat-sensitive parts; a peak below the wetting threshold leaves a dull, grainy joint that never fully formed.

After the peak, the cooling rate sets the solder microstructure and the residual stress in the joint. Slow cooling gives coarse grains and weak joints; very fast cooling induces thermal shock, especially in large ceramic components and thick boards.

Typical rates run 1 to 4 °C/s, with the safe limit set by component type and board construction and verified against the equipment's cooling capability and the component specifications. The cooling segment also decides how long the assembly sits in the range where flux residues char.

theory.h: Reading the profile against your hardware
p: A profile is valid only for the board, paste, oven and measurement point it was built for. A heavy board with large copper planes needs more energy and often a longer soak than a thin signal board, and the same recipe produces a different profile at another conveyor speed or loading density.

Always measure with thermocouples on the actual product rather than a coupon, then compare the measured ramp, soak, time above liquidus, peak and cooling against the paste datasheet window and the J-STD-020 classification temperature for the package size, which is the peak ceiling.

Ramp problems show up as solder balls, tombstoning or board warpage. Soak problems appear as non-wetting, dewetting or cold joints over heavy copper. Time-above-liquidus problems give insufficient intermetallic when short and brittle joints with damaged finishes when long.

Peak problems cause under-reflow or component damage, and cooling problems produce thermal cracking or excessive residual stress. When a defect appears, identify the segment most likely to be responsible, adjust that segment, and re-measure.

calc.task: Build and check a profile for a 1.6 mm FR-4 board with heavy ground planes using SAC305 paste. The measured profile gives: ramp from 25 to 150 °C in 60 s; soak 150 to 190 °C for 90 s; TAL above 219 °C = 45 s; peak = 248 °C; cooling from 248 to 100 °C in 40 s. Check against the J-STD-020 classification temperature for the package size and typical paste guidance.
calc.solution: 1. Ramp rate: (150-25)/60 = 2.08 °C/s. Typical paste guidance is 1 to 3 °C/s; this is within range but verify against paste datasheet. 2. Soak: 90 s in 150 to 190 °C. Many paste datasheets specify 60 to 120 s; this is within range. 3. Peak temperature: measured 248 °C. J-STD-020 sets classification temperatures by package size — 260 °C small, 250 °C large, 245 °C very large (1.6-2.5 mm row; above 2.5 mm thickness the limits fall to 250 °C small and 245 °C large and very large). For a large package 248 °C is inside the limit; for a very large package it exceeds 245 °C by 3 °C, so the package size must be confirmed before disposition. 4. TAL above 219 °C: measured 45 s. J-STD-020 does not set a board-assembly time-above-liquidus limit; its 30 s figure is tp, the time within 5 °C of the classification temperature. The applicable limit is the paste window: IPC-7530B guidance gives 30-90 s, a paste datasheet may narrow it, and 45 s sits inside 30-90 s but below the lower bound of any datasheet that specifies 60 s or more, so it is too short for reliable wetting rather than too long. 5. Cooling rate: (248-100)/40 = 3.7 °C/s. Typical practice is 1 to 4 °C/s; this is within range, and the J-STD-020 classification ramp-down limit is 6 °C/s or less. 6. Conclusion: the binding failure is the too-short time above liquidus, not an excessive one. Lengthen time above liquidus toward the paste window (30-90 s per IPC-7530B, narrowed by the paste datasheet) by adding reflow dwell or slightly raising peak within the package classification temperature, confirm the package size for the peak ceiling, then re-measure.

defect.symptom: Solder joints on large ground-plane pads show dewetting and non-wetting, while joints on small signal pads look normal.
defect.cause: The soak segment is too short or the temperature gradient is too high, so the heavy copper pads never reach the flux activation temperature before the solder melts. The flux cannot reduce oxides on the large pads, and the solder does not wet.
defect.action: Increase soak time or raise the soak temperature band slightly to allow the heavy pads to reach thermal equilibrium. Verify with thermocouples on the actual board that the pad temperature enters the soak window before the liquidus is reached. Re-measure the profile and run wetting tests.

takeaways: Assign each defect to one segment of the curve before adjusting the oven, because the segment names the mechanism.
Keep paste time-above-liquidus guidance separate from the J-STD-020 classification windows, since they answer different questions.
Check the peak against the classification temperature for the package thickness and volume, not against a single remembered figure.

mistakes.mistake: Quoting a 30 s time limit as the board's time above liquidus
mistakes.instead: That is J-STD-020 tp within 5 °C of classification, not the paste window.

mistakes.mistake: Raising the peak to fix weak wetting
mistakes.instead: Check the soak and the time above liquidus first, since wetting usually fails before the peak does.

mistakes.mistake: Using a test coupon as the profile record
mistakes.instead: Measure the actual product, because thermal mass is what the profile describes.

terms.def: The near-isothermal segment where the assembly equalises and the flux works before melting.
The temperature above which an alloy is fully molten.
Solder that spreads and then retracts, leaving thin irregular areas on the pad.
The brittle layer formed between solder and the pad metal during melting.

title: Running a thermal survey: thermocouple attachment, test coupon, worst-case site

goals.text: Run a thermal survey and read the profile at the coolest and hottest locations, not at the oven setpoints.

blocks.alt: A test coupon with several thermocouples attached by different methods, and a board map marking the worst-case thermal sites
blocks.caption: Running a thermal survey: thermocouple attachment, test coupon and the worst-case site

p: A thermal survey records the temperature the board, components and solder joints see as they pass through the oven. The zone setpoints are control targets, not proof that any joint reached temperature.

The measurable outcome is the temperature at the coolest and hottest locations on a representative coupon or production panel, compared with the paste liquidus and solidus, the time above liquidus and the component peak limit. Run the survey at the production panel orientation, conveyor speed and loading pattern; a bare coupon or a different layout measures a process you do not run.
The question the survey answers is whether the actual joint temperatures are inside the window, not whether the oven display matches the recipe.
Use a fine-gauge type K thermocouple with a calibrated logger. Attach the junction to the pad, trace or component body that represents the joint under evaluation.

High-temperature tape works if it is rated for the peak and does not lift in handling. A small solder blob improves thermal contact and changes the local thermal mass, so use one method consistently across surveys. Secure the wire so the junction cannot peel away — a lifted junction reads low because it sees air. A junction on a large copper area can read high or lag the joint.
Check tape, adhesive and logger ratings against your equipment datasheet.
A coupon reproduces the materials and thermal mass of the production board: same laminate, copper distribution, component type, paste deposit and panel position.

Where the product carries a large ground plane, a dense BGA, a heavy connector or mixed SMT and THT, include those features, or run the survey on a sacrificial production panel. A simple strip with small pads gives a clean profile and misses the coolest joint under the ground plane.

Place the coupon where production boards sit, because airflow and radiant heating vary across oven width and length. A coupon that is too light heats faster than the real board and returns a false pass.

theory.h: Finding the coolest and hottest sites
p: The coolest site is usually under a large ground plane, near a cold edge, under a heavy component, or at a panel location with poor airflow. The hottest may be near a heater, on a small low-mass component, or at an edge exposed to radiation.

Run several thermocouples at once and compare the curves. A wide spread between sites means the setpoints no longer describe the process. The coolest site decides whether the paste reaches liquidus and forms a joint; the hottest decides whether anything nearby is overexposed. One thermocouple on a fast pad hides a cold joint elsewhere.

Read the board temperature in each zone. Preheat brings the board up without thermal shock, soak narrows the spread and activates flux, reflow holds the joint above liquidus long enough to wet, and cooling solidifies without excessive stress.

For lead-free paste the liquidus comes from the paste datasheet, and the time above liquidus is checked against the paste and component datasheets. Component peak limits are commonly referenced to IPC/JEDEC J-STD-020, while the component datasheet and the applicable moisture sensitivity level set the final limit. Check every practice-based value against your paste and equipment datasheet.
A measured temperature carries thermocouple error, logger error, attachment lag and placement error. Use a logger with a calibration certificate and record the sampling interval.

Keep the attachment method identical between surveys, so a change in the profile comes from the oven. A junction lifted by tape reads low, one soldered to a large plane reads high or late, a loose wire gives intermittent contact, and a logger resting on a hot conveyor rail shifts its reference junction.
Document thermocouple type, logger model, calibration status, attachment method and the exact location of every junction. Without that record, two surveys can differ while the oven has not changed.
Accept the survey when the coolest joint reaches liquidus with enough time above it and the hottest joint stays below the component and board limits.

A marginal coolest site calls for a profile change or an investigation of heat transfer, panel loading and airflow. A hottest site close to a limit calls for a lower peak or better cooling. A spread too wide between sites needs better uniformity rather than a higher setpoint.

Document the coupon, thermocouple locations, oven settings, measured minimum and maximum temperatures and any deviation. The result should state whether the joints are acceptable, not whether the recipe was followed.

calc.task: A 6-thermocouple survey on a lead-free SAC305 test coupon records a hottest peak of 246 °C and a coolest peak of 238 °C. The paste datasheet gives solidus 217 °C and liquidus 219 °C. The component datasheet allows a peak of 260 °C. Calculate the margin above liquidus at the coolest site and the margin below the component limit at the hottest site.
calc.solution: First, identify the coolest peak: 238 °C. Next, identify the paste liquidus: 219 °C, because SAC305 has a solidus of 217 °C and a liquidus of 219 °C and time above liquidus is measured from the 219 °C crossing. Then subtract the liquidus from the coolest peak: 238 - 219 = 19 °C. This is the margin above liquidus at the coolest site. Next, identify the hottest peak: 246 °C. Then identify the component peak limit: 260 °C. Subtract the hottest peak from the component limit: 260 - 246 = 14 °C. This is the margin below the component limit at the hottest site. Interpretation: the coolest site is above liquidus by 19 °C, and the hottest site is 14 °C below the stated component limit. Verify time above liquidus and cooling rate against the paste and component datasheets.

defect.symptom: Cold or non-wetted solder joints appear on large ground-plane pads after the oven setpoints and a single thermocouple survey look acceptable.
defect.cause: The thermocouple was attached to a small pad or lifted by tape, so it measured a faster-heating location instead of the coolest joint under the ground plane. The test coupon did not reproduce the copper area and component thermal mass.
defect.action: Rerun the survey with a calibrated logger and a test coupon that includes the ground plane and component. Attach the thermocouple junction to the pad or component body at the worst-case site, secure the wire, and compare the coolest and hottest curves. Adjust the soak or peak only after confirming the measurement location.

takeaways: Attach thermocouples to the joint or body under test, because a junction on a convenient pad measures a board you do not build.
Find the coolest and hottest sites together, since one thermocouple can pass a survey that fails at the ground plane.
Record the attachment method and location with every survey, or the next run cannot be compared with this one.

mistakes.mistake: Surveying a bare coupon or test strip
mistakes.instead: Use a coupon with the production copper and components, or a sacrificial production panel.

mistakes.mistake: Reading the oven display as joint temperature
mistakes.instead: Measure on the board, because setpoints say nothing about joint thermal lag.

mistakes.mistake: Changing the profile before checking the attachment
mistakes.instead: Confirm the junction is secure and correctly placed, then adjust the oven.

terms.def: A recorded temperature history from thermocouples on a representative board.
A sample board that reproduces the production laminate, copper and component mass.
The delay between oven air temperature and the temperature reached at the joint.
The location on the board that reaches the lowest or the highest temperature.
