title: Board thermal mass and layout: heavy planes, thermal relief, mixed population, dense vs sparse

goals.text: Build a profile for a given board thermal mass and alloy and check ramp, time above liquidus and peak against limits taken from the cited source.

blocks.alt: Two board layouts side by side, one dense with heavy copper planes and one sparse, with a thermal mass indicator on each
blocks.caption: Board thermal mass and layout: heavy planes, thermal relief, mixed population, dense versus sparse

theory.h: Thermal mass controls the board's response
p: Board thermal mass is the combined heat capacity and heat-transfer resistance of the laminate, copper planes, plated holes, components and fixtures. A thick board with heavy copper reaches oven temperature more slowly than a thin board with sparse copper, so one recipe yields different joint temperatures.
Measure at the pad or component body rather than the oven air, and check the result against the paste and component datasheets.

theory.h: Heavy planes act as heat sinks at the joint
p: Large power and ground planes pull heat away from small pads and can hold a joint below liquidus while the joints around it look normal. The effect peaks when a pad ties directly to a plane with little thermal relief, when the plane sits on an inner layer with short vias, or when the component carries high thermal mass.
Balance the heat flow through pad geometry, paste volume, preheat and airflow instead of simply raising peak temperature.

theory.h: Thermal relief is a heat-balance tool
p: Thermal relief spokes cut the copper area feeding heat away from a pad, which makes the pad easier to lift above liquidus. The relief still has to deliver electrical and mechanical integrity, so spoke count, width and clearance follow the board design rules and the stencil design.
On heavy planes, confirm that the pad reaches liquidus with the chosen paste and component. If it does not, adjust the profile or the layout before raising peak temperature.

theory.h: Mixed populations need a compromise profile
p: A board with large connectors, QFNs, BGAs and small chips holds joints that want different heat input. Large components and heavy planes need enough soak and time above liquidus, while small parts suffer from excessive peak or a long soak.
Build the profile around the most thermally demanding joint and the lowest component temperature limit, then confirm that every part stays inside its own specified limits.

theory.h: Dense and sparse layouts heat differently
p: Dense boards with many components and copper areas heat more uniformly and often need more total energy to reach liquidus. Sparse boards heat quickly and can develop local hot spots near small components or exposed copper.
When one recipe covers different panel designs, compare pad-level profiles, because oven air temperature hides the differences between dense and sparse areas.
For lead-free paste, take the liquidus from the paste datasheet, then set time above liquidus and peak against the applicable standard and the component limits.

The average ramp of 1-3 °C/s comes from IPC-7530 and the paste datasheet. The 60-150 s time-above-liquidus window is J-STD-020 tL, which IPC-7530 typically narrows to 30-90 s. J-STD-020 supplies the classification temperatures that bound the peak: 260 °C small, 250 °C large and 245 °C very large at 1.6-2.5 mm thickness, where the full table is thickness times volume, every volume is 260 °C below 1.6 mm, and above 2.5 mm the limits fall to 250 °C small and 245 °C large and very large. Each carries tp, the time within 5 °C of that temperature, limited to 30 s. Verify the package size, the component datasheet and the paste supplier's recommendation.

When heavy planes hold pad temperature down, lengthen the soak or slow the conveyor to raise the board temperature before liquidus, then confirm that peak and time above liquidus stay inside their limits. Where sparse areas overheat, lower peak or reflow-zone airflow and let preheat bring the whole board up together.
Document thermocouple location, board thickness, copper weight, alloy, and the measured ramp, time above liquidus and peak, so the result can be repeated.

calc.task: A 1.8 mm board with 2 oz copper power planes uses SAC305 paste with solidus 217 °C and liquidus 219 °C. The component limit is the J-STD-020 classification temperature for the package size. A pad-level profile shows ramp from 150 °C to 219 °C in 37 s, time above 219 °C of 85 s, and peak 238 °C. Build and check the profile.
calc.solution: 1. Confirm alloy liquidus: SAC305 solidus 217 °C and liquidus 219 °C from the paste datasheet; time above liquidus is measured from the 219 °C crossing. 2. Apply limits: ramp 1-3 °C/s from IPC-7530 and the paste datasheet; time above liquidus 60-150 s as the J-STD-020 classification window, narrowed to IPC-7530 typical guidance of 30-90 s; the peak ceiling is the J-STD-020 classification temperature for the package size, 250 °C for a large package. 3. Calculate ramp: (219 - 150) / 37 = 1.86 °C/s. 4. Check ramp: 1.86 °C/s is within 1-3 °C/s. 5. Check time above liquidus: 85 s is within 60-150 s. 6. Check peak: 238 °C is below the 250 °C classification temperature and above liquidus by 19 °C. 7. Decision: the profile passes the cited limits, but heavy planes require pad-level confirmation; if pad temperature is low, increase soak or reduce conveyor speed and recheck peak and time above liquidus.

defect.symptom: After reflow, QFN pads on a 2 oz copper plane show incomplete wetting or lifted leads, while small chip components in sparse areas show discoloration or overheating.
defect.cause: The oven profile was tuned to air temperature, and the heavy plane heat sink kept the QFN pad below liquidus; sparse areas heated faster and exceeded the component limit.
defect.action: Profile at the pad, increase soak or reduce conveyor speed to raise pad temperature before liquidus, adjust airflow or zone setpoints, and verify against paste and component limits; if needed, add thermal relief or paste volume and requalify.

takeaways: Profile the hardest joint, because the coolest pad under a heavy plane decides whether the assembly is sound.
Balance heat flow with soak, conveyor speed and thermal relief before raising peak, since a higher peak damages the sparse areas first.
Record thickness and copper weight with the profile, because those numbers explain why the same recipe behaves differently on the next board.

mistakes.mistake: Raising peak temperature to wet one plane-tied pad
mistakes.instead: Lengthen the soak or slow the conveyor, and check the sparse areas for overexposure.

mistakes.mistake: Adding thermal relief after the profile is fixed
mistakes.instead: Design the relief with the electrical and mechanical rules, then requalify the profile.

mistakes.mistake: Copying a recipe between boards of different thickness
mistakes.instead: Measure the new board, because thermal mass changes the whole curve.

terms.def: The heat capacity of the board and its parts, which sets how fast they heat and cool.
Spokes in a plane connection that reduce heat flow into or out of a pad.
A large copper area that conducts heat away from a joint.
A temperature record taken at the joint rather than at the oven air.

title: Alloy systems and profile families: SnAgCu vs SnPb, liquidus basis, nitrogen vs air

goals.text: Build a profile for a given board thermal mass and alloy and check ramp, time above liquidus and peak against limits taken from the cited source.

blocks.alt: Two thermal profile curves overlaid, one for a SAC-type alloy and one for a tin-lead eutectic, with each liquidus marked
blocks.caption: Alloy systems and profile families: SAC305 versus SnPb on a liquidus basis, and nitrogen versus air

p: SnPb eutectic paste is commonly associated with a liquidus of 183 C, while SAC305 is a near-eutectic alloy with a solidus of 217 °C and a liquidus of 219 C.

Those values come from the alloy and paste datasheet, not from J-STD-020, which supplies classification temperatures rather than melting data. The liquidus is where the alloy becomes fully molten, so time above liquidus is measured from the board thermocouple crossing that value, never from the oven setpoint.

theory.h: Alloy families set different thermal budgets
p: SnPb profiles usually run a lower peak, because the J-STD-020 classification temperature for SnPb eutectic is 235 °C for a package thinner than 2.5 mm with a volume below 350 mm³ and 220 °C in every other case.

SAC305 profiles run higher: 260 °C for small packages, 250 °C for large and 245 °C for very large at 1.6-2.5 mm thickness, where the full table is thickness times volume, every volume allows 260 °C below 1.6 mm, and above 2.5 mm the limits fall to 250 °C small and 245 °C large and very large. The practical target peak comes from paste wetting, component rating and board stress, then gets checked against the classification limit.

theory.h: Ramp and soak control flux and gradients
p: IPC-7530B gives typical guidance such as 1-3 °C/s ramp and a soak that reduces thermal gradients.

Heavy boards, large ground planes and dense components need a slower ramp or a longer soak, so the coldest joint reaches liquidus without overheating the hottest. Verify the chosen ramp and soak against the paste and oven datasheets.

theory.h: Time above liquidus is a joint-quality window
p: IPC-7530B gives typical guidance of 30-90 s above liquidus. The 60-120 s figure often quoted beside it is the soak, ts, the time from Tsmin to Tsmax in the J-STD-020 classification profile, not the time above liquidus.

That window allows wetting and intermetallic formation without exhausting the flux or growing intermetallic to excess. Heavy thermal mass may need longer above liquidus, but the limit gets checked against the paste datasheet and component moisture sensitivity.

theory.h: Peak temperature is a ceiling, not a target
p: A SnAgCu peak of 245 °C may be acceptable if the measured board temperature stays below the J-STD-020 classification temperature for the package size — 260 °C small, 250 °C large, 245 °C very large on the 1.6-2.5 mm row, with above 2.5 mm falling to 250 °C small and 245 °C large and very large — and the paste datasheet supports it.
Measure the peak at the joint rather than in the oven air, because board thermal mass and thermocouple placement both shift the apparent value.

theory.h: Nitrogen changes oxidation, not the liquidus
p: Nitrogen reflow cuts oxide formation on paste and pads, which can improve wetting and may allow a lower peak or a shorter time above liquidus. It does not move the SnAgCu liquidus of 219 °C (217 °C is the solidus) or the SnPb liquidus of 183 C.
Verify oxygen level, gas flow and chamber uniformity, because nitrogen also changes heat transfer and profile repeatability.

theory.h: Build the profile from measured board data
p: For a given board thermal mass, attach thermocouples to representative joints, ground planes and component leads. Record ramp rate, time above liquidus and peak.

Compare the measured values with IPC-7530B guidance and the IPC/JEDEC J-STD-020 classification limits, then adjust zones until the coldest joint meets wetting requirements without the hottest joint exceeding its limit.

calc.task: A board with measured thermal mass 90 J/K is reflowed with SnAgCu paste in air. The oven can deliver about 100 W to the board during ramp. The measured profile shows a ramp from 150 °C to 219 °C in 60 s, a time above 219 °C of 75 s, and a peak of 245 C. Build the expected ramp from thermal mass and check ramp, time above liquidus, and peak against IPC-7530B guidance and IPC/JEDEC J-STD-020 limits.
calc.solution: 1. Use the SAC305 liquidus of 219 °C from the paste datasheet as the reference for time above liquidus; 217 °C is the solidus. 2. Estimate ramp rate from heat input and thermal mass: ramp rate = 100 W / 90 J/K = 1.1 °C/s. 3. Estimate time from 150 °C to 219 °C: (219 - 150) / 1.1 = 63 s. This is close to the measured 60 s. 4. Check ramp against IPC-7530B typical guidance of 1-3 °C/s: 1.1 °C/s is within the guidance. 5. Check time above liquidus against IPC-7530B typical guidance of 30-90 s: measured 75 s is within the guidance and clears the J-STD-020 tL minimum of 60 s. 6. Check peak against the J-STD-020 classification temperature for the package size (260 °C small, 250 °C large, 245 °C very large (1.6-2.5 mm row; above 2.5 mm thickness the limits fall to 250 °C small and 245 °C large and very large)): measured 245 °C is below the limit for small and large packages and exactly at the limit for very large packages, so confirm the package size. 7. Confirm the 245 °C peak is supported by the paste datasheet and component temperature ratings; if the board is run in nitrogen, re-run the profile because wetting and heat transfer may shift.

defect.symptom: Small solder balls appear around pads on a heavy ground-plane area after reflow, while the joints themselves look wetted.
defect.cause: The ramp was too fast or the soak was too short for the local thermal mass, causing flux and solvent to boil violently and eject paste material before the joint reached liquidus.
defect.action: Reduce the ramp rate toward IPC-7530B guidance, extend the soak, verify thermocouple placement on the heavy area, and re-run the profile while checking the paste datasheet for recommended ramp and soak limits.

takeaways: Read the liquidus from the paste datasheet for the alloy in use, because J-STD-020 classifies packages and does not give melting data.
Keep the alloy's thermal budget separate from its classification ceiling, since the second bounds the first rather than replacing it.
Re-profile after switching to nitrogen, because the gas changes heat transfer even when the liquidus stays the same.

mistakes.mistake: Quoting a single peak for both SnPb and SAC305 assemblies
mistakes.instead: Check the J-STD-020 classification temperature for the alloy and package, which differ substantially.

mistakes.mistake: Measuring time above liquidus from setpoints
mistakes.instead: Take it from the board thermocouple crossing the alloy liquidus.

mistakes.mistake: Treating the 60-120 s figure as time above liquidus
mistakes.instead: That is the J-STD-020 soak window ts, not the molten time.

terms.def: The temperature below which an alloy is fully solid.
An alloy close to the composition with the lowest melting point in its system.
Reflow in a nitrogen atmosphere that limits oxide formation during melting.
The peak temperature J-STD-020 permits for a package, by thickness and volume.

title: Reflow defect atlas: tombstone, balling, beading, dewetting, voids, distortion

goals.text: Link a defect signature to a profile zone and propose a bounded change with verification.

blocks.alt: Six small joint views labelled with each reflow defect, shown beside a sound joint for comparison
blocks.caption: Reflow defect atlas: tombstone, balling, beading, dewetting, voids and distortion

p: A reflow profile reads as a sequence of zones: preheat, soak, reflow, cooling. Tombstone and beading usually point to preheat or soak imbalance, balling and dewetting to reflow wetting or surface condition, voids to trapped flux or paste rheology, and distortion to cooling restraint or uneven thermal mass.
Link the observed signature to the zone where the defect most likely forms before changing the profile.
Tombstone stands a small chip on end because one pad wets before the other. Beading leaves a rounded ball or bead at a pad edge when wetting is uneven or paste collapses.

Pad thermal imbalance, paste collapse and a ramp that brings the pads to liquidus at different times all drive them. Check pad copper balance, paste volume and preheat ramp against your paste and equipment datasheet.

Balling is a discrete ball separate from the joint, often from paste collapse, excessive preheat, or contamination that prevents coalescence. Dewetting wets the joint and then pulls back, leaving a thin film or an irregular edge.
Dewetting points to surface finish damage, oxide, or a soak too short for flux activity. Compare the defect location with pad finish, storage time and soak behaviour.
Voids are trapped gas or flux residue inside the joint, usually visible by X-ray, and they grow when paste rheology, stencil aperture or ramp rate traps volatiles before the joint closes.

Distortion is board or component movement in reflow, from uneven heating, fixture restraint or cooling contraction. Voids need X-ray or cross-section to confirm, and distortion needs dimensional measurement and a fixture review.

theory.h: From signature to a bounded change
p: A bounded change modifies one profile or process variable and then verifies the result. For tombstone it might reduce ramp rate or extend the soak to balance pad temperature; for dewetting it might adjust soak time or surface cleanliness.
Avoid changing ramp, soak, peak and cooling together unless the failure mode is clearly coupled.
Verification includes thermocouple traces on the suspect pad and a reference pad, visual inspection against the IPC visual acceptance standard, and X-ray or cross-section where voids are suspected.

Accept the change only when the signature is absent on a trial article and the profile stays inside the paste and equipment limits. Record the accepted change with the board, paste, stencil and oven settings.
Values such as ramp rate, soak time and pad thermal relief size are starting points, verified against your paste and equipment datasheet.

The datasheet controls the allowable profile window, and the defect atlas says which zone to adjust. When a change pushes the profile outside the window, stop and re-evaluate paste, stencil, layout or fixture before adding more profile changes.

calc.task: A small chip resistor tombstones on a board where the left pad is isolated and the right pad connects to a copper plane through a thermal relief. Estimate whether pad thermal imbalance is plausible, then propose a bounded profile change and verification.
calc.solution: Start by estimating effective pad area. Assume the isolated pad effective area is 0.30 mm^2 and the plane pad effective area is 0.60 mm^2. The area ratio is 0.60 / 0.30 = 2.0. Copper thickness 35 µm and laminate thickness 1.6 mm are typical starting values; verify against your stack-up. If the plane pad uses a 0.3 mm thermal relief, the plane pad may still have greater thermal mass than the isolated pad, so it can reach liquidus later and increase tombstone risk. Propose a bounded change: reduce ramp rate from 2.0 °C/s to 1.5 °C/s and extend soak by 10 s, not more than 20 s, if paste and oven limits allow. Verify with thermocouples on the suspect pad and a reference pad; confirm pad-to-pad temperature difference before liquidus is reduced. Inspect a trial article against the IPC visual acceptance standard and X-ray if voids are suspected. If tombstone persists, review layout copper balance or paste volume rather than continuing to extend soak.

defect.symptom: Small chip resistor stands on end after reflow, with one terminal soldered and the other lifted.
defect.cause: Pad thermal imbalance and wetting imbalance during reflow; the pad with lower thermal mass reaches liquidus earlier, solder wets that side earlier, and surface tension pulls the component upright.
defect.action: Reduce ramp rate and extend soak within paste and oven limits; add thermal relief or copper balance if layout change is allowed; verify with thermocouple and trial article inspection against the IPC visual acceptance standard.

takeaways: Name the zone from the defect signature before touching the oven, because that choice determines which variable you are allowed to change.
Change one profile variable at a time and verify it on a trial article, unless the failure mode is genuinely coupled.
Treat ramp and soak values as starting points and confirm the limit against the paste and equipment datasheet.

mistakes.mistake: Extending the soak for every tombstone
mistakes.instead: Check pad copper balance and paste volume first, since thermal imbalance is a layout problem.

mistakes.mistake: Chasing voids with a slower ramp alone
mistakes.instead: Review paste rheology, aperture and stencil design with X-ray evidence.

mistakes.mistake: Adjusting ramp, soak and peak in one trial
mistakes.instead: Change one variable, or the result cannot be attributed to any of them.

terms.def: A chip component standing on one end after reflow because one joint wetted first.
Solder that wets and then retracts, leaving a thin irregular film on the pad.
A cavity of trapped gas or flux residue inside a solder joint.
A single, limited change to the process that can be verified against a defined outcome.

title: Profile validation, documentation and change control

goals.text: Evaluate a measured profile and name which zone to change, in which direction, with the expected joint effect.
Link a defect signature to a profile zone and propose a bounded change with verification.

blocks.alt: A validated profile record with thermocouple locations and measured data, beside a change-control request routing the revision
blocks.caption: Profile validation, documentation and change control

p: Profile validation checks whether the measured thermal history at the joint matches the paste, component and board constraints. Put thermocouples on representative joints, not only in the oven air.
Compare the measured curve with the paste datasheet and the component moisture sensitivity limits from the applicable IPC moisture sensitivity guidance.

A reflow profile is reviewed zone by zone. Preheat controls solvent evaporation and prevents thermal shock. Soak activates flux and equalises board temperature. Reflow creates wetting and intermetallic formation. Cooling controls solidification and residual stress.
Each zone gives a different lever, so naming the zone first keeps the adjustment small.
Validation records the location of every thermocouple, the board orientation, the carrier or pallet, the oven setpoints and the measured peak temperature.
A profile is invalid if the thermocouple is loose, the joint is unrepresentative, or the measurement comes from a heavily loaded board with no check against a lightly loaded one.
Attachment affects the result. Use a high-temperature adhesive or a solder point on the joint, and confirm the sensor is not lifted by conveyor vibration.
Measure several joints across the board, because thermal mass and airflow create gradients. On a multi-zone oven, record the measured curve rather than trusting the setpoints.

theory.p: When a signature points to a zone, choose the smallest change that tests the hypothesis. Poor wetting makes the reflow zone the first candidate. A joint that stays cold needs more energy in preheat or soak. Tombstoning points to preheat and soak being too aggressive, or to uneven cooling.

p: Bounded change control means changing one profile variable, recording the old and new values, and verifying with measurement and inspection.
If time above liquidus is short, raise the peak slightly or slow the cooling, then confirm the joint still meets the acceptance criteria in the applicable IPC acceptance guidance.
Document the measured profile, the thermocouple map, the paste lot, the board stackup, the oven recipe, the change reason, the verification data and the disposition.

That record makes the change auditable and stops the next shift repeating the trial and error. Where the change touches moisture-sensitive components, check the applicable IPC moisture sensitivity guidance before releasing the recipe.
Change control separates a recipe adjustment from a process qualification.

A small bounded adjustment is proven by profile measurement and joint inspection. A larger change — new paste, new board design, new oven — needs a formal qualification with statistical confidence and acceptance evidence.

calc.task: A measured lead-free paste profile shows ramp 1.6 °C/s, soak 150-190 °C for 90 s, time above liquidus 45 s, peak 242 °C, cooling 3.0 °C/s. The paste datasheet gives a solidus of 217 °C and a liquidus of 219 °C, recommended time above liquidus 60-90 s, and a recommended peak band of 235-245 °C that must stay below the component's J-STD-020 classification temperature. Evaluate the profile and propose a bounded change.
calc.solution: The measured time above liquidus is 45 s, which is below the datasheet range 60-90 s. The measured peak is 242 °C, which is inside the datasheet band 235-245 °C but only 3 °C below its top, and well below the 250 °C classification temperature of a large package. The soak range 150-190 °C is within the typical window, so the defect signature of dull, grainy, non-wet joints points to the reflow zone rather than the soak zone. Propose a bounded change: raise the peak by 2-3 °C to 244-245 °C, staying at the top of the band and clear of the ceiling, and reduce cooling from 3.0 °C/s to 2.5 °C/s to extend time above liquidus to 60-70 s. Verify against the paste and oven datasheet. Expected joint effect: improved wetting and more complete intermetallic formation, reducing cold solder joints. Risk: excessive peak can damage components or cause solder balling, and excessive slow cooling can enlarge grain size. Verification: remeasure the thermocouple profile, inspect joints against IPC acceptance guidance, check tombstoning and solder balling, and record the change in the recipe document.

defect.symptom: Dull, grainy joints with non-wet pads and insufficient fillet on a board that otherwise shows correct placement and paste volume.
defect.cause: Short time above liquidus and low peak temperature in the reflow zone, leaving incomplete wetting and weak intermetallic formation.
defect.action: Raise the peak temperature within the paste datasheet limit and extend time above liquidus by a bounded amount, then remeasure the profile and inspect joints against IPC acceptance guidance.

takeaways: Validate at the joint with a documented thermocouple map, because a loose or unrepresentative sensor invalidates the run.
Change one profile variable and verify it, so the result can be attributed and the recipe stays inside its limits.
Separate a bounded adjustment from a qualification, since a new paste or oven cannot be proven by a profile alone.

mistakes.mistake: Accepting a profile measured with a detached thermocouple
mistakes.instead: Confirm sensor attachment and location before trusting any curve.

mistakes.mistake: Treating a new paste as a recipe adjustment
mistakes.instead: Run a formal qualification with statistical evidence for a material change.

mistakes.mistake: Changing the peak and the cooling rate together
mistakes.instead: Change one variable at a time, then re-measure both time above liquidus and peak.

terms.def: The record of where each thermocouple was attached and what it measured.
A small, bounded change to oven settings verified by profile and inspection.
Formal evidence that a process meets requirements under defined conditions.
Changing one variable at a time and verifying the outcome before the next change.

title: What each method can see: visual, AOI, 2D X-ray, laminar/3D, boundary scan

goals.text: Choose the inspection method (visual, AOI, 2D X-ray, laminar/3D X-ray, boundary scan) for a stated defect and board feature.

p: Visual inspection, with or without magnification, catches defects that are exposed: missing or wrong components, polarity errors, tombstoned chips, visible bridges on exposed pads, insufficient or excess solder on through-hole leads, mechanical damage, contamination and flux residue.

It suits gross assembly errors and cosmetic acceptability under IPC-A-610, and it cannot reliably judge joints hidden under packages, bottom terminations, BGA balls, QFN wettable flanks, stacked layers, internal voids or barrel fill that no eye can reach.

blocks.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 900 220' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='Inspection coverage stack'><style>text{font-family:'IBM Plex Mono',monospace}</style><rect x='120' y='40' width='660' height='40' rx='10' fill='rgba(83,209,204,.18)' stroke='#53d1cc' stroke-width='1.5'/><rect x='180' y='90' width='540' height='40' rx='10' fill='rgba(83,209,204,.12)' stroke='rgba(83,209,204,.5)' stroke-width='1.5'/><rect x='240' y='140' width='420' height='40' rx='10' fill='rgba(255,152,0,.1)' stroke='#ff9800' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='450' y='65' fill='#edf2f7' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle'>SPI (POST-PRINT) — PASTE VOLUME, HEIGHT, AREA</text><text x='450' y='115' fill='#edf2f7' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle'>AOI POST-PLACEMENT — MISSING, TILT, POLARITY</text><text x='450' y='165' fill='#ff9800' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle'>AOI POST-REFLOW + X-RAY — JOINT QUALITY, HIDDEN</text><text x='450' y='205' fill='#94a3b8' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle'>EVERY LAYER YOU SKIP MOVES ESCAPES DOWNSTREAM</text></svg>
blocks.caption: Inspection layers: each catches a different defect family

blocks.alt: Five stacked inspection bands showing visual, AOI, 2D X-ray of a BGA with voids, laminar 3D slice and a boundary scan chain
blocks.caption: Inspection layers: what visual, AOI, 2D X-ray, laminar 3D and boundary scan can each see

p: Automated optical inspection uses cameras, lighting and image analysis on exposed top and bottom features. It finds component presence, polarity, orientation, wrong and missing parts, tombstoning, visible bridges, coplanarity problems and some fillet or wettable flank features where lighting and 3D height mapping are good enough.

AOI is fast for inline screening, and it misses what sits under a package, behind a tall component, inside a BGA or QFN termination or down a barrel. Check lighting, angle and resolution against the equipment datasheet.

theory.p: 2D X-ray produces a transmission projection and is used when the defect is hidden from optical methods. It can reveal BGA, QFN, PLCC, and CSP termination geometry, missing or collapsed balls, opens, shorts, misalignment, voids, and through-hole barrel fill. Because the image superimposes layers, void size, depth, and bridging location can be ambiguous, and thin wettable flanks may be difficult to judge when overlapped by traces or adjacent balls. Use 2D X-ray for screening hidden joints, and verify magnification and detector resolution against your equipment datasheet.

p: Laminar or 3D X-ray reconstructs slices or volumes, which gives depth discrimination no projection can. Use it to locate a void, estimate its size, inspect stacked packages, separate overlapping BGA rows, judge QFN wettable flanks or evaluate barrel fill in dense boards, and it supports the IPC-7095 guidance on hidden BGA features.

The costs are cycle time, capital, reconstruction artefacts and sensitivity to calibration, so reserve it for cases where 2D X-ray or AOI cannot settle the question, and do not run it as a routine replacement for 2D screening.

Boundary scan, usually JTAG, uses scan cells inside devices to observe and drive package pins. It detects opens and shorts on nets connected to scan-capable pins, which makes it valuable on dense BGA and QFN assemblies where optics are limited.

It does not inspect wetting, component value, non-scan nets, power and ground nets, analog nodes, memory arrays or joints under non-scan devices. It needs design-for-test access, a working scan chain and test vectors that exercise the nets you care about.

theory.h: Choosing from the defect and the feature
p: Match the method to what must be seen. Visual or AOI handles exposed top-side defects, visible through-hole leads, polarity, missing parts and visible bridges, and bottom-side AOI takes the underside.

2D X-ray covers hidden BGA, QFN, PLCC, CSP and barrel features. Laminar or 3D X-ray resolves void size, depth, stacking and overlapping geometry. Boundary scan covers opens and shorts on scan-capable nets in dense packages, combined with physical inspection for non-scan nets and solder quality.

No single method covers every defect. Optical methods depend on lighting, angle, component height and reflectivity; X-ray on magnification, resolution, focus, orientation and reconstruction; boundary scan on chain integrity and coverage.

Acceptance follows the customer-specified IPC-A-610 class and the relevant design guidance such as IPC-7351 and IPC-7525. Take practice-based limits from your equipment and paste datasheets rather than assuming one value.

calc.task: A 0.4 mm pitch BGA has 100 balls. 60 balls are connected to scan-capable signal nets, 20 are power or ground, and 20 are analog nets. The line suspects opens and shorts on signal nets and voiding under all balls. Choose the inspection methods and estimate boundary scan coverage.
calc.solution: First, classify the defects. Opens and shorts on scan-capable signal nets can be tested electrically by boundary scan. Voiding under all balls is a hidden physical defect and requires X-ray. Second, estimate boundary scan coverage. Scan-capable signal balls = 60. Total balls = 100. Coverage = 60/100 = 0.60. Third, interpret coverage. Boundary scan can test 0.60 of the balls for opens and shorts on scan nets, but it does not test the 20 power or ground balls, the 20 analog balls, or solder voiding under any ball. Fourth, choose physical inspection. Use 2D X-ray to screen hidden BGA balls and voids. Use laminar/3D X-ray if void size, depth, or overlapping rows must be measured. Fifth, combine methods. Use boundary scan for scan-net opens and shorts, 2D X-ray for hidden ball screening, and laminar/3D X-ray for ambiguous or acceptance-critical voids. Verify resolution and test coverage against your equipment datasheet and the customer-specified IPC-A-610 Acceptability Requirements for Electronic Assemblies class.

defect.symptom: Boundary scan fails on some scan-capable nets after reflow. AOI shows no visible BGA defect, and 2D X-ray shows collapsed or missing balls under the package.
defect.cause: Insufficient paste release or paste volume, stencil aperture area ratio outside the process window, paste slump, component coplanarity, or reflow profile that did not collapse the balls. Land pattern and stencil design may not match IPC-7351 Land Pattern Design Data Standard for Surface Mount and IPC-7525 Stencil Design Guidelines.
defect.action: Stop the line and quarantine the lot. Confirm the failure with boundary scan and 2D X-ray, then use laminar/3D X-ray to measure void size and ball collapse. Review stencil aperture area ratio, paste type, print pressure, squeegee speed, and reflow profile against IPC-7525 Stencil Design Guidelines and IPC-7095 Design and Assembly Process Implementation for BGAs. Verify ball coplanarity and land pattern, then re-run a qualification lot and accept results against the customer-specified IPC-A-610 Acceptability Requirements for Electronic Assemblies class.

takeaways: Choose the method from what must be seen, because an optical screen cannot answer a question about a joint under a package.
Combine electrical and physical inspection on dense packages, since boundary scan proves connectivity and not wetting.
Check the resolution and coverage limits of the chosen method before accepting its verdict.

mistakes.mistake: Relying on AOI to clear a BGA
mistakes.instead: Use X-ray for hidden terminations, because AOI cannot see under the package.

mistakes.mistake: Treating boundary scan as full joint inspection
mistakes.instead: It proves opens and shorts on scan nets and says nothing about wetting or voids.

mistakes.mistake: Using 2D X-ray to size a void
mistakes.instead: Use laminar or 3D X-ray, because projection overlays layers and distorts depth.

terms.def: An electrical test method that uses scan cells inside devices to drive and observe package pins.
A plated side feature on a QFN that lets optical inspection judge the fillet.
Tomographic X-ray that reconstructs a slice through the assembly.
A 2D X-ray image in which every layer contributes to the same picture.

title: AOI program setup: windows, lighting, thresholds, the false-call/escape trade-off

goals.text: Choose the inspection method (visual, AOI, 2D X-ray, laminar/3D X-ray, boundary scan) for a stated defect and board feature.
Compute escape rate, false-call rate and verification coverage from audit data and state their limits.

blocks.alt: An AOI camera view with component windows, lighting angles and a threshold slider, and a trade-off scale between false calls and escapes
blocks.caption: AOI program setup: windows, lighting, thresholds and the false-call / escape trade-off

theory.h: Match the method to the defect
p: AOI screens optically accessible features: component presence, polarity, tombstoning, skew, rotation, missing solder, visible fillet shape and some coplanarity issues. It is weak on hidden joints, voids, cracks under packages and internal package defects.

Take hidden defects to 2D X-ray or laminar and 3D X-ray: BGA voiding, QFN wetting, bridges under a package, internal lead separation. Take electrical opens and shorts to boundary scan where the nets can be exercised through scan logic, especially on dense BGA and fine-pitch devices, remembering that it does not replace physical inspection for mechanical and solder defects. Use visual inspection for unusual defects, program validation and verifying the AOI calls themselves.

theory.h: Windows define what AOI may see
p: An inspection window is the region assigned to a component or feature plus the expected model, fiducial alignment and tolerance. Windows should allow for placement tolerance, reflow shift, panel handling, warpage and component substitution.

Too tight a window calls a good board because the part shifted slightly. Too loose a window inspects the wrong area or misses a defect near the edge. Build windows from the land pattern and component outline, then validate them with golden boards and known defect samples. On panels, confirm that fiducials, rails and local alignment points stay stable across the panel and through reflow.

theory.h: Lighting and optics set the signal
p: Lighting angle, intensity, colour, focus and camera resolution decide whether a defect produces measurable contrast. Shiny solder, matte components, gold finishes, black packages and reflective pads each confuse a single-light program.

Multi-angle lighting, high dynamic range and separate solder and component channels improve discrimination at the cost of program complexity. Resolution in micrometres has to resolve the smallest feature that matters to the acceptability decision, verified against the equipment datasheet and a test coupon rather than a camera specification.
Thresholds are the numeric limits that convert measurements into pass or fail: solder area, solder height, contrast, coplanarity, pin count, polarity, tombstone angle, skew, rotation.

Derive them from the applicable acceptability standard for soldered assemblies, the land pattern data, the component datasheets and measured process variation. Default thresholds are a starting point, never a release condition. For each threshold record the golden-board value, the process variation, the defect sample value and the chosen limit. Where AOI cannot measure the physical criterion directly, use a surrogate and document its correlation.

theory.h: False calls and escapes are linked
p: Tightening thresholds cuts escapes and usually raises false calls; loosening them does the reverse.

The best setting is not the lowest false-call rate but the point where verification capacity, defect severity, escape cost and throughput balance. A high false-call rate hides real defects, because operators grow impatient and clear calls without verifying. A low one hides escapes behind a permissive program. Decide per defect type, from severity and downstream impact, and expect practice-based false-call rates anywhere from low single digits to higher percentages per board depending on mix and program maturity.

Escape rate, false-call rate and verification coverage only mean something with clear definitions. A call is any AOI output requiring review; a true call is a verified defect; a false call is a verified non-defect.

An escape is a defect AOI did not call but a later audit, test or field return found. Verification coverage is the fraction of calls actually reviewed, and incomplete coverage leaves every estimate uncertain. An audit that samples certain boards, defect types or shifts speaks only for that population.

Sample size, timing and detection capability all bound the metrics. Escapes found after the audit window are missing unless the data are updated, and downstream inspection and test can miss defects, so a measured escape rate is a lower bound.

False calls go underreported when operators clear them without logging. Different board mixes, component substitutions and program revisions change what the same percentage means. Report the denominator, the time window, the board mix and the verification coverage with every rate.

calc.task: A line audits 10000 boards after AOI. AOI made 500 calls. Operators verified 450 calls and found 150 true defects and 300 false calls. The remaining 50 calls were not verified. A downstream audit found 20 escapes that AOI did not call. Compute verification coverage, false-call rate, and escape rate, and state the limits.
calc.solution: First, verification coverage = verified calls / total calls = 450 / 500 = 90 percent. Second, false-call rate among verified calls = false calls / verified calls = 300 / 450 = 66.7 percent. False calls per inspected board = 300 / 10000 = 3.0 percent. If the unverified calls are assumed to have the same false-call rate as verified calls, estimated false calls in the unverified calls = 50 * 300 / 450 = 33.3, total estimated false calls = 333.3, false-call rate among all calls = 333.3 / 500 = 66.7 percent, and estimated false calls per inspected board = 333.3 / 10000 = 3.3 percent. Third, escape rate using verified true calls only = escapes / (verified true calls + escapes) = 20 / (150 + 20) = 11.8 percent. If all 50 unverified calls were false, the escape rate remains 11.8 percent. If all 50 unverified calls were true, true calls = 200 and escape rate = 20 / (200 + 20) = 9.1 percent. If unverified calls are assumed to have the same true-call rate as verified calls, estimated true calls = 150 + 50 * 150 / 450 = 166.7, and estimated escape rate = 20 / (166.7 + 20) = 10.7 percent. Escapes per inspected board = 20 / 10000 = 0.2 percent. Limits: the 90 percent coverage means 50 calls are unverified, so the true false-call and escape rates are uncertain. The downstream audit may miss escapes, so the escape rate is a lower bound. The audit covers only 10000 boards and the sampled board mix, so the rates may not apply to other mixes or program revisions.

defect.symptom: AOI repeatedly calls missing solder fillet on small chip capacitors after reflow, but manual verification finds acceptable solder.
defect.cause: The inspection window was too tight for normal reflow shift, and the solder channel exposure was too high, so the fillet contrast fell below the threshold.
defect.action: Measure the actual placement and reflow shift in millimeters, widen the window to cover the verified variation, reduce or rebalance the solder lighting exposure, retrain the fillet threshold from golden and defect samples, then run a verification audit before releasing the program.

takeaways: Define call, true call, false call and escape before quoting a rate, because each number depends on those definitions.
Balance false calls against escapes at the point verification capacity allows, not at the lowest false-call figure.
Report coverage and the board mix beside every rate, since an incomplete audit understates what it cannot see.

mistakes.mistake: Tightening thresholds until the false-call report looks clean
mistakes.instead: Check the escape data as well, because the two move in opposite directions.

mistakes.mistake: Quoting an escape rate from incomplete verification coverage
mistakes.instead: State the coverage, or the rate describes only the calls someone happened to review.

mistakes.mistake: Comparing defect rates across program revisions
mistakes.instead: Rebaseline after a program or board-mix change, since the denominator moved.

terms.def: A defect the inspection did not call and a later stage or the field found.
An inspection call that verification shows was not a defect.
The share of inspection calls that were actually reviewed.
A known-good reference board used to build and check the inspection program.

title: AOI metrics: escape rate, false calls, first-pass yield, verification workflow

goals.text: Compute escape rate, false-call rate and verification coverage from audit data and state their limits.

blocks.alt: An audit workflow diagram linking inspection result, verification call and disposition, with escape rate and false-call rate readouts
blocks.caption: AOI metrics: escape rate, false calls, first-pass yield and the verification workflow

p: AOI metrics are process indicators built from audit data, not direct measurements of the true defect population. AOI screens, so its reported rejects, passes and escapes depend on program setup, optics, lighting, the component library, panel design, paste, reflow and operator verification.

Stratify the metrics by product, line, shift, program version and defect type before using them for a decision. They are most useful compared over time within one product family, and paired with downstream test, rework and field data. A metric that looks good at the AOI station is incomplete when downstream steps mask defects or nobody audits verification.
Review escape rate, false-call rate, verification coverage and first-pass yield as a set rather than as isolated station scores.

Escape rate is usually defects found after AOI divided by the units, panels or component opportunities inspected. Match the denominator to the question: board-level escapes use boards, joint-level use joints, component-level use components.

Downstream sources include in-circuit test, functional test, manual visual audit, X-ray, rework and field returns. Its limits are the detection capability of those steps, escapes below AOI resolution, intermittent defects, and the time lag before field returns appear.

A low escape rate can mean good detection, downstream masking, or weak downstream detection. Where the downstream audit is weak the rate understates the problem, and where the denominator is too broad a few escapes look insignificant while one component or panel location is failing.
False-call rate is verified good rejects divided by verified AOI rejects. It needs a verification workflow that dispositions every reject as true defect, false call, marginal or other.

Incomplete coverage turns the rate into an estimate from the verified subset, reliable only when that subset represents all rejects. Operator bias, marginal acceptance, duplicate rejects, program changes and differences between the AOI image and the physical board all bend it.

A false call is not automatically waste: some flag marginal conditions that later escape. It can also show that the program is too sensitive for the current paste, stencil or placement process. Keep the disposition categories stable, because redefining them moves the rate without any process change.
First-pass yield is units completed without rework or repair divided by units started.

In the AOI context, separate AOI pass yield, which penalises every AOI reject including false calls, from line first-pass yield, which depends on the final disposition after verification and downstream test. FPY misleads when rework loops, duplicate boards, batch holds or late dispositions are counted inconsistently.

A high FPY with poor verification coverage may hide escapes, and a lower FPY with strong verification may simply reflect better detection. Pair FPY with escape and false-call rates to see whether yield improved because defects were prevented or because detection was relaxed, and keep definitions identical across shifts and products.
A practical workflow runs from the AOI reject to a review of the image and the physical board to a disposition against documented visual acceptance criteria.

Verification coverage is verified rejects divided by total AOI rejects, and it should include random samples of passes, because pass audits estimate the escapes downstream may not catch. Coverage weakens when only high-risk rejects are verified, when operators verify only obvious defects, or when the AOI image is accepted without physical confirmation.

Report coverage beside the false-call rate so the estimate can be read, and add disagreement audits where a second inspector reviews a sample of dispositions, plus clear rules for marginal cases. Otherwise coverage can be high in count and poor in quality.
All three metrics are proportions, so small denominators give unstable results: a few defects in a small audit move the rate substantially.

Control charts, confidence intervals and Pareto analysis by defect type, component, package, panel location, shift and program version say more than a single weekly number. Compare similar products run on similar programs.

Set practice-based thresholds from historical capability, customer requirements and equipment datasheets, and check them against your paste and equipment datasheet. Review them whenever product mix, AOI program, stencil, paste or reflow profile changes, because a target that holds for one family may be wrong for another whose density, packages and panel design differ.
False-call reduction usually starts with program tuning, lighting, fiducial quality, panel layout, component library accuracy and thresholds.

Escape reduction may need better AOI coverage, added X-ray or functional test, and correction of paste, stencil, placement or reflow variation. Coverage improves with training, clear acceptance criteria, disagreement audits and sampled passes.

Let the metrics drive containment and prevention rather than reporting. On THT, AOI sees pin joints poorly, so read escape metrics with X-ray, functional test or manual audit data. Track improvement with before-and-after data on the same denominators and verification rules, so the team can tell whether detection improved, false calls fell, or the problem simply moved to another station.

calc.task: A line inspected 12000 boards through AOI during a week. AOI reported 360 rejects. Quality verified 300 rejects and found 90 false calls. Downstream test and visual audit found 18 defects after AOI. Compute escape rate, false-call rate, and verification coverage, and state the limits of each result.
calc.solution: Escape rate calculation: downstream defects divided by inspected boards = 18 / 12000 = 0.15 percent. This uses a board-level denominator; it does not represent joint-level escape rate and depends on downstream detection. False-call rate calculation: false calls divided by verified rejects = 90 / 300 = 30 percent. This is based on verified rejects only; if unverified rejects differ from verified rejects, the estimate is biased. Verification coverage calculation: verified rejects divided by AOI rejects = 300 / 360 = 83.3 percent. Coverage below full verification means false-call rate is an estimate, not a census. Interpretation: report the three metrics together. A false-call rate of 30 percent with 83.3 percent coverage should be stratified by defect type, component, package, panel location, shift, and program version before setting targets.

defect.symptom: AOI false-call rate rises after a new panel design, while escape rate stays low.
defect.cause: Panel deformation or fiducial variation causes image misalignment, and program thresholds are too tight for the new placement variation.
defect.action: Verify panel and fiducial quality, retune the AOI program with golden boards, audit verified rejects, and monitor false-call rate and verification coverage.

takeaways: Report escape rate, false-call rate and coverage together, because any one of them alone can be improved by worsening another.
Match the denominator to the level you are judging, since board, joint and component escapes answer different questions.
Keep definitions and stratification fixed across comparisons, or a program revision looks like a process improvement.

mistakes.mistake: Reading a falling escape rate as better AOI
mistakes.instead: Check downstream detection and audit coverage, because masking produces the same curve.

mistakes.mistake: Quoting a false-call rate from partial verification
mistakes.instead: State the coverage, or the number describes only the rejects someone verified.

mistakes.mistake: Comparing rates across products with different densities
mistakes.instead: Stratify by product family, since component density changes the detection challenge.

terms.def: Units completed without rework divided by units started.
Verified rejects divided by total AOI rejects, showing how much of the data was actually reviewed.
A second review of a sample of dispositions to test consistency.
Splitting a metric by product, line, shift or defect type so the population is comparable.

title: X-ray interpretation: BGA ball size and voiding, bridging, through-hole fill

goals.text: Classify a defect image into a defect type and an accept / rework / reject disposition with the criterion named.
Choose the inspection method (visual, AOI, 2D X-ray, laminar/3D X-ray, boundary scan) for a stated defect and board feature.

blocks.alt: An X-ray view of a BGA package showing ball size variation, voids and a bridge, beside an X-ray view of through-hole fill
blocks.caption: X-ray interpretation: BGA ball size and voiding, bridging and through-hole fill

p: A 2D X-ray image maps density: solder absorbs more than board laminate, and gas absorbs almost nothing. That is why a void appears dark inside a bright ball, and why a bridge appears as a bright path between two features that should be separate.

Read every image against a named criterion and a known feature size before calling anything. Magnification, detector resolution, focus and sample angle all change what the light and dark shapes appear to be.

Use 2D X-ray as the first method for hidden joints, and turn to laminar or 3D X-ray when overlapping features, multiple layers or true volumetric measurement are required. Boundary scan is not an imaging method: it tests selected digital interconnects electrically and finds opens or shorts only where the design supports it.

In a BGA image each ball should appear as a discrete, roughly circular feature of consistent diameter and spacing across the array. Ball size is read against the expected land pattern, paste volume, component specification and reflow profile.

A ball that is too small points to insufficient paste, paste bleed, poor stencil release or excessive reflow loss. One that is too large points to excessive paste, bleed between adjacent lands, or incomplete paste separation. IPC-7095 gives guidance on land pattern and paste printing design; verify the specific land size, aperture and volume against the component datasheet and your paste and equipment datasheet.

A void is a dark, low-density region inside a ball, because X-rays pass through gas more easily than through solder. Small voids are common and may be acceptable depending on size, location and product class.

IPC-A-610 carries the acceptability criteria for voids in solder balls, and for many Class 3 applications voids are commonly evaluated against a limit such as 25 % of the ball area, with the exact class, revision and customer requirement checked against IPC-A-610 and the contract. Voids at the outer edge of a ball, or voids coalescing across several balls, matter more than an isolated central void, because they cut the effective wetted area and raise thermal and mechanical risk.

theory.h: Bridging under BGA and fine-pitch parts
p: A bridge is a continuous high-density solder path joining two or more balls that should be isolated. On a BGA it often shows as a diagonal or horizontal line between adjacent balls near the array edge or under the die shadow.

Excessive paste volume, paste bleed, misalignment, collapsed balls and a ramp that lets solder flow laterally before wetting all cause it. IPC-7095 gives the land pattern and aperture design guidance; verify aperture size, pitch and stencil thickness against the paste and stencil datasheet. AOI may catch exposed bridges on fine-pitch QFN or QFP, while BGA bridges usually need X-ray.
Through-hole X-ray evaluates solder fill inside a plated hole, particularly when a component body, shielding or a second-side part hides the joint.

A sound through-hole joint shows solder wetting the pad, the hole wall and the lead, with a fill height suited to hole diameter and component class. IPC-A-610 carries the criteria for fill and voids, and for many Class 3 applications voids are commonly evaluated against a limit such as 25 % of the hole circumference, with class, revision and customer requirement confirmed against the standard and the contract. Verify hole diameter, lead diameter and required fill height against the board and component datasheets.
Visual inspection covers exposed joints, polarity, missing components, tombstoning and obvious solder defects. AOI covers exposed SMT placement, fillet shape, tombstoning and many exposed bridges.

A 2D X-ray covers BGA voiding, ball size, hidden bridging and simple through-hole fill where overlapping layers do not obscure the feature. Laminar or 3D X-ray takes over with stacked BGAs, dense routing, many layers, or when void volume and depth must be separated from overlapping features. Boundary scan covers selected digital interconnects where the design supports it, detecting some opens and shorts without replacing X-ray for solder geometry.
Disposition rests on a named criterion, never on appearance. Accept when the measured defect sits inside the applicable IPC-A-610 class and the customer requirement.

Rework when the defect is repairable and the design, package and thermal budget allow repair without damaging nearby features; a localised BGA bridge may be reworkable if the land pattern and component survive the process. Reject when the defect breaks the named criterion and cannot be reworked reliably: a void over the allowed area, a bridge that cannot come out without lifting pads, or a through-hole joint that cannot reach the required fill.
Record the standard, the class, the measured value and the disposition every time.

calc.task: A BGA solder ball has a measured diameter of 0.45 mm. The X-ray image shows a void with an estimated diameter of 0.22 mm. Using a circular approximation, calculate the void area as a percentage of the ball area and classify the defect against a named criterion. Assume the applicable requirement is IPC-A-610 Class 3, voids in solder balls shall not exceed 25% of the ball area, and verify the exact class and revision against the contract.
calc.solution: 1. Ball diameter D = 0.45 mm. Ball radius r_ball = 0.45 / 2 = 0.225 mm. 2. Ball area A_ball = pi * r_ball^2 = pi * (0.225)^2 = pi * 0.050625 = 0.1590 mm^2. 3. Void diameter d = 0.22 mm. Void radius r_void = 0.22 / 2 = 0.11 mm. 4. Void area A_void = pi * r_void^2 = pi * (0.11)^2 = pi * 0.0121 = 0.0380 mm^2. 5. Void percentage = (A_void / A_ball) * 100 = (0.0380 / 0.1590) * 100 = 23.9%. 6. Compare with IPC-A-610 Class 3 criterion: 23.9% is less than 25%. 7. Defect type: void in BGA solder ball. Disposition: accept, provided the void location and any additional voids are also within the applicable IPC-A-610 class and customer requirement.

defect.symptom: 2D X-ray shows a continuous high-density solder path connecting two adjacent BGA balls near the array edge. The balls are otherwise similar in size, but the bridge is located where paste apertures are close together.
defect.cause: Excessive paste volume or paste bleed between adjacent apertures, possibly caused by stencil thickness, aperture design, paste rheology, or reflow profile. IPC-7095 provides BGA land and paste design guidance; verify paste aperture size, stencil thickness, and release behavior against the paste and stencil datasheet.
defect.action: Confirm the bridge with 2D X-ray and, if overlapping features make the extent unclear, use laminar or 3D X-ray. If the bridge is repairable without lifting pads or damaging adjacent balls, rework and re-inspect by X-ray. If the bridge cannot be removed reliably, reject the board. Correct the process by reducing paste volume, adjusting stencil design, improving paste alignment, or modifying the reflow profile, then verify with X-ray and electrical test.

takeaways: Name the criterion and the class before judging an image, because the same void is acceptable in one class and a reject in another.
Compare measured feature sizes on the image itself, since magnification and angle change what the shapes appear to be.
Note the void location as well as its size, because an edge void threatens the joint more than a central one of equal area.

mistakes.mistake: Calling a void from a single 2D projection
mistakes.instead: Confirm size and depth with laminar or 3D X-ray when the joint is stacked or overlapped.

mistakes.mistake: Applying a 25 % void limit without checking the class
mistakes.instead: Read the applicability from IPC-A-610 and the contract before acceptance.

mistakes.mistake: Deciding disposition from appearance rather than a measurement
mistakes.instead: Record the measured value against the criterion so the call can be reproduced.

terms.def: A gas-filled cavity inside a solder joint, visible on X-ray as a dark region.
The reduction in BGA ball height during reflow as the ball settles onto the land.
The area under the die where the package mass changes heat flow and paste behaviour.
Tomographic X-ray that reconstructs a single slice so depth can be resolved.

title: Disposition language: defect, condition and class in workmanship terms

goals.text: State findings in workmanship-standard vocabulary so a second engineer reaches the same disposition.

blocks.alt: Reference sheet: macro photograph of a gull-wing joint under evaluation, schematic section with heel, toe and side fillets, a disposition table accept / process indicator / defect, and the three IPC classes
blocks.caption: Disposition language: the joint, its fillets, accept / process indicator / defect, and the product class

p: In AOI, disposition language turns a visual or geometric call into a repeatable engineering statement. A second engineer should read the finding and reach the same accept, reject or rework decision without hearing the inspector's tone.
The statement names the object, the observed condition, the applicable workmanship class, the evidence and the verification status.

theory.p: Workmanship vocabulary keeps three ideas apart. A defect is a nonconformance to the applicable requirement. A condition is the observable state that may or may not be a defect depending on class and criteria — insufficient solder, a lifted lead, tombstoning, a solder bridge. A class is the workmanship level, commonly IPC-A-610 Class 1, Class 2 or Class 3, which sets the acceptance threshold for that same condition.

theory.h: AOI output is evidence, not disposition
p: AOI indicates a suspected condition from height, area, shape, colour or position. It misses hidden defects and produces false calls from shadows, reflections and component tolerance.
Until measurement, microscopy, X-ray or manual inspection confirms it, say indicated or suspected, or say that it requires verification. Words that assert a defect outrun the evidence.
A useful finding has a fixed order: location, object, condition, evidence, standard or class, proposed action.

For example: "U7 pin 12: suspected insufficient solder fillet; AOI fillet height 0.18 mm; verify against IPC-A-610 Class 2 and paste deposit data." That sentence gives the next engineer where to look, what was measured, which class applies, and what to do next.

theory.h: Class changes what a condition means
p: A condition acceptable in general electronics may be unacceptable in a high-reliability assembly. IPC-A-610 Class 1, Class 2 and Class 3 describe increasing workmanship requirements, so the same fillet, component tilt or solder ball can be dispositioned differently.
State the class on the finding. Do not let the product name imply it.

Workmanship acceptance is normally accept or reject against the applicable standard. A manufacturing disposition may add rework, scrap or use-as-is, and rework has to restore the assembly to the original acceptance criteria.
Rework and repair follow IPC-7711/7721 or the customer-approved equivalent, and the finding says whether rework is proposed or already performed.

A handoff carries enough to reproduce the decision: panel or serial number, coordinate or reference designator, AOI program version, measured value, uncertainty or confidence, applicable standard and class, and verification method.

Where a number is process-based rather than standard-based, label it a process limit and cite the paste, stencil or AOI datasheet. AOI height uncertainty, for instance, may run around 0.02 mm to 0.05 mm, verified against the equipment datasheet.

calc.task: An AOI station reports 'suspected insufficient solder fillet' at Q1 pin 3. AOI measured fillet height = 0.18 mm. The internal process limit for this package is 0.20 mm minimum, and the AOI height measurement uncertainty is ±0.05 mm. The assembly is IPC-A-610 Class 2. Determine whether the finding should be dispositioned as reject, verify, or accept, and write the standardized finding.
calc.solution: 1) Record the evidence: AOI height = 0.18 mm. 2) Apply measurement uncertainty: lower bound = 0.18 mm - 0.05 mm = 0.13 mm; upper bound = 0.18 mm + 0.05 mm = 0.23 mm. 3) Compare with the internal process minimum of 0.20 mm. The upper bound exceeds the minimum, so the AOI call alone does not prove rejection. The lower bound is below the minimum, so acceptance cannot be concluded without verification. 4) Disposition: verify. Use manual inspection, microscopy, or a calibrated AOI re-run; if the confirmed fillet is below the applicable IPC-A-610 Class 2 criterion and the internal minimum, reject or rework per IPC-7711/7721; if confirmed at or above the criterion, accept. 5) Standardized finding: 'Q1 pin 3: suspected insufficient solder fillet; AOI height 0.18 mm ±0.05 mm; internal process minimum 0.20 mm; verify against IPC-A-610 Class 2 before disposition.'

defect.symptom: AOI repeatedly rejects a suspected solder bridge condition on QFP pins 14 and 15 at the same panel location after a stencil change.
defect.cause: Excessive paste deposit, paste release variation, or print misalignment can create bridge risk between fine-pitch leads; verify paste volume, alignment, and stencil condition against the paste and stencil datasheet.
defect.action: Quarantine the affected panel, verify the bridge with microscopy or X-ray if needed, adjust the printer or stencil process, rework confirmed bridges per IPC-7711/7721, then reinspect with AOI and record the disposition using the same workmanship vocabulary.

takeaways: Write the finding in a fixed order — location, object, condition, evidence, class, action — so a second engineer arrives at the same call.
Say suspected or indicated until measurement confirms the condition, because AOI output is evidence and not a verdict.
Name the class and the standard on every finding, since the same condition can pass in one class and fail in another.

mistakes.mistake: Writing a finding that asserts a defect from an AOI call
mistakes.instead: State it as suspected and say what verification is still required.

mistakes.mistake: Leaving the class implicit in the product name
mistakes.instead: Print the applicable IPC-A-610 class on the finding itself.

mistakes.mistake: Quoting a process limit as if it were the workmanship standard
mistakes.instead: Label it as a process limit and cite the datasheet behind it.

terms.def: An observable state that may or may not be a defect depending on the class and criteria applied.
The recorded decision on a nonconforming item: accept, reject, rework, repair, scrap or use-as-is.
Processing that restores a nonconforming item to the original acceptance criteria.
A documented concession to accept an item that does not meet the stated requirement.

title: Classification drill: print, placement, reflow and THT images

goals.text: Classify a defect image into a defect type and an accept / rework / reject disposition with the criterion named.
State findings in workmanship-standard vocabulary so a second engineer reaches the same disposition.

blocks.alt: Four small board images in a row, one per process stage, each with a defect to classify
blocks.caption: Classification drill: print, placement, reflow and through-hole images

p: In a classification drill, name the process stage from the image before naming the defect. A print image shows paste deposits on bare pads, matte and paste-like, with no component bodies and no reflowed solder.

A placement image shows components sitting on paste, with leads or terminations touching paste but not yet wetted. A reflow image shows solidified joints, shiny or dull depending on process, and may show damage or solder morphology. A THT image shows leads through plated holes with solder on the exit side, so the hole wall and the lead-to-hole interface carry the evidence.

Classify the physical condition rather than the machine you suspect. Use workmanship vocabulary: insufficient solder, excess solder, bridging, solder ball, void, dewetting, lifted lead, tombstoning, misalignment, wrong polarity, missing component, insufficient hole fill, icicle, cold solder.
The same condition can arise from different causes, and the defect type and disposition rest on what the image proves about the joint or deposit.
theory.h: Classify by condition, not by suspected cause

p: Compare the paste deposit with the stencil aperture and the paste datasheet. Measure deposit height in micrometres against the stencil and paste datasheet, then verify against your paste and equipment datasheet.

Insufficient paste, bridging, smearing, misprint and incomplete release are judged by whether the deposit can still form an acceptable joint after reflow. Paste outside the intended aperture becomes bridging or smearing, with the pad or net location noted. A thin, broken or absent deposit becomes insufficient paste or misprint. The disposition is usually rework of the print process and removal of the affected boards, unless contamination or damage leaves the board unusable.

Check component presence, orientation, polarity and termination contact. A missing component, wrong component, reversed polarity, rotated chip or lifted termination is a placement or feeder issue until reflow evidence says otherwise.

A component on the right pad but not seated becomes misalignment or lifted termination. A component on the wrong pad, or with the wrong polarity, becomes wrong component or wrong polarity. Rework applies when component and board are undamaged; reject when the component is damaged, the pad is lifted, or the wrong part cannot be identified and replaced.

Judge the joint against the applicable workmanship standard, commonly IPC-A-610, and against the design intent. Tombstoning, solder balls, bridging, insufficient or excess solder, voiding, dewetting and lifted leads are the usual findings.

A solder ball on the board surface may be reworkable if it comes off without damaging the board, and a bridge between adjacent pads is reworkable if the pads and traces survive. Pad lifting, substrate damage or a component crack is a reject, because rework cannot restore reliability.

Inspect the exit side for hole fill, wetting, lead exposure and solder shape. IPC-A-610 gives the criteria for hole fill, wetting angle, excess solder, icicles, solder balls and lifted leads, but the exact limits depend on product class and the current revision, so cite the standard and revision in the finding.

A dull, grainy or non-wetted joint points to insufficient heat, poor flux activity or contamination. A long icicle or excess solder may be reworkable where the hole is sound and the joint can be brought back to an acceptable shape.
Record the finding as location, component or net, defect type, criterion, evidence and disposition.

Accept means the image meets the named criterion with no reliability concern visible. Rework means the condition is repairable under IPC-7711/7721 or an approved procedure and the board can be re-inspected. Reject means the board or component is damaged, the defect is not repairable, or the criterion cannot be met without unacceptable risk. That wording lets a second engineer reach the same disposition from the same image.

calc.task: Classify the following AOI image findings: a paste deposit outside the intended aperture; a chip component with one termination lifted before reflow; a reflowed joint with a bridge between adjacent pads; a THT joint with a dull, grainy surface and no wetting to the hole wall. For each finding, name the defect type and the accept, rework, or reject disposition with the criterion.
calc.solution: Identify the process stage from the image evidence. Name the defect using workmanship vocabulary. Cite the criterion that controls the disposition. Choose accept, rework, or reject based on repairability and damage. Record location, component or net, defect type, criterion, evidence, and disposition. For the paste deposit outside the intended aperture, classify it as bridging or smearing; rework the print process and remove the affected boards unless paste contamination or board damage makes the board unusable; cite the stencil aperture, paste datasheet, and IPC-A-610 joint acceptability after reflow. For the lifted termination before reflow, classify it as lifted termination or misalignment; rework placement if the component and pad are undamaged; reject if the pad is lifted or the component is damaged; cite IPC-A-610 placement and solder joint acceptability. For the reflowed bridge, classify it as bridging; rework if the pads and traces are intact; reject if pad lifting or substrate damage is visible; cite IPC-A-610 solder joint acceptability. For the THT dull non-wetted joint, classify it as cold solder or insufficient wetting; rework per IPC-7711/7721 if the hole wall and lead are sound; reject if hole wall damage or non-repairable contamination is present; cite IPC-A-610 THT solder joint acceptability.

defect.symptom: AOI flags a THT joint with a dull, grainy solder surface, poor wetting to the hole wall, and a lead that appears exposed at the exit side.
defect.cause: Insufficient preheat or dwell, low flux activity, oxidized leads, or hole wall contamination prevented proper wetting and hole fill.
defect.action: Quarantine the board, inspect adjacent joints, rework per IPC-7711/7721 if the hole wall and lead are sound, verify solderability and reflow profile against equipment datasheet, and update incoming inspection if contamination is confirmed.

takeaways: Name the process stage before the defect, because the same shape means different things at print, placement, reflow and THT.
Classify by the condition the image proves, not by the machine you suspect caused it.
Record location, defect, criterion, evidence and disposition, so the call can be repeated by someone else.

mistakes.mistake: Classifying a paste smear as a bridging defect
mistakes.instead: Call it smearing or bridging from the deposit’s position, and let the reflow result decide acceptability.

mistakes.mistake: Rejecting a reworkable board with a surface solder ball
mistakes.instead: Consider rework first where the board and pads are undamaged.

mistakes.mistake: Citing IPC-A-610 without the class or revision
mistakes.instead: State both, since the acceptance limit depends on them.

terms.def: A pointed solder projection formed on a through-hole joint or lead during solidification.
A dull, grainy joint that never wet properly because of insufficient heat or poor flux activity.
A paste deposit that is displaced, incomplete or absent relative to the aperture.
A structured exercise in naming defect type and disposition from images.

title: What stays through-hole and why: connectors, mechanical load, power

goals.text: Calculate plated-hole diameter versus lead diameter, clearance and expected solder fill for a through-hole joint.

p: Through-hole technology still earns its place where a joint must resist mechanical load, hold a heavy connector, carry real current, or survive repeated insertion and removal. A plated through-hole gives the lead a barrel to wet into, and the solder inside that barrel adds retention and a thermal path.
The price is process control: hole diameter, plating thickness, lead diameter, flux activity, preheat and solder dwell all decide whether the hole fills and wets reliably.
