blocks.alt: Reference sheet: macro cross-section of a plated through-hole joint, schematic section with barrel, lead, fill, fillets and land, the load path from a connector through the barrel, and a clearance sketch
blocks.caption: Through-hole joint: barrel, fill and fillets carry the mechanical load; clearance stack in the figure above

p: The drill size is not the final hole size. The finished plated-hole diameter is what remains after copper plating and the final finish.

For solder fill the relevant gap is the finished hole diameter minus the lead diameter. A board supplier may control drill diameter, plated diameter, plating thickness and wall coverage, and the assembly process still has to verify the finished diameter, because that dimension sets both capillary gap and heat transfer.

Connector leads carry a nominal diameter and a tolerance, and the board hole carries its own. The worst-case clearance combines the smallest hole with the largest lead, and the largest clearance combines the largest hole with the smallest lead.

For common small through-hole leads, a diametral clearance of roughly 0.10 mm to 0.30 mm is often workable for wave or selective solder. The right value depends on paste or flux, preheat, solder temperature, dwell, board orientation and pad thermal mass, so verify it against your paste, flux and equipment datasheet.

theory.h: Clearance affects fill, not just fit
p: Too small a gap and flux and solder cannot penetrate, air stays trapped, and the joint shows incomplete fill or voids. Too large a gap and capillary action weakens, heat transfer to the hole falls off, and the barrel may never wet fully.
A radial clearance of roughly 0.05 mm to 0.15 mm is a practical starting range for many plated through-hole joints, confirmed by cross-section or X-ray on the actual board and component.

theory.h: Expected fill is a process result
p: Geometry gives an estimate; the fill height is a process result. The theoretical annular volume is the hole volume minus the lead volume over the hole depth.

Actual fill comes out lower for oxide, weak flux activity, low board temperature, short dwell, poor wall wetting or trapped air. Run a trial, measure the fill height, and use that measured fraction for prediction until the process is stable.
A connector joint may be through-hole for pull-out strength, shear resistance and durability under cable strain.

On a power path the current travels through the plated barrel and the solder joint, so plating quality, solder fill and thermal relief design all matter. Check current rating against the connector specification and the relevant IPC guidance for current carrying and thermal rise rather than inferring it from hole size.
Before releasing a through-hole design, verify finished hole diameter, lead diameter, hole depth, plating thickness and pad geometry.

Then run a solderability trial and inspect cross-sections or X-rays for fill height, wetting, voiding and solder balling. Use IPC-A-610 acceptance for your product class as the pass or fail reference, and treat the calculated fill as a prediction that measurement has to confirm.

blocks.caption: Selection factors: what still earns through-hole its place
head: Factor
Favors through-hole
Favors SMT
rows: Connectors, heavy parts, cable flex, vibration
High mass: needs preheat tuning in wave

calc.task: A through-hole connector lead has nominal diameter 0.80 mm with tolerance plus or minus 0.03 mm. The finished plated hole diameter is nominal 1.10 mm with tolerance plus or minus 0.05 mm. Hole depth is 1.60 mm. A trial wave solder process gives 75 percent hole fill. Calculate minimum and maximum diametral clearance, radial clearance, annular cross-sectional area, theoretical annular volume, expected solder fill height, and expected solder volume.
calc.solution: Step 1: Calculate lead limits. Minimum lead diameter = 0.80 mm - 0.03 mm = 0.77 mm. Maximum lead diameter = 0.80 mm + 0.03 mm = 0.83 mm. Step 2: Calculate finished hole limits. Minimum hole diameter = 1.10 mm - 0.05 mm = 1.05 mm. Maximum hole diameter = 1.10 mm + 0.05 mm = 1.15 mm. Step 3: Calculate diametral clearance. Minimum diametral clearance = minimum hole diameter - maximum lead diameter = 1.05 mm - 0.83 mm = 0.22 mm. Maximum diametral clearance = maximum hole diameter - minimum lead diameter = 1.15 mm - 0.77 mm = 0.38 mm. Nominal diametral clearance = 1.10 mm - 0.80 mm = 0.30 mm. Step 4: Calculate radial clearance. Minimum radial clearance = 0.22 mm / 2 = 0.11 mm. Maximum radial clearance = 0.38 mm / 2 = 0.19 mm. Nominal radial clearance = 0.30 mm / 2 = 0.15 mm. Step 5: Calculate annular cross-sectional area using hole area minus lead area. Minimum area uses minimum hole and maximum lead: area = 0.32 mm squared. Maximum area uses maximum hole and minimum lead: area = 0.57 mm squared. Nominal area uses nominal hole and nominal lead: area = 0.45 mm squared. Step 6: Calculate theoretical annular volume by multiplying area by hole depth. Minimum theoretical volume = 0.32 mm squared x 1.60 mm = 0.52 mm cubed. Maximum theoretical volume = 0.57 mm squared x 1.60 mm = 0.92 mm cubed. Nominal theoretical volume = 0.45 mm squared x 1.60 mm = 0.72 mm cubed. Step 7: Calculate expected fill height from the trial fill fraction. Expected fill height = 0.75 x 1.60 mm = 1.20 mm. Step 8: Calculate expected solder volume by applying the trial fill fraction to theoretical volume. Minimum expected volume = 0.75 x 0.52 mm cubed = 0.39 mm cubed. Maximum expected volume = 0.75 x 0.92 mm cubed = 0.69 mm cubed. Nominal expected volume = 0.75 x 0.72 mm cubed = 0.54 mm cubed. Step 9: Compare the measured fill height and wetting to IPC-A-610 acceptance for your product class, and verify the process against your paste, flux, and equipment datasheet.

defect.symptom: X-ray or cross-section shows connector through-hole joints with solder reaching only the lower half of the hole, while the upper barrel remains dry or lightly wetted.
defect.cause: The hole-to-lead clearance is too small for the selected flux and wave or selective solder parameters, or the board temperature at the hole is too low for the solder to flow and wet the full barrel. Pad thermal mass or a large ground plane can also draw heat away from the joint.
defect.action: Measure finished hole diameter and lead diameter, then calculate actual clearance. Increase preheat or board temperature within the flux and board limits, increase dwell time, verify flux activity and application, and check hole plating quality. If the geometry is the limiting factor, revise the finished hole diameter or lead diameter and re-run a solderability trial with cross-section or X-ray verification.

takeaways: Use the finished plated-hole diameter, not the drill size, because plating and finish change the gap that governs fill.
Stack the lead and hole tolerances to both extremes, since the worst-case gap decides whether the process can fill at all.
Measure a trial fill fraction before predicting fill height, because the geometry calculation gives a ceiling rather than a result.

mistakes.mistake: Calculating clearance from the drill diameter
mistakes.instead: Use the finished plated diameter, which is smaller and is what the solder sees.

mistakes.mistake: Quoting a single clearance figure as universal
mistakes.instead: Check it against your flux, preheat and dwell, since the workable gap depends on all of them.

mistakes.mistake: Treating calculated fill as achieved fill
mistakes.instead: Measure the trial fill height and use that fraction until the process is stable.

terms.def: The radial gap between the finished hole wall and the lead.
The height the solder reaches inside the plated hole, measured from the exit side.
A pad connection pattern that limits heat flow into or out of a through-hole pad.
The copper thickness on the hole wall, which sets current capacity and wall strength.

skills: Lesson m02l06: Case: expired floor life found mid-lot

title: Hole and lead: diameters, tolerance stack-up, placement tolerance, percent fill

goals.text: Calculate plated-hole diameter versus lead diameter, clearance and expected solder fill for a through-hole joint.

blocks.alt: A hole and lead cross-section with the diameter stack-up, the placement tolerance and a barrel fill percentage gauge
blocks.caption: Hole and lead: diameters, tolerance stack-up, placement tolerance and percent fill

theory.h: Plated-hole diameter is the assembly reference
p: For lead insertion the relevant hole size is the finished plated-hole diameter, not the bare drill diameter. The drill is one input to the stack-up: copper plating, wall roughness and drill wear all reduce the usable diameter.

Measure the finished diameter from the assembly side and the component side, because barrel plating can leave the hole slightly non-cylindrical. A measured diameter close to the lead diameter raises insertion force, skew and fill risk. Check the finished diameter against the fabrication drawing and the board supplier's capability report.

Treat the lead diameter as a range, never a single nominal value. Leads may be round, rectangular or formed, and the effective insertion dimension can exceed the nominal wire diameter because of plating, burrs or the forming radius.

Clearance is the finished plated-hole diameter minus the maximum effective lead dimension, and a small nominal clearance can disappear once tolerance stacks up. For production, calculate the worst-case clearance from the minimum plated-hole diameter and the maximum lead dimension, then check it against the insertion equipment's alignment capability and the component datasheet.

Placement tolerance is the positional error between the intended hole centre and the actual lead centre. Feeder repeatability, vision calibration, tape, reel or tube handling, board warpage and lead-forming variation all contribute.

A lead displaced by more than the available radial clearance binds on the hole wall or misses the hole entirely. Manual insertion lets the operator correct some of it; automated insertion has to include placement tolerance in the clearance calculation. Verify the tolerance against the insertion machine specification and the panel datum scheme.
A joint can insert cleanly and still fill badly, because the annular gap is either too small or too large.

Too little clearance traps air, restricts flux flow and stops solder wetting the full wall. Too much lets the lead sit off-centre, opens a void path and weakens capillary control. The desired clearance is therefore a process window, not a number: for wave soldering, the gap must pass solder through the hole while keeping enough capillary action to fill the joint. Verify the acceptable range against the solder process, flux activity, preheat profile and the wave or selective-solder equipment datasheet.

theory.h: Expected fill depends on geometry and process
p: Expected fill is expressed as the percentage of hole depth filled after solidification. Hole aspect ratio, lead-to-hole clearance, surface finish, flux wetting, preheat, solder temperature, dwell time and the soldering method all move it.

A high aspect-ratio hole with tight clearance fills less reliably than a shallow hole with moderate clearance. Use IPC-A-610 acceptance for the applicable product class and confirm actual fill with cross-sections or X-ray where required.

theory.h: Stack tolerances before choosing the hole size
p: A practical stack covers PCB finished-hole tolerance, lead diameter tolerance, lead-forming tolerance, placement tolerance and any allowance for board warpage or panel distortion.

Compare the result with the minimum clearance insertion needs and the minimum gap solder fill needs. A marginal result means a larger hole, a tighter lead tolerance, better placement calibration or a different insertion method, not a hope that nominal values hold. Use worst-case or statistical analysis according to volume and risk.

theory.h: Close the loop with measured data
p: The most reliable clearance and fill predictions come from measured distributions: plated-hole diameter, lead diameter, placement error, and fill results from pilot builds.

If the design clearance sits inside the calculated range and fill is still poor, look at flux activity, preheat, wave height, conveyor speed and hole wall condition. High insertion force points to drill wear, plating thickness, lead burrs or placement repeatability. Record the measured values against the design assumptions so the next hole and lead selection rest on real process capability.

calc.task: A plated through-hole is specified with a nominal finished diameter of 1.00 mm and a PCB tolerance of ±0.05 mm. A component lead has a nominal diameter of 0.60 mm and a tolerance of ±0.03 mm. The insertion placement tolerance is ±0.08 mm. Calculate the minimum radial clearance, the worst-case insertion clearance, and the expected solder-fill range for a wave-soldered joint.
calc.solution: 1. Minimum finished plated-hole diameter = 1.00 mm - 0.05 mm = 0.95 mm. 2. Maximum lead diameter = 0.60 mm + 0.03 mm = 0.63 mm. 3. Nominal radial clearance before placement error = (1.00 mm - 0.60 mm) / 2 = 0.20 mm. 4. Worst-case radial clearance before placement error = (0.95 mm - 0.63 mm) / 2 = 0.16 mm. 5. Placement tolerance consumes radial clearance. If the lead center is displaced by 0.08 mm, the remaining radial clearance on the tight side = 0.16 mm - 0.08 mm = 0.08 mm. 6. Therefore, the worst-case insertion clearance is 0.08 mm radial, or 0.16 mm diametral, assuming the lead and hole remain circular and the lead does not bind. 7. For solder fill, use the nominal gap and the worst-case gap. Nominal gap = 1.00 mm - 0.60 mm = 0.40 mm. Worst-case gap = 0.95 mm - 0.63 mm = 0.32 mm. 8. A typical wave-soldered through-hole joint may show solder fill from about 75% to 100% of hole depth when the gap, flux, preheat, and wave parameters are within the process window. Verify the actual expected fill against the IPC-A-610 acceptance criteria for the applicable product class and against pilot-build cross-sections. 9. If the measured fill is below the required acceptance level, investigate hole wall condition, flux activity, preheat temperature, solder temperature, dwell time, and placement repeatability before changing the hole or lead size.

defect.symptom: Leads insert with high force or partially miss the hole, and wave-soldered joints show incomplete fill, voiding, or solder that does not wet the full hole wall.
defect.cause: The finished plated-hole diameter is smaller than assumed, the lead diameter is at the upper tolerance limit, or placement error consumes the available clearance. The resulting gap is too small for reliable flux flow and solder capillary action.
defect.action: Measure the finished plated-hole diameter and lead diameter on the assembly line. Recalculate the worst-case clearance including placement tolerance. If clearance is marginal, adjust the PCB hole tolerance, tighten lead tolerance, improve placement calibration, or verify the wave-solder process window. Confirm the corrected process with insertion-force data and solder-fill cross-sections.

takeaways: Stack every tolerance — hole, lead, forming and placement — before choosing a hole size, because nominal clearance disappears in production.
Treat clearance as a window with two failure ends, since both a tight and a wide gap spoil fill.
Compare pilot-build fill data with the design assumptions, so the next board is designed against measured capability.

mistakes.mistake: Choosing the hole from the lead nominal plus a rule of thumb
mistakes.instead: Add the tolerances and the placement error, then check both ends of the gap.

mistakes.mistake: Ignoring placement tolerance in an automated line
mistakes.instead: Include it in the radial clearance, because the lead centre moves before it reaches the hole.

mistakes.mistake: Fixing poor fill by enlarging the hole alone
mistakes.instead: Check flux, preheat and dwell first, since too much clearance also ruins fill.

terms.def: The combined worst-case effect of several independent tolerances on one gap.
Hole depth divided by hole diameter, which governs how easily solder fills the barrel.
The force needed to push a lead into a plated hole, an indicator of clearance and burrs.
The range of a parameter that produces acceptable results in production.

title: Insertion: seating, stand-off, polarity, clinch, insertion damage

goals.text: Choose board direction, clinch and masking for a layout to limit shadowing at the wave.
Identify insertion defects from a board image and name the process cause.

blocks.alt: An insertion machine head seating a through-hole lead, with stand-off and clinch callouts and a damaged-lead warning
blocks.caption: Insertion: seating, stand-off, polarity, clinch and insertion damage

p: Shadowing happens when a component, a neighbouring part or a fixture blocks molten solder from reaching a through-hole joint at the wave.

The wave sees the board as a sequence of obstacles: tall parts, dense pin fields, large ground planes and closely spaced components each create local dry zones. Choose board direction, clinch and masking so solder can reach the hole and wet the annular ring without being deflected or trapped.

Pick board direction so the wave reaches the side of the component least likely to shield its own joint. On a rectangular part, the long axis usually runs parallel to the wave direction where the body would otherwise shade its leads. On a connector or tall part, the joint side should face the incoming wave where possible, or the board is angled to shorten the shadow.
The angle is process-dependent: conveyor angles are typically small, often around 3 to 7 degrees, verified against the wave solder equipment datasheet and trial boards.

theory.h: Clinch geometry affects seating and access
p: Clinch holds the component through insertion and transport, and it also sets the gap between body and board.

A tight clinch improves seating and reduces stand-off while closing the gap under the body and restricting solder flow. A loose clinch improves access and allows vibration to lift or misalign the part. Many through-hole components do best with a controlled clinch that keeps the body stable while leaving a small solder-access gap; check clinch force and final stand-off against the insertion machine and the component datasheet.

Stand-off is the distance between body and board surface. Too little traps flux, prevents solder reaching the joint and makes cleaning hard. Too much demands more solder, exposes leads to mechanical stress and costs board density.

For many radial and axial components a practical range is around 0.5 to 1.5 mm, verified against body geometry, pin length, flux activity and the wave profile. Components with moulded bodies or heat-sensitive materials follow the manufacturer's seating or stand-off limits.
Masking protects areas that must not be soldered, and a poor layout worsens shadowing by blocking the wave path or trapping flux.

A good layout exposes the annular ring and lead while avoiding tall mask walls directly in front of the joint. Place mask edges so solder flows around the joint rather than through a narrow channel. Dense layouts often do better with partial masking or local openings than with a continuous band. Verify mask thickness, edge clearance and solder resist compatibility against the wave process.
Polarity errors put a polarised component in the wrong direction: electrolytic capacitors, diodes, LEDs, keyed connectors, ICs with a pin 1 indicator.

Feeder setup, tray orientation, vision misalignment, manual error or a program that disagrees with the physical part all cause them. A polarity error can pass visual inspection when nobody checks the body marking, so the inspection method must confirm marking orientation, not just the presence of the part.
Insertion damage covers bent leads, crushed bodies, cracked ceramics, damaged pin plating and torn lands.

Misaligned feeders, excessive insertion force, worn insertion heads, poor pin straightening and weak board support cause it. The location points to the cause: damage on one board side suggests a feeder or head offset, while damage confined to one component type suggests a tray, tape or feeder setup problem.
Identify component type, pin geometry and board side first, then look for patterns.

One component type affected suggests a feeder or program error; one board location suggests a head or support error; many similar joints suggest wave direction, clinch or masking. For shadowing, look for dry or thin solder on the side away from the wave. For insertion damage, look for lead deformation, body cracks or board damage at the insertion point. For polarity, compare the component marking with the silkscreen and the pin 1 indicator.

theory.h: Match the control to the mechanism
p: For shadowing, adjust board direction, clinch, stand-off or mask layout before touching wave temperature or speed. For insertion damage, correct feeder, head alignment, pin straightening or board support. For polarity, correct feeder orientation, the vision reference, the program or the manual insertion aid.
Remove the physical cause so the process produces acceptable joints without relying on extra solder or rework.

calc.task: A radial electrolytic capacitor has a body diameter of 10.0 mm and a body height of 12.0 mm. The board is moving through the wave at 1.2 m/min. The wave approach angle is 5 degrees relative to the board surface. Estimate the shadow length cast by the component body at the board surface, and decide whether a 0.8 mm stand-off is likely to help or worsen solder access if the adjacent component is 1.5 mm away from the capacitor body.
calc.solution: 1. A straight-ray model with the wave approach angle gives shadow length = height / tan(angle). For a 12.0 mm body and a 5 degree angle, tan(5 degrees) is approximately 0.0875, so 12.0 mm / 0.0875 = 137 mm. 2. Stop at that number: it says the model does not apply. The 5 degree figure is the conveyor incline, and the wave is a flowing body that climbs the component and is pushed into the gap by the turbulent chip wave and by flux action; it is not a ray at 5 degrees. No line observes 137 mm shadows, and common practice keeps about 2.5 mm between a tall through-hole part and the joints behind it. 3. Use the course's screening model instead (lesson 9.5): shadow = height x tan(contact angle from vertical). With a typical 20 degree contact angle, 12.0 mm x 0.364 = 4.4 mm, plus 0.5 to 1.0 mm for turbulence and flux depletion. 4. Compare with the layout: the adjacent component is 1.5 mm from the capacitor body, inside the 4.4 to 5.4 mm zone, so predict shadowing. 5. The 0.8 mm stand-off is small compared with the 10.0 mm body diameter; it may improve seating but reduces solder access under the body, and in a 1.5 mm gap it worsens flux escape and solder flow. 6. Practical conclusion: in this tight layout the 0.8 mm stand-off worsens access unless the wave direction is changed, the clinch is loosened slightly, or the mask and component spacing are adjusted. 7. Verify the final stand-off, clinch force and wave angle with trial boards and the wave solder equipment datasheet. 8. Treat the screening model as a way to rank layouts, not to sign them off.

defect.symptom: A board image shows several electrolytic capacitors with one lead dry or insufficiently wetted on the side away from the wave, while the opposite lead is acceptable. The capacitor bodies are seated close to the board, and the adjacent component is less than 2 mm away.
defect.cause: The joint is being shadowed by the capacitor body and nearby component because the stand-off is too small for the wave approach direction. The tight clinch or seating condition reduces the gap needed for flux escape and solder flow, so the wave cannot reach the far lead reliably.
defect.action: Change the board direction or wave approach angle so the shadow falls away from the joint. Increase stand-off slightly within the component and process limits, or adjust the clinch to hold the part without closing the solder-access gap. If the layout is dense, revise the mask opening or component spacing to expose the annular ring and allow solder flow. Run a trial board and inspect the joint against IPC-A-610 acceptance criteria and your wave solder process specification.

takeaways: Set board direction and stand-off from the component geometry, because the shadow a body casts is what starves its joint.
Use a controlled clinch that holds the part and still leaves solder a path, since either extreme costs a defect.
Separate polarity and damage from solder defects, because they belong to feeder and insertion control rather than the wave.

mistakes.mistake: Raising wave temperature to fill a shadowed joint
mistakes.instead: Fix direction, clinch, stand-off or masking, since heat cannot reach behind an obstacle.

mistakes.mistake: Clamping every part tight to the board
mistakes.instead: Leave a solder-access gap, or the joint starves under the body.

mistakes.mistake: Treating polarity errors as inspection failures
mistakes.instead: Fix feeder and program orientation, and add marking checks to the inspection method.

terms.def: A dry or starved joint caused by geometry blocking the solder wave.
Bending the protruding lead to hold the component during handling and soldering.
The gap between the component body and the board surface.
A joint that received too little solder to wet and form properly.

title: Preparing the board for wave: carriers, pallets, masking, taping, orientation

goals.text: Choose board direction, clinch and masking for a layout to limit shadowing at the wave.

blocks.alt: A board loaded into a carrier with masked and taped areas and an orientation arrow, beside a pallet cross-section
blocks.caption: Preparing the board for wave: carriers, pallets, masking, taping and orientation

p: At the wave the board underside passes over a stationary solder wave, and tall components, connectors, heat sinks, shielding cans and pallet supports deflect it, leaving pads downstream dry, underfilled or poorly wetted.

The preparation job is to find the shadow sources, locate the critical pads, and choose board direction, lead clinch and masking so no critical pad sits in the wake of a tall object. Judge wetting and flux residues against the IPC acceptance criteria for electronic assemblies.
For a single board or panel, rotate the layout so the long axis of tall rectangular components runs perpendicular to the conveyor direction where possible.

Where critical pads cannot move, rotate the board 90 degrees or use a small angle to move the wake off them. Prove the direction on a trial board, because wave turbulence, nozzle design and flux activity change the shadow length.
Where leads are formed or clinched on the wave side, keep bends from lying across downstream pads. Prefer bends perpendicular to the wave, or directed away from critical pads.
Keep wave-side protrusion short and controlled, commonly 0.5-1.5 mm, verified against your equipment and flux datasheet. Long or angled leads act as small dams and lengthen the shadow.
A carrier or pallet holds the board flat, prevents bowing, and lets flux and air escape. Support pins and pallet edges must not block the wave path or cover pads.
Keep clearance under the board, often 1-2 mm, so the wave reaches the underside evenly. Check flatness and support placement: a bowed board creates local shadowing even with the right orientation.
Masking covers areas that should not be soldered and can cut shadowing from large metal parts. Use high-temperature tape or liquid mask that survives preheat and wave contact.

Cover connector bodies, heat sinks, test points and surface-mount devices not meant for the wave. Mask edges should be flat and sealed, and the mask must not trap flux or block drainage. Check the material against your flux and equipment datasheet.
Tape secures masks and protects edges. Use high-temperature adhesive tape whose release does not lift in preheat, and seal the edges so flux cannot wick underneath.

Leave drainage holes and pallet vents clear. After a trial, inspect for lifted tape, trapped flux and residue on adjacent pads, then set tape width and overlap — commonly 6-12 mm — from what the line shows.
Before production, run a trial board with the chosen orientation, clinch, pallet and mask, and inspect pads downstream of tall components for wetting, solder volume and residue.
If shadowing persists, change one variable: rotate the board, change clinch direction, add masking, or adjust pallet support. Record the accepted combination so operators can reproduce it.

calc.task: A 120 mm by 80 mm board has a 12 mm tall connector near the center and critical pads 18 mm downstream of the connector. The line runs at 1.0 m/min with 4 s wave contact. Choose board direction, clinch, and masking to limit shadowing.
calc.solution: 1. Estimate shadow length. For a tall component aligned with the wave, use a practical range of 1.5-2.5 times component height. For 12 mm height, shadow length is 18-30 mm. 2. Compare with critical pad distance. The pads are 18 mm downstream, so they are at the near edge of the estimated shadow and may be at risk. 3. Rotate the board 90 degrees so the connector long axis is perpendicular to the wave. For a perpendicular connector, use a reduced practical range of 1.0-1.5 times height, giving 12-18 mm shadow length. 4. Because 18 mm is still borderline, add high-temperature masking over the connector body and extend the mask 5 mm upstream and downstream of the connector. 5. Set wave-side lead clinch perpendicular to the wave or away from the critical pads, with lead protrusion 0.5-1.5 mm. 6. Run a trial at 1.0 m/min and 4 s contact, then inspect downstream pads. If shadowing remains, increase mask extension by 5 mm or rotate the board a few degrees, and verify against your equipment and flux datasheet.

defect.symptom: Pads downstream of a connector are dry or underfilled, with solder balls near the mask edge.
defect.cause: The board ran with the connector long axis parallel to the wave, and the mask edge lifted, allowing flux to trap solder at the mask boundary.
defect.action: Rotate the board 90 degrees, replace the mask with high-temperature tape sealed at the edges, extend the mask 5 mm past the connector, and run a verification board before releasing the lot.

takeaways: Set orientation before anything else, because a rotated board removes shadows that no amount of flux can cure.
Keep wave-side lead protrusion short and directed away from critical pads, since a bent lead forms its own dam.
Prove the combination on a trial board and record it, so the next shift runs the setup that worked.

mistakes.mistake: Taping over drainage holes to protect a part
mistakes.instead: Leave drainage clear, or flux pools and leaves residue on neighbouring pads.

mistakes.mistake: Choosing orientation by board outline rather than by critical pads
mistakes.instead: Rotate until the pads in the wake are the ones that can tolerate it.

mistakes.mistake: Changing direction, masking and pallet support together
mistakes.instead: Change one variable per trial, or the accepted setup cannot be explained.

terms.def: The region downstream of an obstacle where the solder wave is disturbed or absent.
The length of lead standing proud of the solder side after clinching.
A fixture that holds the board flat through the wave.
The path that lets flux and air escape from under a board or mask.

title: Calculation drill: clearance and expected fill for a real BOM subset

goals.text: Calculate plated-hole diameter versus lead diameter, clearance and expected solder fill for a through-hole joint.

blocks.alt: A calculation panel showing hole diameter, lead diameter, clearance and expected fill for a small set of through-hole parts
blocks.caption: Calculation drill: clearance and expected fill for a real bill-of-materials subset

p: Through-hole joints live on the interaction between plated hole, component lead and solder process. The finished hole diameter, the lead diameter and the board thickness set the annular space that solder must fill.
A calculation drill shows whether a BOM subset is likely to fill properly before the first build, which is cheaper than finding it out at cross-section.
The plated-hole diameter is not the drill diameter. Drill size, copper thickness and plating thickness combine to set the finished diameter.

Work from the approved land-pattern library and the fabrication drawing, and verify the finished size against the drill and plating capability. IPC-7351 gives land-pattern and hole-size guidance, and the final value still has to match what fabrication can hold.
The component supplier controls the lead diameter, and handling modifies it. Measure at the seating plane and at the exit side where the lead is bent or deformed.
A tight fit blocks capillary flow; a loose fit lets solder drain away and leaves a weak joint. Record nominal and worst-case dimensions rather than leaning on one nominal value.
Clearance is normally evaluated as diametral clearance, the hole diameter minus the lead diameter, with radial clearance at half that.

Both matter: diametral clearance affects assembly and alignment, and radial clearance is the capillary gap that draws solder through the hole. The window is not a design value alone; it must suit the wave or selective solder equipment.
Capillary action, flux activity, preheat and contact time fill the joint. A clean, wettable hole and lead are what let solder climb and fill the annulus.

Preheat too low leaves the hole cold and produces partial fill, and excessive preheat oxidises the joint or dries the flux. Verify preheat and wave settings against your paste and equipment datasheet.

The applicable IPC-A-610 class defines acceptance. IPC-A-610 sets a minimum vertical barrel fill of 75 % for both Class 2 and Class 3, and Class 3 additionally requires visible fillets on the primary and secondary sides.

A documented exception allows about 50 % fill, or 1.2 mm, for parts with fourteen or more leads whose barrels tie into internal thermal or conductor planes. Some customers specify 100 % fill contractually, and that is a customer requirement rather than an IPC-A-610 class limit. Set the process target above the minimum for the required class, and never let the target stand in for the acceptance criteria.

For a drill, use nominal dimensions first, then the worst-case tight and loose cases. Calculate annular volume and expected fill volume, then compare the result with the required class and the process capability.
Where expected fill sits close to the minimum, plan cross-section or X-ray verification before production.

calc.task: For a single axial resistor in the BOM subset, the lead diameter is 0.50 mm nominal and 0.55 mm maximum. The plated through-hole diameter is 0.90 mm nominal, 0.85 mm minimum, and 0.95 mm maximum. The board thickness is 1.60 mm. Calculate nominal diametral clearance, worst-case tight and loose diametral clearance, nominal annular volume, and expected solder fill at a 90% process target. Compare the expected fill with IPC-A-610 minimum hole fill for the applicable class.
calc.solution: Nominal radii: hole radius 0.45 mm, lead radius 0.25 mm. Nominal diametral clearance: 0.90 - 0.50 = 0.40 mm. Worst-case tight: hole minimum 0.85 mm, lead maximum 0.55 mm, diametral clearance 0.85 - 0.55 = 0.30 mm. Worst-case loose: hole maximum 0.95 mm, lead minimum 0.50 mm, diametral clearance 0.95 - 0.50 = 0.45 mm. Nominal hole volume: pi * 0.45 * 0.45 * 1.60 = 1.018 cubic millimetres. Nominal lead volume: pi * 0.25 * 0.25 * 1.60 = 0.314 cubic millimetres. Nominal annular volume: 1.018 - 0.314 = 0.704, which rounds to 0.70 cubic millimetres. Expected fill volume at 90% target: 90% of 0.704 = 0.63 cubic millimetres. The 90% target is above the IPC-A-610 minimum vertical barrel fill of 75% that applies to both Class 2 and Class 3; a customer requirement for 100% fill is contractual and is not an IPC-A-610 class limit. Verify the required class and process capability.

defect.symptom: X-ray or cross-section shows hole fill below the applicable IPC-A-610 minimum, with dull solder at the exit side and occasional open at the lead shoulder.
defect.cause: The hole-to-lead clearance is too tight for the wave or selective solder process, or preheat is too low, so capillary flow stalls before the hole fills. Verify against your paste and equipment datasheet.
defect.action: Quarantine the lot, measure finished hole diameter and lead diameter, check drill and plating records, adjust preheat and contact time within equipment limits, and requalify with cross-section or X-ray.

takeaways: Compare expected fill with the IPC-A-610 minimum for the required class, and remember Class 3 also needs visible fillets on both sides.
Run the worst-case tight and loose clearances, because the tight case is what stalls capillary flow.
Treat a contractual 100 % fill requirement as a customer requirement and record it separately from the class limit.

mistakes.mistake: Assuming the drill diameter is the finished hole
mistakes.instead: Use the plated diameter, since plating shrinks the hole the solder must fill.

mistakes.mistake: Quoting 75 % fill as sufficient for every class and contract
mistakes.instead: Check Class 3 fillet requirements and any customer specification above the class limit.

mistakes.mistake: Setting a process target and calling it acceptance
mistakes.instead: Keep the target above the minimum but judge boards against the standard and the contract.

terms.def: Hole diameter minus lead diameter at the joint.
Half the diametral clearance, the gap on one side of the lead.
The percentage of the plated hole depth filled with solder.
A stated allowance in the standard that permits a lower value under defined conditions.

title: Wave architecture: flux, preheat, wave types (single/dual, lambda, micro-wave)

goals.text: Set flux type and amount, preheat level and fog/wave height for a given board and justify each setting.

p: A wave soldering window is the interaction of flux application, preheat, wave contact and cooling.

On lead-free alloy the window narrows, because wetting and intermetallic formation both need adequate board temperature and short contact. Set the window by thermocouple profiling and cross-section, then verify against your paste and equipment datasheet.

blocks.caption: Wave soldering line: fluxer, preheat, dual wave (turbulent chip wave first, laminar main wave second), cooling; single, dual, lambda and micro-wave types

blocks.alt: Reference sheet: side view of a wave soldering machine with fluxer, preheat, a solder pot with the turbulent chip wave first and the laminar main wave second, and cooling; a solder wave photograph; wave type profiles
blocks.caption: Wave soldering architecture: fluxer, preheat, chip wave then main wave, cooling; single, dual, lambda and micro-wave

p: Preheat activates flux, drives off solvents and brings board and leads to a temperature where solder wets without thermal shock.

Establish the top-side temperature before the wave by profiling. Common practice uses a soak plateau, and the exact value depends on board mass, flux and equipment. Place thermocouples on heavy ground planes and on small pads, and follow IPC-7530 for the profiling method.
Wave length and conveyor speed set contact time. Too short gives insufficient fill and cold joints; too long brings excess solder, bridging and thermal stress.
Adjust conveyor speed together with wave height and pump condition, and verify the result with cross-sections and solder weight rather than with the display.
Wave height controls wetting pressure and contact. A wave too high floods through-holes and makes icicles; one too low misses pads.
Nozzle clogging and pump wear change the effective contact time even when the speed has not moved, which is why wave height belongs in the same check as speed.
Nitrogen reduces oxidation of solder and flux residue, improves wetting, lowers dross and can cut bridging. It does not replace correct preheat or flux selection.
Control and monitor the oxygen level. The benefit is largest on fine-pitch and high-density boards, where the same wetting margin buys more.
Flux solids, activation and application density decide residue, wetting and cleaning. Too little flux gives non-wetting and shading; too much leaves residue, bridges and a cleaning burden.
Measure and trend flux density, and evaluate residue by cross-section and ion chromatography or an equivalent method.

Cross-sections show whether the window is right. Shading points to oxidation or insufficient flux activity. Excess solder points to too high a wave, too long contact or poor drainage. Insufficient fill points to low preheat, short contact, blocked holes or poor wetting.
Judge the result against the IPC-A-610 acceptance criteria for the product class.

calc.task: A board requires 4 s wave contact time. The wave contact length is 250 mm. Set conveyor speed. The board top surface must reach 105 °C before wave, starting from 25 °C, over 90 s. Calculate average preheat ramp rate.
calc.solution: First, convert wave length to meters: 250 mm = 0.250 m. Next, conveyor speed = wave length / contact time = 0.250 m / 4 s = 0.0625 m/s. Then convert to m/min: 0.0625 m/s * 60 s/min = 3.75 m/min. Next, preheat ramp = (105 °C - 25 °C) / 90 s = 80 °C / 90 s = 0.889 °C/s. Finally, convert to °C/min: 0.889 °C/s * 60 s/min = 53.3 °C/min. Verify the selected speed and ramp against your equipment, flux, and board thermal mass.

defect.symptom: Shading on through-hole barrels and pads after wave, with dull gray surface and poor wetting at hole entrance.
defect.cause: Flux activity too low, preheat too low, oxygen in wave zone high, or contaminated nozzle.
defect.action: Verify flux density and activation, profile board temperature, reduce oxygen, clean nozzle, and run cross-section.

takeaways: Set conveyor speed from the wave contact length and the required contact time, then check it against cross-sections rather than the display.
Profile the top-side temperature on heavy planes and small pads, because preheat is what decides wetting without thermal shock.
Treat nitrogen as a wetting aid, not as a substitute for preheat and flux selection.

mistakes.mistake: Lowering conveyor speed to fix insufficient fill without checking preheat
mistakes.instead: Profile the board first, since cold holes cannot be filled by dwelling longer.

mistakes.mistake: Judging the wave by its height on the pump only
mistakes.instead: Look at the wetting pressure across the board, because nozzle clogging changes it locally.

mistakes.mistake: Adding nitrogen to compensate for a weak flux
mistakes.instead: Fix the flux selection and density, then measure the oxygen benefit separately.

terms.def: The interval a board spends in contact with the solder wave.
Incomplete wetting on a through-hole or pad caused by oxidation or insufficient flux activity.
Oxide and intermetallic debris that forms on molten solder.
A test that measures ionic contamination left by flux residues.

title: Flux selection and application: solids, activity, amount, pattern, verification

goals.text: Set flux type and amount, preheat level and fog/wave height for a given board and justify each setting.

blocks.alt: A fluxer head spraying a pattern onto a board underside, with a solids readout, an activity class label and a verification coupon
blocks.caption: Flux selection and application: solids, activity, amount, pattern and verification

p: Flux selection for wave and selective wave starts from the condition of board and termination: base metal, finish, oxidation, hole geometry, component mass and acceptable residue.

On THT the flux must reach hole walls and lead surfaces. On a selective wave for SMT it must wet pad and termination without leaving excess residue under components. IPC J-STD-004 classifies flux by residue type and activity; confirm compatibility with the finish and the cleaning process on the datasheet.

Solids content drives residue, bridging and post-solder cleanliness. Low-solids no-clean flux leaves less visible residue and may need tighter preheat. Higher-solids rosin or water-soluble flux improves wetting on oxidised surfaces and carries more residue and cleaning.
Take the solids from the flux datasheet and check spray viscosity and residue acceptability against your paste and equipment datasheet.
Activity must be high enough to remove oxides through preheat and wave contact, and low enough to avoid corrosion, solder balling or residue that traps moisture.

The IPC J-STD-004 activity classes guide the choice: low activity for clean, fresh finishes, higher activity for oxidised surfaces or high-thermal-mass joints. Verify both by wetting and residue tests.
Apply enough flux to wet every solderable surface and not enough to pool in holes, under components or on non-solderable areas.

With jetted or fogged flux, pattern uniformity matters more than peak thickness. Check coverage with flux indicator paper, residue inspection or cross-section. Nozzle pattern, pressure, board speed and solids set the amount; verify against your paste and equipment datasheet.

Preheat activates flux, drives off solvent and reduces thermal shock. The board temperature must be high enough to activate the flux before the wave and below the damage limits of board and components.
Measure with thermocouples on heavy pads and component bodies, and check the target against your paste, equipment datasheet and board material limits.
Wave height sets the contact area and the turbulence. Too low gives incomplete hole fill; too high gives bridging, solder balls and pad erosion.
Set fog or selective wave height against board thickness and hole pattern, then verify by cross-section and visual inspection.

theory.p: Verification covers first-article wetting, hole fill, residue, cleanliness and reliability. IPC J-STD-001 and IPC-A-610 supply the acceptance criteria for soldered assemblies, used alongside your internal residue and cleaning limits.

calc.task: A 1.6 mm glass-epoxy board, 50 mm x 40 mm, has 100 through-hole pads with fresh finish. Select no-clean flux type, amount, preheat level, and fog/wave height, and justify each setting.
calc.solution: First, board area = 50 mm x 40 mm = 20 cm2. Next, select no-clean organic flux with low-to-moderate activity per IPC J-STD-004 because the finish is fresh and residue must remain acceptable without cleaning. Then set flux amount as a deposition of flux solids: a starting range of 0.08-0.23 mg/cm2 of board bottom area, which is 500-1500 µg/in² of solids and about 0.8-2.3 g/m². For 20 cm2 that is 1.6-4.6 mg of solids; take the mid value 0.15 mg/cm2, giving 3.0 mg of solids. With a 2.0% solids flux within a 1.5-2.5% starting range, the solution mass is 3.0 mg / 0.02 = 150 mg. If the fluxer output is 300 mg/min of solution, spray time = 150 mg / 300 mg/min = 0.5 min, about 30 s. State the basis before comparing numbers: figures quoted per unit of liquid, for example 0.5-1.0 g/ft², are several times larger than solids-based figures. Verify the solids deposition with a fluxometer in µg/in² or by weighing a witness card, and verify the range against your flux and equipment datasheet. Set preheat target to 100 °C within a 90-110 °C starting range, measured with thermocouples, to activate flux and reduce thermal shock; verify against your paste/equipment datasheet and board limits. Set fog/wave height to 1.5 mm within a 1.2-1.8 mm starting range above the board underside for hole fill without top-side overflow; verify by cross-section and visual inspection. Finally, justify: low-to-moderate activity matches fresh finish, 0.15 mg/cm2 of flux solids and 2.0% solids balance wetting and residue, 100 °C preheat supports activation, and 1.5 mm wave height supports hole fill while limiting bridging.

defect.symptom: Solder balls and partial hole fill on the underside after wave soldering.
defect.cause: Flux amount or solids too high for the preheat setting, causing flux to boil and eject solder; wave height may be too low for hole fill.
defect.action: Reduce flux amount or solids, increase preheat until board top reaches the verified activation range, and adjust wave height upward only after checking for bridging; verify with cross-section and residue inspection.

takeaways: Choose flux activity from the finish and the oxide on the board, then prove it by wetting and residue tests rather than by class alone.
Control flux solids rather than liquid volume, and state the basis whenever a deposition figure is quoted.
Set preheat from a board thermocouple, since flux activation happens at board temperature and not at the oven display.

mistakes.mistake: Quoting flux deposition per unit of liquid when the specification is solids-based
mistakes.instead: State the basis, because the two figures differ by several times.

mistakes.mistake: Raising flux activity to fix a cold joint
mistakes.instead: Check preheat and wave contact first, since activity cannot compensate for a cold board.

mistakes.mistake: Judging flux coverage by the machine setting
mistakes.instead: Measure with fluxometer or witness card, because pattern uniformity decides the result.

terms.def: The non-volatile fraction of a flux that remains after the solvent evaporates.
The ability of a flux to remove oxides from the metal surface during soldering.
An instrument that measures the flux solids deposited per unit area.
The height of the flux fog applied to the board underside before the wave.

title: Preheat: board top vs bottom temperature, flux activation, thermal limits

goals.text: Set flux type and amount, preheat level and fog/wave height for a given board and justify each setting.

blocks.alt: A board cross-section with top and bottom temperature probes, a preheat curve, and a flux activation temperature band
blocks.caption: Preheat: board top versus bottom temperature, flux activation and thermal limits

theory.h: The thermal path in wave soldering
p: Heat enters a wave-soldered board mainly from the bottom, so the bottom surface rises quickly while the top lags.

The top surface temperature is the practical control point for flux activation and solvent evaporation. Put thermocouples on the bottom near the wave contact zone and on the top over a representative component or pad. For a typical 1.6 mm FR-4 board, a top-surface target of 90-130 °C just before the wave is a common starting point, verified against the flux datasheet, board thickness, copper content and component sensitivity.
Select flux by residue requirement, cleaning capability and hole-fill need.

No-clean fluxes suit lines without cleaning and where residue can stay, and they may leave visible residue and demand tighter preheat control. Water-soluble fluxes serve through-hole fill where aqueous cleaning exists, and they can be more corrosive when left on. Rosin-based fluxes remain in some repair and legacy processes. Take the classification and residue requirements from IPC J-STD-004 and confirm compatibility with the finish and the cleaning process.
Flux has to wet every bottom pad, lead tip and hole wall without boiling violently, lifting components or creating fog.

For spray application the controlled quantity is solids per unit of bottom area: a starting range of 0.08-0.23 mg/cm2, which is 500-1500 µg/in² of solids and about 0.8-2.3 g/m², with the lower end for thin boards and the higher end for heavy copper or through-hole walls. Figures quoted per unit of liquid, such as 0.5-1.0 g/ft², are several times larger and not comparable.

For foam application, set foam height and dwell so flux reaches the hole walls without dripping. Verify the amount by weighing a test board before and after fluxing, against the supplier's solids and activity data.
Preheat raises the board enough to activate flux and evaporate solvents without thermal shock or premature flux degradation.

A practical target is 90-130 °C on the top surface and 100-140 °C on the bottom immediately before wave contact, on a controlled ramp. Thin boards need less preheat to protect components, while thick boards and heavy copper planes need more to lift the top surface. Profile to IPC-7530 guidance and adjust until hole fill and wetting are stable.
Wave height must wet bottom pads and lead tips without flooding the top side or stirring up turbulence.

For a 1.6 mm board a starting height of 0.5-1.5 mm above the bottom surface is common, checked visually and by looking for solder balls, bridging and top-side contamination. Spray pressure, nozzle distance, flux viscosity and preheat control the fog: a fine even mist is what you want, and dripping flux or visible fog on nearby surfaces means too much application or poor atomisation.

theory.h: Setting a process for a given board
p: A thin board with light copper and small through-hole leads starts with lower flux density, lower preheat and lower wave height.

A thick board, heavy copper or large leads gets more preheat first, then more flux, then more wave height only if wetting is still short. A cold top side calls for more preheat or a slower conveyor; an overheating bottom calls for less wave height or lower wave temperature. Record the settings that give acceptable fill without solder balls, bridging or component damage.
Verify with thermocouple data, flux weight gain and joint inspection. Check hole fill, wetting angle, residue, solder balls, bridging and component damage against IPC-A-610 for the required class.
Document flux type, flux density, preheat setpoints, wave height, conveyor speed and wave temperature. After any change, re-run the profile and inspect a representative board before production.

calc.task: A 1.6 mm FR-4 board, 100 mm x 150 mm, 28 µm copper, 0.6 mm pitch SMT on top, 0.8 mm diameter through-hole leads on bottom, no-clean flux, aqueous cleaning not available. Set flux type and amount, preheat level, and fog/wave height, and justify each setting.
calc.solution: 1. Flux type: choose no-clean low-residue flux because cleaning is not available; verify flux activity and residue against IPC J-STD-004 and supplier datasheet. 2. Flux amount: bottom area = 100 mm x 150 mm = 15000 mm2 = 150 cm2. Set the target as a deposition of flux solids, 0.15 mg/cm2 within the 0.08-0.23 mg/cm2 (500-1500 µg/in²) starting range for mixed SMT/THT with no-clean flux, giving 150 cm2 x 0.15 mg/cm2 = 22.5 mg of solids. Add 10-20% for through-hole hole walls if spray does not fully wet holes; target 25-27 mg of solids. At 2.0% solids that is 1250-1350 mg of flux solution. Verify by weighing a test board or witness card before and after fluxing and converting the result to µg/in² of solids with a fluxometer. 3. Preheat: set top-surface target 110 °C and bottom-surface target 120 °C before wave. Use a controlled ramp and verify with thermocouples. This activates no-clean flux and evaporates solvents while limiting thermal stress on 0.6 mm pitch SMT. 4. Fog: set spray pressure 0.15-0.25 MPa and nozzle distance 100-200 mm. For this board choose 0.18 MPa and 150 mm. Verify that the spray forms a fine mist, not drips, and that nearby surfaces are not coated with flux fog. 5. Wave height: for a 1.6 mm board, set wave height 1.0 mm above the bottom surface. This is within the 0.5-1.5 mm starting range and leaves 0.6 mm clearance to the top side. Adjust up only if hole fill is poor; adjust down if solder balls, bridging, or top-side contamination appear. 6. Justification: no-clean flux requires controlled preheat, so 110 °C top and 120 °C bottom are reasonable starting targets. A flux-solids density of 0.15 mg/cm2 is enough to wet pads and leads without excessive fog. A wave height of 1.0 mm should wet the bottom side without flooding the top. Verify all settings with thermocouple data, flux weight, and IPC-A-610 inspection.

defect.symptom: Solder balls and small bridges on bottom pads after wave, with flux residue on the top side.
defect.cause: Flux amount or fog is too high, preheat is too low causing violent flux boiling, and wave height is too high causing turbulence and splashing.
defect.action: Reduce flux density to the lower end, reduce spray pressure or adjust nozzle distance, increase preheat slightly, lower wave height, then re-profile and inspect a representative board.

takeaways: Control the top-surface temperature before the wave, because the bottom heats faster and hides a cold top side.
Work in flux solids per unit area, since liquid-volume figures differ by several times and cannot be compared.
Raise preheat before flux and wave height when a thick board fills poorly, because temperature is usually the first limit.

mistakes.mistake: Measuring preheat on the bottom side only
mistakes.instead: Add a top thermocouple, because flux activation depends on the top surface.

mistakes.mistake: Comparing a g/ft² liquid figure with a solids deposition
mistakes.instead: Convert to solids per unit area before comparing the two.

mistakes.mistake: Raising wave height to improve fill on a heavy board
mistakes.instead: Increase preheat first, since a higher wave brings bridging and top-side contamination.

terms.def: The height of the flux mist applied to the board underside.
The mass of flux solids left per unit of board area.
The board temperature on the component side just before wave contact.
Rapid temperature change that can crack components or delaminate the board.

goals.text: Calculate wave contact (dwell) time from conveyor speed and contact length and judge the result against the process window.

blocks.alt: Reference sheet: board over a solder wave with effective contact length, conveyor speed, fog height and board clearance dimensions, the formula t equals L over v, a photograph of a board meeting the wave, and too-high versus too-low wave sketches
blocks.caption: Contact time t = L / v, fog height and board clearance; worked numbers in the figure above

theory.h: Contact time and why it matters
p: Contact time or dwell is how long the board underside stays in the wave. Calculate it as t = L / v, where L is the effective contact length in mm and v the conveyor speed in mm/s.

Dwell governs heat transfer, flux activation, hole fill and solder penetration. Too little leaves icicles, poor wetting and incomplete fill; too much overheats the board, burns off flux, damages components and bridges.
Use the effective contact length, not the nozzle length. Turbulence, wave height, board clearance and capillary action in the holes extend the wetted zone beyond the nozzle.
Measure it with a witness board, thermal paper or a short test run with a marked board. On a dual-wave machine, record the contact length of each wave and the total residence in the combined zone.

Dwell windows are machine-, flux- and board-specific, and published practice is narrower than folklore suggests. A typical window is 2 to 4 s, lead-free processes commonly run 3 to 5 s, and only heavy boards or a chip-wave plus main-wave pair push contact beyond that, to about 6 s.

A single-wave window of 6 to 12 s would overheat thin boards and burn off flux long before it filled a barrel, so treat any figure above 6 s as something your own trial data has to justify. Verify against the flux and equipment datasheet and your trials.
Judge dwell by hole fill, wetting, residue and thermal stress rather than by clock time. A high-thermal-mass board may need longer dwell, while small components and thin boards may need less.

Choose flux type from the board design and the cleaning capability. No-clean low-solids flux is common on mixed SMT and THT boards where residue is acceptable; water-soluble flux suits heavy oxidation or dense through-hole fill and requires cleaning.

Flux amount is specified as a deposition of flux solids in micrograms per square inch, measured with a fluxometer, with a typical recommended range of 500 to 1500 µg/in² of solids, about 0.8 to 2.3 g/m² (1 in² = 6.45 cm², 1 m² = 1550 in²). State the basis before comparing numbers: figures quoted per unit of liquid, for example 0.5 to 1.0 g/ft², are not comparable with solids-based figures and are several times larger.
Take the range from the flux datasheet and check it against the equipment datasheet. Too little flux gives poor wetting and dewetting; too much gives spatter, residue and solder balls.
Preheat brings the board underside to a temperature that activates flux and removes solvent before wave contact.

Measure on the board underside near wave entry, not in the air. A common starting range is 90-130 °C, verified against your paste and equipment datasheet. Low preheat leaves solvent in the flux and causes solder balls or poor wetting; high preheat burns flux, oxidises pads and stresses components.
Fog height, or wave crest height above the nozzle, sets how far the wave reaches toward the board. Board clearance is the gap between the crest and the board underside at entry.

A wave too high or a clearance too small lets the board meet the wave too early, which brings excessive dwell, bridging and board damage. A wave too low or a clearance too large stops the wave penetrating the holes, giving icicles and non-fill. Set height and clearance together, and check board bow and support.
Set flux type and amount first, then preheat, then wave height and board clearance, then conveyor speed.

Run a coupon with representative through-holes, pads and components. Adjust speed to bring dwell into the window, then adjust wave height or clearance to improve fill without pushing dwell out of it. Inspect the coupon against IPC-A-610 and record the settings.

calc.task: A 1.6 mm FR-4 board with 0.8 mm through-holes and small SMT components is run on a single-wave machine. Conveyor speed is 1.0 m/min. Effective contact length measured with a witness board is 180 mm. The flux datasheet gives a dwell window of 2-5 s for this lead-free process. Calculate dwell time, judge it against the window, and set flux type and amount, preheat level, and fog/wave height with board clearance for this board.
calc.solution: 1. Convert speed: 1.0 m/min = 1000 mm / 60 s = 16.7 mm/s. 2. Calculate dwell: t = L / v = 180 mm / 16.7 mm/s = 10.8 s. Step 3: Judge: 10.8 s is far above the 2-5 s window, more than twice its upper bound, so the line is running too slowly whatever the hole fill looks like. Raise conveyor speed to bring dwell into the window: the 180 mm contact length at 1.0 m/min is an over-long contact zone, and the window is reached at v = 180 mm / 4 s = 45 mm/s = 2.7 m/min for the top of the window or 180 mm / 3 s = 60 mm/s = 3.6 m/min for a mid-window 3 s. Pair the faster line with a check of wave height and clearance, because contact that long also means the board is riding deeper into the wave than intended. 4. Flux setting: use no-clean low-solids flux for mixed SMT/THT if residue is acceptable. Set spray density from the flux datasheet range, for example 500-1500 µg/in² of flux solids (about 0.8-2.3 g/m²), measured with a fluxometer by the wet or dry method; adjust tank pressure and traversing speed, then verify coverage and residue against your flux and equipment datasheet. 5. Preheat setting: set board-underside temperature near wave entry to 105-120 °C to activate flux and remove solvent while limiting thermal shock; verify against your paste/equipment datasheet. 6. Fog/wave height and clearance: set wave crest height to 10-12 mm above the nozzle and set board support so the board underside is 0-0.5 mm above the wave crest at entry, giving light contact without forcing the board into the wave. 7. Validate: run a coupon at the new speed, inspect hole fill, wetting, residue, and component damage, then adjust speed, wave height, or clearance in small steps; a 3 s dwell that fills the barrels has replaced the 10.8 s dwell that also overheated the board.

defect.symptom: Solder icicles and partial hole fill on 0.8 mm through-holes at board exit, with wetted pads but no bridging.
defect.cause: Wave height is too low and board clearance too large, so the wave never penetrates the holes; flux coverage may also be low, and the conveyor speed has to be checked against the 2-5 s window at the same time.
defect.action: Increase dwell by reducing conveyor speed or increasing effective contact length; raise wave height or reduce board clearance within machine limits; verify flux coverage and preheat; re-run a coupon and inspect against IPC-A-610 acceptability criteria.

takeaways: Measure effective contact length with a witness board, because turbulence extends the wetted zone beyond the nozzle.
Bring dwell into the 2 to 5 s range by speed before adjusting wave height, since contact length is what the window describes.
State the flux basis in µg/in² of solids, because liquid-volume figures are several times larger and not comparable.

mistakes.mistake: Calculating dwell from the nozzle length
mistakes.instead: Use the measured effective contact length, or the dwell comes out short.

mistakes.mistake: Slowing the conveyor to fill barrels
mistakes.instead: Check wave height and clearance first, since a slow line overheats the board without filling.

mistakes.mistake: Quoting a g/ft² liquid figure against a solids specification
mistakes.instead: Convert to solids per unit area before comparing.

A test board used to measure the effective contact length and wave footprint.
An instrument that measures flux solids deposition per unit area.
The gap between the wave crest and the board underside at wave entry.

title: Shadowing and orientation: shading, pallets, board direction, lead geometry

goals.text: Predict shadowing from layout and orientation and change direction, masking or sequence to remove it.

blocks.alt: A wave with a component casting a solder shadow behind it, a pallet blocking the path, and an orientation arrow showing board direction
blocks.caption: Shadowing and orientation: shading, pallets, board direction and lead geometry

theory.h: What shadowing means at the wave
p: Shadowing is a wetting or fill defect caused when a component, pallet, fixture or neighbouring part blocks the solder wave, flux or preheat from reaching a pad, lead or joint.

At the wave it is more than optical obstruction: local cooling, flux depletion, turbulence and poor drainage all contribute. Predict it by asking two questions — can solder reach the joint from the wave side, and can the joint drain after contact?

theory.h: Layout and orientation as the first predictor
p: Layout predicts shadowing when a tall or wide component sits upstream of a smaller joint in the wave direction. A connector, shield, transformer or tall electrolytic capacitor leaves a low-energy zone behind it.

Draw the wave direction on the assembly drawing and mark the solder-side access path. A downstream joint behind a body, pallet wall or neighbouring part will show incomplete fill, voiding or cold joints. Confirm on a test coupon, because turbulence can stretch or shorten the affected zone.
Board direction changes the shadow length, because the same component presents a different projected height to the wave.

A long body parallel to the wave direction can shade a whole row of joints, while rotating the panel or the component 90 degrees cuts the projected length. Check conveyor direction, wave angle and board angle together. Where the line allows panel rotation, compare the shadowed side before and after; where it does not, use pallet clearance or masking to compensate.
Pallets shadow when holes are too small, walls too thick, or support rails cover pads. They also trap flux, shield preheat and hold heat that changes drainage.

A good pallet opens the solder side around each joint, leaves clearance around leads, and avoids covering adjacent pads. Masking tape, kapton or pallet masking removes shadowing by blocking solder from areas that should stay dry, and the mask edge must not bridge into the joint. Check the pallet material, adhesive and wave equipment datasheet.
Lead geometry controls how much solder enters the hole and wets the pad. Long leads, tight lead-to-hole clearance, bent leads and large bodies all reduce capillary action and drainage.

Axial and radial parts behave differently: an axial lead can be shaded by a body sitting close to the board, while a radial lead can be shaded by adjacent leads or a pallet wall. Check lead diameter, hole diameter, pad size and seating height against your drill and plating data.

Sequence can change at layout, pallet or line level. Place shadow-prone joints where the wave has stabilised, keep them out of the wake of tall parts, and use a pallet that exposes the joint from the wave side.

On some lines a second wave, a different wave angle or a selective wave improves access. Where a downstream part blocks drainage, move the part, rotate the panel or add a pallet opening. Confirm the change with cross-section or wetting inspection, not only with appearance.
Start with a simple line-of-sight model: project the component height along the wave angle to estimate the shadow zone, then add a margin for turbulence and flux depletion.

Treat that model as a screening tool and not a guarantee. For production, run a coupon in the suspected orientation, inspect the joint, and adjust direction, masking or sequence. Check against your paste, wave and pallet datasheets, because the same layout behaves differently on other conveyors and wave types.

calc.task: A wave line runs left to right. A 10 mm tall connector with a 25 mm long body is placed 2 mm upstream of a row of 1.0 mm through-hole pads. The wave contact angle is estimated at 20 degrees from vertical. Predict whether the downstream pads are shadowed, then propose one orientation change, one pallet change, and one sequence change.
calc.solution: 1. Draw the wave direction left to right and mark the connector body. 2. Estimate shadow length using a line-of-sight model: shadow length = height * tan(angle). For 10 mm and 20 degrees, shadow length = 10 mm * 0.364 = 3.6 mm. 3. Compare with the gap: downstream pads are 2 mm behind the connector, so 2 mm is less than 3.6 mm; predict shadowing. 4. Add a turbulence and flux-depletion margin of 0.5 mm to 1.0 mm; the affected zone may extend to 4.1 mm to 4.6 mm. 5. Orientation change: rotate the connector 90 degrees so the 2 mm wide end faces the wave; shadow length = 2 mm * tan(20 degrees) = 0.7 mm, which is less than the 2 mm gap; verify with a coupon. 6. Pallet change: open the pallet hole around the downstream pads and add 1.0 mm clearance around the connector body; ensure the pallet wall does not cover the pads. 7. Sequence change: move the shadowed row downstream of the connector by at least 5 mm, or place it after a stabilizing wave zone; if layout cannot move, use masking or a selective wave to expose the joint.

defect.symptom: Downstream through-hole pads show partial fill and voiding only on the side away from the wave, while upstream pads are acceptable.
defect.cause: A tall connector body and pallet wall shadow the wave, and the board direction places the pads in a low-energy zone with poor flux and solder access.
defect.action: Rotate the panel or component, open the pallet around the pads, and re-run a coupon; if the defect persists, adjust wave angle or use masking to expose the joint.

takeaways: Check whether solder can reach the joint and whether it can drain, because both halves of the shadow problem need fixing.
Change the projected height — by rotating board or component — before adding fixtures, since geometry is the cheapest lever.
Screen with a line-of-sight model and confirm on a coupon, because turbulence decides the real edge of the shadow.

mistakes.mistake: Judging shadowing from the top-side appearance
mistakes.instead: Inspect the solder side and cross-section, since the top looks the same either way.

mistakes.mistake: Adding masking without checking the mask edge
mistakes.instead: Keep the edge clear of the joint, or the mask itself bridges the gap.

mistakes.mistake: Trusting the geometric shadow calculation alone
mistakes.instead: Add a turbulence margin and confirm on a coupon.

terms.def: The region behind an obstacle where the wave arrives weakened and cooled.
The obstacle dimension that faces the wave travel direction.
The cut-out that exposes a joint to the wave through the fixture.
How readily solder leaves the joint after the wave passes.

title: Wave defect atlas: bridging, balling, insufficient fill, bypass, lifted lead, blowholes

goals.text: Diagnose a wave defect from a solder-side image and name the parameter responsible.

blocks.alt: Reference sheet: six through-hole joint tiles with macro photographs and cross-sections for bridging, balling, insufficient fill, bypass, lifted lead and blowhole
blocks.caption: Wave soldering defect atlas: bridging, balling, insufficient fill, bypass, lifted lead, blowhole

p: A wave defect atlas starts on the solder side, because the defect shape records the last thermal and wetting events.

Read fill height, meniscus, wetting angle, solder volume, and whether the defect is isolated or repeats with component mass. Compare images in the same field of view. Acceptance limits live in IPC-A-610, so confirm the applicable class and revision before judging a joint.
Bridging is solder between adjacent pads or leads after the wave. Too much solder volume, poor drainage, low preheat, a slow conveyor or flux residue all cause it.
On fine pitch, check wave height, solder temperature and flux coverage. Wave height windows depend on the equipment, so verify against your paste and equipment datasheet.

Balling is separate solder balls on pads, traces or component bodies, and it usually means poor wetting or premature solidification: low preheat, oxidised leads, weak flux activity, or a solder temperature too low for the alloy.

Excessive turbulence and poor drainage can also throw balls. Compare the ball location with the wave contact pattern, and check preheat and solder temperature against your paste and equipment datasheet.
Insufficient fill shows as a low solder column in a through-hole, often with a shiny meniscus at the bottom and little wetting on the lead.

The responsible parameter is usually preheat ramp or dwell: the top of the hole never reaches the temperature capillary action needs. High aspect ratio, board thickness and lead-to-hole clearance all contribute. Typical preheat ramps are 1.0 to 3.0 °C/s and dwell 2 to 5 s, with 3 to 5 s for lead-free, verified against the flux and equipment datasheet.
Bypass is a joint the wave never wetted, showing a dry pad or lead with little solder.

Wave height too low, board warpage, poor flux coverage, a conveyor too fast, or a shielding effect from nearby components all produce it. Check the wave contact line and board support, then verify wave height, conveyor speed and spray pattern against the equipment datasheet.
A lifted lead has separated from the pad or barrel after wave contact, sometimes leaving a small solder remnant.

It is usually thermal-mechanical: high component mass, rapid heating, board expansion or insufficient preheat create differential movement. Handling and mounting contribute too. Check preheat ramp, component mass and board support against the process specification.
Blowholes appear as voids or craters in the joint, often near the hole wall or under the component. Trapped moisture, solvent or flux volatiles boiling during wave contact cause them.

A fast preheat ramp, low top-side temperature, high aspect ratio or a contaminated board all raise the risk. Check preheat ramp, dwell and board bake requirements against your paste and equipment datasheet and the IPC-A-610 acceptance criteria.
Classify the image by shape first: bridging, balling, low fill, dry joint, lifted lead or void.

Then map the shape to a parameter — volume and drainage for bridging, wetting temperature for balling, preheat and dwell for insufficient fill, wave contact for bypass, thermal mass and support for a lifted lead, moisture and volatiles for blowholes.
Confirm with a short DOE that changes one parameter at a time, and record the image, the profile and the datasheet limits behind the change.

calc.task: A solder-side image shows a through-hole with board thickness 1.6 mm, hole diameter 0.8 mm, lead diameter 0.5 mm, fill height 1.1 mm, preheat ramp 0.8 °C/s, dwell 2.5 s, and solder temperature 245 °C. Diagnose the defect and name the parameter most likely responsible.
calc.solution: Step 1: Classify the image. Low fill with a meniscus at the bottom is insufficient fill, not bridging or bypass. Step 2: Calculate hole aspect ratio: 1.6 mm / 0.8 mm = 2.0. A high aspect ratio increases the need for adequate preheat and dwell; verify the threshold for your board stackup and paste. Step 3: Calculate fill fraction: 1.1 mm / 1.6 mm = 0.6875, or 68.75%. Compare with the acceptance limit in IPC-A-610 for the applicable class; if the limit is higher, the joint fails. Step 4: Compare process values with typical windows: preheat ramp 0.8 °C/s is below the 1.0 to 3.0 °C/s range often used for through-hole fill, and dwell 2.5 s is inside the 2 to 5 s window but short of the 3 to 5 s lead-free band. Verify against your paste/equipment datasheet. Step 5: Check solder temperature: 245 °C may be acceptable for some alloys but can be low for high thermal mass joints; verify against the paste/equipment datasheet. Step 6: Conclusion: the image and profile point to insufficient fill caused primarily by low preheat ramp and short dwell; adjust preheat ramp toward the verified range and dwell toward the verified range, then re-run with a single change at a time.

defect.symptom: Solder-side image shows low fill in through-holes with a shiny meniscus at the bottom, little wetting on the lead, and no bridging.
defect.cause: Preheat ramp is too low and dwell is too short for the hole aspect ratio, so the hole top surface does not reach the temperature needed for capillary action.
defect.action: Increase preheat ramp and dwell within the verified paste/equipment datasheet range, confirm top-side temperature at the hole, and re-run with a single parameter change.

takeaways: Read the solder side first, because fill height and meniscus record what the wave actually did.
Map each shape to one parameter before touching the machine, since the appearance already narrows the candidates.
Confirm with a single-parameter DOE and keep the image with the profile, so the fix is reproducible.

mistakes.mistake: Raising solder temperature to cure balling
mistakes.instead: Check preheat, lead oxidation and flux activity first, since cold preheat is the usual cause.

mistakes.mistake: Treating a lifted lead as a solder defect
mistakes.instead: Review preheat ramp, component mass and board support, which is where the movement comes from.

mistakes.mistake: Reading fill height without the aspect ratio
mistakes.instead: Note hole depth and diameter, because a deep narrow hole needs more energy to fill.

terms.def: A joint that the wave failed to wet at all.
A void or crater in the joint caused by expanding trapped volatiles.
Hole depth divided by hole diameter, the same name as the stencil ratio but a different quantity.
The curved solder surface at the top of a filled hole or at the joint edge.
