title: Wave process control: bath contamination, tin consumption, records, first article

goals.text: Set flux type and amount, preheat level and fog/wave height for a given board and justify each setting.
Diagnose a wave defect from a solder-side image and name the parameter responsible.

blocks.alt: A solder pot with a contamination analysis readout and a tin consumption chart, beside a record sheet and a first-article board
blocks.caption: Wave process control: bath contamination, tin consumption, records and first article

p: Wave control sets the thermal and chemical conditions that let solder wet through-hole barrels and solder-side terminations without bridges, non-wetting or spatter.

The controls are flux type and amount, preheat temperature, wave or fog height, conveyor speed and pot temperature. For a given board, justify each one from board mass, copper content, component heat sinks, the flux activation range and the alloy liquidus.
Choose the flux from the contamination level and the residue requirement.

Rosin mildly activated flux is common on general through-hole assemblies where residues are cleaned or acceptable. Water-soluble flux suits a high oxide load or a planned cleaning step. No-clean fluxes appear less often at the wave, because residue and spatter are harder to manage there; check compatibility against the flux datasheet and the cleaning process.

Control flux as a deposition of solids per unit area of the bottom side. A practical starting range is 0.08 to 0.23 mg/cm2 of solids, which is 500-1500 µg/in² and about 0.8-2.3 g/m², verified against the flux datasheet and the spray pattern.

Wet mass per unit area is several times larger because the flux is roughly 2 % solids, so state whether a figure is on a solids or a liquid basis before comparing it. Too little flux gives non-wetting and dull joints; too much gives spatter, residue and poor fill. Weight a test coupon or board before and after fluxing to confirm coverage.
Preheat activates flux, removes volatiles and reduces thermal shock.

Measure the top surface or a representative thermal mass with a thermocouple. A practical entry range is 90 to 120 °C for many boards, with the flux activation temperature and the board maximum setting the final value. A cold board boils flux violently and spatters; a hot one burns the flux out before the wave arrives.
Wave height decides how much solder contacts the board bottom.

On a single wave, a crest 1 to 2 mm above the nozzle is a common starting point. On a dual-wave machine the first wave may sit near 1 to 2 mm and the second near 0.5 to 1 mm, with fog height often 2 to 5 mm above the nozzle. Check the equipment manual, because nozzle geometry changes the relationship between crest height and board immersion.
Contact time is wave length divided by conveyor speed. A practical range is 2 to 4 s for many boards, adjusted for hole fill and component heat sinks.

Pot temperature must sit above the alloy liquidus: 245 to 255 °C is common for Sn63/Pb37 and 250 to 260 °C for SAC305. Verify against the alloy datasheet and equipment capability, and record the actual pot temperature.

Bath condition changes wetting and the defect rate. Copper, nickel, iron and flux residues reach the bath from boards, fixtures and nozzles, so monitor contamination against the solder supplier's limits and change or filter the bath when wetting degrades.
Tin leaves through dross, drag-out, evaporation and replenishment losses. Track solder added per board or per hour, dross handling and pot level to keep wave height stable.
Record flux type, lot, wet flux density, preheat temperature, wave height, fog height, conveyor speed, pot temperature and any deviation.

For the first article, run the board, inspect the solder side against IPC-A-610 Class 2 or 3, measure hole fill and keep a solder-side image. If it fails, change one parameter at a time and record the result.

calc.task: A 1.6 mm FR-4 mixed assembly has 17 µm copper, 2 mm through-hole connectors, and small chip passives. The bottom area is 100 mm by 150 mm. Select flux type, flux amount, preheat level, wave height, fog height, and conveyor speed for a single-wave process, and justify each setting.
calc.solution: First, identify thermal behavior. The board is moderate mass with through-hole connectors that act as heat sinks, so preheat must be sufficient to bring the joint area to flux activation temperature without overheating the top side. Second, select flux. Use rosin mildly activated flux for general through-hole wetting, assuming residues are acceptable or cleaned; verify the flux activation range against the flux datasheet. Third, set flux amount. Target 0.20 mg/cm2 of flux solids on the bottom side, within the 0.08-0.23 mg/cm2 (500-1500 µg/in²) starting range. Bottom area is 100 mm x 150 mm = 15000 mm2 = 150 cm2. Required flux solids is 0.20 mg/cm2 x 150 cm2 = 30 mg per board; at 2.0% solids that is about 1500 mg of flux solution. Verify the solids deposition with a fluxometer or a weighed witness card. Fourth, set preheat. Target top surface temperature of 105 °C at wave entry, within the practical 90 to 120 °C range, then verify with a thermocouple on a test coupon. Fifth, set wave height. Use a single-wave crest height of 1.5 mm above the nozzle, within the 1 to 2 mm starting range, so the board bottom contacts the crest without excessive immersion. Sixth, set fog height. Use 3 mm fog height above the nozzle to pre-wet the underside before the main wave; verify against the machine manual. Seventh, set contact time. If the wave length is 80 mm and conveyor speed is 25 mm/s, contact time is 80 mm / 25 mm/s = 3.2 s, within the 2 to 4 s practical range. Eighth, set pot temperature. For SAC305, use 255 °C, above the SAC305 liquidus of 219 °C (217 °C is the solidus), and verify against the alloy and equipment datasheet. Ninth, justify. The flux amount supports wetting without excess residue, preheat activates flux and reduces spatter, wave height and contact time provide hole fill without excessive bridging, and pot temperature maintains solder fluidity.

defect.symptom: Solder-side image shows scattered small solder balls and spatter around through-hole connector leads, with some dull non-wetted pads nearby.
defect.cause: Preheat temperature was too low for the flux activation range, so flux volatiles boiled during wave contact and caused spatter; the same condition can reduce wetting and leave dull joints.
defect.action: Increase preheat so the top surface reaches 100 to 110 °C at wave entry, verify with a thermocouple, confirm flux activation range from the flux datasheet, and re-run first article. If spatter persists, reduce wave height or fog height slightly and check for board moisture or excessive flux volume.

takeaways: Justify each setting from board mass, copper and alloy, since the same recipe moves everything when the board changes.
State flux figures on a solids or liquid basis before comparing them, because the two differ by several times.
Keep the first-article image with the parameter record, so the next run starts from evidence rather than memory.

mistakes.mistake: Setting pot temperature below the alloy liquidus
mistakes.instead: Confirm the liquidus from the alloy datasheet, since a cold pot cannot wet.

mistakes.mistake: Recording settings without the flux lot
mistakes.instead: Include the lot, because bath and flux condition drift with it.

mistakes.mistake: Changing preheat, wave height and speed together on a failing first article
mistakes.instead: Change one parameter at a time, or the cause is lost.

terms.def: The temperature of the molten solder in the wave reservoir.
The height of the solder wave above the nozzle opening.
Oxide and intermetallic debris that forms on the molten solder surface.
The temperature band in which the flux removes oxides effectively.

title: Where selective beats wave: mixed assembly, heat-sensitive neighbours, throughput

goals.text: Choose nozzle and flux strategy for a joint group and defend the choice against the joint geometry.

p: Selective soldering serves mixed assemblies where through-hole joints cannot go through a full wave without damaging nearby surface-mount parts, plastic connectors or heat-sensitive devices.

The process localises heat and flux to one joint group, so neighbours stay protected while the joint stays repeatable. The choice is a joint geometry decision rather than a question of machine availability.

The group must be reachable from the bottom side, have clearance for the nozzle, and let flux reach the joint without being absorbed by adjacent paste or trapped under a component. Agree the IPC-A-610 acceptance class before the trial, because the same visual defect passes in one class and fails in another. Confirm too that the process brings no new risk of its own: flux migration, solder balls, or thermal damage to neighbouring joints.

blocks.caption: Selective soldering: a programmable micro-wave wets only targeted pads

blocks.alt: A mixed assembly with through-hole joints beside surface-mount parts, and a selective nozzle soldering one joint while the neighbours stay cool
blocks.caption: Where selective beats wave: mixed assembly, heat-sensitive neighbours and throughput

p: A joint group is a set of joints served by one nozzle path, one flux application and one thermal profile. Isolated pins, connector rows, mixed through-hole and surface-mount pads, and repair zones are typical.

Geometry decides the choice: pin diameter, hole plating, pad size, standoff height, body height and the distance to the nearest heat-sensitive part tell you whether a mini-wave, dip or jet nozzle can reach the joint. A tall connector may need a taller nozzle or a different flux delivery method, and a low-standoff part may need a shallow wave to avoid flooding.

Check against the board layout and nozzle datasheet before committing to a path. Where a group mixes technologies, confirm that surface-mount joints are already reflowed or that the selective process will not disturb them.
Nozzle choice balances wetting energy, thermal exposure and reach.

A mini-wave makes a small solder wave and suits exposed through-hole pins and mixed joints. A dip nozzle gives more uniform immersion for small groups and raises the heat seen by nearby pads. Jet or spray-assisted nozzles improve flux delivery and wetting on tight pitch and demand control of splash and solder mist.

With heat-sensitive neighbours, take the smallest nozzle that still wets completely, and verify nozzle height, wave height and dwell against the equipment datasheet. Record practice values such as orifice size, wave height and standoff as a range until capability is established, and keep the nozzle compatible with the alloy and flux chemistry.
Flux strategy has to match joint geometry and contamination level.

Clean boards with plated through-holes may need only a low-solids liquid flux applied by controlled spray or jet. Oxidised pins, high-thermal-mass connectors or joints with limited access may need higher activity or a pre-applied flux preform, with residue and corrosion risk evaluated first.

Give enough flux to wet the joint and the wall without migrating to nearby surface-mount joints or throwing solder balls. With aerosol or ultrasonic delivery, verify droplet size, pressure and solids against the paste and flux datasheets, because the same nozzle behaves differently with another chemistry. Check flux placement visually and by cross-section before release.
Neighbours are the reason for the process, so the thermal budget has to be controlled at the joint rather than at the nozzle.

Preheat should bring board and joint to a stable temperature before solder contact, which cuts thermal shock and improves wetting without a long dwell. Set peak and dwell from the component moisture sensitivity level and the alloy liquidus, with a margin agreed by the design and reliability teams.

Measure the surface temperature at the neighbour's body or pin, not only the pot temperature, and check a plastic connector, electrolytic capacitor or small-signal device against its datasheet and the IPC J-STD-001 thermal exposure guidance. Profile the worst-case joint and the nearest sensitive component together.
Throughput follows the number of joint groups, path length, dwell, flux application time and preheat stabilisation.

A single group runs quickly, while a mixed assembly often needs several passes, nozzle changes or flux applications. Model cycle time as fixed plus variable elements: flux application, preheat, solder dwell, cooling and a rework allowance.

When throughput is short, cut unnecessary path length or combine compatible groups first, then adjust dwell and flux within the wetting window. Never shorten dwell below the point where fill and wetting hold unless a qualified alternate process is approved. Confirm the joint against IPC-A-610 and guide any rework by IPC-7711/7721.
A defensible decision starts with geometry. Draw the joint group, mark the nozzle access path, and identify the nearest heat-sensitive component.

Then choose the nozzle that reaches the joint with the least thermal exposure, and the flux that wets without migrating. A low-standoff joint near a plastic connector suits a shallow mini-wave with low-solids flux. A high-thermal-mass connector with oxidised pins suits a dip nozzle, higher activity and longer preheat. Tight-pitch mixed joints often want a jet-assisted nozzle with controlled flux volume.
Defend the choice by showing that geometry, neighbour clearance and thermal budget fit the nozzle and flux, and back it with trial data rather than vendor claims.
Verify with cross-sections, hole fill, wetting angle, residue inspection and thermal profiling at both the joint and the neighbour.

Record nozzle type, nozzle height, wave height, dwell, preheat, peak temperature, flux type, flux volume and spray parameters. Use a small trial matrix to find the window, then confirm on production samples.

State practice-based values as ranges and verify them against the paste, flux and equipment datasheets. Accept against the agreed IPC-A-610 class and the IPC J-STD-001 workmanship requirements. Rework a failed joint per IPC-7711/7721 and update the window when the failure shows a systematic nozzle or flux mismatch, so the documentation lets another engineer repeat the choice.

blocks.caption: Wave vs selective: where each process wins
head: Criterion
Wave
Selective
rows: Poor: whole board committed to the line

calc.task: A mixed assembly has a 40-pin through-hole connector, a 0.65 mm pitch surface-mount QFP 8 mm away, and an electrolytic capacitor 12 mm away. The connector pins are 1.0 mm diameter and the board is 1.6 mm thick. Select a nozzle and flux strategy, then estimate cycle time and thermal margin.
calc.solution: Define the joint group as the 40 through-hole pins, because they share access, thermal mass, and flux requirements. Select a small mini-wave nozzle with an orifice of 1.5-2.5 mm, a wave height of 0.5-1.0 mm, and a standoff of 0.5-1.5 mm, because the joint is accessible from below and the nearby surface-mount QFP is 8 mm away. Select low-solids liquid flux delivered by controlled spray at 15-30 uL per joint group, because the pins are plated and the nearby joints do not require high-activity flux. Set preheat to 90-120 °C board surface temperature, peak solder temperature to 245-255 C, and dwell to 2-4 s, then verify against the solder alloy liquidus and the component datasheet. Measure the capacitor body temperature during profiling; if the datasheet limit is 105 °C and the measured value is 85-95 C, the margin is 10-20 C. Estimate cycle time as flux application 3 s, preheat 20 s, solder dwell 3 s, cooling 10 s, and nozzle path 15 s, giving 51 s per board. Defend the choice by showing that the mini-wave nozzle reaches the 1.0 mm pins without flooding the 0.65 mm pitch QFP, the flux volume is low enough to limit migration, and the thermal margin protects the capacitor. Confirm acceptance against IPC-A-610 and rework any defective joint according to IPC-7711/7721.

defect.symptom: After selective soldering, a through-hole connector shows intermittent opens and dull, grainy joints, while nearby surface-mount joints look acceptable.
defect.cause: The preheat was too low for the connector thermal mass, and the dwell was too short, so the hole wall and pin did not reach a stable wetting temperature; flux may have been insufficient or poorly distributed.
defect.action: Re-profile the joint group with a higher preheat and longer dwell, verify board surface temperature at the connector, confirm flux volume and nozzle standoff against the equipment datasheet, and rework affected joints according to IPC-7711/7721. Re-inspect against IPC-A-610.

takeaways: Choose selective soldering from joint geometry and neighbour clearance, not from machine availability.
Take the smallest nozzle that wets completely, because thermal exposure to the neighbour is the constraint being managed.
Profile the nearest sensitive component as well as the joint, since the neighbour sets the ceiling.

mistakes.mistake: Selecting a dip nozzle for the whole group because it wets quickly
mistakes.instead: Check neighbour temperature first, since the extra heat is what damages it.

mistakes.mistake: Raising flux activity without checking residue
mistakes.instead: Verify the residue class and cleaning plan, or corrosion risk replaces the wetting problem.

mistakes.mistake: Shortening dwell to meet takt time
mistakes.instead: Confirm fill and wetting on a cross-section before accepting the faster cycle.

terms.def: A set of joints processed with one nozzle path, flux application and thermal profile.
A small localised solder wave formed by a nozzle, used for selective joints.
The gap between the component body and the board surface.
Flux travelling away from the intended joint onto neighbouring pads or components.

title: Nozzle strategy: size and shape, flux-on-the-fly, dwell per joint, multi-pass

goals.text: Choose nozzle and flux strategy for a joint group and defend the choice against the joint geometry.
Build a selective program — path, order, dwell per joint, passes — for a given board.

blocks.alt: A set of interchangeable nozzles with a joint beside each, a flux-on-the-fly applicator, and a multi-pass sequence
blocks.caption: Nozzle strategy: size and shape, flux-on-the-fly, dwell per joint and multi-pass

p: Nozzle strategy starts with the joint, not with a favourite nozzle.

On a through-hole lead the opening must be large enough to wet the lead and pad without dragging adjacent joints and small enough to keep the meniscus stable. For common leads of 0.5 mm to 1.2 mm, an inside diameter of 0.8 mm to 2.0 mm is a practical starting range, verified against your equipment and the adjacent pad spacing.
On a surface-mount pad the nozzle footprint controls heat transfer and flux delivery, so the same joint fails when the nozzle edge lands on a neighbouring pad or misses the thermal mass.
Shape changes thermal and wetting behaviour. A conical nozzle concentrates heat on a small joint, which suits isolated pins and small surface-mount pads.

A flat or annular nozzle spreads heat over a larger area, which helps large pads, ground planes and multi-pin connectors where the joint must fill from the pad edge inward. A slot nozzle presents a narrow solder edge along a joint line, which suits row connectors, shield cans and long joints.
Match the shape to the joint outline, then check clearance to nearby components and pads.

Flux-on-the-fly applies flux immediately before the wave or nozzle contact, so it is still active when the joint reaches wetting temperature. The variables are volume, pattern, viscosity and solids content.

A practical starting density is 0.05 mg/mm^2 to 0.25 mg/mm^2 on the joint area, or a joint volume of 0.5 uL to 3.0 uL for many selective nozzles, verified against the flux datasheet and the residue requirement. Too little flux gives poor wetting and pinholes; too much leaves residue, throws solder balls or destabilises the meniscus.

Note the basis before comparing numbers: this is flux per unit of joint area for selective application, while the Module 09 figures are flux solids per unit of board bottom area, so the two must never be compared directly.

Dwell is the time a joint spends under the wave or nozzle. It must be long enough to heat the joint, activate flux and let solder flow, and short enough to limit intermetallic growth, component damage and flux burn-off.

For many through-hole joints 0.5 s to 3.0 s is a reasonable starting range, and small surface-mount joints may need only 0.2 s to 1.5 s. Large thermal masses such as connectors with ground tabs need longer dwell or a preheat pass. Verify actual joint temperature with thermocouples rather than relying on bath temperature alone.
Multi-pass programs separate functions that would compete in a single pass: a preheat pass, a flux pass and a solder pass, or a wetting pass followed by a fill pass.

For high thermal mass joints, a preheat pass of 100 °C to 160 °C reduces thermal shock and shortens the solder dwell. Lead-free bath temperatures commonly sit around 250 °C to 260 C, verified against the alloy datasheet and the equipment.
Multi-pass improves fill on large pads, and every pass adds cycle time and thermal exposure, so use the fewest passes that still meet the joint.
Building the program means translating the joint list into path, order, dwell and passes.

Group joints by nozzle type and flux pattern first, then order the path to keep the meniscus stable and avoid dragging solder across unsoldered joints. A practical order runs from low thermal mass joints to medium and high, which stabilises the process, though board layout and component mass can reverse it — check with test coupons.
Keep the path away from tall components, avoid sharp direction changes over fresh joints, and drive each group from its own dwell table.
Defend the choice against the joint geometry by giving the physical reason behind every parameter.

State lead diameter, pad area, component mass, access and adjacent spacing. Then show that the nozzle size and shape cover the joint without bridging, that flux reaches the joint interface, that dwell heats the joint into the wetting range, and that the passes manage thermal mass.
When a joint fails, change one variable — nozzle size, flux volume, dwell or pass order — and record the result against your visual acceptance criteria.

calc.task: A board has 12 through-hole connector pins with 0.8 mm lead diameter and 1.6 mm pad diameter, 4 surface-mount power pads of 4 mm by 4 mm, and 1 ground pad of 8 mm by 8 mm. Choose nozzle size and shape, flux strategy, dwell per joint, and passes for a selective soldering program. Assume lead-free solder and verify against equipment datasheet.
calc.solution: Group the joints into 12 through-hole pins, 4 surface-mount power pads, and 1 ground pad. For the through-hole pins, choose a conical nozzle with inside diameter 1.2 mm to 1.6 mm, giving clearance around the 0.8 mm lead while avoiding adjacent 1.6 mm pads. For the 4 mm by 4 mm power pads, choose a flat or annular nozzle with footprint 4.5 mm to 6.0 mm to cover the pad edge and heat the copper. For the 8 mm by 8 mm ground pad, choose a slot or large annular nozzle with footprint 8.5 mm to 10.0 mm, or use a 2-pass strategy if the nozzle cannot cover the pad without adjacent risk. Use flux-on-the-fly with 0.10 mg/mm^2 to 0.20 mg/mm^2 on the joint area (a per-joint-area basis, not the flux-solids-per-board-area basis used for wave soldering in Module 09); for the ground pad, aim near 0.20 mg/mm^2 if residue allows. Set dwell: through-hole pins 1.2 s to 1.8 s; power pads 0.8 s to 1.5 s; ground pad 2.0 s to 3.0 s. Use 2 passes for the board: pass 1 preheat at 120 °C to 140 °C over high thermal mass joints, pass 2 solder at 255 °C to 260 C. If the ground pad shows incomplete fill, add another pass with flux-only or lower dwell solder, then recheck.

defect.symptom: A 4 mm by 4 mm surface-mount power pad shows a dull, cratered fillet and lifted pad edge after selective soldering.
defect.cause: The nozzle footprint was too small, dwell was near 0.5 s, and flux density was near 0.05 mg/mm^2, so the pad did not reach wetting temperature and flux burned off before solder flowed.
defect.action: Increase nozzle footprint to 4.5 mm to 6.0 mm, raise flux density to 0.10 mg/mm^2 to 0.20 mg/mm^2, add a preheat pass at 120 °C to 140 C, and increase dwell to 0.8 s to 1.5 s; verify with thermocouples and visual acceptance criteria.

takeaways: Size the nozzle from the lead and the adjacent pad spacing, because both the clearance and the meniscus depend on it.
State flux figures on the joint-area basis, since the wave numbers in Module 09 use board area and cannot be compared.
Add passes only for thermal mass, because each one costs cycle time and heat.

mistakes.mistake: Choosing a nozzle by the joint outline alone
mistakes.instead: Check adjacent pad spacing and component clearance, or the nozzle drags solder.

mistakes.mistake: Reusing a wave flux density on a selective nozzle
mistakes.instead: Convert to the joint-area basis first, since the two are not interchangeable.

mistakes.mistake: Extending dwell on every joint to fix one large pad
mistakes.instead: Add a preheat pass instead, because dwell loads the neighbours as well.

terms.def: Flux applied immediately before solder contact so it stays active at wetting temperature.
The curved solder surface that forms at the nozzle and the joint.
A nozzle with a narrow linear opening, used for rows and long joints.
The heat capacity of the joint and its surrounding copper and component.

skills: Lesson m10l01: Where selective beats wave: mixed assembly, heat-sensitive neighbours, throughput

title: Thermal budget of the neighbours: heat spread, monitoring, sensitive parts

goals.text: Estimate the heat exposure of neighbouring parts and specify the mitigation and the verification.

blocks.alt: A board cross-section showing heat spreading from a soldered joint into adjacent copper and components, with a temperature map
blocks.caption: Thermal budget of the neighbours: heat spread, monitoring and sensitive parts

theory.h: Thermal budget as a shared resource
p: The thermal budget is more than the target joint profile: it is the cumulative heat reaching nearby parts by conduction, convection and radiation.

In reflow, wave and hand soldering, the board, copper planes, leads, fixtures and air all carry heat. A neighbour can pass its datasheet limit while the target joint sits comfortably inside specification.

Conduction through copper planes and component leads usually dominates close to the heat source. Convection from oven air or wave flux vapour sets the background temperature. Radiation matters less at soldering temperatures, though hot fixtures or a solder pot can contribute.
The path with the lowest thermal resistance controls the peak temperature the neighbour sees, so that is the path to interrupt.
Large copper areas, thick board material, high-conductivity substrates, dense placement and low standoff carry heat further.

High paste volume, long time above liquidus, high peak and slow cooling extend the exposure in time. A fixture touching the board either sinks heat or traps it, depending on material and contact area.
Parts that need watching include electrolytic capacitors, plastic connectors, LEDs, MEMS devices, sensors, adhesive-bonded components and anything with a moisture sensitivity level.

Their limits are usually a maximum body temperature, a maximum time at temperature, a moisture sensitivity class and a limit on mechanical deformation. Set the allowable budget from the component datasheet and the assembly process specification.
Early in layout, estimate neighbour exposure from the heat source temperature and an attenuation factor based on distance, copper connectivity and local thermal mass.
For production, replace the estimate with thermocouple profiling at the worst-case location. The estimate screens; the profile is the evidence.
Mitigate at layout, process or fixture level.

Layout options are more spacing, thermal relief, less copper connectivity and moving sensitive parts away from heat sources. Process options are a lower peak, a shorter time above liquidus, selective soldering, less paste and an adjusted conveyor speed. Fixtures and shields cut radiant or convective heat, and heat sinks pull heat away.
Verify with a thermal profile recorded at the target joint and at the most exposed neighbour, plus functional test after exposure and inspection for deformation, discolouration or solder defects.

Record the profile, the thermocouple locations and the acceptance criteria. Where a neighbour sits near its limit, repeat the profile after any change to paste, oven setup, fixture or component supplier.

calc.task: A wave-soldering line has a solder pot temperature of 250 °C (typical 245-260 °C; verify against equipment datasheet). The board top surface near the wave is 100 °C (typical 80-120 °C; verify against profile). An electrolytic capacitor is 8 mm from the wave contact and has a maximum body temperature of 105 °C. Estimate the capacitor body temperature using an attenuation length of 4 mm (typical 3-6 mm; verify against board and fixture trials).
calc.solution: Step A: Calculate the temperature difference between the pot and the board top: 250 °C - 100 °C = 150 °C. Step B: Apply exponential attenuation: rise = 150 °C × exp(-8 mm / 4 mm). Step C: Evaluate: exp(-2) ≈ 0.14, so rise ≈ 21 °C. Step D: Estimated body temperature = 100 °C + 21 °C = 121 °C. Step E: Compare with 105 °C; the estimate exceeds the limit. Mitigation: move the capacitor away from the wave contact, add a thermal shield, or use selective soldering. Verification: attach a thermocouple to the capacitor body, run a wave-soldering profile, and confirm the peak body temperature remains below 105 °C and the part passes functional test.

defect.symptom: After wave soldering, an electrolytic capacitor near the wave contact shows bulging, electrolyte leakage, or reduced capacitance.
defect.cause: Heat spread from the wave contact raised the capacitor body above its datasheet limit because the part was too close to the heat source and the profile was not verified at the capacitor.
defect.action: Stop the line, attach a thermocouple to the capacitor body, rerun the wave-soldering profile, increase spacing or add a thermal shield or selective soldering, then verify the peak body temperature and functional performance.

takeaways: Place thermocouples on the neighbour as well as the joint, because the joint can pass while the neighbour fails.
Interrupt the lowest-resistance path, since that is what sets the neighbour's peak rather than distance alone.
Re-profile after any fixture, paste or supplier change, because the assumption that produced the old margin has moved.

mistakes.mistake: Watching the pot temperature as a proxy for neighbour temperature
mistakes.instead: Measure the body, since attenuation and thermal mass change the number entirely.

mistakes.mistake: Relying on a layout estimate for release
mistakes.instead: Profile the production board, because the estimate only screens.

mistakes.mistake: Accepting a neighbour close to its limit
mistakes.instead: Keep margin and repeat the profile after any process change.

terms.def: The distance over which the temperature rise from a source falls by a factor of e.
How strongly a path resists heat flow; the lowest-resistance path carries the most heat.
The J-STD-020 class that states how long a package may sit in factory ambient before reflow; it does not raise or lower the peak temperature the package tolerates.
A physical barrier that reduces radiant or convective heat reaching a part.

skills: Lesson m10l02: Nozzle strategy: size and shape, flux-on-the-fly, dwell per joint, multi-pass

title: Programming a run: path, order, fixtures, air knife, cycle time

goals.text: Build a selective program — path, order, dwell per joint, passes — for a given board.

blocks.alt: A machine screen showing a soldering path with numbered joints, a fixture, an air knife and a cycle-time breakdown
blocks.caption: Programming a run: path, order, fixtures, air knife and cycle time

p: A selective soldering program is a machine-readable recipe for one board, not a list of coordinates.

It defines where flux lands, how long the board preheats, how the air knife behaves, which joints go first, how the nozzle moves, how long each joint dwells, how many passes run, and how the board cools before handling.

The inputs are board geometry, component list, pad and hole dimensions, copper area, component height, board thickness, fixture design, flux type, alloy, nozzle temperature and machine limits. The output is a repeatable cycle that wets properly without excess heat, flux carryover, bridging or mechanical disturbance.

Each path, dwell, pass and fixture decision should trace to a board feature or a measured thermal result, so another engineer can audit the program and reproduce it on the same equipment, fixture and material set.
Path planning starts from the bottom side, because selective soldering normally reaches through-hole pins and bottom-side pads from below.

On a through-hole joint the path centres on the hole or pad and approaches from a direction that drags no solder across neighbouring pads. A continuous wave path works for pin rows when nozzle width, flux coverage and pad spacing allow it; isolated joints are usually safer point to point, which limits solder dragged into nearby gaps. Bottom-side surface-mount pads follow the pad geometry and avoid crossing between pads unless the method is qualified.

Keep lead-in and lead-out short, predictable and outside the final wetted area. Account for shadowing from tall components, connectors and shielding cans, and verify nozzle-to-board, nozzle-to-component and pin-to-support clearance on the first article rather than assuming them.

theory.h: Ordering joints for heat and flux
p: The order of joints is a thermal decision. Group by access and thermal mass, then run from low-mass to high-mass joints while the board is still warm from preheat.

High-mass joints such as ground-plane pins and heavy connectors need more energy, and placing them too early cools the nozzle or wave; placing them too late overheats the board near sensitive parts. Avoid scheduling a high-mass joint immediately before one near a heat-sensitive component unless a cooling pause or fixture airflow is available.

Grouping also cuts travel: joints sharing a row, a connector footprint or a nozzle approach run together, and grouping must not force the nozzle across completed joints or drag solder over unprocessed pads. Use parallel fluxing or preheat only after confirming that flux activation, board temperature and wetting stay inside the qualified window. Document the reason for each group, because later troubleshooting needs to know whether a defect came from path, thermal mass or sequence.
The fixture is part of the program: it sets board height, exposure, support and thermal behaviour.

A good fixture holds the board flat, exposes the bottom side, supports areas that would flex, and blocks neither nozzle, fluxer nor air knife. Insulating, low-heat-transfer materials such as PEEK or phenolic are common for temperature stability and stiffness.

Vacuum hold-down helps, and vacuum holes must not pull flux into unwanted areas or seat the board unevenly. Support pins sit under large components, connector bodies and board edges, not so close to through-hole pads that they block solder access. Pin height sets the board-to-nozzle relationship, so a change in board thickness may need a z-height change even when the coordinates stay put.

The fixture should drain flux and stop it pooling on the top side, and mixed-technology boards may need cutouts or shields against flux mist and radiant heat. Check flatness, pin wear and seating on the first article, because a small height error changes dwell contact and either starves the joint or floods it.

The air knife is a programmed air or nitrogen curtain that strips excess flux from the board surface and, on some machines, limits flux carryover toward the nozzle or pot. It controls how much flux reaches the joint.

Too little leaves excess flux that boils during soldering and causes blowback, voids or dross. Too much cools the joint, disturbs small components, oxidises the wetting surface or dries the flux before it activates.

Define whether the knife runs, when it fires relative to fluxing and soldering, its pressure, distance and angle. Starting ranges are 20-60 kPa, 5-15 mm and 15-45 degrees, verified against the paste, flux and equipment datasheet. Dry filtered air is common; nitrogen serves where oxidation control matters, with gas purity and flow qualified.

Check for clogging, uneven flow and leakage, because a partly blocked knife leaves a local flux imbalance that shows up as a random wetting defect. In troubleshooting, compare knife settings with defect location: defects near the flux application edge usually point to flux volume or knife timing rather than dwell.
Dwell is how long the solder source stays in contact with, or close enough to, the joint. Set it from thermal mass, pad size, hole size, lead material, flux activity and nozzle temperature.

Small pins and small bottom-side pads need less dwell than ground-plane pins or heavy connector leads. A practical starting range is 0.8-2.5 s for low-mass joints and 1.5-4.0 s for high-mass joints, with the qualified value coming from thermocouple data and cross-sections.

On high-mass joints, several short passes usually beat one long dwell, because heat spreads without overheating neighbours. Include cooling between passes when board temperature climbs too fast, and record the pass count with its reason: one pass for simple joints, two or more for high copper area, thick leads or a poor wetting history.

Never raise dwell to compensate for low preheat, thin flux coverage or a wrong nozzle height. A joint wanting excessive dwell points to path, fixture height, flux volume or the thermal profile, and those come first.
Cycle time sums board handling, flux application, preheat, air-knife action, solder movement, dwell, cooling and fixture exchange. Calculate it from the program, then verify it on the machine.

Optimise by cutting non-value-added travel, grouping joints logically, and using machine features only where they preserve wetting. Never shorten preheat or cooling for throughput unless the profile and acceptance criteria still hold.

Verification covers first-article inspection, thermocouples at representative joints, cross-sections on critical joints and acceptance against IPC-A-610. Rework follows IPC-7711/7721 rather than improvised extra heat cycles.

Prevention is built into the program: path geometry prevents bridging, order prevents heat damage, fixture support prevents flex, air-knife control prevents flux carryover, and dwell and pass strategy prevent cold joints. Version-control the program with board revision, fixture revision, flux lot, nozzle condition and measured cycle time, so a good run can be compared with a bad one and the difference traced to material, fixture wear, nozzle condition or settings.

calc.task: A board has 84 through-hole pins and 26 bottom-side surface-mount joints. Twelve of the through-hole pins are high-mass ground-plane pins. The program uses single-pass soldering for the remaining through-hole pins and surface-mount joints, and two passes for the high-mass pins. Dwell is 1.2 s for low-mass through-hole pins, 1.8 s for surface-mount joints, and 2.4 s for high-mass pins. Travel overhead is 0.35 s per pass for low-mass through-hole pins and surface-mount joints, and 0.55 s per pass for high-mass pins. Flux application takes 18 s, preheat takes 45 s, air-knife action takes 6 s, cooling takes 12 s, and board handling takes 10 s. Calculate the solder time, total cycle time, and effective joints per minute.
calc.solution: Step 1: Determine the number of low-mass through-hole pins. Total through-hole pins are 84. High-mass through-hole pins are 12. Low-mass through-hole pins are 84 - 12 = 72. Step 2: Calculate low-mass through-hole solder time. Each low-mass through-hole pin uses one pass. Time per pass is dwell plus travel overhead: 1.2 + 0.35 = 1.55 s. Total low-mass through-hole time is 72 * 1.55 = 111.6 s. Step 3: Calculate surface-mount solder time. Each surface-mount joint uses one pass. Time per pass is 1.8 + 0.35 = 2.15 s. Total surface-mount time is 26 * 2.15 = 55.9 s. Step 4: Calculate high-mass through-hole solder time. Each high-mass pin uses two passes. Time per pass is 2.4 + 0.55 = 2.95 s. Total high-mass time is 12 * 2 * 2.95 = 70.8 s. Step 5: Sum solder time. Solder time is 111.6 + 55.9 + 70.8 = 238.3 s. Step 6: Add non-solder cycle elements. Flux application is 18 s, preheat is 45 s, air-knife action is 6 s, cooling is 12 s, and board handling is 10 s. Non-solder time is 18 + 45 + 6 + 12 + 10 = 91 s. Step 7: Calculate total cycle time. Total cycle time is 238.3 + 91 = 329.3 s. Step 8: Calculate total joints. Total joints are 84 + 26 = 110. Step 9: Convert total cycle time to minutes. 329.3 / 60 = 5.488333... minutes. Step 10: Calculate effective joints per minute. 110 / 5.488333... = 20.04 joints per minute. Rounded for reporting, the effective rate is 20.0 joints per minute.

defect.symptom: A row of through-hole pins shows incomplete wetting on the far side of a connector, while the first pins in the row are acceptable. The defect repeats at the same location on multiple boards.
defect.cause: The path or order causes heat loss and flux depletion before the nozzle reaches the far end of the row. The connector body may shadow preheat or flux, the fixture may allow local board flex, or the air knife may dry the flux before the last joints are soldered. The dwell may be adequate for the first joints but insufficient for the cooler far-end joints.
defect.action: Measure board temperature at the first and last joints with thermocouples. Check fixture support near the connector and verify board height. Review the path direction and consider reversing the row or splitting it into two groups. Verify flux coverage and air-knife pressure, distance, and timing. If the far-end joints are cooler, increase preheat or add a short cooling pause before the row rather than only increasing dwell. Qualify the change with cross-sections and acceptance review against IPC-A-610.

takeaways: Trace every path, dwell and pass back to a board feature or a thermal measurement, so the program can be audited.
Keep lead-in and lead-out outside the wetted area, because that is where dragged solder bridges neighbours.
Record the pass count with its reason, since a later investigation needs to know whether the joint needed the extra heat or the extra time.

mistakes.mistake: Raising dwell to fix a cold joint
mistakes.instead: Check preheat, flux coverage and nozzle height first, since dwell is the most expensive lever.

mistakes.mistake: Using vacuum hold-down without checking the holes
mistakes.instead: Confirm flux cannot be pulled into unwanted areas and the board seats evenly.

mistakes.mistake: Optimising cycle time by shortening cooling
mistakes.instead: Keep the profile and acceptance criteria intact, or the boards leave too hot to handle.

terms.def: The non-soldering travel into and away from a joint.
A timed air or nitrogen curtain that removes excess flux from the board surface.
A fixture method that pulls the board flat against a support surface.
Keeping each program revision tied to the board, fixture and material set it was qualified with.

title: Selective defects and validation: cross-section, pull test, documentation

goals.text: Build a selective program — path, order, dwell per joint, passes — for a given board.
Estimate the heat exposure of neighbouring parts and specify the mitigation and the verification.

blocks.alt: A joint cross-section, a pull-test fixture holding a lead, and a validation record sheet
blocks.caption: Selective defects and validation: cross-section, pull test and documentation

p: Selective soldering exists because a full wave would overheat nearby SMT or temperature-sensitive THT parts.

Validation proves two things at once: the joint is mechanically and electrically sound, and the neighbours stay inside their allowed thermal budget. Use IPC-A-610 for visual acceptance, IPC-7711/7721 for rework and repair, and IPC-7530 for thermal process control where it applies.
Start from the board layout and define each joint as a solder target.

Order the joints so heat-sensitive parts go last where possible, and so the nozzle approaches without disturbing adjacent components. Set dwell per joint from the time needed to wet pad and hole, then add a short margin for paste variability.
One pass covers simple through-hole joints; multiple passes come in only when pad, hole or paste volume needs more heat. Verify against your paste, nozzle and equipment datasheet.
Estimate exposure from preheat, wave or jet temperature, contact time, board thickness, copper area, lead mass and standoff.
The first estimate is a measurement: record the temperature rise at the nearest sensitive part with a thermocouple or thermal probe during a dry run, then repeat with paste and a sacrificial board.
Where direct measurement is impossible, use a conservative model based on thermal mass and contact time, and check it against the equipment datasheet.

Mitigate by reducing preheat, lowering jet temperature within paste limits, shortening dwell, increasing standoff, shielding the sensitive part, using a smaller nozzle, or moving the sensitive joint later in the sequence.

Verification covers a thermal profile at the sensitive part, visual inspection after cooling, and functional or electrical test where the part is thermally sensitive. Document the profile and the accepted program revision.
Cross-sections answer what the eye cannot: joint geometry, hole fill, intermetallic formation and crack risk.

Prepare the sample so the section passes through pad, hole and lead, then inspect for wetting, voiding, cracks and excessive intermetallic. Accept against IPC-A-610 and repair per IPC-7711/7721. Take sections from representative boards rather than from one ideal sample.
Pull testing suits THT leads and selected SMT terminations where mechanical strength is the concern.

Fix the board, pull the lead perpendicular at a controlled rate, and record force and failure mode. Acceptance rests on the specified minimum strength or a validated process capability, not on a single pass or fail sample. Follow the applicable component and board standards, and document sample size, temperature and failure mode.

Documentation carries board revision, component placement, program file, nozzle, paste lot, preheat and jet settings, dwell per joint, pass count, thermal profile, cross-section results, pull-test results and any deviation.
When a defect appears, record the symptom, the suspected cause, the corrective action and the revalidation evidence, so the program stays auditable and repeatable.

calc.task: A 1.6 mm FR-4 board has a THT joint with a 0.8 mm lead in a 1.0 mm hole. A 0402 capacitor is 2.0 mm from the joint. The selective jet is set to 250 °C, preheat is 100 °C, and dwell is 2.5 s. Estimate the peak temperature at the capacitor and specify mitigation and verification.
calc.solution: Step 1: Define the thermal budget. The nearby capacitor should remain below the temperature limit specified by its datasheet. For this screening estimate, use a conservative internal target of 150 °C at the capacitor body, then verify against the component datasheet. Step 2: Estimate heat input at the joint. Use the lead surface area in the hole as the heat-transfer area. Lead circumference is pi times 0.8 mm, which is about 2.5 mm. Multiply by board thickness 1.6 mm to get about 4.0 mm². Step 3: Estimate heat flow. Use an effective heat-transfer coefficient of 500 W/m²K for the solder jet contact zone, then verify against equipment data. The temperature difference is 250 °C minus 100 °C, which is 150 K. Heat flow is 500 W/m²K times 4.0e-6 m² times 150 K, which is about 0.3 W. Step 4: Estimate energy input. Multiply 0.3 W by dwell 2.5 s to get about 0.75 J. Step 5: Estimate heat reaching the capacitor. Assume 10 percent of the joint heat reaches the capacitor through the board and copper, then verify with a thermocouple. Heat reaching the capacitor is about 0.075 J. Step 6: Estimate capacitor thermal mass. Use a mass of about 1.2 mg for a 0402 capacitor and a specific heat of about 0.8 J/gK, then verify against component data. Step 7: Estimate temperature rise. Divide 0.075 J by 0.0012 g times 0.8 J/gK to get about 78 K. Add this to preheat 100 °C to get an estimated peak of about 178 °C. Step 8: Compare with the target. The estimated 178 °C exceeds the 150 °C screening target, so mitigation is required. Step 9: Apply mitigation. Reduce dwell to 1.5 s, lower preheat if paste limits allow, add a thermal shield near the capacitor, and move the capacitor-sensitive joint later in the sequence if possible. Step 10: Recalculate with mitigation. Energy input becomes 0.3 W times 1.5 s, which is about 0.45 J. Heat reaching the capacitor becomes about 0.045 J. Temperature rise becomes about 47 K. Estimated peak becomes 100 °C plus 47 K, which is about 147 °C. Step 11: Verify. Run a thermocouple profile at the capacitor on a sacrificial board, inspect the joint visually, perform cross-section if hole fill or crack risk is uncertain, and perform pull testing on representative leads. Document the accepted program revision, thermal profile, cross-section result, and pull-test result.

defect.symptom: Adjacent 0402 capacitor shows discoloration and an open circuit after selective soldering of a nearby THT joint.
defect.cause: Excessive dwell and preheat allowed heat to propagate through the pad and copper plane, and shielding was not used near the temperature-sensitive part.
defect.action: Reduce dwell, lower preheat within paste limits, add a thermal shield, rerun the thermal profile at the capacitor, inspect the joint and capacitor, perform cross-section if needed, and update the program revision with revalidation evidence.

takeaways: Validate the neighbour and the joint in the same run, because selective soldering protects one by risking the other.
Measure the sensitive part on a sacrificial board before release, since a thermal estimate only screens.
Record the program revision with the profile and the section, so a later change can be traced to its evidence.

mistakes.mistake: Verifying only the joint that was soldered
mistakes.instead: Profile the nearest sensitive part, which is what the process was chosen to protect.

mistakes.mistake: Accepting a pull test on one sample
mistakes.instead: Use a documented sample size and the failure mode, not a single pass.

mistakes.mistake: Releasing a program after a mitigation without re-profiling
mistakes.instead: Repeat the profile, because the mitigation changed the thermal path.

terms.def: A production-equivalent board used for thermal or destructive testing.
A mechanical test that measures the force needed to separate a joint.
The temperature and time a part may tolerate without damage.
The versioned record of path, dwell, pass and process settings.

title: The hand soldering station: tip selection, temperature setting, ESD and fume control

goals.text: Select iron, tip, temperature and technique for a joint and state the thermal budget applied.

theory.h: Station anatomy and the control loop
p: A hand soldering station is a closed loop: controller, heater, tip, sensor and ground path.

The setpoint is the tip temperature at the heater, not the joint temperature. A good station recovers quickly when a cold joint draws heat, so choose a station whose tip holds a stable temperature while it touches the pad, and confirm the actual tip temperature with a calibrated thermocouple or probe against the equipment datasheet.
IPC J-STD-001 expects workmanship that does not damage the base material, which makes a controlled, clean and grounded station part of the requirement rather than a convenience.

blocks.alt: A closed-loop soldering station with controller, heater, tip and sensor, a set of interchangeable tip shapes, a grounded mat and a fume extraction arm
blocks.caption: The hand soldering station: tip selection, temperature setting, ESD and fume control

p: The tip is the heat-transfer interface, so geometry follows the joint.

Small conical or chisel tips suit chip components, wider chisel or hoof tips suit through-hole leads and ground planes, and specialty shapes cover fine-pitch or BGA rework. Low thermal mass recovers faster on small joints; higher thermal mass holds temperature on large pads.

The contact face must be clean, tinned and free of oxidation. Check tip compatibility and power rating against the iron datasheet, because an undersized tip drives long dwell while an oversized one heats neighbouring parts.
Setpoint selection starts with the alloy, the flux and the thermal mass.

Lead-free SAC alloys generally need higher process temperatures than eutectic tin-lead, and the exact range depends on paste, iron and board design, so verify against your paste and equipment datasheet.

A higher setpoint shortens contact time and can also oxidise flux, damage laminate or lift pads. A lower one produces cold joints when the tip cannot recover. Use the lowest temperature that wets and forms a fillet inside an acceptable cycle time.
Good technique is repeatable contact, not scraping.
Clean the tip, add a little fresh solder, touch the tip to pad and terminal, feed solder into the joint, remove the tip, and hold the part until the solder solidifies.

The thermal budget combines tip temperature, contact time, heat-transfer area and the number of heat cycles. Record setpoint, tip type, contact time and any preheat, and validate the budget on scrap or test coupons, because IPC J-STD-001 requires a sound wetted joint without heat damage.
Hand soldering means handling bare boards and components, so the station belongs to an ESD control program.

ANSI/ESD S20.20 and IEC 61340-5-1 cover grounded equipment, personnel grounding, conductive or dissipative work surfaces, and verification. Bond the iron tip and body to a common ground point, and ground the operator where the program requires it.
Verify the iron ground path and the wrist strap or footwear system with the tester your ESD program specifies, and replace damaged cords, mats and straps.
Solder fume carries flux decomposition products and particulate, so local exhaust is the practical control.

Place the extraction inlet close to the joint without blocking the operator's view, and hold the capture velocity the ventilation design calls for. Check airflow, filter condition and face velocity against the equipment datasheet and local occupational exposure limits.
On a shared hood, keep the inlet near the source and never between the operator's breathing zone and the joint.
After soldering, inspect wetting, fillet shape, solder volume, lifted pads, charred laminate, solder balls and disturbed components.
IPC-A-610 gives the visual acceptance criteria and IPC J-STD-001 covers workmanship and repair practice. Use a magnifier or microscope sized to the component.
When a joint fails, decide whether heat, contamination, insufficient solder or mechanical damage caused it, then correct the process rather than reworking repeatedly without a root cause.

blocks.caption: Iron setpoint guidance — follow tip maker and alloy TDS
head: Joint type
Tip mass and shape
Setpoint approach
rows: Higher end: heat the joint, not the part
Time over temperature: heat mass first

calc.task: A small chip resistor must be hand soldered to a thin copper pad on a multilayer board using no-clean paste. Select iron, tip, temperature, technique, and state the thermal budget applied.
calc.solution: Step 1: Check the paste and component datasheets for maximum temperature and recommended process window; verify against your paste/equipment datasheet. Step 2: Choose a temperature-controlled, grounded, ESD-safe iron rated for rework, typically 40-60 W. Step 3: Choose a small chisel or conical tip with a 0.5-1.0 mm contact face, clean and tinned. Step 4: Set the iron to 340-360°C for lead-free SAC-type solder, then verify actual tip temperature with a probe. Step 5: Pre-tin the pad, place the resistor, touch the tip to the pad and terminal, feed a small amount of solder, remove the tip, and hold the part until solidified. Step 6: Apply a thermal budget of about 350°C tip temperature, 1.5-3.0 s tip contact per joint, and a target pad/component temperature of about 220-250°C for 1-2 s. Step 7: Estimate heat input as 0.1-0.3 J for the small joint, recognizing that board copper and adjacent pads can increase the required energy. Step 8: Inspect the joint for wetting, fillet, lifted pad, and laminate damage, using IPC-A-610 and IPC J-STD-001 as the workmanship references.

defect.symptom: A pad lifts or the laminate discolors after a few seconds of soldering.
defect.cause: The thermal budget exceeded the board material limit because the setpoint was too high, the tip was too small, the tip was oxidized, or the operator held the iron too long while trying to wet the joint.
defect.action: Reduce the setpoint within the paste and iron datasheet range, use a larger or better-tinned tip to improve heat transfer, shorten contact time, pre-tin the pad, and inspect the board with IPC-A-610. If laminate damage is visible, reject or rework according to IPC J-STD-001 and record the corrected thermal budget.

takeaways: Measure the tip temperature with a calibrated probe, because the setpoint is the heater temperature and not the joint temperature.
Pick the tip by joint geometry and thermal mass, since an undersized tip forces long dwell and an oversized one heats the neighbours.
Record the thermal budget with the setpoint, tip and contact time, so a rework can be reproduced and audited.

mistakes.mistake: Setting the iron as hot as it goes to shorten contact
mistakes.instead: Use the lowest temperature that wets, because excess heat lifts pads and chars laminate.

mistakes.mistake: Reworking a failed joint repeatedly without a cause
mistakes.instead: Identify whether heat, contamination or solder volume caused the failure first.

mistakes.mistake: Checking ESD grounding once at installation
mistakes.instead: Verify the iron and the operator grounding at the interval the program defines.

terms.def: The combination of tip temperature, contact time and heat cycles a joint receives.
The spreading of molten solder into a continuous metallurgical bond with the pad and lead.
The air speed at the extraction inlet needed to pull fume away from the joint.
A curved tip shape that carries a solder bead to a joint, useful on through-hole and large pads.

title: Technique: contact order, dwell, feed, lead-free discipline, technique defects

goals.text: Select iron, tip, temperature and technique for a joint and state the thermal budget applied.

blocks.alt: A sequence of four panels showing tip contact on pad and lead, dwell, solder feed and removal, with a cold-joint warning callout
blocks.caption: Technique: contact order, dwell, feed, lead-free discipline and technique defects

theory.h: Contact order sets the thermal path
p: Manual rework works when heat reaches the joint before solder does.

Preheat the board where thermal mass is high, place the tip so it touches lead and pad together, feed solder to the joint, remove the solder, and then remove the tip. That order leaves the interface hot when the solder arrives and keeps cold joints out.

Withdraw the tip too early and the joint solidifies while the operator is still feeding, which gives a disturbed or incomplete fillet. Feed before the interface is hot and the solder balls on the tip or sits on the pad without wetting.
Use thermocouple data on a thick board, a large copper area or a heat-sensitive component, and confirm that the technique suits the joint geometry and the board material.

Dwell is the time the tip and solder stay in thermal contact with the joint. It must be long enough for lead, pad and solder to reach a wetting condition and short enough to protect board, component and flux.
Dwell follows tip geometry, iron recovery, board thickness, copper area and preheat. A joint on a large copper plane or a long lead needs more heat than a small isolated pad.

Find the minimum dwell that wets on a sacrificial joint, then check it against your paste and equipment datasheet. When wetting is poor, change tip, preheat or technique before extending dwell, because longer contact is not a substitute for better thermal contact and it damages neighbours, darkens flux and weakens the board interface.

theory.h: Feed controls volume, flux and bridging
p: Feed solder wire to the joint, never melt it on the tip.

Wire diameter and feed length should match the joint size, so the operator can place enough solder for a fillet without excess. Flux-cored wire cleans the interface, and too much feed traps flux, creates voids or bridges adjacent pads.

Use short touches and let the joint draw solder into the fillet, watching the flow rather than counting on a remembered amount. A small joint wants a smaller diameter for control; a large joint can take a larger one, still fed to the joint and never flooded over the area. Check diameter, flux activity and technique against your paste and equipment datasheet.
SAC-type lead-free solder needs higher wetting temperatures and more active flux than tin-lead, and it forgives less: contamination, mixed alloys and a poor tip condition all show up faster.
Dedicated tips and clean work areas limit cross-contamination. Choose setpoints and dwell from the solder or paste datasheet, then confirm on the actual board.

Lead-free discipline also controls the thermal history of the joint, because repeated rework changes wetting behaviour and intermetallic formation. Never share a tip between tin-lead and lead-free work unless the process is qualified and the tip cleaned, and document the alloy and flux system for each rework task.

theory.h: Iron and tip must match the joint
p: The iron has to recover temperature during contact, and the tip has to transfer heat without blocking inspection or forcing the operator to press.
A fine tip suits small SMD joints, and a chisel or hoof tip with real contact area suits through-hole joints. Match the tip face to the lead and pad geometry.

An undersized tip cools during contact and pushes the operator into a longer dwell; an oversized one damages nearby parts and is hard to control. Check tip condition at the start of every shift, because oxidation, wear and poor plating cut heat transfer and wetting, and confirm with calibration records that the displayed temperature matches the measured one.

theory.h: Technique defects are thermal or mechanical
p: Insufficient wetting usually comes from a low interface temperature, short dwell, an oxidised tip or contaminated surfaces.

Disturbed joints happen when the component moves while the solder solidifies. Bridging and excess solder come from overfeeding or poor tip withdrawal. Lifted pads follow excessive dwell, high preheat or mechanical prying. Voids come from trapped flux, moisture or heating fast enough to drive volatiles through the joint, and burned flux leaves residue that hampers inspection and may reduce corrosion resistance.
Inspect against the IPC acceptance standard and correct the process parameter that caused the defect rather than touching up repeatedly.

theory.h: State the thermal budget before rework
p: A thermal budget is the controlled combination of tip setpoint, board preheat, contact time, number of contacts, tip geometry and alloy.

Write it down for each rework task so another engineer can reproduce the result. Measure board temperature with a thermocouple where the joint is thermally significant, and record the values actually used rather than the nominal setpoint.

Align the budget with the IPC acceptance standard and the solder, paste and equipment datasheets. State whether the joint was repaired with an initial contact or whether more contacts were allowed, and define the maximum board temperature the component tolerates. That makes the technique auditable and stops technique defects becoming routine.

calc.task: A manual rework operator must repair a through-hole joint on a 1.6 mm glass-epoxy board with a 0.8 mm lead and a 35 µm copper annular ring. The board is preheated to 100 °C. The solder is a SAC-type lead-free solder. Select iron, tip, temperature, and technique, and state the thermal budget applied.
calc.solution: Choose a temperature-controlled iron with enough thermal recovery for a through-hole joint; verify against the iron datasheet. Choose a chisel or hoof tip whose contact face is slightly wider than the lead; for a 0.8 mm lead, use a 1.0-1.5 mm tip face. Set tip temperature to 330-350 °C for SAC-type solder on a preheated board; verify against the solder and iron datasheet. Use contact order: place the tip on lead and pad, feed solder to the joint, remove solder, then remove tip. Apply dwell of 1.5-2.5 s per contact; if the joint does not wet, stop and reassess rather than extending dwell. Feed 0.5-1.0 mm solder wire in short touches; the amount should form a concave fillet without bridging. State thermal budget: tip setpoint 330-350 °C, board preheat 100 °C, contact time 1.5-2.5 s, initial contact; thermal budget index = (tip setpoint - board preheat) × contact time = 230-250 °C × 1.5-2.5 s = 345-625 °C·s per contact. Record actual tip temperature, contact time, preheat, tip geometry, solder alloy, flux, and board temperature; inspect against the IPC acceptance standard.

defect.symptom: A reworked through-hole joint shows a dull, grainy surface and poor wetting at the pad.
defect.cause: The interface did not reach wetting temperature because dwell was too short, tip recovery was insufficient, or the tip was oxidized.
defect.action: Recheck iron calibration and tip condition, increase preheat or use a higher thermal mass tip, repeat with correct contact order, and verify against your paste/equipment datasheet.

takeaways: Heat the joint before feeding solder, because the interface temperature decides whether the solder wets or balls.
Find the minimum dwell that wets and stop there, since extra contact damages the board without improving the fillet.
Write the thermal budget down, so the next engineer reproduces the joint instead of guessing at it.

mistakes.mistake: Melting solder on the tip to carry it to the joint
mistakes.instead: Feed to the joint, because solder on the tip arrives without a wetted interface.

mistakes.mistake: Extending dwell when a joint will not wet
mistakes.instead: Change tip, preheat or technique first, since dwell is already the expensive variable.

mistakes.mistake: Recording only the iron setpoint in the budget log
mistakes.instead: Record measured tip and board temperature, because the display can drift from reality.

terms.def: A joint whose component moved while the solder was solidifying, leaving a rough surface.
The written combination of setpoint, preheat, contact time and alloy allowed for a rework.
Solder wire with a flux core that cleans the interface as it melts.
The temperature at the boundary between solder and the surfaces being joined.

title: Rework: hot air, preheat, paste-in-pad, BGA/QFN removal and replacement

goals.text: Specify or perform a rework operation within the allowed cycles and thermal budget and record what was applied.

blocks.alt: A hot-air rework station with a preheated board, a component being lifted, and a replacement part being placed with paste in the pads
blocks.caption: Rework: hot air, preheat, paste-in-pad, BGA and QFN removal and replacement

p: Rework is a controlled thermal operation, not a repair shortcut.

Before starting, define the thermal budget: preheat temperature, peak temperature measured at the joint, time above liquidus, dwell, cooling behaviour, and the number of thermal cycles the board and component have already seen.

The budget must suit the laminate, the surface finish, the moisture sensitivity level of the component and the paste or solder-ball material. Take the assembly document, the board supplier guidance, the component datasheet and the paste or ball datasheet as the controlling references.
Where the allowed cycle count is not stated, treat any additional cycle as a deviation that needs engineering approval.
Preheat softens the thermal shock and lets the joint reach reflow temperature without an extreme air temperature.

Measure board temperature near the component rather than trusting the air setting. A workable practice preheats the board to a measured temperature that supports paste activation and ball collapse while the component body stays inside its rated limit, verified against the paste, component and equipment datasheets.
Use a nozzle that covers the footprint without blasting neighbours. On a large board or a thermally massive part, raise preheat or fit a larger nozzle rather than raising peak air temperature.
Paste-in-pad suits QFN, MLF and some small land-pattern replacements where design and process allow it.

The paste must be compatible with the existing finish and reflow profile, and the deposit volume controlled by stencil, syringe or dispenser. For BGA replacement, paste-in-pad is less common than new solder balls or a pre-balled component, though a qualified repair method may use it.
Clean the pads, avoid contamination, and confirm paste lot, expiry and storage. IPC J-STD-001 gives the general soldering requirements; apply the qualified method and record the material.
During removal, heat the joint until the solder collapses, then lift with minimal force. Never pry a component that solid solder still locks in place.

On a BGA, watch for warpage, lifted pads and disturbed neighbours; on a QFN, watch thermal-pad adhesion and corner lifting. If the part will not release, improve preheat or heat distribution before raising peak temperature.

After removal, inspect the pads under magnification and clean residual solder with a qualified method. IPC-7530 gives rework, modification and repair guidance, so use it together with your process qualification and work instruction.
Align the replacement with fiducials, land patterns or a placement aid.
Alignment matters most on a BGA because the joints are hidden: use a qualified placement method and verify with X-ray after reflow. On a QFN, check coplanarity, paste volume and thermal-pad wetting.

Reflow on a measured profile that meets the paste or ball specification and the board thermal limits. Where the component is moisture-sensitive, follow IPC/JEDEC J-STD-033 and record floor-life status before the rework begins.
Inspect after rework by the method the assembly calls for: magnification on QFN and passives, X-ray on BGA and hidden joints, and functional test where specified.
IPC-A-610 gives visual acceptance criteria, applied at the class and criteria the contract defines. Record the rework as a process step, not as an undocumented exception.
The record carries operator, date, station, nozzle, preheat setpoint, measured peak temperature, dwell, cycle count, paste or ball lot, flux lot, inspection result and any deviation.
Every thermal exposure spends part of the component and the board budget. Count cycles per component and per board area, because neighbours see the heat too.

If a component needs several attempts, stop and decide whether the failure is alignment, paste volume, contamination, pad damage or an unsuitable profile. Repeated hot-air attempts without a new root cause lift pads, delaminate the board or damage the part.
Where the contract or board specification gives a maximum cycle count, do not exceed it without engineering approval.

calc.task: A BGA replacement is planned on an assembly that allows 2 rework cycles. One cycle has already been used. The proposed second cycle uses a measured peak temperature of 245 °C and a dwell time of 45 s. The paste datasheet states a maximum peak temperature of 250 °C and a recommended dwell range of 30-60 s. Determine whether the proposed operation is within the stated thermal budget and list what must be recorded.
calc.solution: 1. Count the cycles: one previous cycle plus one proposed cycle equals 2 cycles. 2. Compare the cycle count with the allowed limit: 2 cycles is within the allowed 2 cycles, assuming no other rework has occurred in the same area. 3. Compare the measured peak temperature with the paste limit: 245 °C is below the stated maximum of 250 °C. 4. Compare the dwell time with the recommended range: 45 s is within the stated 30-60 s range. 5. Confirm that the peak temperature was measured at the joint or component, not only from the hot-air controller, and that preheat, ramp, and cooling were controlled according to the qualified profile. 6. Record the rework: operator, date, station, nozzle, preheat setpoint, measured peak temperature, dwell time, cycle count, paste lot, flux lot, inspection method, and inspection result.

defect.symptom: After BGA replacement, X-ray shows incomplete collapse or bridging on several balls, and the component sits slightly tilted.
defect.cause: Likely causes include uneven preheat, excessive hot-air temperature on one side, misalignment during placement, insufficient paste or solder-ball volume, contaminated pads, or board warpage during reflow.
defect.action: Stop the rework. Inspect the pads and component under magnification, clean the pads, verify alignment, and repeat only if the cycle count and thermal budget allow it. Use a more uniform preheat and a qualified nozzle or profile. After replacement, inspect by X-ray and record the corrected profile, materials, and inspection result.

takeaways: Count cycles per component and per area before the hot air goes on, because the budget is spent in exposures and not in minutes.
Measure peak temperature at the joint, since the controller display is the air temperature and the joint is what the specification limits.
Raise preheat or nozzle size instead of air temperature, because extra air heat warps the board and blasts the neighbours.

mistakes.mistake: Prying a component that has not fully collapsed
mistakes.instead: Keep heating until the solder is liquid, because force lifts pads and cracks the part.

mistakes.mistake: Trusting the hot-air setpoint as the joint temperature
mistakes.instead: Profile with a thermocouple at the joint, since air and joint differ by a wide margin.

mistakes.mistake: Repeating hot-air attempts when the first one failed
mistakes.instead: Stop and find the root cause, because each attempt spends the cycle budget.

terms.def: A repair method that prints or dispenses paste onto the land pattern before placing the component.
One complete heating and cooling exposure counted against the allowed rework budget.
The stage at which a solder ball melts and settles onto its pad during reflow.
Bending of the board under heat that can tilt a component or open joints.
