title: Repair limits: IPC-7711/7721 classes, conductor cut, annular ring, laminate damage

goals.text: Classify a reworked or repaired joint against IPC-7711/7721 class criteria and state the class the product requires.
Decide repairable versus scrap and record the basis and the residual risk.

blocks.alt: A repaired trace with a conductor cut, an annular ring measurement and a laminate damage callout, beside a class limits table
blocks.caption: Repair limits: IPC-7711/7721 classes, conductor cut, annular ring and laminate damage

theory.p: This lesson covers repair limits for reworked or repaired electronic assemblies using IPC-7711/7721 Class 1, IPC-7711/7721 Class 2, and IPC-7711/7721 Class 3 acceptance criteria. The required class is not chosen by the repair operator; it is set by the product specification, drawing, contract, or reliability plan. A Class 1 product may tolerate a cosmetic laminate scratch that would be unacceptable on a Class 3 product, so the first step is to record the required IPC-7711/7721 class before inspecting the damage.

p: A joint or board area is repairable when the damage sits inside the applicable IPC-7711/7721 limits, the repair method is qualified for the materials and thermal exposure, and the repaired area can be inspected and documented.
It is scrap when the damage violates IPC-7711/7721 acceptance, when the repair would need unqualified materials or processes, or when the residual risk is beyond what the product owner will accept.

The disposition record states the measured condition, the class applied, the repair method and the residual risk, such as thermal fatigue, insulation degradation or mechanical weakness. IPC-7711/7721 is the standard the record cites for the acceptance decision.
A conductor cut is judged as a reduction of conductor width against the designed width.

IPC-7711/7721 does not set the number itself: its conductor-repair procedures require only that width, spacing and current-carrying capacity stay within the allowable tolerances, and leave the limit to the drawing and the bare-board standards. A width figure quoted from IPC-7711/7721 alone would be misread for exactly that reason.

The figure comes from IPC-A-600 §3.5.3.1, which caps the reduction of minimum conductor width at 20 % for Class 2 and 10 % for Class 3, with the controlled revision and customer specification still to be verified. Measure the original width from the drawing or a known-good reference, measure the repaired width, and calculate the reduction. Beyond the limit for the class, the repair is unacceptable unless the customer authorises a deviation.
Annular ring is the copper left around a drilled hole after plating and rework.

IPC-7711/7721 requires the repaired hole to retain the annular ring the class calls for, and the number comes from IPC-A-600 §2.10.3: 0.050 mm [0.0020 in] minimum external annular ring at Class 3, with up to 20 % local reduction for pits, dents, nicks, pinholes or splay. Check the controlled revision and the product specification as well.

Insufficient annular ring cuts current capacity, weakens the thermal relief and raises the risk of cracking in thermal cycling, so a hole below the limit is normally scrap unless a qualified repair restores the copper geometry.
Laminate damage is assessed for delamination, blistering, separation, exposed conductors and loss of dielectric insulation.

IPC-7711/7721 does not accept damage that creates delamination, blistering, separation or exposed conductors. A shallow cosmetic scratch may be repairable where a qualified repair restores insulation and no prohibited condition exists.

IPC-7721 sets no laminate-damage depth limit. Its laminate-repair procedures, epoxy and film-adhesive, are judged on what they restore: insulation and electrical clearance held, no epoxy in the hole or on internal pad walls, no reduction in hole diameter, no exposed adjacent circuitry. Where a depth limit is needed, take it from the controlled IPC-A-600 or IPC-6012 revision and the customer specification, not from IPC-7721, which describes the laminate-repair procedures and not the limit itself.
The repair method must be qualified for the laminate system, the copper finish, the solder mask, the component package and the thermal profile.
Practice-based values such as preheat rate, peak temperature, dwell and cleaning solvent compatibility come from the paste, flux, solder mask and equipment datasheets, and are confirmed by trial.

A repair that meets the IPC-7711/7721 geometry limits can still be rejected if the process blisters or delaminates the laminate, lifts solder mask, damages a component, or leaves contamination that cannot be removed. Qualification belongs with the method, and IPC-7711/7721 acceptance applies to the result.
The disposition record must be specific enough for another engineer to repeat the decision.

It carries the class, the measured conductor width reduction, the measured annular ring, the laminate condition, the repair method, the inspection result and the residual risk. Residual risk can include reduced current margin, greater sensitivity to thermal cycling, lower insulation resistance or reduced mechanical strength.
If that residual risk is unacceptable to the product owner, the correct disposition is scrap even where the repair is technically possible, and IPC-7711/7721 accepts that outcome as a valid decision.

calc.task: A Class 2 assembly requires IPC-7711/7721 Class 2. A repaired trace originally 0.30 mm wide is now 0.24 mm wide. A repaired plated through hole has an annular ring of 0.06 mm. A laminate scratch is 0.08 mm deep, with no delamination, no blistering, no separation, and no exposed conductors. Decide whether the assembly is repairable or scrap and state the basis.
calc.solution: Step 1: Confirm the required class is IPC-7711/7721 Class 2. Step 2: Calculate conductor width reduction: (0.30 mm - 0.24 mm) / 0.30 mm = 0.06 mm / 0.30 mm = 0.20, or 20%. Step 3: Compare with the IPC-A-600 §3.5.3.1 conductor width reduction limit for Class 2, which is 20% of the minimum conductor width. The trace is exactly at the limit and acceptable only if the controlled revision and customer specification allow 20% for Class 2. Step 4: Compare annular ring: 0.06 mm is greater than the IPC-A-600 §2.10.3 Class 3 minimum of 0.050 mm, so the hole is acceptable if the controlled revision confirms that minimum for the class. Step 5: Evaluate laminate damage: the scratch is 0.08 mm deep with no delamination, blistering, separation or exposed conductor, so no prohibited condition exists. IPC-7721 sets no depth limit; a shallow cosmetic scratch is repairable if a qualified repair restores insulation and electrical clearance. Step 6: Disposition: repairable, provided the repair method is qualified, the laminate is restored or accepted as cosmetic by the customer, and the residual risk is documented. Basis: conductor width reduction at the IPC-A-600 §3.5.3.1 Class 2 limit of 20%, annular ring above the IPC-A-600 §2.10.3 minimum, and laminate damage without prohibited defects. Residual risk: reduced trace current margin, possible thermal cycling sensitivity at the repaired hole, and possible insulation resistance risk at the laminate scratch if the repair material is not qualified.

defect.symptom: After rework, a plated through hole shows a crescent-shaped copper gap around the hole, and the adjacent trace is visibly narrower than the original trace.
defect.cause: Excessive heat or mechanical abrasion during component removal and pad cleaning removed copper from the annular ring and reduced the trace width.
defect.action: Measure the annular ring and trace width, compare them with the applicable IPC-A-600 class limits, and record the result. If the annular ring or conductor width reduction is outside the IPC-A-600 limit, scrap the assembly or request a customer deviation. If within limits, inspect for delamination, blistering, and exposed conductors, qualify the repair method, and document the residual risk.

takeaways: Fix the class before inspecting the damage, because the same scratch is acceptable on one product and scrap on another.
Take the numeric limits from IPC-A-600 and IPC-6012 rather than IPC-7721, which describes procedures and leaves the numbers to those documents.
Record the measured condition and the residual risk, so the next engineer can repeat or challenge the disposition.

mistakes.mistake: Repairing to the operator's own idea of good
mistakes.instead: Apply the class the contract sets, because acceptance is a product decision.

mistakes.mistake: Treating IPC-7721 as a source of depth or width limits
mistakes.instead: Use IPC-A-600 and IPC-6012 for the numbers, since IPC-7721 gives procedures.

mistakes.mistake: Scrapping a repairable board because the repair looks difficult
mistakes.instead: Judge against the measured limits and the qualified method, not against comfort.

terms.def: The width of copper remaining around a drilled hole after plating.

title: Acceptance and re-inspection of rework and repair; documenting the operation

goals.text: Classify a reworked or repaired joint against IPC-7711/7721 class criteria and state the class the product requires.
Decide repairable versus scrap and record the basis and the residual risk.

blocks.alt: A magnified reworked joint under inspection with a fillet and wetting check, beside a record sheet listing method, cycles and thermal exposure
blocks.caption: Acceptance and re-inspection of rework and repair, and documenting the operation

p: Acceptance after rework or repair is not a glance at the touched joint.

The inspector confirms that the affected area, the adjacent joints, the nearby components and the board surface still meet the required class, and that the repair method introduced no new defect. IPC-7711/7721 gives acceptability criteria for reworked and repaired assemblies, IPC-A-610 gives the visual and construction baseline for the original assembly, and IPC J-STD-001 carries the process requirements for materials, cleanliness, solderability and thermal stress.
Rework restores a nonconforming assembly to the original design and specification.

Repair makes a nonconforming assembly acceptable for use, and the result may not restore the original design intent. Because repair can leave a deviation, it usually needs engineering approval, a qualified repair method and a documented risk assessment.
IPC-7711/7721 is the primary standard for judging whether a reworked or repaired joint is acceptable, though the product specification may also call up IPC-A-610 and IPC J-STD-001.
The customer, the product specification or the reliability requirement sets the class, and it must be stated before inspection.

IPC-A-610 and IPC-7711/7721 both use class-based criteria, commonly Class 1, Class 2 and Class 3, with Class 3 generally reserved for high-reliability products where a defect has greater consequence. The inspector never infers the class from the component type: the work order, drawing, contract or quality plan confirms it.
Re-inspection covers the repaired joint, the adjacent joints, the component body and leads, the pad and trace area, the solder mask, nearby components and local cleanliness.

On joints, look for wetting, fillet formation, solder volume, cracks, exposed copper, lifted pads, damaged traces, disturbed solder mask, flux residue, contamination and mechanical damage. On components, look for lifted leads, cracked bodies, discolouration, thermal damage and missing or damaged markings.
IPC-7711/7721 gives the repairability and acceptability guidance, and IPC-A-610 supplies the visual baseline.
A joint is repairable when a qualified method can correct the defect, the required class can be achieved, and the repair creates no unacceptable residual risk.
Scrap applies when the damage is too severe, the method is not qualified, the board material is thermally or mechanically damaged, or the repair would need an unapproved deviation.

IPC-7711/7721 supports repairability decisions from defect type, component type, board condition and required class. IPC J-STD-001 supports the process controls that keep the repair from creating a new defect.

theory.h: Documenting the basis and the residual risk
p: The record states the original defect, the required class, the repair method, the materials, the operator, the equipment, the inspection result and the disposition.

It also states the reasoning behind repair against scrap, and the residual risk the organisation has accepted: reduced thermal fatigue life, contamination, flux residue, mechanical weakness, trace or pad damage, component thermal damage, or uncertainty about future reliability.
IPC-7711/7721 supports documentation of the operation, while the quality system defines the record format and the approval route.
On the line, the inspector confirms the class first, then inspects the repaired area against IPC-A-610 and IPC-7711/7721.

A joint that meets the class with a qualified method is accepted. A joint that does not meet the class goes on to the question of whether a qualified repair can restore compliance; if it cannot, the assembly is scrapped or routed for engineering disposition.
Every repair is re-inspected, and the residual risk is recorded alongside the disposition.

calc.task: A reworked QFP solder joint on a high-reliability assembly shows a lifted pad and exposed copper after hot-air rework. The product specification requires IPC-A-610 Acceptability of Electronic Assemblies Class 3 and IPC-7711/7721 Acceptability of Rework, Modifications, and Repairs for Electronic Assemblies Class 3. Classify the joint, decide repairable versus scrap, and record the basis and residual risk.
calc.solution: Step 1: Confirm the required class from the work order or product specification. In this case, the required class is IPC-A-610 Acceptability of Electronic Assemblies Class 3 and IPC-7711/7721 Acceptability of Rework, Modifications, and Repairs for Electronic Assemblies Class 3. Step 2: Inspect the repaired joint and adjacent area. The observed condition is a lifted pad and exposed copper, with possible thermal disturbance to the solder mask and nearby joints. Step 3: Compare the condition against IPC-A-610 Acceptability of Electronic Assemblies Class 3. A lifted pad and exposed copper indicate that the original visual and construction acceptability condition is not met. Step 4: Compare the condition against IPC-7711/7721 Acceptability of Rework, Modifications, and Repairs for Electronic Assemblies Class 3. The repairability decision depends on whether the pad, trace, and board material can be restored to the required class using a qualified repair method. Step 5: Determine whether a qualified repair exists. If the pad is lifted and the copper is exposed, repair may require pad or trace restoration, which is a deviation from the original design and requires engineering approval. If no qualified repair method exists, the joint is not repairable under the required class. Step 6: Decide repairable versus scrap. If the pad lift is minor, the trace is intact, the board material is not thermally damaged, and a qualified repair method is available, the joint may be repairable with engineering approval. If the pad is detached, the trace is damaged, the board material is delaminated, or the repair cannot restore Class 3, the assembly should be scrapped or routed for engineering disposition. Step 7: Record the basis. The record should state the defect, required class, inspection result, repairability decision, approval status, and disposition. Step 8: Record residual risk. If repaired, residual risk may include reduced thermal fatigue life, contamination, flux residue, mechanical weakness, trace or pad damage, component thermal damage, or future reliability uncertainty. If scrapped, residual risk is avoided, but the cost is the loss of the assembly.

defect.symptom: After rework, the solder joint appears acceptable at first glance, but the pad is slightly lifted and the copper is exposed at the edge of the land.
defect.cause: Excessive heat or mechanical force during rework lifted the pad from the laminate, exposing copper and disturbing the solder mask.
defect.action: Stop the repair, inspect the pad, trace, and adjacent joints, and compare the condition against IPC-A-610 Acceptability of Electronic Assemblies and IPC-7711/7721 Acceptability of Rework, Modifications, and Repairs for Electronic Assemblies. If the required class cannot be restored with a qualified repair method, scrap the assembly or route it for engineering disposition. Record the defect, required class, repairability decision, and residual risk.

takeaways: Confirm the class from the work order before inspecting, because the same defect passes one product and fails another.
Treat repair as a deviation that needs approval, since rework restores the design and repair may not.
Record the residual risk with the disposition, so the accepted weakness is visible to whoever inherits the assembly.

mistakes.mistake: Accepting a repair on the visual look of the touched joint
mistakes.instead: Inspect the neighbours, the mask and the cleanliness too, because the repair changed all of them.

mistakes.mistake: Inferring the class from the component type
mistakes.instead: Read it from the work order or contract, since class is a product decision.

mistakes.mistake: Leaving the repair out of the build record
mistakes.instead: Log it as a process step, because an undocumented repair cannot be audited.

Making a nonconforming assembly acceptable without necessarily restoring the design.
The inspection of a repaired area and its surroundings against the required class.
The formal decision on whether a nonconforming assembly may be used, repaired or scrapped.

title: Practice: rework one joint and document it against criteria

goals.text: Specify or perform a rework operation within the allowed cycles and thermal budget and record what was applied.
Classify a reworked or repaired joint against IPC-7711/7721 class criteria and state the class the product requires.

blocks.alt: A single reworked joint with measurement callouts and a completed documentation form beside it
blocks.caption: Practice: rework one joint and document it against criteria

p: This practice asks you to rework a solder joint, document the operation, and classify the result against the IPC-7711/7721 rework and repair requirements at the acceptance class the product specifies.
The product owner normally states the required IPC-A-610 class, Class 2 for instance, and the reworked joint must meet that class unless an approved deviation exists.

Record the budget before the iron goes near the joint: allowed rework cycles, peak temperature, dwell, preheat temperature and cooling method, taken from the product specification, IPC-7711/7721 and the paste, component and equipment datasheets.

Use the lowest thermal input that produces wetting, and check it against your datasheet, because alloy, board finish, mass and nearby components all move the working window. A budget written after the fact is a description, not a control.
Inspect the joint, clean the area, and remove old solder, flux residue and moisture-sensitive residues with approved materials.

Confirm that pad, land and nearby components are not lifted, cracked or delaminated. If damage is already there, stop and evaluate a repair under IPC-7711/7721 instead of carrying on with rework, which would only deepen it.
Apply heat in a controlled way, with hot gas, a soldering iron or a local rework station as approved.

Add only the solder and flux needed to wet the joint, then let it solidify without disturbance. Record the tool, the tip or nozzle, the temperature setpoint, the measured peak temperature, the dwell, the number of thermal cycles and any cleaning performed.
A rework record identifies the assembly, serial number, date, operator, station, original defect, action taken, thermal data, materials used and the post-rework inspection result.
It also states the required IPC-A-610 class and whether the joint meets IPC-7711/7721 rework or repair acceptance for that class, because the record is the evidence behind the class claim.
Inspect against the IPC-A-610 acceptance criteria for the required class, then confirm the method is acceptable under IPC-7711/7721.
A joint that fails becomes a repair candidate, a deviation candidate or scrap under the approved process. Rework is never automatically acceptable just because the inspector did it.

The usual problems are insufficient wetting, lifted pads, thermal damage to components or laminate, excess flux residue, disturbance of an adjacent joint, and mechanical stress from component removal.
Record each with evidence and disposition it against IPC-7711/7721 and IPC-A-610, so the failure is traceable to a cause and a decision rather than to a retry.

calc.task: A product requires IPC-A-610 Class 2. The product specification allows up to 2 rework thermal cycles and a peak temperature of 250 °C for up to 10 s. A technician preheats the board to 150 °C, applies hot gas with a measured peak of 248 °C for 8 s, then uses a 350 °C iron tip for 2 s to touch up the joint. Determine whether the operation is within the stated budget and what must be recorded for IPC-7711/7721 documentation.
calc.solution: Begin by counting thermal cycles. The hot-gas pass counts as a cycle and the iron touch-up counts as another cycle, so the total is 2 cycles, which equals the allowed maximum. Compare peak temperature. The measured hot-gas peak is 248 °C, which is below the 250 °C limit. Compare dwell time. The hot-gas dwell is 8 s, which is below the 10 s limit. Check the iron touch-up. The iron tip temperature is 350 °C, but the joint peak must be compared with the 250 °C limit; if the measured joint peak during the 2 s touch-up remains at or below 250 °C, the thermal budget is met. Record the result. Record preheat 150 °C, hot-gas peak 248 °C for 8 s, iron tip 350 °C for 2 s, total cycles 2, materials used, inspection result, IPC-7711/7721 rework acceptance, and the required IPC-A-610 Class 2 disposition.

defect.symptom: After rework, the joint shows a lifted pad, insufficient wetting, and a dark ring around the land.
defect.cause: Excessive heat or dwell, combined with mechanical force during component removal, weakened the pad adhesion and disturbed the solder interface.
defect.action: Stop further rework, quarantine the assembly, and evaluate the condition under IPC-7711/7721. If a repair is approved and the joint can meet IPC-A-610 Class 2, perform the approved repair and document it; otherwise scrap or route for engineering disposition.

takeaways: Write the thermal budget before applying heat, because a budget recorded afterwards cannot constrain the operation.
Count every heat application as a cycle, including the iron touch-up, since the allowance is spent in exposures and not in passes.
Record the class and the evidence with the rework, so the acceptance claim can be defended later.

mistakes.mistake: Treating the iron touch-up as outside the cycle count
mistakes.instead: Count it, because it is a thermal exposure like any other.

mistakes.mistake: Reworking on top of a lifted pad
mistakes.instead: Stop and evaluate a repair, since more heat makes the damage worse.

mistakes.mistake: Claiming acceptance without the thermal record
mistakes.instead: Record peak temperature and dwell, because the class claim rests on that evidence.

terms.def: A short iron pass used to correct a joint after the main rework heating.
An approved departure from the specified acceptance criteria.
The recorded decision to accept, repair, rework or scrap an assembly.
One heating and cooling exposure counted against the allowed rework allowance.

title: What residue is and why it matters: ionic residue, SIR, CAF, contact failure

goals.text: Select a cleaning method and chemistry for a stated residue and assembly type, including MSL/ESD constraints.
Interpret cleanliness test results and decide pass or rework, stating the criterion.

p: Residue is any unwanted material left on a board after assembly: flux solids, solder paste residues, no-clean flux polymer films, fingerprints, dust, handling oils and ionic salts.

It matters because it holds moisture, supports electrochemical migration, changes surface energy, interferes with coating adhesion and raises contact resistance. In coating and ESD stages it can also create localised charge paths or blunt the effect of ionised air blowers.
Treat residue as a process defect with a source, a mechanism and a verification method, not as a cosmetic issue.

blocks.alt: A board surface with flux residue between close conductors, with a surface insulation resistance test cell and a filament-growth callout
blocks.caption: What residue is and why it matters: ionic residue, surface insulation resistance, conductive anodic filament and contact failure

theory.h: Ionic residue, ROSE and what it does not prove
p: Ionic residue is contamination that dissolves in water and can carry current once a thin water film forms.
ROSE tests measure soluble ionic contamination as sodium chloride equivalent, usually with IPC-TM-650 methods and the cleanliness requirements that IPC J-STD-001 references.

A low ROSE value is useful and it does not prove the board is free of organic, hydrophobic or particulate residue. A board can pass its ROSE limit and still carry a no-clean flux film that absorbs moisture, lowers surface insulation resistance or stops the coating wetting. Use ROSE as a gate, and pair it with visual inspection, SIR or CAF testing where the product has fine pitch, high-impedance nodes or long-term reliability requirements.

theory.h: SIR and CAF: residue becomes a reliability failure
p: Surface insulation resistance measures how well a surface blocks current between conductors under humidity and bias, commonly evaluated with IPC-TM-650 methods.

Low SIR can come from ionic residue, absorbed moisture, flux films or contamination bridging fine-pitch lands. Conductive anodic filament is a related failure in which copper migrates along glass fibres in the laminate, accelerated by moisture, bias and residue that lowers local insulation resistance, and it is normally screened with IPC-TM-650 CAF methods.
SIR and CAF are different tests that say the same thing: the surface or the laminate is not electrically stable under the intended service condition.

theory.h: Contact failure: residue at the interface
p: Contact failure happens when residue changes the metal-to-metal interface at edge connectors, spring contacts, press-fit pins or test points.

Thin organic films raise contact resistance, cause intermittent opens, or promote fretting corrosion by changing lubricity and moisture retention. Gold plating tolerates some contamination without being immune: particulate and ionic residue still cause intermittent contact or corrosion under the contact.

Cleaning chemistry must suit the plating, the elastomers and the connectors. On ESD-sensitive assemblies, cleaning and handling follow ANSI/ESD S20.20 or IEC 61340-5-1, because a clean board can still be damaged by uncontrolled charge transfer.
Select cleaning by residue type, assembly geometry and downstream constraints.

Water-soluble flux usually wants aqueous cleaning with a saponifier or alkaline cleaner and a thorough deionised water rinse. No-clean flux may need a semi-aqueous solvent, a low-surface-tension aqueous cleaner, or a solvent rinse followed by an aqueous wash, depending on how much residue remains and whether reflow has turned it into a polymer film.

Rosin residues often respond to alcohol or solvent cleaning, and the solvent choice has to consider flammability, material compatibility and environmental permits. Verify cleaner concentration, temperature and rinse quality against your paste and equipment datasheet.
For bottom-terminated packages, high-aspect-ratio gaps and under-component spaces, the method has to wet, penetrate and rinse.
That rules out a spray that only reaches the visible surface and points towards agitation, vacuum-assisted cleaning, or ultrasonic cleaning where the assembly tolerates it.
A cleaner that cannot reach the residue cannot remove it, and the board leaves the line looking clean while the gap stays contaminated. That reach is part of method selection, not a separate step.

theory.h: MSL and ESD constraints on cleaning
p: Moisture-sensitive devices need moisture control before and after cleaning.

Where an assembly has been exposed beyond the floor life that IPC/JEDEC J-STD-033 assigns, bake it before reflow or rework according to the MSL level and the product specification. Cleaning can reintroduce moisture, so the drying, bake and reflow windows need control.

For ESD-sensitive work, use grounded surfaces, wrist straps, ionisers and ESD-safe containers as ANSI/ESD S20.20 or IEC 61340-5-1 requires, and avoid high-velocity dry air and uncontrolled plastic film that generate charge. Where cleaning happens inside an ESD-controlled area, confirm that the equipment, baskets and transport materials suit the ESD program.

theory.h: Interpreting cleanliness results and deciding rework
p: Decide pass or rework against a written criterion, never against operator opinion.

The criterion may come from IPC J-STD-001, a customer specification, a reliability plan, or an IPC-TM-650 method applied to a coupon or an assembly. A typical decision tree reads: visual residue means rework; ROSE above the limit means rework; a failed SIR or CAF minimum means rework even where ROSE passes.

On a marginal result, repeat the test on a fresh coupon or a defined area and document the sampling location. When reworking, find the residue source, adjust chemistry or rinse, retest and record the result; if the rework touches components, follow IPC-7711/7721 and re-evaluate MSL exposure.

calc.task: A no-clean flux assembly contains bottom-terminated QFNs and fine-pitch connectors. It is classified MSL 3 and is processed in an ESD-controlled area. After cleaning, ROSE coupons read 0.82 µg NaCl/cm². The product cleanliness limit is 1.00 µg NaCl/cm². SIR testing under the specified humidity and bias condition reads 8.5 × 10^7 Ω. The reliability specification requires at least 1.0 × 10^8 Ω. Select a cleaning method and chemistry, state the pass or rework decision, and state the criterion.
calc.solution: Step 1: Identify the residue. The stated residue is no-clean flux, which can leave an organic film plus ionic activators. Step 2: Check assembly constraints. Bottom terminations and fine-pitch connectors require a cleaning method that can wet, penetrate, and rinse narrow gaps. MSL 3 requires moisture control per IPC/JEDEC J-STD-033; if floor life is exceeded, bake before rework. ESD controls must follow ANSI/ESD S20.20 or IEC 61340-5-1. Step 3: Select cleaning method and chemistry. Use a low-surface-tension aqueous cleaner or a semi-aqueous solvent followed by deionized water rinse. If the no-clean flux has polymerized, use a compatible solvent or semi-aqueous chemistry first, then aqueous rinse. Verify cleaner concentration, temperature, and rinse conductivity against your paste and equipment datasheet. Step 4: Apply the cleanliness criterion. The 1.00 µg NaCl/cm² value here is a product-specific limit; the widely used published reference is 1.56 µg NaCl/cm² per IPC-TM-650 method 2.3.25, and high-reliability customers often work tighter. ROSE 0.82 µg NaCl/cm² is below the 1.00 µg NaCl/cm² limit, so ROSE passes. Step 5: Apply the reliability criterion. SIR 8.5 × 10^7 Ω is below the required 1.0 × 10^8 Ω, so SIR fails. Step 6: Decide pass or rework. Rework the assembly. The governing criterion is the SIR minimum, not the ROSE pass. Suspect insufficient rinse, hydrophobic residue, or residue trapped under bottom terminations. Re-clean with improved rinse or a semi-aqueous/solvent step, dry, bake if required by MSL exposure, and retest ROSE and SIR.

defect.symptom: Edge-card connectors show intermittent opens and variable contact resistance after conformal coating. Boards pass visual inspection and ROSE, but functional test fails.
defect.cause: No-clean flux residue was trapped under connector contacts, and the aqueous rinse did not remove a hydrophobic film. The cleaning process was not qualified for the connector geometry, and ESD-safe transport was not maintained between cleaning and coating.
defect.action: Quarantine the lot. Re-clean using a semi-aqueous or compatible solvent step followed by deionized water rinse. Verify cleanliness with IPC-TM-650 methods and contact resistance or SIR testing. Control MSL exposure per IPC/JEDEC J-STD-033 and ESD handling per ANSI/ESD S20.20 or IEC 61340-5-1. If component rework is needed, follow IPC-7711/7721.

takeaways: Read ROSE as a gate rather than a verdict, because it measures ionic species and says nothing about a hydrophobic flux film.
Let the failed SIR result decide when ROSE passes, since impedance under bias is closer to the service condition.
Pick the chemistry from the residue and the geometry, because a cleaner that cannot reach under a bottom termination cannot remove what is there.

mistakes.mistake: Accepting a board on the ROSE number alone
mistakes.instead: Test SIR where the product calls for it, since organic residue passes ROSE.

mistakes.mistake: Choosing the strongest solvent available as a default
mistakes.instead: Match chemistry to plating and elastomers, because the cleaner can damage the assembly it saves.

mistakes.mistake: Cleaning after floor life has expired without a bake
mistakes.instead: Bake per IPC/JEDEC J-STD-033 first, because cleaning adds moisture rather than removing it.

The resistance measured across a surface between conductors under humidity and applied bias.
A copper filament that grows through laminate along glass fibres under bias and moisture.

title: Cleaning methods: aqueous, semi-aqueous, solvent, ultrasonic; material compatibility

goals.text: Select a cleaning method and chemistry for a stated residue and assembly type, including MSL/ESD constraints.

blocks.alt: A cleaning line with a wash chamber, rinse, ultrasonic tank and dryer, with a material compatibility matrix beside it
blocks.caption: Cleaning methods: aqueous, semi-aqueous, solvent and ultrasonic, with material compatibility

p: Cleaning on SMT and through-hole assemblies removes flux residue, particulates, ionic contamination and process aids before coating, inspection, test or final assembly.

Select the method from the residue type, the assembly construction, the component sensitivity and the downstream process. Rosin, no-clean, water-soluble and solder paste residues plus mixed contamination all behave differently, so chemistry and mechanical action are matched to the residue rather than picked by convenience.
For coating, cleaning also has to leave a surface the coating can wet and bond to, which is a stricter target than visual cleanliness.
Aqueous cleaning uses water-based chemistry, often with surfactants, saponifiers or alkaline additives, and may add spray, immersion, ultrasonic or agitation.

It works well on water-soluble flux residues, ionic contamination and some no-clean residues where the residue is accessible and the chemistry compatible. Typical process temperatures sit in the range of 40 to 70 degrees Celsius, and the exact temperature, concentration, contact time and rinse quality are verified against the paste, flux and equipment datasheet.
The method needs good rinsing and drying, because water left in a barrel or under a component is the next defect.
Semi-aqueous cleaning combines a solvent or solvent-like chemistry with water or water-based rinsing, often using alcohols, glycol ethers or modified alcohols.

It suits residues that are partly soluble in water but also carry organic or rosin-like components needing stronger organic chemistry. Drying time can be shorter than a fully aqueous process, while rinse water quality, drying and chemical compatibility still need control.
On mixed SMT and through-hole assemblies it is a practical compromise where water-soluble and rosin residues occur together.
Solvent cleaning dissolves flux residues, oils, adhesives and some coating residues with organic solvents or blends.

It is effective for localised cleaning, rework and residues that water-based chemistry removes poorly. Selection has to weigh flammability, toxicity, regulatory restrictions, material compatibility and drying behaviour.

Solvents attack plastics, labels, markings, conformal coatings, adhesives and some elastomers, so compatibility is tested before production. On ESD-sensitive assemblies, solvent cleaning needs the same ESD controls as any other bench operation.

Ultrasonic cleaning uses high-frequency acoustic energy in a liquid bath to generate cavitation, which lifts contamination out of complex geometry, blind holes, through-holes and under-component spaces.

Typical ultrasonic frequencies are often selected in the range of 25 to 40 kHz for general cleaning, with higher frequencies used for more delicate parts, and this band is confirmed against the equipment datasheet. It reaches particulates and flux residue that spray cleaning misses. The same energy can damage delicate components, thin wires, fragile terminations, unsecured parts and some optical or MEMS devices, so power density, frequency, bath chemistry and exposure time are all controlled and the frequency band is confirmed against the equipment datasheet.
Compatibility is evaluated for laminate, solder mask, silkscreen, component bodies, terminations, labels, connectors, seals, adhesives, coatings and protective films.

Cleaning chemistry causes swelling, crazing, discolouration, marking removal, adhesion loss or corrosion, and the risk rises with temperature, concentration and dwell. Through-hole and mixed assemblies need attention to trapped liquid and cleaning-agent residue in barrel holes and under leads.
For an assembly headed for coating, wetting and adhesion are part of the compatibility question, not a separate one.
Moisture sensitivity follows the applicable MSL classification and floor-life rules, commonly referenced through IPC/JEDEC J-STD-033.

Cleaning exposes moisture-sensitive devices to water, heat and extra handling time, which can consume floor life or force a re-bake before reflow. For MSL 3 or higher, plan the process so total exposure, drying time and storage stay inside the limits.
Where cleaning happens after placement and before reflow, the assembly may need drying according to the MSL rules before it goes into the oven.
Cleaning brings ESD risk through fluid flow, spraying, wiping, handling and the movement of insulating materials.

Handle assemblies with ESD-sensitive parts in an EPA consistent with ANSI/ESD S20.20, with grounded surfaces, wrist straps where appropriate, ESD-safe containers and controlled handling. Solvent wiping, compressed air and dry cloth wiping generate charge when the materials are not ESD-safe, so material choice and humidity control matter.
At the coating stage the assembly may already be sensitive, so the cleaning step belongs inside the ESD program rather than beside it.
A practical sequence: identify the residue, define the assembly type, list the material and MSL/ESD constraints, then pick the least aggressive method that meets the cleanliness requirement.
Water-soluble residues favour aqueous cleaning, rosin and no-clean residues may favour semi-aqueous or solvent cleaning, and trapped particulates favour ultrasonic or immersion assistance.

For conformal coating, validate the cleaning process with post-clean inspection and coating adhesion testing rather than visual cleanliness alone, and keep MSL-sensitive assemblies inside their exposure windows.

calc.task: Select a cleaning method for a mixed SMT/THT assembly with water-soluble flux residue, trapped particulates in through-holes, MSL 3 components, and a downstream conformal coating requirement. Estimate whether a 60 minute aqueous cleaning and drying cycle can be completed within a 4 hour floor-life window, and define the minimum verification checks before coating.
calc.solution: Step 1: Identify residue and constraints. The residue is water-soluble flux with particulates, the assembly is mixed SMT/THT, components are MSL 3, and the assembly must be clean before conformal coating. Step 2: Select candidate method. Aqueous cleaning is suitable for water-soluble flux, and ultrasonic or agitation assistance may help remove particulates from through-holes. Step 3: Estimate cycle time. Assume cleaning 10 minutes, rinse 5 minutes, drying 45 minutes, and handling 10 minutes, giving a total of 70 minutes. Step 4: Compare with floor-life window. The available window is 4 hours, or 240 minutes. Remaining floor life after cleaning is 240 minus 70, which equals 170 minutes. Step 5: Check MSL handling. MSL 3 floor-life rules are governed by IPC/JEDEC J-STD-033, so the actual floor life must be taken from the component specification and the current exposure record. If the assembly has already used more than 170 minutes of floor life, re-baking or a shortened cleaning route is required. Step 6: Define verification before coating. Perform visual inspection for residue and trapped liquid, check drying completion, verify cleanliness with a suitable method such as ion chromatography or surface insulation resistance testing, and perform coating adhesion testing on a representative coupon or sacrificial assembly. Step 7: Define ESD controls. Handle the assembly in an ESD-controlled area consistent with ANSI/ESD S20.20, using grounded surfaces and ESD-safe containers during cleaning, drying, and coating.

defect.symptom: After conformal coating, localized coating lifting and white discoloration appear near through-hole connectors and under large SMT components, with occasional low surface insulation resistance readings.
defect.cause: Cleaning removed visible flux but left trapped aqueous rinse residue or surfactant film in through-holes and under components. The assembly was dried insufficiently before coating, and the cleaning process was not validated for trapped-liquid removal or coating adhesion.
defect.action: Stop coating release. Re-clean affected assemblies using a validated semi-aqueous or aqueous process with extended rinse and drying, then verify dryness and cleanliness before re-coating. Add through-hole drainage orientation, increased drying time, and post-clean surface insulation resistance or ion contamination checks. Update the cleaning process to include trapped-liquid inspection and coating adhesion qualification.

takeaways: Match the chemistry and the mechanical action to the residue, because a method chosen for convenience usually leaves the hardest fraction behind.
Choose the least aggressive method that meets the criterion, since aggressive cleaning trades contamination for material damage.
Validate cleaning for coating by adhesion, not by sight, because a wetting film that fails adhesion looks clean.

mistakes.mistake: Cleaning everything with the strongest solvent available
mistakes.instead: Select by residue and compatibility, because solvents attack plastics, labels and coatings.

mistakes.mistake: Skipping drying control after aqueous cleaning
mistakes.instead: Dry barrels and under-component spaces, since trapped water becomes corrosion and coating lift.

mistakes.mistake: Ignoring floor life while the board sits in a cleaning line
mistakes.instead: Track exposure per IPC/JEDEC J-STD-033, because cleaning time counts against MSL.

terms.def: A process using solvent chemistry followed by an aqueous rinse.
The formation and collapse of vapour bubbles in a liquid that dislodges contamination.
An alkaline additive that turns flux residue into a water-soluble soap.
An ESD protected area, the controlled zone where sensitive assemblies are handled.

title: Cleanliness verification: ROSE, ion chromatography, particle count, visual

goals.text: Interpret cleanliness test results and decide pass or rework, stating the criterion.

blocks.alt: A ROSE tester extracting a board, an ion chromatography trace, a particle count readout and a magnified visual check
blocks.caption: Cleanliness verification: ROSE, ion chromatography, particle count and visual

theory.h: Cleanliness verification at the coating and ESD stage
p: Cleanliness verification asks whether residues from soldering, cleaning, handling or coating can compromise adhesion, surface insulation resistance, corrosion resistance or ESD protection.

At this stage the board may be inspected before conformal coating, after cleaning, and again after coating where the coating is expected to protect an ESD path. The result is a comparison against a defined criterion, never a measurement on its own: a pass means the measured contamination is below the limit for the tested area and the visual condition is acceptable, and a fail means the area is reworked, retested or dispositioned by engineering.
Write the criterion before testing, and state the method, the sampled area, the reporting units and the action on failure.
A cleanliness result means something only when the sampled area, extraction method, blank correction and reporting units are known.

ROSE and ion chromatography usually normalise to area, such as micrograms of sodium chloride equivalent per square centimetre or micrograms of a specific ion per square centimetre, and the tested area must match the area the result represents. Test a small high-risk area and the result applies to that area, not to the whole board.

Blank correction removes what the solvent, container and handling contributed. For a rework decision, record method, area, instrument, date, operator, visible defects, whether the sample was destructive, whether the area was masked, and whether the result was averaged.
ROSE extracts residues into a solvent and measures conductivity or resistivity.

It is fast and useful for process control, and it does not identify the ion, does not measure non-ionic residue and can be disturbed by weakly ionic or volatile material. Compare the result with the limit in the customer or internal process specification: above the limit the tested area fails; below it the area may pass for ionic contamination while visual inspection and ion-specific testing are still required on a high-reliability, fine-pitch or to-be-coated assembly.

ROSE is most useful when the process is stable and the same solvent, temperature and extraction time are used. A shift without a process change sends you to the blank, the solvent, the cell calibration and the sampling technique.
Ion chromatography separates and quantifies individual ions such as chloride, sulfate, nitrate, acetate and formate.

It is used when ROSE fails, when a specific flux chemistry is suspected, or when corrosion risk has to be understood. Interpretation needs individual ion limits and, where specified, a total ionic limit, because a total can pass while one ion fails and the reverse can also happen.

The laboratory reports detection limits, and a value below detection is not zero. For rework, the failed ion and the process that put it there guide the cleaning: chloride usually points to paste, water or handling, and organic ions point to flux residue. Ion chromatography is slower than ROSE, so it serves qualification, failure analysis and periodic verification rather than every board.
Particle count verifies that particulate contamination is controlled before coating and inside the ESD-controlled area.
Airborne counts are compared with cleanroom classes from the ISO cleanroom particle count standard, and surface counts come from wiping, flushing or a counter over a defined area.

The criterion states the particle size threshold, the area or volume sampled and the maximum count. A particle count proves nothing about chemical cleanliness: it shows only that particles above the selected size are inside the allowance. For coating, particles cause pinholes, poor adhesion or localised corrosion where they hold moisture; on ESD surfaces they interrupt coating continuity or create high-resistance spots. Sample location matters, because a cleanroom can pass while the board surface fails.
Visual inspection finds residue, flux staining, corrosion, handling marks, coating defects and particles large enough to see.

It runs under controlled lighting and magnification against the IPC visual acceptability standard or a customer-approved visual standard. A visual pass means no unacceptable residue or defect is present in the inspected area.

Visual inspection cannot find all ionic contamination, so it is combined with chemical tests where the risk is high. A visible defect fails the area even when chemical tests pass, unless engineering issues a documented deviation. Look under connectors, near stencil apertures and along board edges where cleaning solution struggles to reach, and keep photographs and annotated drawings for marginal results and retests.
The pass decision uses the most restrictive applicable criterion: customer specification, internal specification or standard method guidance.

A common sequence is visual pass, ROSE pass, ion chromatography pass and particle count pass. When any test fails, rework the area with a validated cleaning process and retest the same or a representative area. On a marginal result, repeat the test and check sampling technique, blank and calibration before accepting.

For coating and ESD work, ask whether residue could be trapped under the coating or shift surface resistivity; if so, require ion-specific confirmation before coating. The disposition states accepted, reworked, scrapped or released under deviation, and the retest is compared with the original criterion, not with a relaxed limit chosen after the fact.

theory.h: Where the acceptance numbers come from
p: A cleanliness criterion is never invented at the bench: it comes from the customer specification, the reliability plan or a published reference.

The most widely used reference is 1.56 microgram NaCl equivalent per square centimetre, reported per IPC-TM-650 method 2.3.25 and historically applied to assembled boards through IPC J-STD-001 and to bare boards through IPC-6012. Many high-reliability customers tighten it: about 1.0 microgram per square centimetre for high-impedance analogue and telecom hardware, about 0.75 for aerospace and military, and about 0.5 for medical assemblies, with ion chromatography per IPC-TM-650 method 2.3.28 confirming the specific ions.

Two cautions follow. ROSE reports a conductivity equivalent rather than a named ion, so two boards with the same ROSE value can carry very different corrosion risk. And a limit taken from another product family is a starting point for discussion, not an acceptance criterion.

calc.task: A cleaned board area is tested before conformal coating. The internal cleanliness specification is: ROSE <= 0.25 microgram NaCl equivalent per square centimeter; individual ion <= 0.10 microgram per square centimeter; particles >= 5 micrometer <= 100 per square centimeter; visual inspection shows no visible residue. The ROSE extract measured 0.34 microgram NaCl equivalent per square centimeter, and the blank was 0.03 microgram NaCl equivalent per square centimeter. Ion chromatography reported chloride 0.12 microgram per square centimeter and sulfate 0.06 microgram per square centimeter. A surface particle sample over 10 square centimeters counted 1400 particles at or above 5 micrometers. Visual inspection found no visible residue. Decide pass or rework and state the criterion.
calc.solution: Correct ROSE for blank: 0.34 - 0.03 = 0.31 microgram NaCl equivalent per square centimeter. Compare ROSE to limit 0.25 microgram NaCl equivalent per square centimeter. 0.31 is above 0.25, so ROSE fails. Compare individual ions to limit 0.10 microgram per square centimeter. Chloride 0.12 is above 0.10, so ion chromatography fails. Sulfate 0.06 is below 0.10, so sulfate alone passes. Normalize particle count: 1400 particles divided by 10 square centimeters = 140 particles per square centimeter. Compare particle count to limit 100 particles per square centimeter. 140 is above 100, so particle count fails. Visual inspection passes because no visible residue was found. Overall decision is rework because the most restrictive criterion is not met: ROSE, ion chromatography, and particle count all exceed their limits. Rework with validated cleaning, then retest the same area and adjacent high-risk areas before coating.

defect.symptom: After conformal coating, localized corrosion and intermittent ESD path failures appear near a connector.
defect.cause: Residual ionic flux from wave solder was not removed; ROSE sampling averaged a large area and missed a local residue pocket, while particles trapped under coating increased moisture retention.
defect.action: Quarantine the lot, remove coating if possible, re-clean with validated ultrasonic or flush process, retest the connector area with ion chromatography and local ROSE, verify particle control, then recoat and retest.

takeaways: Write the criterion before the test, because a limit chosen after the result is a rationalisation.
Report the sampled area with the number, since a localised pocket disappears inside a whole-board average.
Treat a marginal result as a reason to check the method, not as a reason to relax the limit.

mistakes.mistake: Comparing ROSE readings from different solvents and extraction times
mistakes.instead: Keep solvent, temperature and time fixed, because the value is only comparable within one method.

mistakes.mistake: Reading a below-detection ion result as zero
mistakes.instead: Treat it as below the reporting limit, since the laboratory cannot resolve less.

mistakes.mistake: Accepting a board because the chemical tests passed while a visible defect remains
mistakes.instead: Fail the area, because a documented deviation is the only route past it.

terms.def: Subtracting contamination contributed by solvent, container and handling from the measured result.
A method that separates and quantifies individual ionic species in an extract.
The number of particles above a stated size in a defined area or volume.
The smallest value an analytical method can report as distinguishable from background.

blocks.alt: Reference sheet: five coating cross-sections acrylic, urethane, silicone, parylene and UV cure, each rated for moisture barrier and removability in words, with a macro photograph of a coated assembly under UV light
blocks.caption: Coating types and selection: acrylic, urethane, silicone, parylene and UV cure; thicknesses in the figure above

p: Conformal coating goes on after assembly to cut moisture ingress, ionic contamination, dust, fungal growth and some mechanical abrasion.
In process engineering the choice of chemistry is the small part: coating also changes cleaning, masking, inspection, rework, test access, thermal behaviour and reliability under thermal cycling.

Drive the selection from the service environment, board density, component sensitivity, cleaning requirements and the rework strategy. A dense SMT board with bottom-terminated parts may need a low-viscosity coating and careful masking, while a through-hole power board may tolerate a thicker silicone or urethane film.
Acrylic coatings suit products where rework and repair access matter.

They come off easily by mechanical means or with compatible solvents, and they go on by brushing, spraying, dipping or selective coating. Typical dry-film thickness is often in the range of 25 to 75 micrometers, and the target is verified against the coating datasheet and the IPC-CC-830 qualification for the specific product.

Acrylics give good dielectric performance and reasonable moisture protection, with less resistance to solvents, fuels and aggressive chemicals than urethane or silicone. That makes them a common choice for consumer and industrial electronics with a rework path.

Urethane coatings generally give better chemical and abrasion resistance than acrylic systems and suit industrial, automotive and outdoor electronics, in moisture-cure, heat-cure and UV-cure variants.
Typical dry-film thickness may be around 25 to 100 micrometers depending on product and application method, and the process window is verified against the coating datasheet and IPC-CC-830 test data.

The tougher film protects better and reworks harder: mechanical removal, localised solvent softening or thermal removal may be needed, and the method must be qualified so pads, solder mask and adjacent parts survive.
Silicone coatings are chosen for high temperature, high humidity and applications that need flexibility.

They stay flexible over a wide temperature range and often take thermal cycling better than rigid coatings. Typical dry-film thickness is often around 25 to 100 micrometers, verified against the datasheet and IPC-CC-830 qualification.

Removal is mechanical or by selected solvents, and it can smear or leave residue that interferes with soldering. The larger process issue is silicone near connectors, switches, relays or gold-plated contacts, because silicone migration raises contact resistance and is hard to undo.
Parylene is vapour-deposited and forms a very thin, uniform, pinhole-free film.

Typical thicknesses are often in the range of 1 to 25 micrometers, with many applications using 5 to 15 micrometers, checked against the coating specification and IPC-CC-830 or equivalent qualification data.

Because it arrives as a vapour, it covers complex geometry and high-aspect-ratio features without the bridging or pooling of liquid coatings, which suits dense SMT assemblies, medical electronics and products where added thickness is critical. It is hard to remove selectively, so mask before deposition rather than repair afterwards.
UV-cure coatings serve processes that need fast handling and short cycle times, applied by spray, jet or selective coating and cured by ultraviolet light.
Typical dry-film thickness may be around 25 to 75 micrometers, verified against the datasheet and IPC-CC-830 qualification.

The limitation is line of sight: areas under components and connectors, inside deep cavities or behind tall parts may receive too little UV energy to cure fully, leaving tacky or uncured material that attracts contamination and ruins adhesion. UV systems are often paired with moisture-cure or heat-cure chemistry to reach shadowed areas.
Masking protects connectors, test points, switches, heatsink interfaces, optical sensors, antennas and any area that must stay uncoated.
Methods include tape, caps, plugs, liquid mask and selective coating. The mask has to survive coating, cleaning and any rework temperature without lifting, bleeding or leaving residue.

For cleaning, the mask material and adhesive must suit the solvent or aqueous chemistry, because some adhesives bleed under solvent exposure. For rework, the coating must come off without damaging neighbours or leaving residue that stops solder wetting, and IPC-7711/7721 gives the rework guidance while IPC-A-610 gives the coverage and finish criteria the coated board is judged against. Following IPC-7711/7721 in the rework instruction is what keeps a coated assembly repairable at all.

theory.p: A practical selection method starts with the environmental requirement: humidity, temperature, chemicals, dust, vibration, and expected service life. Next, define the board constraints: component height, bottom-terminated packages, test points, connectors, thermal interfaces, and rework frequency. Then match coating chemistry to those constraints. Acrylic is often selected when easy rework is needed. Urethane is often selected when chemical and abrasion resistance are higher priorities. Silicone is often selected for high temperature and flexibility. Parylene is often selected for thin, uniform coverage on dense assemblies. UV cure is often selected for fast throughput when line-of-sight cure is achievable. Finally, verify the selected coating against IPC-CC-830 qualification data, IPC-A-610 inspection requirements, IPC-7711/7721 rework guidance, and the assembly cleaning process. The final choice should be documented with coating type, target thickness, application method, cure method, masking method, inspection criteria, and rework method.

calc.task: Select a coating and masking strategy for a dense SMT/THT control board that must operate in a humid industrial environment, be reworkable at the board level, and must not contaminate a nearby gold-plated edge connector. Estimate coating coverage volume and check whether the selected coating thickness is compatible with a 0.50 mm connector mating clearance.
calc.solution:
Step 1: Define requirements. The board needs moisture protection, rework access, and connector protection. A urethane coating is selected for balanced moisture and chemical resistance, with acrylic selected as a backup if rework becomes difficult. Silicone is rejected near the gold-plated edge connector because silicone migration can increase contact resistance. Parylene is considered but rejected for this example because local rework is required and parylene removal is difficult. UV cure is considered but rejected as the primary coating because the board has tall connectors and shadowed areas.

Step 2: Select target thickness. The coating datasheet and IPC-CC-830 qualification data are checked. A target dry-film thickness of 50 micrometers is selected, with an acceptable process range of 25 to 75 micrometers. This range is verified against the coating datasheet and IPC-A-610 inspection requirements for coating coverage and thickness.

Step 3: Estimate board area. The coated area is estimated as 120 mm by 80 mm, or 9600 mm². The area is converted to square meters: 9600 mm² = 0.0096 m².

Step 4: Estimate coating volume. Volume = area × thickness. For 50 micrometers: 50 µm = 0.000050 m. Volume = 0.0096 m² × 0.000050 m = 0.00000048 m³. Convert to milliliters: 0.00000048 m³ = 0.48 mL. This is the theoretical dry-film volume only; actual dispensed volume will be higher because of overspray, masking, and process losses.

Step 5: Estimate wet volume. If the coating has 40 percent solids by volume, wet volume = dry volume / solids fraction = 0.48 mL / 0.40 = 1.20 mL. The 40 percent solids value is a practice-based example and must be verified against the coating datasheet.

Step 6: Check connector clearance. The gold-plated edge connector has a mating clearance of 0.50 mm. The coating is masked from the connector contact area. If the coating edge is allowed to approach the connector, the coating thickness must not create a step that interferes with mating. A 50 micrometer coating is 0.050 mm, which is 10 percent of the 0.50 mm clearance. This is acceptable only if the coating edge is outside the mating interface and the mask prevents coating creep. The mask boundary is set 1.0 mm from the connector contact area to allow for process variation. The 1.0 mm margin is a process example and should be verified against the coating viscosity, application method, and IPC-A-610 inspection criteria.

Step 7: Check rework compatibility. The urethane coating is tested on a sacrificial board using the planned rework method. Removal is checked against IPC-7711/7721 guidance for damage to pads, solder joints, and adjacent components. If the urethane cannot be removed without damaging nearby components, the process is changed to a localized acrylic coating or a masked urethane coating with a defined rework window.

Step 8: Final selection. The selected strategy is urethane coating at 50 micrometers nominal, masked from the gold-plated edge connector with a 1.0 mm boundary margin, applied by selective coating, and qualified for rework according to IPC-7711/7721. The process is accepted only after coating thickness, adhesion, cure, masking boundary, and rework damage checks pass.

defect.symptom: After conformal coating and thermal cycling, a board fails ICT at a connector test point. Visual inspection shows a thin, clear coating film bridging between adjacent test pads, and the coating appears glossy and tacky under a shadowed connector.
defect.cause: The coating was applied too thickly near the test-point array, and the UV-cure step did not fully cure the shadowed area under the connector. The uncured or partially cured material remained tacky, attracted contamination, and allowed capillary flow into the pad gap. Masking was not sufficient to keep the coating away from the test-point spacing.
defect.action: Stop the lot and quarantine affected boards. Remove the coating from the affected area using a qualified rework method that does not damage the pads or adjacent components, following IPC-7711/7721 guidance. Re-clean the area and verify solderability and insulation resistance. Correct the process by reducing coating viscosity or application pressure, adding a mask or cap over the test-point array, and verifying UV energy dose in shadowed areas. Add a post-cure inspection step for shadowed regions and requalify the coating process against IPC-CC-830 and IPC-A-610 requirements.

takeaways: Choose the coating from the service environment and the rework strategy together, because a better barrier that cannot be opened is a liability.
Keep silicone away from gold contacts, since migration raises contact resistance permanently.
Mask before deposition rather than repairing after it, which matters most with parylene.

mistakes.mistake: Selecting the most protective chemistry by default
mistakes.instead: Match protection to service and rework, because rework cost rises with every step up.

mistakes.mistake: Coating a board before cleaning is verified
mistakes.instead: Verify cleanliness first, since coating seals contamination against the surface.

mistakes.mistake: Assuming UV cure reaches under a component
mistakes.instead: Check line of sight, because shadowed material stays tacky and attracts dirt.

terms.def: The coating thickness remaining after solvents have evaporated and cure is complete.
The qualification and performance standard for conformal coating materials.
The transfer of low-molecular silicone to nearby surfaces, raising contact resistance.
An area that line-of-sight cure cannot reach under a component or behind a tall part.

title: Application and masking: spray, dip, selective, thickness, cure, repairability

goals.text: Choose a coating and masking strategy and check its compatibility with cleaning, rework and the assembly.

blocks.alt: A coating line with a selective spray head, a masked connector, a thickness measurement and a cure oven
blocks.caption: Application and masking: spray, dip, selective, thickness, cure and repairability

theory.h: Selecting a coating for mixed assemblies
p: Coating selection starts with the service environment and the thermal, chemical and electrical requirements of the assembly.

Acrylics are easy to remove and repair, urethane gives good abrasion and chemical resistance, silicone tolerates high temperature and humidity, epoxy gives strong mechanical protection at the cost of removability, and parylene gives thin uniform coverage at the cost of vacuum deposition and careful masking.
On a mixed SMT and through-hole board, verify that the coating does not attack flux residue, potting compound, connectors or test points. IPC-CC-830 is the qualification standard to check against.
Spray coating is common at low and medium volume and on assemblies with complex topography.

Typical spray viscosity is adjusted to the equipment range, often around 10 to 100 mPa·s for air-assisted systems, with the exact value taken from the coating supplier's process window and the spray equipment manual.

Atomisation pressure, nozzle size, travel speed and distance set the film thickness and the overspray. On mixed assemblies, keep high pressure away from small components, exposed vias, connectors and test pads. Measure wet film with a comb or gauge, then confirm dry film after cure; target values are commonly 25 to 130 µm depending on the coating class and IPC-CC-830 qualification, but the final range should match the qualified coating system.
Dip coating gives good coverage on through-hole assemblies and boards with open component spacing.

The board is immersed and withdrawn at a controlled rate, commonly 100 to 300 mm/min, with dwell adjusted so the film drains without bridging. Viscosity, temperature and withdrawal speed set the wet film thickness; a typical process may aim for 50 to 150 µm dry film thickness, verified against the coating datasheet and IPC-CC-830 qualification.
Dip coating traps solvent under large components and bottom-terminated packages, so preheat, dwell and ventilation are controlled to limit voids and skips.

theory.p: Selective coating is used when only part of the assembly requires protection, such as high-voltage areas, exposed copper, or moisture-sensitive regions, while connectors, test points, heatsinks, and mechanical interfaces must remain uncoated. The process uses programmed dispensing or jetting to place coating only on defined areas. Key controls are nozzle path, coating volume, cure schedule, and edge definition. For SMT/THT boards, selective coating reduces masking labor and improves repair access, but it requires good CAD or Gerber data and verification of component height, pin spacing, and connector sealing. Check that the coating does not creep into connector contacts or under component terminations where IPC-A-610 class requirements for cleanliness and solder joint visibility apply.

Masking protects areas that must remain uncoated, such as connectors, test pads, heatsink interfaces, potting areas, and repair zones. Common masks include high-temperature tape, silicone caps, liquid photoimageable masks, and removable wax or polymer masks. Mask selection depends on coating solvent, cure temperature, dwell time, and cleaning chemistry. For example, solvent-based coatings may attack some tapes, while high-temperature cure may lift adhesive or leave residue. Verify mask compatibility by running a coupon through the full coating, cure, and cleaning sequence. If cleaning is required after coating, confirm that the cleaning solvent does not swell, soften, or craze the coating; IPC-CC-830 includes chemical resistance testing, but production cleaning should still be validated on the actual assembly.

p: Dry film thickness drives insulation, mechanical protection, thermal behaviour and repairability.

Too thin a coating may not meet IPC-CC-830 qualification or IPC-A-610 acceptability for the intended class; too thick a coating traps solvent, cracks in thermal cycling or interferes with connectors and test probes.

Measure wet film before cure and dry film after, on flat areas, at edges and near components. Verify cure by the supplier's method: solvent rub, hardness, adhesion, or FTIR conversion where applicable. On heat-sensitive assemblies the cure temperature is the constraint that decides the chemistry.
Repairability depends on the removal method, the access to the joints and the thermal exposure during rework.
Acrylics come off with solvent or mechanical action, while urethane, silicone and epoxy may need stronger solvents, abrasion or thermal assistance, and parylene may need plasma or specialist removal.

For rework and repair, follow IPC-7711 and IPC-7721 for acceptable methods, including preheat, temperature control and post-rework inspection. Leave enough uncoated area for probe access, soldering and inspection.
A coating strategy has to survive the whole flow: soldering, cleaning, inspection, functional test and repair.

Residual flux, ionic contamination, moisture or dust under the coating cause corrosion, insulation failure or adhesion loss, so cleaning before coating is validated against laminate, solder mask and component materials, and the board is dry before coating.

After coating, inspect for pinholes, bridging, voids, peeling, contamination and coverage of exposed copper, using IPC-A-610 acceptance criteria at the applicable class. At connectors and test points, confirm the masking held.

calc.task: A mixed SMT/THT board is coated by spray with a target dry film thickness of 75 µm. The coating has a volume solids content of 45% by volume. The wet film thickness measured on a coupon is 165 µm. Determine whether the wet film thickness is reasonable for the target dry film thickness, and calculate the expected dry film thickness from the measured wet film thickness.
calc.solution: Step 1: Use the relationship between wet film thickness, dry film thickness, and volume solids: DFT = WFT × volume solids fraction. Step 2: Convert volume solids to a fraction: 45% = 0.45. Step 3: Calculate expected dry film thickness: DFT = 165 µm × 0.45 = 74.25 µm. Step 4: Compare with target: 74.25 µm is within a practical tolerance of the 75 µm target, assuming the process tolerance allows approximately ±10 µm or the tolerance specified by the coating supplier. Step 5: Verify the result on the actual assembly after cure, because solvent evaporation, drainage, and surface roughness can change the final thickness. If the qualified IPC-CC-830 coating system or IPC-A-610 inspection class requires a different thickness range, adjust the spray parameters and re-measure.

defect.symptom: After conformal coating and cure, a connector area shows white residue and intermittent contact resistance. The coating appears to have crept under the connector housing and left a soft film on the contacts.
defect.cause: The masking or selective coating boundary was too close to the connector, the coating viscosity was too low, or the spray/dispense volume was too high, allowing capillary creep into the connector. The cleaning solvent used after coating may also have softened the coating and redistributed it onto the contacts.
defect.action: Stop the affected lot and inspect other boards for coating creep. Remove the assembly from the line and clean or replace affected connectors according to IPC-7711 and IPC-7721 rework and repair guidance. Requalify the masking layout or selective coating path with a larger keep-out margin, reduce dispense volume or spray pressure, and verify coating creep on a connector test coupon. If cleaning is required, confirm solvent compatibility with the coating and connector materials before returning to production.

takeaways: Pick the chemistry from the service environment and the rework method together, because a coating that cannot be opened turns a repair into a scrap.
Measure wet film before cure and dry film after, since thickness is the property the specifications judge.
Prove mask and coating compatibility on a coupon, because the full sequence reveals attacks a single step hides.

mistakes.mistake: Spraying at high pressure over small components and vias
mistakes.instead: Reduce pressure near fine features, because the jet drives coating into places masking cannot protect.

mistakes.mistake: Coating a board that is not fully dry
mistakes.instead: Dry first, since trapped moisture blisters the film and corrodes under it.

mistakes.mistake: Assuming cure from the schedule alone
mistakes.instead: Verify cure by the supplier's method, because shadowed or cool areas stay undercured.

terms.def: The coating thickness measured immediately after application, before solvent loss.
The fraction of the wet coating that remains as dry film after cure.
An area that must stay uncoated, defined in the coating program or mask layout.
A spectroscopic check of how completely the coating has cured.
