title: Contamination and coating defect cases: residue, white residue, corrosion, fish-eye, dewetting

goals.text: Interpret cleanliness test results and decide pass or rework, stating the criterion.
Choose a coating and masking strategy and check its compatibility with cleaning, rework and the assembly.

blocks.alt: Five magnified coated-surface defects shown side by side, each labelled, beside a sound coated surface
blocks.caption: Contamination and coating defect cases: residue, white residue, corrosion, fish-eye and dewetting

theory.h: Cleanliness testing as a decision tool
p: A cleanliness result is read against the defect risk of the assembly, not only against a generic limit.

On coated electronics the real question is whether residue, ionic contamination, particulate, flux or masking material can cause corrosion, insulation failure, solderability loss, coating defects or an ESD handling problem. A result that is acceptable on a low-density through-hole board can be unacceptable on fine-pitch SMT, bottom-terminated components or high-impedance analogue circuits.
The pass or rework criterion therefore combines the applicable standard, the customer requirement and the process capability behind it.
Visual inspection under magnification finds visible residue, flux, solder balls, masking bleed and particulate.

Solvent extraction conductivity or ion chromatography estimates ionic contamination, reported as sodium chloride equivalent or as individual ions such as chloride, sulfate, nitrate and bromide. Surface insulation resistance measures electrical leakage and can reveal contamination that no eye will find.
Cleanliness patch tests, ROSE-type, give a rapid ionic estimate and can miss non-ionic residue, rosin, polymers and masking films, so no single test answers the whole question.

theory.h: Choosing a pass or rework criterion
p: A practical criterion states the test method, the area sampled, the acceptance limit, the inspection magnification and the action when the limit is exceeded.

For example, a board may pass if no visible residue is present at the magnification IPC-A-610 requires for the product class and if ionic contamination is below the limit agreed for that assembly and coating system.

On a marginal result, rework is usually better than retest where the residue type is known to interfere with coating adhesion or wetting. Where the result is clean but the coating shows fish-eye, the contamination lives on the surface or in the coating itself, not in the extract.
Flux residue survives under components, in thermal relief pads and under bottom-terminated packages.

Rosin-based residue resists aqueous cleaning and causes poor wetting or coating adhesion. No-clean residue may be electrically acceptable in some designs and still create coating defects when the coating solvent reactivates or lifts it.

Masking tape adhesive, silicone release agents and cured masking material leave low-surface-energy films that cause fish-eye or dewetting, and particulate from paste, cutting, grinding or handling creates coating defects and local corrosion sites.
White residue often appears after cleaning, drying or humidity exposure, and it may be a salt, a flux reaction product, a mineral deposit or a corrosion product.

Where the residue is conductive or hygroscopic it lowers insulation resistance and promotes corrosion under the coating. Corrosion may start as discolouration, green or white deposits, lifted metallisation, or an intermittent electrical fault.

A coating hides the early stage, which is why pre-coating cleanliness and drying matter so much. White residue found after coating sends you back to whether it formed before coating, migrated through, or came from the coating.
Fish-eye appears as small circular areas where the coating fails to wet the substrate; dewetting is the coating pulling back and leaving thin or uncovered regions.

Both usually trace to low-surface-energy contamination: silicone, mould release, adhesive residue, skin oils or certain masking materials. They also occur when substrate surface energy is too low for the coating, or when viscosity, solvent balance or drying schedule is wrong.
The first corrective action is to find the contamination source and remove it, then verify by coating a coupon of the same lot.

Choose the coating from the protection required: acrylic where rework matters, urethane for chemical and moisture resistance, silicone for thermal cycling and humidity, epoxy for hard chemical resistance where rework is rare, and parylene for pinhole-free coverage at the cost of vacuum deposition and special masking.
Masking protects connectors, test points, heatsink interfaces, optical surfaces and mounting areas, and must survive cleaning, cure and assembly without bleeding, lifting or leaving residue.

Before releasing a coating and masking plan, confirm three things: cleaning does not attack the mask, the mask leaves no residue after removal, and the coating does not swell or soften in the rework solvent.

For rework, confirm that the coating can be removed locally without lifting adjacent coating or damaging component bodies. For assembly, confirm that coated surfaces do not foul press-fit connectors, screw threads, thermal pads, snap fits or grounding contacts.
Where an area must stay conductive, mask it or use a selected removal method, and verify continuity afterwards.
Conformal coating changes surface resistance and can affect handling of ESD-sensitive assemblies.
Some coatings insulate enough to let charge accumulate on the surface unless the assembly is handled inside the ESD program. Masking tapes can generate charge when they are peeled.

For ESD-sensitive assemblies, verify the surface resistance of the coated area and of the handling path, use ESD-safe masking and removal procedures, and where the design needs dissipative behaviour, confirm that the coating and mask do not leave isolated insulating islands near sensitive devices.

calc.task: A fine-pitch SMT board is cleaned, inspected, and tested before conformal coating. Visual inspection at 10x finds no visible residue. A solvent extraction cleanliness test reports 18 micrograms per square centimeter sodium chloride equivalent. The agreed acceptance limit for this product class and coating system is 15 micrograms per square centimeter sodium chloride equivalent. The board also shows two small fish-eye defects on a nearby test board coated with the same lot. Decide whether the board passes or requires rework, state the criterion, and calculate the percentage exceedance of the cleanliness limit.
calc.solution: 1. State the pass/rework criterion: the board passes only if visual inspection at the required magnification shows no visible residue and the ionic cleanliness result is at or below the agreed limit of 15 micrograms per square centimeter sodium chloride equivalent. 2. Compare the measured cleanliness result with the limit: measured value is 18 micrograms per square centimeter, limit is 15 micrograms per square centimeter. 3. Calculate exceedance: 18 minus 15 equals 3 micrograms per square centimeter. 4. Calculate percentage exceedance: 3 divided by 15 equals 0.20, which is 20 percent above the limit. 5. Decision: the board fails the cleanliness criterion and requires rework or additional cleaning, followed by retest. 6. Additional action: because fish-eye defects appeared on a test board from the same coating lot, do not recoat immediately. Investigate low-surface-energy contamination, masking residue, silicone sources, and coating lot compatibility before cleaning, retesting, and recoating.

defect.symptom: After conformal coating and cure, small circular uncovered areas appear around several QFN pads, and a white powdery residue is visible near a connector after humidity exposure.
defect.cause: The fish-eye areas are consistent with low-surface-energy contamination, likely masking adhesive residue or silicone transfer, preventing coating wetting. The white residue near the connector is consistent with ionic contamination or flux reaction product that was not fully removed before coating, then migrated or absorbed moisture through the coating edge.
defect.action: Stop coating release for the affected lot. Remove the coating locally or fully if needed, clean the board with a validated cleaning process, retest cleanliness using visual inspection and ionic or surface insulation resistance testing, and verify surface energy or coating adhesion on a test coupon. Replace or qualify the masking material if adhesive residue is found, control silicone sources in the area, and rework only after the cleanliness and coating wetting criteria are met.

takeaways: Set the criterion from the assembly's defect risk, because the same reading passes one board and fails another.
Test for the contaminant you actually fear, since a patch test cannot see a non-ionic film.
Chase fish-eye to its source on the surface, because the extract can read clean while the coating refuses to wet.

mistakes.mistake: Accepting a board on the extract value alone
mistakes.instead: Inspect and coat a coupon, since adhesion is the property that fails.

mistakes.mistake: Reworking without finding the residue source
mistakes.instead: Identify the process that left it, because cleaning the same way will leave it again.

mistakes.mistake: Peeling ESD-safe masking tape without grounding yourself
mistakes.instead: Handle inside the ESD program, since peeling generates charge.

terms.def: A circular area where coating fails to wet the surface, leaving bare substrate.
Coating pulling back from an area and leaving it thinly covered or uncovered.
A rapid extraction test that estimates ionic contamination over a defined area.
A surface resistance range that bleeds charge away slowly enough to protect sensitive devices.

title: Test levels and what each catches: ICT, flying probe, boundary scan, functional

goals.text: Compare ICT, flying probe, boundary scan and functional test for a given assembly and choose a strategy with reasons.

theory.h: Test level starts with defect modes and access
p: A test strategy is a coverage decision, not a machine preference.

The main defect modes are opens, shorts, wrong or missing components, wrong polarity, solder defects, damaged traces and assembly errors that affect function. The chosen level catches defects near their point of occurrence, gives repairable diagnostics and fits the production volume.
Access, netlist quality and component mix usually decide whether a bed-of-nails fixture, probe access, scan chains or functional stimulus is practical.

blocks.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 900 280' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='Test strategy pyramid'><style>text{font-family:'IBM Plex Mono',monospace}</style><polygon points='450,40 590,110 310,110' fill='rgba(244,67,54,.15)' stroke='#f44336' stroke-width='1.5'/><polygon points='450,40 690,180 210,180' fill='none' stroke='#ff9800' stroke-width='1.5'/><polygon points='450,40 800,250 100,250' fill='none' stroke='#53d1cc' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='450' y='92' fill='#f44336' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle'>BURN-IN / FIELD</text><text x='450' y='152' fill='#ff9800' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle'>FUNCTIONAL TEST (FCT)</text><text x='450' y='222' fill='#53d1cc' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle'>ICT / BOUNDARY SCAN — HIGH COVERAGE, LOW COST PER TEST</text><text x='60' y='24' fill='#edf2f7' font-size='14' font-weight='600'>TEST STRATEGY PYRAMID</text><text x='60' y='272' fill='#94a3b8' font-size='12'>COST PER DEFECT CAUGHT RISES AS YOU GO UP</text></svg>
blocks.caption: Test pyramid: cheapest coverage first, most expensive last

blocks.alt: A test pyramid with the four levels, each annotated with the defect modes it catches, its relative cost and its coverage
blocks.caption: Test levels and what each catches: in-circuit test, flying probe, boundary scan and functional test
Test method comparison
head: Method
Catches
Cost per board
Coverage
rows: Opens, shorts, wrong/rotated parts, some values

p: In-circuit test drives a bed-of-nails fixture onto the test points and measures electrical structure in ohm, farad and volt.
It finds opens, shorts, wrong passive values, missing components and some polarity errors, which makes it strong on high-volume assemblies with good test-point access and a stable netlist.

It misses faults hidden under devices and in nets without access, and it is disturbed by guard circuits, power paths and component tolerance. Fixture cost and cycle time go into the choice as well, checked against the equipment datasheet.

theory.h: Flying probe is flexible structural test
p: Flying probe moves its probes to pads, vias or test points without a dedicated fixture.

That makes it the practical option for prototypes, low-volume builds and boards where fixture cost cannot be justified. It finds opens, shorts and some component errors, at the cost of longer cycle time and access limited by probe reach, pad size and obstruction.
It is usually paired with functional test when the structural coverage it delivers is incomplete.
Boundary scan uses JTAG cells inside compliant devices to drive and observe pins while the board is powered.

It detects opens, shorts and some solder defects between scan-capable devices, including fine-pitch and ball-grid-array connections that are hard to probe. It does not measure passive values or power delivery, and it cannot see non-scan devices unless they are observable through scan logic.
Coverage depends on device support, scan chain integrity, and whether the netlist carries the relevant pins.

theory.h: Functional test proves behavior under intended conditions
p: Functional test applies inputs and checks outputs, timing in second, power in volt and ampere, communication behaviour and thermal behaviour in degree Celsius.
It catches the assembly errors that stop the board working: wrong firmware, connector faults, power problems and some component mismatches.

It misses latent defects, marginal joints and wrong values that do not change behaviour under the test conditions. It is a good final screen, though diagnosis gets harder when the fault is intermittent or outside the exercised path.

theory.h: Coverage tradeoffs between structural and functional levels
p: Structural tests locate a defect at the point where it occurs, and functional tests prove that the system behaves.

A structural test can pass a board that fails functionally, because it does not exercise dynamic loading, timing or analogue performance. A functional test can pass a board with a latent defect, because the fault is never excited.
A practical strategy combines structural coverage for manufacturing defects with functional coverage for operational requirements, and states which defect classes each level owns.
Rank defect risk, access, volume and repair data, then choose.

High-volume dense assemblies with good test points usually take in-circuit test plus functional test. Low-volume and prototype builds take flying probe plus functional, which avoids fixture cost. Dense digital assemblies with strong JTAG support take boundary scan plus functional to cover the hard-to-probe nets.

Mixed-signal and power assemblies need power-path checks in the structural level and load plus thermal conditions in the functional level. Check coverage against the probe and equipment datasheet before committing the line.

calc.task: A 1200-component assembly has 18% BGA, 40% boundary-scan coverage, 2000 units/month, and 30% of nets lack test points. Choose a test strategy and justify it.
calc.solution: First, map defect risk: BGA and fine-pitch solder defects are high, so structural coverage is needed. Second, compare access: 30% of nets lack test points, so in-circuit test alone leaves gaps. Third, use boundary scan for the 40% scan-covered digital nets, especially BGA connections. Fourth, use flying probe or in-circuit test for accessible passives and power nets, depending on volume. Fifth, add functional test to verify power in volt and ampere, timing in second, and thermal behavior in degree Celsius. Sixth, choose in-circuit test plus boundary scan plus functional for 2000 units/month if fixture cost is justified; choose flying probe plus boundary scan plus functional for lower volume. Verify coverage against your paste, probe, and equipment datasheet.

defect.symptom: Boundary scan reports an open on a BGA net, but functional test passes under nominal conditions.
defect.cause: A marginal solder joint or cracked BGA connection may remain conductive when the pin is not exercised under load, thermal stress, or vibration.
defect.action: Re-run boundary scan with known good boards, inspect with X-ray or cross-section if available, exercise the net under load and temperature, and rework or reject the board if the fault persists.

takeaways: Use structural test to locate and functional test to prove, because each answers a question the other cannot.
Read a coverage number with its access limit, since a net without a test point has no in-circuit coverage however dense the fixture.
Add functional load and temperature where the product will see them, because nominal conditions hide marginal joints.

mistakes.mistake: Claiming full structural coverage from a fixture with missing test points
mistakes.instead: Subtract the inaccessible nets, because a bed of nails only touches what it can reach.

mistakes.mistake: Treating a functional pass as proof of a sound joint
mistakes.instead: Add boundary scan or X-ray on hidden joints, since a marginal connection can conduct under no load.

mistakes.mistake: Buying a fixture for a prototype run
mistakes.instead: Use flying probe, because fixture cost needs volume to spread over.

terms.def: A fixture with spring-loaded probes that contact all test points at once.
A driven node that isolates a component so its value can be measured in circuit.
A test architecture that drives and observes device pins through internal scan cells.
A fault that is present but does not show under the test conditions applied.

title: In-circuit test: fixture, node access, test-point design, analog limits

goals.text: Compare ICT, flying probe, boundary scan and functional test for a given assembly and choose a strategy with reasons.
Specify design-for-test requirements as design requests with rationale.

blocks.alt: A bed-of-nails fixture with spring probes contacting test points, a node access diagram and an analog measurement panel
blocks.caption: In-circuit test: fixture, node access, test-point design and analog limits

theory.p: In-circuit test uses spring probes to contact test points and measure analog electrical parameters such as resistance, capacitance, inductance, diode junctions, transistor junctions, open nets, and shorted nets. The fixture holds the board, aligns probes, applies controlled force, and isolates nodes from adjacent circuitry. A good fixture reduces false failures by controlling contact resistance, guarding, shielding, board support, and thermal drift. For dense assemblies, fixture complexity grows with net count, guarded analog nodes, fine-pitch access, and mixed power domains. Verify probe force and contact resistance against your probe and equipment datasheet; a common production target is contact resistance below 100 mΩ, but acceptance limits should be set from golden-board data and equipment repeatability.

theory.h: Comparing ICT, flying probe, boundary scan and functional
p: In-circuit test gives high throughput and strong component-level coverage where test points exist, at the price of a fixture that low volume or frequent design changes cannot justify.

Flying probe avoids the dedicated fixture and suits prototypes, small lots and boards with limited access, and it is slower with less high-speed and guarded analogue capability. Boundary scan tests interconnects and selected device pins through JTAG, which makes it valuable on BGA, QFN and fine-pitch devices that no probe can reach.
Functional test proves system behaviour, including the analogue performance, power sequencing, RF and firmware interaction the other three cannot verify.

theory.h: Choosing a strategy for an assembly
p: Choose in-circuit test when volume justifies the fixture, test-point access is adequate and component-level analogue coverage is needed.

Choose flying probe when volume is low, the design changes often, or fixture cost cannot be justified. Add boundary scan when BGA, QFN or fine-pitch devices create inaccessible nets and the devices support scan. Add functional test when analogue performance, power sequencing, RF behaviour, firmware interaction or system timing falls outside component-level coverage.
Fixture design accounts for probe pitch, tip diameter, board support, alignment pins, hold-down method, thermal effects and guard shielding.

Spring probes need annular clearance around the test point so the tip lands cleanly without shorting adjacent copper. Probe force must break minor contamination without damaging the pad; typical spring-probe force ranges are often around 0.5 N to 1.5 N, and a common production target is contact resistance below 100 mΩ, with acceptance limits set from golden-board data and equipment repeatability.
Ask for a test point on every net where practical, with clear naming and netlist correlation.

For through-hole or large SMT test points, a diameter of 1.0 mm to 1.5 mm and spacing of 2.54 mm to 3.81 mm are common starting points, verified against probe pitch and the paste process. For fine-pitch access, via test points may be used at a diameter of 0.3 mm to 0.6 mm with an annular ring of 0.15 mm to 0.3 mm, subject to probe tip size and drill capability.
Test points also have to survive assembly: mask clearance, no paste on the pad, and enough copper to take repeat probing.
Derive analogue limits from component tolerance, fixture residual, leakage, temperature, solder effects and measurement repeatability.

Use four-wire measurement for low-resistance checks and guard high-impedance nodes to cut leakage error. Diode junction tests often use small currents, for example 50 µA to 100 µA, and low voltages, for example 0.1 V to 0.5 V, so the test does not forward bias an adjacent junction or disturb the circuit.

Power-rail tests need controlled voltages and current limits, so a wrong rail clamp does not damage the board it is testing. A common starting guard band is around ±5% of nominal, confirmed against production variation. Temperature also moves junction and resistor measurements, so limit development often runs inside a controlled window such as 25 °C to 40 °C.

Issue design-for-test requests early, before layout freeze, and include a netlist with the test-point list, the boundary-scan chain definition, the analogue net classification, the power-domain map, test access points, keep-out zones, fiducials and test-point naming rules.

The rationale is fewer fixture iterations, better coverage, fewer false failures and faster debug. Name the guarded analogue nodes so guard rings and test limits can be planned, and flag inaccessible nets before they are designed in rather than after.
Validate the fixture with golden boards before production release: contact resistance, open and short coverage, analogue limits, and repeatability across boards and fixture cycles.
Track failures by test point, net, component and probe location. When failures cluster, check probe wear, board coplanarity, solder mask residue, fixture alignment and guard integrity.
Then use boundary scan and functional test to separate a fixture access problem from a solder joint problem.

calc.task: A multilayer assembly has 1,200 nets, several BGA packages, and annual volume 25,000. A design review finds that 82% of nets can be accessed with a single test point, 12% require paired test points for guarded analog nodes, and 6% are inaccessible. The planned test-point diameter is 1.2 mm, the probe tip diameter is 0.9 mm, and the required annular clearance is 0.15 mm. The available fixture has a 1,500 probe limit. Calculate accessible test points, total test points, minimum pad diameter, and choose a test strategy with reasons.
calc.solution: Step 1: Calculate single-point accessible nets. 1,200 nets × 82% = 984 nets. Step 2: Calculate guarded nets requiring paired test points. 1,200 nets × 12% = 144 nets. Step 3: Double the guarded net count to get test points for those nets. 144 nets × paired test points = 288 test points. Step 4: Calculate inaccessible nets. 1,200 nets × 6% = 72 nets. Step 5: Calculate total test points. 984 single-point test points + 288 paired test points = 1,272 test points. Step 6: Calculate minimum pad diameter. Minimum pad diameter = probe tip diameter + clearance + clearance = 0.9 mm + 0.15 mm + 0.15 mm = 1.2 mm. Step 7: Compare total test points with fixture limit. 1,500 probe limit - 1,272 test points = 228 probes of margin. Step 8: Choose strategy. Use ICT as the primary production test because annual volume 25,000 supports fixture cost, total test points fit within the 1,500 probe limit, and component-level analog coverage is needed. Add boundary scan for inaccessible nets and BGA interconnect coverage. Add functional test for analog performance, power sequencing, and system-level acceptance. Flying probe is not the primary strategy because volume is high enough to justify ICT, but it may be useful for early prototypes or fixture debug.

defect.symptom: ICT reports intermittent opens on guarded analog nets after extended production, with failures moving between adjacent test points and contact resistance rising above 100 mΩ.
defect.cause: Spring probe tip wear, solder mask residue, or fixture alignment drift reduces effective contact area. Guarded high-impedance nodes are sensitive to small increases in contact resistance and leakage, so the measurement shifts into the open or out-of-limit region.
defect.action: Stop production release, inspect and replace worn probes, clean the fixture and board test points, verify alignment with a golden board, and confirm contact resistance below the accepted limit. Re-run limit development with golden-board data, then review test-point placement and guard design for the next fixture revision.

takeaways: Size the fixture against volume, because a bed of nails on a low-volume build spends money to add cycle time.
Derive analogue limits from measured repeatability, since a limit tighter than the fixture resolves creates false failures.
Validate the fixture on golden boards before release, because probe wear and alignment drift appear as product defects.

mistakes.mistake: Probing a test point with no mask clearance
mistakes.instead: Design clearance around the pad, since a short to adjacent copper reads as a fault.

mistakes.mistake: Setting limits from component tolerance alone
mistakes.instead: Include fixture residual and repeatability, because the measurement chain has its own spread.

mistakes.mistake: Chasing clustered failures in the solder process first
mistakes.instead: Check probe wear and alignment, because clustering follows the fixture as often as the board.

terms.def: A known-good assembly used to validate the fixture and develop limits.
The resistance added by the probe-to-pad interface, which must stay low and stable.
A driven node that isolates a component or net so it can be measured in circuit.
A pad or via reserved for probing, sized for the probe tip and clearance.

title: Flying probe: when it wins, throughput ceiling, program effort

goals.text: Compare ICT, flying probe, boundary scan and functional test for a given assembly and choose a strategy with reasons.

blocks.alt: A flying-probe machine with movable probes contacting a board, beside a throughput-versus-volume chart and a program effort gauge
blocks.caption: Flying probe: when it wins, the throughput ceiling and program effort

theory.h: What flying probe is and when it wins
p: Flying probe is a test method in which movable probes contact test points sequentially or in parallel.
It wins when fixture cost and lead time dominate, when volume is low to medium, when the design changes often, or when component density makes a bed-of-nails fixture impractical.
It does not replace every in-circuit or functional test: it is a strategy choice made on coverage, throughput, program effort and design maturity.

theory.h: Comparison with ICT, boundary scan and functional test
p: In-circuit test uses a bed-of-nails fixture and can isolate components for shorts, opens, resistance, capacitance, inductance, diodes and some powered tests. It gives high throughput and good analogue coverage where test points exist, and fixture cost plus access are its limits.

Flying probe applies the same electrical principles without a dedicated fixture, so it is flexible, while probe movement sets a throughput ceiling. Boundary scan uses JTAG or similar chains to control and observe device pins.
Functional test sits above all three and proves that the assembly behaves as designed.

theory.h: When flying probe is the better strategy
p: Choose flying probe when volume is low to medium, prototypes and pilot lots are frequent, test points are sparse or access is difficult, and design iterations are expected.
A practical check is to count accessible test points and estimate probe access: if a bed-of-nails fixture would need many pogo pins, complex fixturing or would foul components, flying probe wins.
Verify probe reach, probe force and minimum pad size against the tester datasheet and IPC-7351 land-pattern guidance.
Mechanical motion sets the ceiling far more than electrical measurement does.

A rough model: time per point equals average probe move time plus dwell plus measurement overhead, divided by the number of probes working in parallel, then adjusted for probe sequencing efficiency. Probe speed, acceleration, dwell and collision avoidance come from the equipment datasheet.

In practice dense boards, small pitch, double-sided probing, calibration cycles and many component tests all pull the achieved rate below the model. Typical flying-probe point rates can range from about 10 to 100 points/min, but verify against your tester, board size and test program.
Program effort is not just the test sequence.

It includes importing CAD, BOM, netlist and test-point data; defining limits from component tolerance and simulation; writing probe access rules; checking for collisions; calibrating probes; and validating the false-call rate.

Flying probe programs start faster than in-circuit fixtures because no bed of nails has to be built, while complex analogue tests, powered tests and tight limits need engineering time close to a fixture program.
A 50-piece prototype with 0.4 mm pitch components, limited test points and no JTAG gets early coverage from flying probe without fixture cost.

A stable 100,000-piece product with good test-point access usually finds in-circuit test plus boundary scan cheaper per unit and faster. A mixed-technology assembly with BGAs and critical analogue circuits uses boundary scan for interconnect coverage, in-circuit or flying probe for component-level checks, and functional test for system verification.
The risks are probe marks, contamination, false calls, probe wear and damage to small pads or components.
Evaluate probe marks against IPC-A-610 acceptability criteria and your product quality requirements. Keep probe pads clean, verify probe force and dwell, and use calibration standards.
When flying probe throughput falls short, add test points, increase probe count, reduce coverage, move high-volume lots to in-circuit test, or use boundary scan to relieve the probe.

calc.task: Estimate the flying-probe throughput ceiling for a prototype assembly with 1,200 test points, 4 probes, average probe move 250 mm, probe speed 100 mm/s, dwell 0.20 s, measurement overhead 0.10 s, parallel efficiency 0.65, board handling 15 s, and availability 85%. Assume each point requires one probe move and one dwell.
calc.solution: 1. Move time per point = 250 mm / 100 mm/s = 2.5 s. 2. Electrical time per point = dwell + overhead = 0.20 s + 0.10 s = 0.30 s. 3. Serial time per point = 2.5 s + 0.30 s = 2.8 s. 4. Ideal parallel time per point = 2.8 s / 4 probes = 0.70 s/point. 5. Effective time per point = 0.70 s / 0.65 = 1.077 s/point. 6. Test time = 1,200 points * 1.077 s/point = 1,292 s = 21.5 min. 7. Cycle time = 1,292 s + 15 s = 1,307 s = 21.8 min. 8. Theoretical boards/h = 3,600 s/h / 1,307 s/board = 2.75 boards/h. 9. Availability-adjusted boards/h = 2.75 * 0.85 = 2.34 boards/h. 10. Points/min = 1,200 points / (1,292 s / 60 s/min) = 55.7 points/min. This is an upper-bound estimate; real throughput will be lower if probe collisions, calibration, component access, or test sequencing reduce parallel efficiency.

defect.symptom: Flying probe reports intermittent opens on fine-pitch test pads, and the same board passes after reflow cleaning and retest.
defect.cause: Flux residue, probe contamination, or oxide on small test pads increases contact resistance; probe dwell or force may be too low for the pad finish and probe tip condition.
defect.action: Clean the board and probe tips, verify probe force and dwell against the tester datasheet, inspect pad finish and probe marks against IPC-A-610 acceptability criteria, and re-run the program with a contact-resistance check or calibration standard before releasing the lot.

takeaways: Choose flying probe when volume cannot pay for a fixture, because the fixture is the cost the method removes.
Model throughput from probe movement, not from measurement time, since the mechanical motion dominates.
Watch probe marks on small pads, because a test method that damages the product has failed even when it caught the defect.

mistakes.mistake: Buying a fixture for a prototype lot
mistakes.instead: Use flying probe, because fixture cost needs volume to justify it.

mistakes.mistake: Assuming flying probe limits match in-circuit limits
mistakes.instead: Loosen them to the probe's repeatability, because a tighter limit only raises false calls.

mistakes.mistake: Ignoring probe contamination between production lots
mistakes.instead: Clean tips and verify force, since flux and oxide raise contact resistance and read as opens.

terms.def: A spring-loaded contact used in bed-of-nails fixtures to press onto a test point.
The indentation or witness mark a probe leaves on a test pad.
The fraction of the ideal multi-probe throughput a tester actually achieves.
A failure reported by the tester on a board that is actually good.

title: Boundary scan / JTAG: BGA access, structure, what it cannot find

goals.text: Compare ICT, flying probe, boundary scan and functional test for a given assembly and choose a strategy with reasons.
Specify design-for-test requirements as design requests with rationale.

blocks.alt: A scan chain of devices connected through BGA packages, with the test access port at one end and a shaded region it cannot reach
blocks.caption: Boundary scan and JTAG: BGA access, structure, and what it cannot find

theory.h: Why boundary scan matters for BGA assemblies
p: Boundary scan earns its place on BGA assemblies because the package hides the solder joints and the escape routing, so a tester cannot reach every net with a probe.
IEEE Std 1149.1 (JTAG) defines a serial test access port and boundary-scan cells that let a tester drive or observe device pins through a handful of control lines.
At 0.5 mm pitch the value is not in replacing every other method but in giving electrical access to digital nets that would otherwise have none.

theory.p: A scan-capable device contains a TAP controller, an instruction register, and data registers. Boundary-scan cells sit between the internal core and the package pins. In EXTEST, the tester shifts a pattern into the boundary-scan chain, updates the cells, then captures the pin states. TCK clocks the state machine, TMS controls state transitions, TDI shifts data in, TDO shifts data out, and TRST is optional. Chains can be daisy-chained across devices. Keep chain length and TCK frequency within the limits of the package, board, and tester; verify against IEEE Std 1149.1 (JTAG) and your tester datasheet.

p: Boundary scan finds digital interconnect defects between scan cells: opens, shorts, stuck-at faults and some bridging where both ends of the net are scan-capable.
It reads IDCODE to confirm device presence and orientation, and SAMPLE/PRELOAD observes normal operation. That makes it useful in-system and on boards where probe access is poor.
Coverage depends on the accuracy of the BSDL file and the netlist, and on whether the pins in question are actually configured as scan cells.
Boundary scan cannot find a defect that leaves the scan cell's logic state unchanged, or one outside the chain.

Non-scan passives, analogue circuits, power distribution, clocks, reset, configuration pins and high-speed interfaces stay invisible unless extra test structures exist. It says nothing about solder joint quality, mechanical strength, contamination, thermal behaviour or parametric performance such as rise time, noise margin or current draw.
A short on a net with one non-scan end waits for another method to catch it. The scan port itself is defined by IEEE Std 1149.1, and nothing outside that definition is visible to it.

theory.h: Compare ICT, flying probe, boundary scan and functional test
p: Compare by access, coverage, speed and cost.

In-circuit test uses a bed of nails and can check many passive and pin-level faults quickly, at the cost of test points and fixture design, and fine-pitch BGA escapes may still be out of reach. Flying probe avoids the fixture and suits prototypes, and it is slower and still needs probe access.

Boundary scan needs few access points and works well on BGA digital nets, given scan-capable devices, BSDL files and design discipline. Functional test proves the system and is the slowest to diagnose.
Choose from the assembly mix.

A high-volume BGA board with many scan-capable digital devices takes boundary scan for digital interconnect, functional test for system behaviour, and in-circuit or flying probe for non-scan passives where test points exist.

A prototype of a few boards gets faster feedback from flying probe plus boundary scan plus functional test than from a full fixture. On a mixed-signal board boundary scan may cover a minority of nets, so functional test carries more of the weight.
Specify DFT as design requests with a rationale.

Ask for boundary-scan support on all digital devices with BSDL files, IDCODE values and a netlist so the tester can build chains. Ask for a stable JTAG header or test points, with TCK, TMS, TDI, TDO and optional TRST routed per IEEE Std 1149.1 (JTAG).
Ask for test points on non-scan passives, power, ground, clocks, reset and configuration pins, and for chains short enough for the cycle time the tester needs.
Chain length, TCK frequency, power state and pin multiplexing are the practical limits.

Some devices need power and configuration before scan access, others support limited unpowered modes, so check the device datasheet. Long chains raise test time and can degrade signal integrity; short, balanced groups help.
Keep JTAG traces away from high-speed clocks and sensitive analogue nets, and verify signal quality by simulation or measurement before the design freezes.

calc.task: A BGA assembly has 1200 nets. Boundary scan can access 720 digital nets. Flying probe can access 600 nets and takes 18 min per board. Functional test catches 480 system-level defects but misses 240 latent opens. The boundary-scan chain has 1000 cells and runs at 10 MHz. Each vector shifts 1000 bits. Choose a test strategy for 5000 boards and state reasons.
calc.solution: Step 1: Boundary-scan net coverage = 720 / 1200 = 0.60 = 60%. Step 2: Nets not covered by boundary scan = 1200 - 720 = 480 nets. Step 3: Shift time per vector = 1000 bits / 10 MHz = 100 µs. Step 4: For 1000 vectors, shift time = 1000 * 100 µs = 100 ms; allow overhead and use 0.2 s per board. Step 5: Flying-probe coverage = 600 / 1200 = 50%. Step 6: Flying-probe time for 5000 boards = 18 min * 5000 = 90000 min = 1500 h. Step 7: Functional test catches 480 system-level defects but misses 240 latent opens, so it should not be the only method. Step 8: For the first 50 boards, use flying probe plus boundary scan plus functional test to debug access, chain integrity, and system behavior. Step 9: For the remaining 4950 boards, use boundary scan plus functional test as the production baseline. Step 10: Add ICT or flying probe only for non-scan passives if the 480-net coverage gap is unacceptable after reviewing fault risk, test-point availability, and fixture cost.

defect.symptom: Boundary scan passes all digital interconnect tests, but the board fails functional test with intermittent resets and missing clock activity.
defect.cause: The reset and clock nets are not covered by boundary scan, and a marginal solder joint or missing decoupling capacitor affects power integrity rather than scan-cell logic state.
defect.action: Add test points or functional vectors for reset, clock, and power rails; review the coverage report for untested nets; verify the BGA escape routing and decoupling layout; re-run boundary scan, functional test, and a targeted flying-probe check on the affected nets.

takeaways: Read boundary scan as coverage of digital nets, because everything outside the chain is untested however clean the report looks.
Keep chains short and balanced, since chain length spends cycle time on every vector.
Ask for scan support and BSDL files at design review, because a device chosen without them has no coverage to add later.

mistakes.mistake: Treating a passing scan report as full board coverage
mistakes.instead: Publish the untested net list, because reset, clock and power usually sit outside the chain.

mistakes.mistake: Designing long daisy chains for layout convenience
mistakes.instead: Split into short chains, because every bit shifts on every vector.

mistakes.mistake: Assuming scan access needs no power sequencing
mistakes.instead: Check the device state requirement, since some devices need configuration before scan works.

terms.def: The boundary-scan description language file that tells the tester how a device's scan cells are arranged.
The scan instruction that drives and observes package pins for interconnect testing.
A device identification register readable through the scan port.
The state machine inside a scan-capable device that sequences test access port operations.

title: Coverage math: node vs defect coverage, escape risk, where inspection ends and test starts

goals.text: Estimate test coverage and name the defect classes left uncovered by the chosen strategy.

blocks.alt: Two overlapping coverage circles, one for nodes exercised and one for defect modes detected, with the uncovered region marked
blocks.caption: Coverage math: node versus defect coverage, escape risk, and where inspection ends and test starts

p: Node coverage counts the electrical nodes or nets a test method exercises; defect coverage estimates the share of likely defect modes it can actually detect.

A board can carry high node coverage and low defect coverage at the same time, if the test only checks connectivity at nominal conditions and misses marginal joints, parametric drift or thermal opens.
Reporting one number without the other hides the gap.
Visual inspection, AOI and X-ray look for physical evidence: missing or wrong component, polarity, tombstoning, solder bridging, insufficient solder, foreign material and visible component damage.

They work on defects with an optical or radiographic signature and they do not prove electrical behaviour under power, temperature or signal loading. A joint can look perfect and be open, and a joint can look marginal and conduct.

theory.h: Test detects electrical and functional faults
p: In-circuit test, boundary scan and functional test apply electrical stimulus and measure the response.

They find opens, shorts, wrong component values, inverted orientation where it changes electrical behaviour, power faults and functional errors. They miss defects that are physically present and electrically invisible, such as a cosmetic solder issue or contamination that does not affect current.

theory.h: Coverage math needs a defect model
p: To estimate coverage, list the expected defect classes and assign each a detection probability per method.

Take the probabilities from your own process capability data, test logs or pilot builds, not from a vendor headline. Use a range rather than a point estimate, and check it against your paste and equipment datasheet.
Use SI units such as millimetre and micrometre for physical inspection limits, and ppm as the dimensionless rate for escape risk.

theory.h: Escape risk is coverage plus occurrence
p: Escape risk combines detection coverage with defect occurrence.

Where a defect class occurs at a known rate and a method detects a fraction of it, the residual escape rate is the occurrence rate multiplied by the undetected fraction. That gives a ppm figure for planning, never a guarantee: real escapes follow process drift, test program quality and intermittent defects.

theory.h: Where inspection ends and test starts
p: Inspection ends where the defect has no reliable physical signature, or the signature is too small, hidden or variable to inspect consistently.

Test starts where the question becomes whether the assembly behaves electrically or functionally. On hidden joints, X-ray or boundary scan bridges part of the gap, and neither replaces a test that exercises the node under representative conditions.

theory.h: Choosing a strategy defines the uncovered classes
p: A strategy built only on AOI leaves electrical opens under packages, shorts under components, wrong values inside tolerance and parametric faults uncovered.
A strategy built only on in-circuit test may leave cosmetic solder defects, intermittent joints, thermal opens and functional timing errors uncovered.
Document the chosen strategy with the defect classes it does not cover and the compensating controls used, so the gap is a decision rather than an accident.

calc.task: A board has 1200 electrical nodes. ICT exercises 980 nodes. Functional test exercises 150 nodes, of which 30 overlap with ICT. A defect model gives occurrence rates: visible solder and placement defects 1500 ppm, electrical open and short defects 800 ppm, parametric and wrong-value defects 200 ppm. AOI detects 70 percent of visible defects, ICT detects 90 percent of electrical defects, and functional test detects 60 percent of parametric defects. Estimate node coverage, weighted defect coverage, and residual escape ppm. Name defect classes left uncovered.
calc.solution: Node coverage: union of ICT and functional nodes is 980 + 150 - 30 = 1100 nodes. Node coverage = 1100 / 1200 = 91.7 percent. Weighted defect coverage: visible contribution = 1500 * 0.70 = 1050 ppm detected; electrical contribution = 800 * 0.90 = 720 ppm detected; parametric contribution = 200 * 0.60 = 120 ppm detected. Total detected = 1050 + 720 + 120 = 1890 ppm. Total occurrence = 1500 + 800 + 200 = 2500 ppm. Weighted defect coverage = 1890 / 2500 = 75.6 percent. Residual escape = 2500 - 1890 = 610 ppm, or 2500 * 0.244 = 610 ppm. Defect classes left uncovered include under-component opens and shorts not exercised, intermittent solder joints, thermal opens, wrong values within tolerance, parametric drift, contamination, cosmetic solder defects, functional timing errors, and firmware errors.

defect.symptom: AOI passes a QFN assembly, but ICT finds an open on the exposed pad net after reflow.
defect.cause: solder paste volume under the QFN was low or the pad was not wetted, so the joint was electrically open but visually acceptable.
defect.action: check stencil aperture and paste release, verify paste height with SPI, review reflow profile, and add X-ray or boundary scan coverage for hidden pad nets; rework per IPC acceptability guidance.

takeaways: Publish node coverage and defect coverage together, because the first number flatters any test that only checks connectivity.
Weight coverage by occurrence, since a method that catches a rare class adds little to the escape rate.
List the uncovered classes with the strategy, because the gap is where escapes come from.

mistakes.mistake: Quoting a single coverage percentage for the whole board
mistakes.instead: Report per defect class, because coverage is a property of a defect model.

mistakes.mistake: Using vendor detection figures as your capability
mistakes.instead: Measure on your own process data, since the same method behaves differently on different products.

mistakes.mistake: Treating an AOI pass as an electrical pass
mistakes.instead: Add a test that exercises the node, because visual signature and electrical behaviour are different questions.

terms.def: The fraction of electrical nodes a test method exercises.
The fraction of expected defect modes a method can detect, weighted by occurrence.
A defective assembly that passes the inspection and test strategy and reaches the customer.
The likelihood that a method reports a present defect of a given class.

title: Choosing a strategy for a product mix: volume, complexity, cost, rework loop

goals.text: Compare ICT, flying probe, boundary scan and functional test for a given assembly and choose a strategy with reasons.
Estimate test coverage and name the defect classes left uncovered by the chosen strategy.

blocks.alt: A decision matrix of product volume against assembly complexity, with a test strategy recommended in each quadrant and a rework loop
blocks.caption: Choosing a strategy for a product mix: volume, complexity, cost and the rework loop

p: Product mix is a test-strategy problem because volume, complexity, cost and the rework loop interact.

High volume favours methods with short cycle time and repeatable contact, since fixture cost spreads over many units and line balance starts to matter. High complexity favours methods that reach dense interconnects, verify presence and value, and isolate faults quickly. Cost pressure favours whatever reduces escapes, rework and test time, which is rarely the cheapest tester on the quotation.
The strategy follows the mix, not the other way round.
In-circuit test uses a dedicated fixture with pogo pins to contact the test points.

It is strong on opens, shorts, missing components, wrong values and some solder defects where the net is accessible and the program is well built. Coverage is not the number of test points: it also depends on double-sided access, fine-pitch access, component orientation, and whether power, analogue and high-speed nets are included.
Fixture cost and design lead time are the price of that speed. Verify coverage against the fixture design, the equipment datasheet and the applicable IPC acceptance standard for solder defects.
Flying probe replaces the fixture with movable probes that reach test points under program control.

It suits prototypes, low volume, high mix and debug, because fixture cost disappears and program changes come quickly. It gives broad net coverage where test points are accessible, with cycle time usually longer than in-circuit test and probe reach limiting dense or double-sided boards.
Test-point placement and clearance matter more here, because a probe has to land on what the layout gives it.
Boundary scan controls device pins through JTAG and tests interconnects without physical probes.

It is valuable where access is limited, test points are scarce, or the interconnects are too dense to probe, and it detects opens, shorts and some device-level faults on scan-capable interconnects, plus programming and debug support.
Its coverage stops at scan-capable devices and scan-capable nets, and non-scan components stay outside it.
Functional test applies power, signals and loads to verify that the assembly behaves as intended.
It catches programming errors, gross functional failures, some marginal defects and system-level interactions the structural tests miss.

It may not isolate the failed net or component, and its coverage depends on the program, the stimulus conditions and the measurement resolution. Functional test is slow and needs specialised fixtures, software and skills, which is why it usually closes the line rather than opens it.
On high-volume, high-complexity assemblies the common combination is in-circuit test, boundary scan and functional test, which balances coverage, cycle time and rework loop time.

In-circuit test gives fast structural coverage, boundary scan covers where probes cannot reach, and functional test closes the gross functional defects. On low-volume or prototype work, flying probe plus boundary scan plus functional test often beats building a fixture.
State coverage for nets, components and defect classes, never as one standalone figure.

A strategy can cover most nets and still miss under-component solder defects, non-scan analogue faults, thermal and mechanical defects, intermittent contacts, contamination, programming errors and marginal parametric drift.

Coverage also depends on the conditions: temperature, voltage and timing, because some defects only appear under stress. Name the uncovered classes when the strategy is chosen, and name the control that compensates.
The rework loop runs from defect detection to corrected unit, and it drives both cost and quality.

A strategy that localises defects quickly shortens diagnosis and stops repeated functional debugging. Structural tests isolate opens, shorts, missing parts and wrong values, while functional tests may only say that a subsystem failed.
Total cost includes fixture, test time, maintenance, program development, escapes, rework and scrap. The cheapest tester is often the expensive choice once the loop is counted.

calc.task: A high-density assembly has 1400 nets, 30% BGA, 25% non-scan devices, and monthly volume 4000 units. Flying probe cycle time is 180 s, ICT cycle time is 25 s, boundary scan adds 8 s, and functional test adds 45 s. Estimate coverage and choose a strategy with reasons.
calc.solution: Define total nets as 1400. Estimate ICT net coverage. With accessible test points and double-sided probing, assume 85% of nets are testable; verify against fixture design. ICT coverage = 1400 x 85% = 1190 nets. Estimate boundary-scan coverage. Scan-capable share is 75%. Assume scan tests 80% of scan-capable interconnects; verify against boundary-scan tool. Scan coverage = 1400 x 75% x 80% = 840 nets. Combine coverage conservatively. Assume scan adds 7 percentage points beyond ICT because many scan nets overlap with ICT. Combined structural coverage = 85% + 7% = 92%. Add functional test. Assume functional test adds 3 percentage points for gross functional and programming defects. Estimated total coverage = 95%. Compare cycle time. ICT + boundary scan + functional = 25 s + 8 s + 45 s = 78 s per unit. Flying probe + boundary scan + functional = 180 s + 8 s + 45 s = 233 s per unit. At 4000 units/month, the ICT-based strategy is more practical for the rework loop because it reduces test time per unit and keeps fixture cost amortized. Choose ICT + boundary scan + functional. Reasons: high volume amortizes fixture cost, ICT gives fast structural coverage, boundary scan adds coverage where probe access is limited, functional test closes gross functional defects, and cycle time supports the rework loop. Name defect classes left uncovered: under-BGA opens/shorts not detected by structural or functional tests, non-scan analog faults, thermal or mechanical defects, intermittent contacts, contamination, marginal parametric drift, and programming errors not exercised by the functional program. Verify residual risk against your acceptance criteria and failure history.

defect.symptom: Intermittent open after reflow on a fine-pitch QFP, with the fault appearing only after thermal cycling or handling.
defect.cause: Insufficient solder paste volume, poor paste release, misalignment, or contaminated pad surface can create a marginal joint that tests good initially but opens under stress.
defect.action: Check stencil aperture, paste release, SPI data, alignment, and pad cleanliness; review reflow profile; add stress screening or targeted inspection if the defect class is not covered by the chosen test strategy.

takeaways: Choose the strategy from volume, complexity and the rework loop, because each driver points at a different method.
State coverage per defect class, since a net percentage says nothing about under-component joints.
Count the rework loop in the cost, because a slow diagnosis turns a cheap tester into an expensive one.

mistakes.mistake: Buying a fixture for a high-mix low-volume line
mistakes.instead: Use flying probe, because fixture cost cannot spread over a few hundred units.

mistakes.mistake: Reporting coverage for the board as one number
mistakes.instead: Break it down by class and condition, because defects live in the gaps.

mistakes.mistake: Leaving functional test to find structural faults
mistakes.instead: Cover structure early, because functional failures are the hardest to debug.

terms.def: A production profile with many different assemblies in small quantities.
The time and cost from detecting a defect to producing a corrected unit.
A spring-loaded contact that presses onto a test point in a fixture.
A defective unit that passes the strategy and reaches the customer.

title: Defect data before opinions: taxonomy, Pareto by stage, measurement integrity

goals.text: Structure a defect problem with measured data (taxonomy, Pareto by stage, measurement integrity) before analysis.

theory.h: Start with measured defect data, not with opinions
p: A defect problem becomes manageable once measured data describes it, before any analysis starts.

The first task is not to decide whether the printer, the placer, the oven, the wave or the operator is at fault. The first task is to define what was measured, where, in what unit, and against which acceptance rule.

"The oven is causing tombstoning" is an opinion until stage-specific counts, component references, board identifiers, lot data, process parameters and inspection results support it. "Reflow-stage confirmed defects are the largest contributor this week" is a measured observation, provided the taxonomy and the inspection integrity are known.
Treat defect data as a measurement system: if the measurement system is weak, every conclusion built on it is weak too.

blocks.alt: A Pareto chart of defects by process stage with a data-integrity check panel beside it
blocks.caption: Defect data before opinions: taxonomy, Pareto by stage and measurement integrity

p: A useful defect taxonomy records the defect mode, the assembly stage, the inspection or test point, the product, the board or lot identifier, the line, the shift, the equipment, the recipe and the disposition.

The defect mode says what was found: insufficient solder, excess solder, misalignment, tombstoning, bridging, voiding, lifted lead, solder ball, component damage or contamination. The stage says where it was detected and, where known, where it was created.
A taxonomy only pays off when the fields are filled the same way every shift, which is a discipline problem before it is a database problem.

theory.h: IPC acceptance and rework standards as the defect language
p: For visual and workmanship decisions, IPC-A-610 gives the acceptance criteria and IPC-7711/7721 gives the rework and repair guidance.
These standards matter because they supply a common language for classification and disposition. Acceptance still depends on product class, customer requirements and the specific defect condition.
Do not assume every visible anomaly is a reject, and do not assume every reject is a confirmed process defect.
A Pareto by stage answers which stage contributes the largest share of confirmed defects, escapes, rework, scrap or test failures.
A final-test Pareto alone hides upstream causes: a functional failure can come from a reflow defect, a placement defect, a through-hole insertion problem or a test setup issue.

A stage-based Pareto separates incoming material, paste print, placement, reflow, through-hole insertion, wave solder, in-circuit test and functional test, so the contribution is visible where it was made.

theory.h: Measurement integrity determines whether the Pareto is trustworthy
p: Measurement integrity asks whether the inspection or test system detects the defect it is meant to detect and whether it avoids false calls.

On SMT the measurement systems are SPI for paste volume and area, AOI for component and solder condition, X-ray for hidden joints, in-circuit test for connectivity, functional test for operation and manual visual inspection. On through-hole work they are insertion verification, wave inspection and the same electrical tests.
An unaudited measurement system produces a Pareto of its own biases.

theory.h: Record process parameters in SI units and trace them to the defect
p: Defect data becomes actionable when it is linked to process parameters in consistent SI units.

Print data may include stencil thickness in mm, aperture dimensions in mm, paste volume in mm³, squeegee pressure in Pa or N depending on the printer interface, print speed in mm/s and paste temperature in °C. Placement data may include nozzle force in N, placement speed in mm/s, component offset in mm and feeder pickup accuracy in mm. Reflow data may include zone temperatures in °C, conveyor speed in mm/s and atmosphere in ppm oxygen.

Trace each parameter to the defect it is suspected of causing, or the correlation stays a story. Verify the actual ranges against your paste datasheet, stencil design, printer datasheet, oven profile, wave or selective solder machine datasheet, and IPC-7525, IPC-7526, IPC-7530 or IPC-7711/7721 guidance where applicable.

theory.h: Define the denominator before comparing stages
p: A defect count without a denominator misleads.

The denominator may be boards produced, boards inspected, components placed, joints inspected, test cycles or units shipped, and a stage defect rate must state which. Defects per board, per thousand boards, per million joints and failures per test cycle are different metrics.
Where one stage inspects every board and another samples a subset, raw counts cannot be compared directly.

theory.h: Use the Pareto to select the next measurement, not to assign blame
p: The output of a stage-based Pareto is a short list of stages and defect modes that justify further measurement.

If reflow-stage confirmed defects dominate, stratify by component type, package size, board location, paste lot, stencil design, oven profile or AOI program. If paste print defects dominate, review SPI data, stencil condition, squeegee settings, paste rheology and registration. If through-hole or wave defects dominate, review insertion, hole fill and wave parameters.
Assigning blame is not an output; choosing the next measurement is.

calc.task: A mixed SMT/THT line produced 12,000 boards during a week. The MES defect table before measurement-integrity audit contained these stage defect calls: incoming 18, paste print 145, placement 92, reflow 270, THT insertion 34, wave solder 56, ICT 71, functional test 48. An AOI audit reviewed the 270 reflow calls and confirmed 210 defects, with 60 false calls. A detection audit used 50 seeded reflow defects and found that AOI detected 48 and missed 2. Calculate the raw stage defect rate per 1000 boards, the raw Pareto ranking, the corrected confirmed stage defect rate per 1000 boards, the corrected Pareto ranking, the AOI false-call rate, the AOI detection rate, and the seeded escape rate. State whether the reflow stage is still the top stage after correction and what data action is needed before root-cause analysis.
calc.solution: 1. Raw total defect calls = 18 + 145 + 92 + 270 + 34 + 56 + 71 + 48 = 734. 2. Raw stage defect rate per 1000 boards = stage count / 12,000 x 1000. Incoming = 18 / 12,000 x 1000 = 1.5. Paste print = 145 / 12,000 x 1000 = 12.1. Placement = 92 / 12,000 x 1000 = 7.7. Reflow = 270 / 12,000 x 1000 = 22.5. THT insertion = 34 / 12,000 x 1000 = 2.8. Wave solder = 56 / 12,000 x 1000 = 4.7. ICT = 71 / 12,000 x 1000 = 5.9. Functional test = 48 / 12,000 x 1000 = 4.0. 3. Raw Pareto ranking by count: reflow 270, paste print 145, placement 92, ICT 71, wave solder 56, functional test 48, THT insertion 34, incoming 18. 4. Raw percentage of total = stage count / 734 x 100. Reflow = 270 / 734 x 100 = 36.8%. Paste print = 145 / 734 x 100 = 19.8%. Placement = 92 / 734 x 100 = 12.5%. ICT = 71 / 734 x 100 = 9.7%. Wave solder = 56 / 734 x 100 = 7.6%. Functional test = 48 / 734 x 100 = 6.5%. THT insertion = 34 / 734 x 100 = 4.6%. Incoming = 18 / 734 x 100 = 2.5%. 5. Raw cumulative percentage: reflow 36.8%, paste print 56.6%, placement 69.1%, ICT 78.8%, wave solder 86.4%, functional test 92.9%, THT insertion 97.5%, incoming 100.0%. 6. Corrected confirmed total = 18 + 145 + 92 + 210 + 34 + 56 + 71 + 48 = 674. 7. Corrected stage defect rate per 1000 boards: incoming = 18 / 12,000 x 1000 = 1.5. Paste print = 145 / 12,000 x 1000 = 12.1. Placement = 92 / 12,000 x 1000 = 7.7. Reflow = 210 / 12,000 x 1000 = 17.5. THT insertion = 34 / 12,000 x 1000 = 2.8. Wave solder = 56 / 12,000 x 1000 = 4.7. ICT = 71 / 12,000 x 1000 = 5.9. Functional test = 48 / 12,000 x 1000 = 4.0. 8. Corrected Pareto ranking by confirmed count: reflow 210, paste print 145, placement 92, ICT 71, wave solder 56, functional test 48, THT insertion 34, incoming 18. 9. Corrected percentage of total = stage count / 674 x 100. Reflow = 210 / 674 x 100 = 31.2%. Paste print = 145 / 674 x 100 = 21.5%. Placement = 92 / 674 x 100 = 13.6%. ICT = 71 / 674 x 100 = 10.5%. Wave solder = 56 / 674 x 100 = 8.3%. Functional test = 48 / 674 x 100 = 7.1%. THT insertion = 34 / 674 x 100 = 5.0%. Incoming = 18 / 674 x 100 = 2.7%. 10. Corrected cumulative percentage: reflow 31.2%, paste print 52.7%, placement 66.3%, ICT 76.8%, wave solder 85.1%, functional test 92.2%, THT insertion 97.2%, incoming 99.9% before rounding to full total. 11. AOI false-call rate = false calls / AOI calls x 100 = 60 / 270 x 100 = 22.2%. 12. AOI detection rate = detected seeded defects / seeded defects x 100 = 48 / 50 x 100 = 96.0%. 13. Seeded escape rate = missed seeded defects / seeded defects x 100 = 2 / 50 x 100 = 4.0%. 14. Optional estimate of true reflow defects, assuming the seeded detection rate applies to the confirmed population and false calls have been removed: estimated true reflow defects = confirmed reflow defects / detection rate = 210 / 0.96 = 218.8. 15. Conclusion: reflow remains the top stage after correction, but the gap between reflow and paste print narrows from 125 raw calls to 65 confirmed defects. The data action is to remove false calls from the Pareto, record confirmed versus called defects separately, verify AOI program settings and defect library, and stratify reflow defects by component, package, board location, paste lot, stencil design, and oven profile before root-cause analysis.

defect.symptom: AOI reports a high number of reflow-stage solder defects, especially insufficient solder and bridging, but repair confirmation shows that many boards pass IPC-A-610 acceptance or are repaired without a confirmed process defect. The reflow stage dominates the Pareto, and operators blame the oven while the paste printer and stencil condition are not being reviewed.
defect.cause: The defect database is counting AOI calls as confirmed defects without separating false calls, and the AOI program has not been audited against IPC-A-610 acceptance conditions or a seeded defect library. The measurement system is therefore inflating the reflow stage and hiding the true upstream contribution from paste print or stencil-related defects.
defect.action: Freeze the current Pareto, rebuild the defect table with separate fields for AOI call, confirmed defect, false call, escape, disposition, and IPC-A-610 acceptance decision. Run an AOI false-call and detection audit using known-good boards and seeded defects. Correct the Pareto using confirmed defects only. If the corrected reflow Pareto still dominates, stratify by component, package, board location, paste lot, stencil design, and oven profile. If the corrected paste print Pareto rises, review stencil condition, aperture design, paste rheology, squeegee settings, and SPI data against IPC-7525, IPC-7526, and IPC-7530 guidance and your equipment datasheets.

takeaways: Separate calls from confirmed defects before plotting, because a false-call rate becomes a Pareto bar if nobody audits it.
Keep the denominator with every rate, since stage comparisons collapse when one stage samples and another inspects everything.
Let the Pareto choose the next stratification, because a chart that ends in a person produces no measurement.

mistakes.mistake: Ranking stages by raw inspection calls
mistakes.instead: Rank by confirmed defects, because inspection bias is not process performance.

mistakes.mistake: Auditing the defect database once and assuming it is stable
mistakes.instead: Re-audit after program or product changes, since the bias returns with them.

mistakes.mistake: Comparing a sampled stage with a fully inspected stage
mistakes.instead: Normalise the denominator, because sampling changes the count and not the process.

terms.def: A ranked bar chart of defect counts or rates by category, used to choose where to work first.
An inspection or test failure reported on an assembly that is actually acceptable.
The ability of an inspection system to detect defects without inventing them.
Splitting a defect population by a second variable to find where the effect concentrates.

title: Cause analysis tools: 5-Why, fishbone, fault tree, change-point analysis

goals.text: Separate root cause, contributing causes and the detection escape in a structured cause analysis.

blocks.alt: Four small diagrams side by side: a five-why chain, a fishbone with six bones, a fault tree and a change-point chart
blocks.caption: Cause analysis tools: five-why, fishbone, fault tree and change-point analysis

theory.h: Separate the failure, the causes and the escape
p: Cause analysis starts by separating three questions: what physical failure occurred, what process conditions made it likely, and why the defect was not detected.

A root cause is the condition that, once corrected, prevents recurrence under the same operating assumptions. Contributing causes raise probability or severity without being sufficient alone. A detection escape is a gap in inspection, test or sampling.
Most bad investigations collapse these three into one sentence, and then fix the detection while the cause stays in the process.
The why-chain, the 5-Why, suits a narrow failure mode with a mostly linear sequence.

Ask why until the answer points at a controllable process parameter, a design condition or a management-system gap, then stop and verify with evidence. Tombstoning can run from uneven wetting to asymmetric paste deposit, to stencil alignment or paste rheology, to setup verification.
Avoid stopping at operator error, which is usually a description of the process rather than a cause.
A fishbone works better when many cause families may interact.

Use categories such as machine, method, material, measurement, environment and management, and populate them with testable hypotheses: reflow profile drift, paste viscosity or metal content, stencil aperture wear, placement nozzle force, feeder misalignment, wave conveyor speed, flux activity, humidity and inspection coverage.
The diagram organises the investigation; it does not prove anything until each branch is tested.

theory.h: Fault tree for combined causes and escapes
p: Fault tree analysis helps when the top event can result from several independent or combined causes.

Define the top event narrowly, such as an open joint or a tombstoned component, then decompose it with AND and OR gates. An open joint may need both insufficient wetting and mechanical disturbance, while a tombstone may follow from severe paste asymmetry or severe placement offset.
Fault trees make detection escapes explicit, because the tree shows the branch that should have caught the defect and did not.
Change-point analysis compares behaviour before and after a suspected change.

Common changes are paste lot, stencil, reflow profile, placement nozzle, feeder setup, wave chain speed, flux lot or AOI program revision. Use a before and after defect rate, a control chart, or a change-point statistic where data allow.
Confirm that the change occurred before the shift, that it affected the product and process in question, and that nothing else moved at the same time.
Separate root cause, contributing causes and detection escape in the final report.

The root cause is the item for corrective action, such as an unqualified paste lot property or a stencil aperture outside the qualified range. Contributing causes may be a marginal reflow profile, a worn nozzle or high placement speed, and they can be reduced by risk controls even when they are not primary.

The detection escape is closed by inspection or test changes, such as AOI program limits, X-ray sampling, functional test coverage or the IPC-A-610 visual acceptability criteria, and it needs its own owner.

theory.h: Close with verification and updated controls
p: Close with verification.

Containment protects the customer, corrective action removes the root cause, and effectiveness checks confirm that the defect rate, escape rate or process parameter has returned to an acceptable state. Update the control plan, the FMEA, the work instructions and the inspection program.

Use SI units for temperatures, times, distances and volumes, and state the uncertainty or the sampling limits behind the numbers. Avoid absolute language: standards and contracts allow exceptions, so record the applicable IPC-A-610 class and the IPC/JEDEC J-STD-001 requirements alongside any approved deviation.

calc.task: A line produces 1000 boards/day. Tombstone defect rate for small chip resistors was 0.2% over 10 days. After a paste lot change, the rate was 1.5% over 10 days. AOI detects 80% of tombstones. Functional test detects 5% of the tombstones missed by AOI. Estimate daily escaped defects before and after the change, and state how to classify root cause, contributing causes, and detection escape.
calc.solution: First, convert defect rates to defects per day. Before: 1000 boards/day x 0.2% = 2.0 defects/day. After: 1000 boards/day x 1.5% = 15.0 defects/day. Second, estimate defects missed by AOI. AOI detects 80%, so it misses 20%. Before: 2.0 x 0.20 = 0.4 missed/day. After: 15.0 x 0.20 = 3.0 missed/day. Third, estimate defects missed by functional test. Functional test detects 5% of AOI misses, so it misses 95%. Before: 0.4 x 0.95 = 0.38 escaped/day. After: 3.0 x 0.95 = 2.85 escaped/day. Fourth, interpret the change point. The escaped defect rate rises from 0.38/day to 2.85/day after the paste lot change, so the paste lot change is a strong candidate change point if the timing matches. Fifth, classify causes. A likely root cause is a paste lot property outside the qualified range, such as viscosity or metal content, verified against the paste datasheet. Contributing causes may include stencil alignment drift, nozzle wear, or marginal reflow profile. The detection escape is the AOI program and functional test coverage that failed to remove the remaining tombstones.

defect.symptom: Tombstoned chip resistors after reflow; some passed AOI and reached functional test or downstream assembly.
defect.cause: A paste lot with viscosity or metal content outside the qualified range, combined with stencil alignment drift, produced asymmetric paste deposits and uneven wetting. The AOI program limits did not flag small tombstones, and functional test coverage did not reliably detect them.
defect.action: Quarantine the suspect paste lot and verify viscosity and metal content against the paste datasheet. Requalify stencil alignment, reflow profile, and placement setup. Update the AOI program and add targeted X-ray or functional test coverage. Run an effectiveness check on subsequent lots and update the control plan and FMEA.

takeaways: Name the failure, the cause and the escape separately, because fixing detection on an unproven cause hides the defect rather than removing it.
Stop the why-chain at a controllable parameter, since operator error describes the process without changing it.
Verify effectiveness against a rate, because a corrective action without a measured before and after is a claim.

mistakes.mistake: Closing a case at operator error
mistakes.instead: Trace to the process condition that allowed it, because the same error recurs with a new operator.

mistakes.mistake: Treating a contributing cause as the root cause
mistakes.instead: Keep the categories apart, since the risk control differs from the corrective action.

mistakes.mistake: Fixing detection first because it is faster
mistakes.instead: Address the escape and the cause with separate actions, because a better inspection finds more of the same defect.

terms.def: The condition whose correction prevents recurrence under the same assumptions.
A defect that passed the inspection or test intended to catch it.
A top-down logic diagram using AND and OR gates to decompose a failure event.
A point in time at which a process measurement shifts, often following a deliberate change.
