title: Containment and traceability: quarantine scope, lot trace, retroactive search

goals.text: Write a complete 8D with containment, corrective action, owners, dates and an effectiveness metric.

blocks.alt: A containment boundary drawn around work in process, finished goods and shipped units, with a lot trace chain and a retroactive search arrow
blocks.caption: Containment and traceability: quarantine scope, lot trace and retroactive search

theory.h: Containment and traceability are separate controls
theory.p: Containment protects the customer while the cause is unknown, and traceability tells you what to contain. In SMT/THT, a defect can be created by paste, component, stencil, placement, reflow, wave solder, insertion, cleaning, or test escape. A good containment record starts with the detection point and works backward to the last verified good point. It should identify the product, process step, equipment, operator, program, material lot, and time window. If records are incomplete, the scope should be widened until the uncertainty is bounded, then narrowed with evidence. The goal is not to quarantine the whole factory; it is to isolate the population that could plausibly contain the defect. A clear scope also reduces the cost of investigation, because the team can focus on the process window, material lots, and equipment settings that actually produced the suspect units. When the scope is vague, teams often inspect too much product, lose line capacity, and still miss the escape. When the scope is too narrow, the escape can continue downstream, and the company may need to notify the customer under the applicable requirement in ISO 9001 or IATF 16949.

p: Quarantine scope is a bounded suspect population.

Use timestamps from MES, ERP, test logs and line audits. The scope covers work in process, finished goods, shipped goods, returns, and anything made between the last verified good inspection and detection.

Include adjacent shifts and changeovers where the process was not verified afterwards. A paste lot change, stencil change, feeder change or wave program change usually widens the window, because the change itself is a candidate cause.
Scope too narrow lets the escape continue downstream, and the company may then have to notify the customer under the applicable requirement in ISO 9001 or IATF 16949.

theory.h: Lot trace in SMT and through-hole
p: Lot trace connects the assembly to the materials and process parameters that affected it.

On SMT, trace the component lot, solder paste lot, stencil, placement program, feeder setup, reflow profile and oven zone settings. On through-hole work, trace the component lot, insertion program, wave solder program, flux density, preheat temperature, conveyor speed and solder pot temperature.
Verify the settings against the equipment datasheets before quoting them as fact in the report.
Retroactive search looks for other units that may share the latent cause.

Search forward from the suspect materials and backward from the defect signature. Include units made before and after detection where the process was not verified, and units from the same equipment, operator, program or material lot.

Where the population is too large to inspect fully, use a sampling plan matched to the risk and state its confidence, because an unstated sample is an unstated claim. ANSI/ASQ Z1.4 can supply the plan when one is needed, and the plan is documented and approved rather than chosen at the bench.
An 8D report is a structured problem-solving record.

It names the team, describes the problem with product, quantity, location and detection point, and states the interim containment. It identifies the root cause and the escape point, then defines the permanent corrective action with implementation dates, owners and effectiveness checks.
Prevention comes next: update the control plan, the FMEA, the work instructions and the inspection program so the same escape cannot recur silently.
Every containment and corrective action needs a named owner and a due date.
Containment actions are short-term and are verified before suspect material is released. Corrective actions get a longer validation window.

Measure effectiveness with a metric tied to the defect: solder defect ppm, first pass yield, rework rate, test escape rate or audit findings. Set the target from historical performance rather than from ambition, and re-measure after the fix is in place.

theory.p: Closure requires evidence that the suspect population is dispositioned, the cause is corrected, and the process is stable. Disposition options include rework, scrap, use-as-is, or customer concession, depending on contract and product requirements. Rework should follow IPC-7711/7721 and be documented. Soldering acceptance should be checked against IPC-A-610 and IPC/JEDEC J-STD-001 where applicable. Update the control plan and FMEA, train affected staff, and add an initial-article check or layered process audit for a defined period. Keep the 8D open until the effectiveness metric is met and the records are archived. The closure package should include the quarantine record, disposition record, root cause evidence, corrective action evidence, effectiveness data, and updated documents. If the customer requires a formal report, use the customer format while keeping the same evidence. If the issue is internal, the same package supports the next audit and reduces the chance of recurrence. Closure is not complete when the line is running; it is complete when the process control is updated and the evidence shows the defect is no longer escaping.

calc.task: A line produced 1200 boards/h. A solder bridge was detected at 14:20. The last verified good inspection was at 13:50. The line stopped at 14:25. A paste lot change occurred at 13:45. Calculate the suspect window, suspect board count, and quarantine quantity. Then draft the containment, corrective action, owners, dates, and effectiveness metric for an 8D.
calc.solution: Start by choosing the earliest credible suspect time. The paste lot change at 13:45 is earlier than the last verified good inspection at 13:50, so use 13:45 as the conservative start of the suspect window. The line stopped at 14:25, so the suspect window is 13:45 to 14:25. The window length is 40 min. Convert the production rate to boards per minute: 1200 boards/h divided by 60 min/h equals 20 boards/min. Multiply 20 boards/min by 40 min to get 800 boards. Quarantine the 800 boards plus any work in process, finished goods, and shipped units from the same window. Containment owner: SMT process engineer; due date: 24 h. Corrective action owner: process engineer; due date: 7 days. Corrective action: verify flux density, preheat temperature, conveyor speed, and solder pot temperature against your equipment datasheet; rework per IPC-7711/7721; add an initial-article check after changeover. Effectiveness metric: solder bridge ppm; baseline 500 ppm; target 100 ppm; measured over 30 days. Close when the target is met and the control plan, FMEA, and work instructions are updated.

defect.symptom: Solder bridges between adjacent THT leads on a fine-pitch header after wave solder, detected at ICT.
defect.cause: Flux application was too heavy and preheat was below the range recommended by the wave solder equipment datasheet, leaving flux residue that prevented solder coalescence.
defect.action: Quarantine product back to the last verified good inspection, rework per IPC-7711/7721, adjust flux density and preheat within the equipment datasheet range, and add an initial-article check after each changeover.

takeaways: Bound the suspect population before releasing anything, because containment without a window is a promise rather than a control.
Trace the material and the process settings to each assembly, since a signature without a candidate cause leads nowhere.
Attach a metric and a date to every action, because an action without a measurement cannot be closed.

mistakes.mistake: Setting the window at the detection time
mistakes.instead: Start from the last verified good point, because defects created earlier were passing until now.

mistakes.mistake: Quarantining without the shipping and returns data
mistakes.instead: Include shipped and returned units, because the customer holds the rest of the population.

mistakes.mistake: Closing an 8D on the corrective action alone
mistakes.instead: Verify effectiveness after implementation, because a fix that was not measured is a hope.

terms.def: The immediate action that stops suspect product reaching the next process or the customer.
The record linking an assembly to its materials, equipment, programs and time window.
Identifying other units that share a suspect cause with the detected defect.
An eight-discipline problem-solving report structure used for escapes and recurring defects.

title: 8D discipline: D1–D8 content and where 8D reports fail

blocks.caption: The eight disciplines D1-D8 and where 8D reports usually fail: containment sold as correction, root cause without data, closure without an effectiveness metric

blocks.alt: Reference sheet: eight hexagons D1 team to D8 closure with D3, D4 and D8 marked as common failure points, a whiteboard fishbone photograph, and evidence examples
blocks.caption: The eight disciplines D1-D8 and the usual failure points

p: An 8D report is a structured problem-solving record for internal escapes, customer complaints or repeated process defects.

In SMT and through-hole work it connects the complaint to traceable evidence: product, lot, line, process step, component, paste, stencil, feeder, reflow or wave and selective solder parameters, inspection program and test data.
The report is useful only if another engineer can follow the logic, repeat the verification and see where the conclusions came from.

theory.h: D1 team and D2 problem description
p: D1 names a small working team with authority and knowledge: process engineering, production, quality, materials, equipment maintenance, design, and supplier support where materials or tooling are involved.

D2 describes the problem as observed, not as a conclusion. Include product, line, process step, defect mode, quantity, date, lot, measurement method, customer impact, and whether the defect is an occurrence or a detection escape.
A problem statement that already names the cause has skipped the investigation.
Containment protects the customer while the root cause is still under investigation.

Typical actions are quarantining suspect lots, sorting outgoing stock, adding inspection, holding shipments, notifying the customer, freezing process changes, and reworking only under a controlled method.
Each action needs an owner, a date and a verification method. Containment is not corrective action: it reduces risk without removing the cause.

theory.h: D4 root cause, occurrence and detection
p: A complete 8D separates the occurrence root cause from the detection escape.

Occurrence may involve paste rheology, stencil aperture design, reflow ramp and soak, component coplanarity, feeder accuracy, placement pressure, wave dwell, selective nozzle condition, flux activity, preheat, cooling or thermal mass. Detection may involve AOI coverage, in-circuit coverage, visual inspection limits or test escape.
Both sides need evidence, and the evidence should be traceable to lot or program records rather than recalled.

theory.h: D5 corrective action and D6 validation
p: Corrective action addresses the proven root cause, not the visible symptom.

Examples: changing stencil aperture geometry, updating the reflow profile inside the paste and component datasheet window, replacing a feeder, adjusting wave or selective solder parameters, updating an AOI program, adding a poka-yoke, or changing supplier control.
Implementation needs an owner and a date, and validation should show the effect on the metric rather than the completion of the task.

Prevention updates the management system so the class of problem is less likely to recur: PFMEA, control plan, work instructions, operator training, design rules, incoming inspection, supplier agreements, tooling maintenance, and horizontal deployment to similar products or lines.
Closure is supported by evidence: containment records, root-cause data, validation results, updated documents, and a measured effectiveness check.

The usual failures are presenting containment as correction, stating a root cause without data, ignoring the detection escape, missing owners or dates, vague language, missing traceability, and closure without an effectiveness metric.
Another frequent failure is no horizontal deployment, so the same defect returns on a similar product.
A good 8D is auditable: it shows what was found, what was done, who did it, when, and what the data said afterwards.

calc.task: Write a complete 8D for an SMT line where a customer reports tombstoned chip resistors on a production lot. Include containment, corrective action, owners, dates, and an effectiveness metric.
calc.solution:
D1 Team: SMT process engineer as lead, production supervisor, quality engineer, materials engineer, AOI programmer, and supplier representative if paste or component data are needed.
D2 Problem: customer reported tombstoned chip resistors on product X, line Y, reflow process step, defect mode tombstoning, lot traceability recorded, quantity reported by customer, measurement method visual and AOI, date of complaint recorded. The problem is both occurrence and detection because the defect reached the customer.
D3 Containment: quarantine suspect lots, sort outgoing stock, add AOI and visual inspection, notify customer, freeze process changes, and hold shipments until containment is verified. Owner: quality engineer. Date: 2026-01-15. Verification: audit sorted lots and outgoing inspection records.
D4 Root cause: occurrence root cause identified from data as unbalanced wetting caused by stencil aperture imbalance and reflow ramp rate outside the preferred window for the paste and component. Detection root cause identified as AOI program did not reliably flag tombstone on small chip components.
D5 Corrective action: update stencil aperture design, adjust reflow profile within the paste and component datasheet window, update AOI program, and add feeder and placement verification to the setup checklist. Owner: SMT process engineer. Date: 2026-01-22.
D6 Validation: run validation lots, measure tombstone defect rate, and compare to the effectiveness metric. Effectiveness metric: tombstone defect rate in ppm over validation lots, target from customer specification or internal control limit. Owner: quality engineer. Date: 2026-02-05.
D7 Prevention: update PFMEA, control plan, work instructions, operator training, and horizontal deployment to similar products using the same component family or stencil design. Owner: process engineering manager. Date: 2026-02-12.
D8 Closure: close when containment is verified, corrective action is validated, documents are updated, and the effectiveness metric is met. Owner: quality manager. Date: 2026-02-19.

defect.symptom: AOI flags tombstoned chip resistors on one side of the PCB after reflow, and the defect rate rises on the night shift.
defect.cause: Stencil aperture for one pad is too large and the reflow ramp is too fast, causing unbalanced wetting; the AOI program did not detect tombstone on small components.
defect.action: Quarantine suspect lots, sort outgoing stock, reduce aperture imbalance, adjust reflow profile per paste and component datasheets, update AOI program, validate with short runs, and monitor defect rate in ppm.

takeaways: Keep occurrence and detection separate through D4, because one corrective action rarely closes both.
Treat containment as a holding action, since releasing on containment alone leaves the cause in the process.
Close on a measured metric, because a completed action list is not evidence that the defect rate moved.

mistakes.mistake: Writing the cause into the D2 problem statement
mistakes.instead: Describe what was observed, because a leading statement biases every later step.

mistakes.mistake: Closing on the corrective action date
mistakes.instead: Verify the metric afterwards, since implementation and effect are different events.

mistakes.mistake: Skipping horizontal deployment to similar products
mistakes.instead: Apply the fix to similar products, because the same design repeats across the line.

terms.def: The process condition that created the defect.
The defect that passed the inspection or test meant to catch it.
A design or process feature that prevents an error from being made.
Applying a corrective action to other products, lines or sites with the same risk.

title: Corrective vs preventive action and effectiveness verification

goals.text: Write a complete 8D with containment, corrective action, owners, dates and an effectiveness metric.
Feed the result back into PFMEA, control plan and the auditor checklist through change control.

blocks.alt: Reference sheet: flow from nonconformity detected through corrective and preventive action to an effectiveness verification gate with a reopen loop, and a macro photograph of a reworked chip resistor joint
blocks.caption: Corrective vs preventive action, verified with data at the effectiveness gate

p: Corrective action responds to a detected nonconformity, such as a solder defect found by AOI, X-ray, functional test or a customer complaint.
Preventive action addresses a credible potential failure before it happens: a stencil aperture close to a paste-release limit, or a wave pot temperature drifting towards its control limit.
In an 8D, containment protects the customer before the root cause is known, corrective action removes the cause, and preventive action keeps the next product out of the same hole.

A usable 8D records the problem statement, affected part numbers and lots, containment quantity and disposition, team roles, root cause, corrective action, implementation evidence, effectiveness metric and closure decision.

Name owners by role: SMT process engineer, line supervisor, quality engineer, PFMEA owner. Use actual dates from the CAPA or 8D record, not assumed ones, and keep the evidence attached rather than summarised.
An auditor follows the chain from the complaint to the changed control, so every link needs a document.
Containment can be quarantine of suspect lots, full inspection, rework, a temporary parameter lock, or a hold on shipping.
Match the method to the risk: a safety-related joint defect may need full inspection and customer notification, while a cosmetic issue may need sampling and disposition by a documented plan.
Verify containment by checking the inspected population against the population you believed you had. A containment claim with no count behind it is a statement of intent.
For SMT and through-hole defects, separate the cause that created the defect from the cause that let it escape.

Occurrence causes include paste volume, stencil aperture design, reflow profile, wave solder temperature, flux activity, component coplanarity, feeder calibration and handling damage. Detection causes include AOI program coverage, X-ray sampling, test coverage and operator judgement. Systemic causes include missing controls, unclear work instructions and absent verification.
All three belong in the report, because each needs a different action.

theory.h: Choosing a corrective action that survives production
p: Select the action that addresses the verified root cause and can be sustained.
Examples: changing a stencil aperture, adding a poka-yoke fixture, revising a reflow profile, replacing a worn feeder, changing a supplier lot, or adding a sensor check.

A parameter adjustment is valid where the root cause is drift or misconfiguration, provided the data and the equipment datasheet support the setting, and provided the correction cannot be quietly reversed on the next shift.
Define the effectiveness metric before implementation.

Common metrics are defect rate in ppm, first pass yield, AOI escape rate, X-ray void percentage, wetting quality and functional test failure rate. Verification needs enough production time and sample size to detect recurrence, and the acceptance criterion should be agreed with quality and, where required, the customer.
If the metric misses the target, the 8D stays open.

theory.p: A practical closure record can show: containment date 2026-01-15, owner line supervisor; corrective action implementation date 2026-01-22, owner SMT process engineer; effectiveness verification date 2026-02-05, owner quality engineer; effectiveness metric defect rate in ppm with target 500 ppm; PFMEA and control plan update owner PFMEA owner. The dates, owners, and metric should be copied into the 8D from the CAPA or change control record.

theory.h: Feeding the result into PFMEA, control plan and audit checklist
p: When the 8D closes, update the PFMEA with the failure mode, cause, current controls, occurrence, detection and reaction plan.
Update the control plan with the new parameter, inspection method, frequency and reaction plan. Add or revise auditor checklist questions so the next audit verifies the new control.
Use change control to approve the revision, train the affected personnel, and record the effective date.

calc.task: A THT wave solder line had 180 defects in 12000 boards before corrective action. After corrective action, 24 defects occurred in 15000 boards. Calculate the before and after defect rate in ppm, the reduction, and whether the after rate meets a target of 500 ppm.
calc.solution: Before rate = 180 / 12000 = 0.015 = 15000 ppm. After rate = 24 / 15000 = 0.0016 = 1600 ppm. Reduction = (15000 - 1600) / 15000 = 0.8933 = 89.3 percent. The after rate is 1600 ppm, which is above the target of 500 ppm, so the corrective action is not yet effective by the agreed metric. Continue monitoring, increase sample size, or strengthen the corrective action before closing the 8D.

defect.symptom: THT wave solder joints on fine-pitch IC leads show insufficient wetting and dewetting after wave solder, with AOI flagging a higher reject rate on a panel side.
defect.cause: The wave solder pot temperature reading was lower than the verified actual temperature because the thermocouple had drifted, and the setpoint was adjusted without a documented change control record. The resulting thermal profile did not meet the wetting requirement for the lead finish and flux used.
defect.action: Quarantine suspect boards, recalibrate the thermocouple, verify the pot temperature against the equipment datasheet, restore the approved setpoint through change control, revalidate with wetting and X-ray checks, update the PFMEA and control plan, and add a daily thermocouple check to the auditor checklist.

takeaways: Separate corrective from preventive action, because the complaint and the risk are different populations.
Size containment to the risk and prove it by count, since an unverified containment is a hope.
Define the effectiveness metric before the fix, because a target chosen afterwards always looks met.

mistakes.mistake: Closing an 8D when the action is implemented
mistakes.instead: Verify the metric first, since implementation is not an effect.

mistakes.mistake: Adjusting a parameter without change control
mistakes.instead: Record the change, because an undocumented setting cannot be restored after a shift change.

mistakes.mistake: Updating the 8D but not the control plan
mistakes.instead: Revise the control plan and audit checklist, because the fix lives in the documents the line follows.

terms.def: Corrective and preventive action, the quality-system record behind the 8D.
Process failure mode and effects analysis, the risk document the 8D updates.
The measurable rate used to prove that a corrective action worked.
The approval route for a documented change to a process or specification.

title: Closing the loop: PFMEA, control plan, auditor checklist, change control

goals.text: Feed the result back into PFMEA, control plan and the auditor checklist through change control.

blocks.alt: A loop diagram linking corrective action to a process failure mode analysis update, a control plan revision, an auditor checklist and change control
blocks.caption: Closing the loop: PFMEA, control plan, auditor checklist and change control

theory.h: Closing the loop means changing the control system
p: A corrective action is not complete when the line returns to normal output.
It is complete when the learning is written into the PFMEA, the control plan, the auditor checklist and the change-control record.

The PFMEA records the failure mode, cause, detection method and risk priority. The control plan records the process parameter, specification, measurement method, sample size, frequency and reaction plan. The checklist asks whether the control is being executed, and the change record shows who approved it and when.

theory.p: Change control is the route by which a process change is proposed, reviewed, approved, implemented, verified, and closed. In electronics assembly, changes may include paste type, stencil aperture, reflow profile, wave solder temperature, flux density, conveyor speed, component substitution, feeder change, nozzle change, placement program revision, or inspection criteria. A change should be controlled when it can affect fit, form, function, reliability, solderability, or inspection acceptance. For example, a change in peak reflow temperature or dwell time above the liquidus can affect solder joint microstructure and should be reviewed against the paste and component datasheets and against IPC-7530 Guidelines for Convection Reflow Soldering where applicable.

theory.h: PFMEA should reflect the current process
p: The PFMEA is a living risk document.

After an investigation, update the failure mode when a new cause is found, update the cause when the root cause differs from the original assumption, and update the detection method when the current inspection cannot reliably find the defect.
Update severity, occurrence or detection ratings only when evidence justifies it. A rating changed to make the chart look better is worse than no rating at all.
A control plan cannot say only that the operator checks quality.
It states what is checked, how often, with what method, against what limit, and what happens when the result falls outside specification.

For paste printing that means stencil cleanliness, paste viscosity or rheology per the paste datasheet, print alignment, paste height, paste volume and post-print inspection. For reflow it means zone temperatures, conveyor speed, atmosphere and profile verification.
The auditor checklist asks whether the control exists and whether it is followed.

Useful questions: is the current revision of the control plan available at the station, are measured values recorded at the required frequency, are out-of-limit results handled per the reaction plan, are calibration labels valid, is rejected material segregated, and are change-control records complete?
A checklist that only asks whether a document exists audits the filing cabinet.

A practical package contains the problem statement, defect data, root cause, proposed change, affected documents, risk assessment, verification plan, implementation date, responsible owner and closure evidence.

For an SMT example, a new paste lot causing insufficient solder on fine-pitch QFN pads brings in paste lot traceability, a stencil design review, a reflow profile comparison against IPC-7530, first-article results and the updated control plan.
When updating inspection criteria, use the applicable acceptance standard and the customer or internal specification.
IPC-A-610 gives the acceptance classes and visual criteria for solder joints, components and cleanliness, and IPC-7711/7721 gives the rework and repair methods.
Where a change affects rework, the rework instruction changes with it, so the new criteria and the old method do not sit side by side in the same document set.

theory.h: Close with verification, not only approval
p: After implementation, verify that the defect rate has fallen and that no new failure mode has appeared.
Verification may use first-article inspection, in-process data, final inspection data, field return data, reliability test data or audit findings.
A temporary change carries an expiry date or a condition for permanent adoption in the change record itself, so it cannot become permanent by neglect.

calc.task: A 0402 SMT placement line shows a tombstoning rate of 180 ppm on a fine-pitch board. Investigation shows the peak reflow temperature was 232 °C and time above liquidus was 48 s, while the paste datasheet recommends a peak temperature range of 235 °C to 245 °C and time above liquidus of 40 s to 70 s. A change-control proposal raises the peak temperature to 240 °C and time above liquidus to 55 s. Calculate the change in peak temperature and time above liquidus, determine whether the proposed values are inside the paste datasheet range, and define the minimum verification sample needed to confirm that tombstoning is reduced to below 50 ppm with 95% confidence if the observed rate after the change is 0 defects in the sample.
calc.solution: 1. Calculate the peak temperature change: proposed peak temperature minus current peak temperature = 240 °C - 232 °C = 8 °C. 2. Calculate the time above liquidus change: proposed time above liquidus minus current time above liquidus = 55 s - 48 s = 7 s. 3. Check the proposed peak temperature against the paste datasheet range: 235 °C to 245 °C. The proposed 240 °C is inside the range. 4. Check the proposed time above liquidus against the paste datasheet range: 40 s to 70 s. The proposed 55 s is inside the range. 5. For a zero-defect verification sample, use the binomial rule for zero failures: the probability of observing zero defects if the true defect rate is p is (1 - p)^n. To demonstrate with 95% confidence that the true rate is below p = 50 ppm = 0.00005, solve (1 - 0.00005)^n <= 0.05. 6. Take natural logs: n >= ln(0.05) / ln(1 - 0.00005). 7. ln(0.05) = -2.9957. ln(1 - 0.00005) ≈ -0.000050001. 8. n >= -2.9957 / -0.000050001 ≈ 59,913. 9. Round up to a practical sample size: inspect at least 60,000 units with zero tombstoning defects to claim 95% confidence that the true tombstoning rate is below 50 ppm. 10. If 60,000 units are not practical, use a lower confidence level, a higher target ppm, or combine inspection with process data such as reflow profile logs, paste volume data, and placement accuracy data. 11. Update the PFMEA cause to include reflow profile deviation, update the control plan to require profile verification at the defined frequency, update the auditor checklist to verify profile logs and calibration, and close the change-control record only after the verification result is accepted.

defect.symptom: After a paste change, the line shows intermittent insufficient solder on 0.5 mm pitch QFN pads. Final inspection passes visually, but X-ray shows reduced heel fillet and small voiding on some joints. The defect rate rises from about 20 ppm to about 150 ppm over three shifts.
defect.cause: The new paste has a different viscosity and slump behavior, but the stencil aperture and reflow profile were not requalified. The control plan still uses the old paste print parameters and the auditor checklist does not require paste lot traceability or post-print paste height verification. The PFMEA did not include paste rheology change as a cause for insufficient solder on fine-pitch QFN pads.
defect.action: Open a change-control record for the paste substitution. Requalify the stencil aperture and reflow profile using the new paste datasheet and verify against IPC-7530 Guidelines for Convection Reflow Soldering where applicable. Add paste lot traceability, paste height or volume measurement, and QFN X-ray sampling to the control plan. Update the PFMEA to include paste rheology change as a cause of insufficient solder. Add a checklist item requiring the auditor to verify that the current paste lot, stencil revision, reflow profile, and X-ray results match the approved control plan. Run a verification lot and close the change only when the defect rate returns to the target range and the documents are updated.

takeaways: Write the learning into the documents the line follows, because an action that lives only in the 8D changes nothing.
Attach a measurable control to every change, since "operator checks" is not a control.
Verify the defect rate after implementation, because a new failure mode often arrives with the fix.

mistakes.mistake: Approving a change and skipping the control plan update
mistakes.instead: Update the plan and the checklist, because the station follows the plan.

mistakes.mistake: Leaving a temporary change in place indefinitely
mistakes.instead: Set an expiry date, since temporary settings become permanent by default.

mistakes.mistake: Editing PFMEA ratings to reflect the hoped-for improvement
mistakes.instead: Rate from evidence, because the rating drives the next risk decision.

terms.def: The document stating what is measured, how often, against what limit, and the reaction when it fails.
Process failure mode and effects analysis, the living risk record for the process.
The defined response when a measured value falls outside its limit.
A full check of the first unit produced after a change.

skills: Lesson m14l05: Corrective vs preventive action and effectiveness verification

title: 8D workshop: full case from symptom to closure

goals.text: Structure a defect problem with measured data (taxonomy, Pareto by stage, measurement integrity) before analysis.
Separate root cause, contributing causes and the detection escape in a structured cause analysis.
Write a complete 8D with containment, corrective action, owners, dates and an effectiveness metric.

blocks.alt: A case timeline from observed defect through containment, root cause, corrective action and closure, with the evidence recorded at each step
blocks.caption: Eight-discipline workshop: a full case from symptom to closure

theory.h: Define the symptom with measured data
p: Start with the observed defect, not a suspected cause.
Record product, lot, stage, time in seconds, operator, equipment, and the measured attribute: solder volume in cubic millimetres, component offset in millimetres, hole fill as a percentage.
Use a taxonomy that separates symptom families: insufficient solder, excess solder, misalignment, voiding, non-wet. The taxonomy has to stay stable across lots, or nothing can be compared later.

theory.h: Pareto by stage before root cause
p: Sort defect counts by process stage: paste print, placement, reflow, wave, inspection.
A Pareto by stage shows where the largest measured loss is, not where the most obvious cause is. A stage with few defects but high cost or high field risk stays visible anyway.
Use the stage Pareto to set containment priority and to decide where to collect the next data, not to name the culprit.
A Pareto is only as good as the measurement behind it.

Verify the inspection method, the sample plan and the agreement between operators. For dimensional checks, confirm that the gauge resolution in millimetres is fine enough for the tolerance, and that measurement uncertainty is small against process variation.
For visual defects, use boundary samples and cross-check independent inspectors. Where disagreement is large, fix the measurement before sorting the data.

theory.h: Separate root cause, contributing causes and detection escape
p: The root cause is the process condition that, once removed, prevents recurrence under normal conditions.

Contributing causes make the defect more likely or more severe: paste viscosity drift, feeder wear, thermal profile variation in degrees Celsius, conveyor speed variation in millimetres per second. The detection escape explains why the defect was not found before shipment, such as a missing AOI program revision or a sampling plan that never covered the feature.
Each category gets its own action, and the report keeps them apart. A complete 8D report must address all three, because a corrected process with an open escape still ships defects.

theory.h: Containment must be measurable and time-bound
p: Containment protects the customer while the cause is being confirmed: quarantine, full inspection, rework, or a temporary process limit.

State the containment owner, the start time, the review interval and the exit condition. The exit condition rests on measured evidence, such as a clean inspection window or verified process capability, not on elapsed time alone.
Corrective action removes the root cause and closes the detection escape.
Examples: changing the stencil design, updating feeder calibration, adding a profile check, modifying an AOI program. Each action has an owner, a due date and a verification method.
Verification should show that the action works under normal production conditions, and that the defect returns if the action is removed — which is the honest test of whether it was a cause.
Closure is not complete until the effectiveness metric is defined and measured.

A common metric is no escapes inside a defined verification window, with the window chosen from production volume and risk. Record the baseline defect rate, the post-action defect rate and the inspection method used.
If the metric is not met, reopen the analysis rather than closing the report.

calc.task: A line records 100 defects in a production window: paste print 40, placement 30, reflow 20, wave 10. Calculate the stage Pareto and cumulative percentage. Before using the result, confirm that the inspection method has adequate resolution and repeatability for the measured attribute; verify against your paste/equipment datasheet.
calc.solution: Total is 100. Paste print share is 40 divided by 100, which is 40 percent, cumulative 40 percent. Placement share is 30 divided by 100, which is 30 percent, cumulative 70 percent. Reflow share is 20 divided by 100, which is 20 percent, cumulative 90 percent. Wave share is 10 divided by 100, which is 10 percent, cumulative 100 percent.

defect.symptom: Wave solder line shows insufficient hole fill on through-hole connectors, with exposed land visible at the bottom of the hole.
defect.cause: Root cause is a preheat temperature setpoint drift in degrees Celsius that reduced flux activation; contributing causes are board loading density and conveyor speed variation in millimetres per second; detection escape is that final visual inspection did not include a hole fill check aligned with IPC-A-610 acceptance criteria.
defect.action: Containment: quarantine suspect lots and perform full inspection with boundary samples; owner: wave solder process engineer; date: containment due at end of shift. Corrective action: restore preheat setpoint, add a logged preheat check, and update inspection to include hole fill criteria from IPC-A-610; owner: wave solder process engineer; date: corrective action due before next monthly review. Effectiveness metric: no escapes in the next 10 verification lots.

takeaways: Fix the measurement before reading the Pareto, because inspection noise sorts into a chart like real signal.
Set the containment exit on evidence, since a time-based exit simply ends attention.
Prove the cause by removing the action, because a fix that cannot be reversed cannot be demonstrated.

mistakes.mistake: Reading the stage Pareto as a diagnosis
mistakes.instead: Use it to choose the next measurement, since it ranks symptoms and not causes.

mistakes.mistake: Closing on a clean week of output
mistakes.instead: Measure the metric across a defined window, because a short quiet period proves little.

mistakes.mistake: Keeping a containment in place with no exit condition
mistakes.instead: Define the evidence that ends it, because permanent containment becomes the process.

terms.def: Defect counts sorted by the process stage where they were detected or attributed.
A physical specimen showing the limit of acceptability, used to align inspectors.
The third cause category of an 8D: why the defect passed the inspection or test meant to catch it.
How well a process holds its specification, stated as a measurable index.

title: How designers read process feedback: language, format, what gets acted on

goals.text: Convert a process limitation into a specific, testable design rule change.
Write and defend an ECN/DCR request against typical design objections.

p: Designers act on feedback written as a constraint, not a complaint.

A useful process note names the affected component or layer, the observed failure mode, the measurable process variable and the proposed design rule. "Small chip passives tombstone on the right side of the panel when paste apertures are asymmetric" is actionable; "the board is bad" is not.
The request should be short enough to read quickly and specific enough that a designer can change a rule file, a land pattern or a stencil without asking for clarification.

blocks.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 900 280' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='Process capability distribution'><style>text{font-family:'IBM Plex Mono',monospace}</style><line x1='60' y1='230' x2='860' y2='230' stroke='#94a3b8' stroke-width='1'/><line x1='250' y1='230' x2='250' y2='40' stroke='#f44336' stroke-width='1.5' stroke-dasharray='6 4'/><line x1='650' y1='230' x2='650' y2='40' stroke='#f44336' stroke-width='1.5' stroke-dasharray='6 4'/><line x1='450' y1='230' x2='450' y2='50' stroke='#53d1cc' stroke-width='1' stroke-dasharray='3 3'/><path d='M120,228 C260,220 330,70 450,70 C570,70 640,220 780,228' fill='rgba(83,209,204,.1)' stroke='#53d1cc' stroke-width='2.5'/><text x='250' y='30' fill='#f44336' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle'>LSL</text><text x='650' y='30' fill='#f44336' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle'>USL</text><text x='450' y='30' fill='#53d1cc' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle'>MEAN</text><text x='450' y='258' fill='#cbd5e1' font-size='14' text-anchor='middle'>Cp = (USL - LSL) / 6 sigma — spread vs tolerance</text><text x='450' y='276' fill='#94a3b8' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle'>Cpk also asks: is the mean centered?</text><text x='60' y='20' fill='#edf2f7' font-size='14' font-weight='600'>PROCESS CAPABILITY</text></svg>
blocks.caption: Capability compares the process spread to the tolerance band

blocks.alt: A process note written as a constraint, with the affected component, the observed condition and the requested change highlighted
blocks.caption: How designers read process feedback: language, format and what gets acted on
Cp / Cpk interpretation — thresholds are industry convention
head: Index
Reading
Action

theory.h: Translate process language into design variables
p: Use language that maps a process observation onto a design variable.
Instead of "the solder is not wetting well", name what controls wetting: pad finish, copper area, paste aperture area, stencil thickness, reflow ramp, component mass.

On SMT the designer can change land-pattern geometry, paste apertures, copper balance and thermal relief. On through-hole work they can change hole size, annular ring, solder mask clearance and component selection. The designer cannot change "wetting"; they can change those variables.
The format that gets action is an ECN or DCR with a clear decision point.

Start with the problem statement, then evidence, affected part numbers, proposed change, test plan, cost, schedule and risk. Name the exact layer or file: paste stencil layer, solder mask layer, copper layer, component library, assembly drawing.
Where the change touches acceptance, land pattern, board fabrication or BGA design, name the relevant IPC standard and the clause it applies.

theory.h: Make the change bounded and testable
p: Designers prioritise changes that reduce a measured risk, fit the existing board and can be verified without a full requalification.

"Make the pads bigger" invites rejection, because it can affect routing, impedance, assembly density or solder mask bridges. "Increase the paste aperture area on the low-volume side by 8 % to 12 % and verify SPI paste volume inside the process window" gives a bounded change and a test that proves it.
The difference between the two requests is the difference between a wish and a proposal.

theory.h: Convert a limitation into a design rule
p: To turn a process limitation into a design rule, identify the physical cause, express it as a design variable, and set a measurable limit.

For tombstoning the causes are unequal paste volume, unequal pad copper area, asymmetric thermal mass and placement offset. A testable rule reads: for small chip passives, the paste apertures on both ends shall have areas within ±10 % of each other, the copper pads shall be symmetric, and the placement centre shall be within ±0.05 mm of the pad centre.
Each clause is measurable, which is what makes it a rule rather than an intention.

theory.h: Apply the same logic to THT
p: On wave soldering, insufficient fill and solder balls follow from hole-to-lead clearance, pad size and flux activity.

A design rule can specify a clearance range, an annular ring and the solder mask web between pads. Because hole plating, drill wear and the wave profile vary, state the range and verify it against the board fabricator and the assembly equipment.
Ask the fabricator for the expected drilled hole tolerance and plated hole size, then set the rule from the achievable process rather than from a nominal drawing value.
Expect objections: the board worked before, the change costs money, the supplier cannot support it, test coverage is incomplete, the change touches another product.
Answer with data and a bounded plan: defect rate before and after, affected part numbers, test sample, fallback if the change fails, and the parts or files that will not change.
Where the change is too large for one step, propose a pilot panel or a product with high volume enough to prove it first.

theory.h: Close with a rule and a proof
p: A good process feedback note ends with what the designer must change and what the process team will prove.

Example: "Change the small chip passive paste apertures to symmetric rectangles with equal area; process will verify SPI paste volume, AOI tombstone rate and reflow profile on 300 boards before release."
That gives the designer a rule change and the process team a testable commitment, and neither is asked to do the other's job.

calc.task: A small chip passive tombstone issue appears on 18 boards out of 4000 boards. Convert this into a design rule change and an ECN/DCR request. Determine the current defect rate, a target rate, the sample size needed to show the target with 95% confidence if no tombstones are observed, and the paste aperture area balance needed to support the rule.
calc.solution: Current rate: 18 / 4000 = 0.0045 = 0.45%. Target: set a target of <=0.10% (1000 ppm) based on line capability and risk; verify against internal quality targets. Sample size: for a no-defect demonstration at 95% confidence, use the binomial upper bound. With confidence = 0.95 and target = 0.0010, n = ln(0.05) / ln(0.999) = 2995. Round up to 3000 boards. Design rule: for small chip passives, paste apertures on both ends shall have equal area within ±10%; for a nominal aperture area of 0.011 mm^2, the allowable range is 0.0099 mm^2 to 0.0121 mm^2. Process checks: SPI paste volume per pad within ±15% of nominal, placement center within ±0.05 mm of pad center, and reflow profile within paste and component limits. ECN/DCR: change the paste stencil layer for small chip passives to symmetric apertures, remove asymmetric copper or thermal relief on the affected pads, and add SPI verification. Defense: show the current 0.45% rate, the target 0.10% rate, the 3000-board no-defect test, the affected part numbers, the fallback to the previous stencil if the test fails, and the fact that the change does not alter the BOM or board outline.

defect.symptom: AOI flags tombstones on small chip passives on the right side of the panel after reflow, and SPI shows paste volume low on the left pads of the same components.
defect.cause: Asymmetric paste apertures or stencil aperture damage create unequal solder volume on the two ends of the component, and placement offset may increase the imbalance.
defect.action: Stop release of the affected stencil, quarantine suspect boards, rework or scrap as required, correct the stencil apertures to symmetric geometry, verify SPI paste volume within ±15% of nominal, and update the design rule to require aperture area balance within ±10%.

takeaways: Name the design variable rather than the symptom, because a designer can only change a layer, a dimension or a rule.
Bound the request with a number and a test, since an unbounded change asks for trust instead of evidence.
Offer the proof with the request, because a designer approves a change they can see verified.

mistakes.mistake: Sending a defect report with no design variable in it
mistakes.instead: Convert the symptom to a variable, because nothing on the drawing changes otherwise.

mistakes.mistake: Asking for a rule with no measurable limit
mistakes.instead: Set the limit in percent or millimetres, since a rule that cannot be measured cannot be audited.

mistakes.mistake: Raising the same request every quarter
mistakes.instead: Close it with a rule and a verification, because an open request loses credibility.

terms.def: Engineering change notice, the formal record that authorises a design change.
A drawing, layer, dimension or library attribute the designer controls.
A measurable constraint applied during layout or stencil design.
A limited build used to prove a change before full release.

title: The evidence pack: measured data, images with scale, defect rate, cost of poor quality

goals.text: Build an evidence pack that quantifies the process impact of the current design.

blocks.alt: Reference sheet: macro photograph of a solder bridge between QFP leads with a scale bar, a measurement table, a defect-rate trend with control limits and a cost-of-poor-quality donut chart
blocks.caption: The evidence pack: measurement, image with scale, defect rate with its basis, cost of poor quality

p: An evidence pack is a compact set of records showing what the SMT or through-hole process is actually doing, not what it was intended to do.

For a working process engineer it lets another engineer or a manager answer three questions without visiting the line: what is being measured, what the physical evidence shows, and what the financial consequence of the defect is.
If the pack cannot answer those three, it is a folder rather than evidence.

theory.h: Measured data that belongs in the pack
p: Measured data covers both process parameters and output quality.

Typical inputs are stencil thickness, aperture area, paste volume, reflow peak temperature, time above liquidus, placement accuracy and oven profile repeatability. Typical outputs are joint quality, defect counts, first-pass yield, rework count and scrap count.
For each parameter record the unit, the measurement method, the sample size, the time window and the acceptance limit, because a number without those is not comparable to anything.
An image is evidence only when it can be interpreted later.

Each image carries a scale reference: a calibrated ruler, a scale bar or a known component dimension, plus the magnification or field of view. The file name or caption identifies board, panel, station, defect type, date and shift.

For solder defects, take a close-up and a wider view showing the component, adjacent pads and the surrounding land, because the close-up alone cannot show where it sits. Include the stencil side, the board side and, where it matters, a 3D measurement or a cross-section.
Define the defect rate clearly.
A common board-level metric is defects per million opportunities, and the opportunity count must be stated: one joint, one pad, one component or one inspection point.
On surface-mount work, defect density is often more useful than a pass percentage, because it compares across board sizes and mixes where a simple percentage does not.
A single shift misleads when the line runs a mixed product or a changeover happened.

State the sampling window: one shift, one day, one week, one production order. For a process comparison, use matched conditions — same product, same line, same paste lot family, same stencil, similar board mix.
Where matched conditions are impossible, state the differences and treat the comparison as indicative rather than conclusive.
Cost of poor quality includes scrap, rework labour, inspection labour, line downtime, expedited freight, warranty or field failure exposure, and lost capacity.

For a line-level estimate start with direct costs: scrapped boards, rework time, additional inspection time and machine time consumed by rework. For a product-level estimate add downstream test failures, repair and customer returns.
Keep the calculation transparent enough that someone can check one of the terms.
The pack connects data, images, defect rate and cost into one argument.
For insufficient solder, show the measured paste volume distribution, images of the affected joints, the defect rate by station or product, and the rework cost per affected board.
The conclusion states the impact in operational terms: yield loss, throughput loss, rework burden, or risk of escape.
The pack can be a short report, a spreadsheet or a slide set, and it must be traceable.

Include a cover page with product name, line, date range, author and revision, attach the raw data or give the path where it is stored, and use consistent units, preferably SI: millimetres, micrometres, grams, seconds and degrees Celsius.
For images, embed captions in the report and keep the original files with their metadata.

calc.task: Build a simple cost-of-poor-quality estimate for a surface-mount line producing 12,000 boards per week. The line has a first-pass yield of 96.5 percent. Of the failed boards, 70 percent are reworked successfully, 20 percent are scrapped, and 10 percent are held for further analysis. Rework labor is 18 minutes per board at a loaded labor rate of 45 euros per hour. Scrap cost is 120 euros per board. Additional inspection and handling cost is 3.50 euros per failed board. Calculate weekly rework labor cost, scrap cost, inspection and handling cost, total cost of poor quality, and cost per good board.
calc.solution: 1. Calculate failed boards per week: 12,000 boards per week multiplied by 1 minus 0.965 equals 12,000 multiplied by 0.035 equals 420 failed boards per week. 2. Calculate reworked boards: 420 failed boards multiplied by 0.70 equals 294 reworked boards per week. 3. Calculate rework labor hours: 294 boards multiplied by 18 minutes per board equals 5,292 minutes. 5,292 minutes divided by 60 equals 88.2 hours per week. 4. Calculate rework labor cost: 88.2 hours multiplied by 45 euros per hour equals 3,969 euros per week. 5. Calculate scrapped boards: 420 failed boards multiplied by 0.20 equals 84 scrapped boards per week. 6. Calculate scrap cost: 84 boards multiplied by 120 euros per board equals 10,080 euros per week. 7. Calculate inspection and handling cost: 420 failed boards multiplied by 3.50 euros per board equals 1,470 euros per week. 8. Calculate total cost of poor quality: 3,969 euros plus 10,080 euros plus 1,470 euros equals 15,519 euros per week. 9. Calculate good boards per week: 12,000 boards minus 420 failed boards equals 11,580 good boards per week. 10. Calculate cost of poor quality per good board: 15,519 euros divided by 11,580 good boards equals 1.34 euros per good board. 11. Interpretation: the current process consumes 15,519 euros per week in direct rework, scrap, and handling, equivalent to 1.34 euros per good board. This figure should be checked against your actual labor rate, scrap value, inspection cost, and any downtime or expedite costs before using it in a business case.

defect.symptom: After reflow, several 0402 chip resistors show tombstoning on one side of the board, and the defect rate rises from a baseline of about 200 defects per million placements to about 1,800 defects per million placements on the affected panel location.
defect.cause: The evidence pack links the defect to uneven paste release and thermal imbalance. Images with scale show one pad has paste volume near the lower end of the process window while the adjacent pad is near the upper end. The stencil design for that panel location has slightly different aperture areas, and the reflow profile shows a faster ramp rate than the paste datasheet recommends for the board thermal mass.
defect.action: Reduce the defect rate by adjusting the stencil aperture area balance for the affected pads, verifying paste release with 3D solder paste inspection, and slowing the preheat ramp rate within the paste and component thermal limits. Re-run a short production window, collect images with scale, record defect rate by panel location, and update the evidence pack with before and after data.

takeaways: Build the pack so it answers what is measured, what the evidence shows and what it costs, because those three questions decide whether anyone acts.
Put the unit and the window with every number, since a bare figure cannot be compared with the next build.
Keep images interpretable later, because a close-up without scale is an anecdote.

mistakes.mistake: Reporting a defect rate without the opportunity count
mistakes.instead: State what is counted, because a joint and a board give different numbers for the same line.

mistakes.mistake: Comparing two shifts running different products
mistakes.instead: Match conditions or label the comparison as indicative, since product mix dominates the rate.

mistakes.mistake: Quoting a cost of poor quality with no terms
mistakes.instead: Show the build-up, because a total nobody can check is not persuasive.

terms.def: A defect rate normalised by the number of countable opportunities in the product.
Defects normalised to board area or joint count, allowing comparison across sizes.
The cost of scrap, rework, inspection and lost capacity caused by defects.
A comparison where product, line, materials and process settings are held comparable.

title: Writing the change request: problem, impact, proposal, alternatives, risk, verification

goals.text: Write and defend an ECN/DCR request against typical design objections.

blocks.alt: A change request form with the six sections laid out, each with a short example entry
blocks.caption: Writing the change request: problem, impact, proposal, alternatives, risk and verification

theory.h: Frame the change request as a contract
p: An ECN or DCR states what is wrong, what is being changed, and how acceptance will be proven.

It identifies affected part numbers, drawings, BOM levels, routings, test programs and documents. For SMT and through-hole work, add board revision, panelisation, feeder or insertion head, stencil, wave or selective solder, and inspection method.
Write it so design, manufacturing, quality and purchasing can all read it without a translator.
The problem statement carries defect mode, location, occurrence, detection method and consequence.

Use measurable terms: solder voiding on QFN pads detected by X-ray, tombstoning at a specific feeder, lead seating error at a connector row. State sample size, lot, date, equipment and operator where they matter.
Where acceptance criteria are needed, cite IPC-A-610 and verify the applicable class against the product specification.
The impact section covers electrical, mechanical, thermal, assembly, test, reliability, inventory and qualification effects.

For a land-pattern change, cite IPC-7351 for footprint geometry and IPC-7095 for BGA. For through-hole work, cover lead forming, seating, wave dwell, clearance and interference with adjacent components.
Say whether existing inventory can be consumed, reworked or scrapped, and who pays for it.
The proposal specifies old and new values, the drawing revision, the BOM change, process parameter changes and work instruction updates.

For paste changes, state stencil thickness, aperture dimensions and paste type, verified against the paste and printer datasheet. For through-hole work, state lead finish, seating tolerance and wave or selective profile limits.
Include traceability, first-article requirements and the list of documents that change.
Consider at least two alternatives: process adjustment, component substitution, layout change, or test change.

Compare technical feasibility, cost, schedule, inventory and risk. A rejected alternative states why, for example a process window too narrow, no qualified component, insufficient test coverage, or an unacceptable rework burden.
This section is what defends the request against the objection that it was chosen before the analysis.
Use a simple risk table: failure mode, severity, occurrence, detection, mitigation, residual risk.

For rework and repair limits cite IPC-7711/7721, and for soldering process qualification cite IPC J-STD-001. State the controls: SPC, AOI, X-ray, in-circuit test, functional test, environmental stress screening.
Do not claim zero risk. State the residual risk you accept and who accepts it.
Verification includes the sample plan, acceptance criteria, data format and disposition.

Measure dimensional changes with calibrated tools. Inspect solder joints by cross-section or X-ray against IPC-A-610 where required. Where the change affects joint stress, define the thermal cycling or vibration test.
Close the ECN or DCR only when the data, the updated documents and the inventory disposition are all complete.

calc.task: A proposed ECN reduces a chip resistor stencil aperture from 0.50 mm by 0.50 mm to 0.45 mm by 0.45 mm, with stencil thickness 0.12 mm. Calculate the paste volume change and a simple verification sample using n = 1 / target defect rate, with target 0.5% per board.
calc.solution: Step 1: Old aperture area = 0.50 mm x 0.50 mm = 0.25 mm^2. Step 2: New aperture area = 0.45 mm x 0.45 mm = 0.2025 mm^2. Step 3: Old paste volume = 0.25 mm^2 x 0.12 mm = 0.03 mm^3. Step 4: New paste volume = 0.2025 mm^2 x 0.12 mm = 0.0243 mm^3. Step 5: Volume change = (0.0243 - 0.03) / 0.03 = -0.19, or 19% reduction. Step 6: Target defect rate = 0.5% = 0.005 defects per board. Step 7: Simple screening sample n = 1 / 0.005 = 200 boards. Step 8: This is a screening sample, not a confidence statement; verify the final sample size against your quality plan and customer requirements.

defect.symptom: AOI flags missing or tombstoned small chip components on one feeder lane, while adjacent lanes pass.
defect.cause: Stencil aperture or paste release may be out of process, placement nozzle vacuum may be low, feeder timing may be misaligned, or the component may be sticking to the nozzle.
defect.action: Stop the lane, quarantine suspect boards, measure paste volume, check stencil thickness and aperture condition, verify printer and placement parameters against the equipment datasheet, clean or replace the nozzle and feeder, then run a first article and requalify before release.

takeaways: State what changes and how acceptance is proven, because a change request without a proof is an opinion.
Show impact and alternatives before the proposal, since reviewers approve what they can see was compared.
Name the residual risk and its owner, because a claim of zero risk invites rejection.

mistakes.mistake: Sending a change request that names only the desired outcome
mistakes.instead: Give old and new values, because the implementer needs the difference.

mistakes.mistake: Omitting the inventory and document impact
mistakes.instead: List them, since a change that leaves stock stranded gets deferred.

mistakes.mistake: Verifying with an unstated sample plan
mistakes.instead: State the sample and the criterion, because acceptance without a plan is a judgement.

terms.def: Design change request, the engineering request that initiates a change before formal approval.
The first unit built to a changed design, inspected in full.
The risk that remains after mitigation, accepted by a named owner.
The arrangement of boards on a production panel, which a design change can affect.

title: DFM/DFT asks that work: pad geometry, paste relief, spacing, test points, fiducials, panelization, hole/lead spec

goals.text: Convert a process limitation into a specific, testable design rule change.

blocks.alt: A board layout with pad geometry, paste relief, spacing, test points, fiducials and panelization callouts, beside a hole-to-lead specification table
blocks.caption: Design-for-manufacture and test asks that work: pad geometry, paste relief, spacing, test points, fiducials, panelization and hole-to-lead specification

theory.h: From line limitation to testable rule
p: A DFM or DFT ask is useful only when it becomes a measurable rule.

Start with the process limitation, not the component name. Poor placement repeatability points to a larger pad or a larger component-to-component keepout. An unstable stencil print points to paste relief, a different aperture shape or a thickness change. Insufficient wave fill points to a larger annular ring or a different hole-to-lead clearance.
Each of those is a drawing dimension a designer can change and a process engineer can verify.
Pad geometry controls paste volume, wetting, self-alignment and bridging risk.

For passives, land length and width should support the intended fillet while leaving room for the neighbour. For QFN, MLF and other exposed-pad packages, the centre pad needs paste relief, because full-area paste pushes the package up, traps flux or creates voids.
Frame the land pattern against IPC-7351, check paste aperture changes against IPC-7525, and verify both against your paste and printer datasheet and your own placement accuracy.

theory.h: Paste relief is a process control
p: Paste relief is a stencil or aperture change used to control volume, bleed and bridging.

Methods include reducing aperture area, splitting a large pad into sub-apertures, adding a step stencil, or changing wall geometry. On fine-pitch packages a small area reduction can stop paste collapse without starving the joint, and on thermal pads splitting the aperture into several openings improves release and cuts voiding.
Treat it as a process control with a measured window, not as a cosmetic tweak to the stencil.

theory.h: Spacing must satisfy assembly and inspection
p: Spacing rules have to satisfy electrical clearance, assembly access, inspection and thermal or wave-solder shielding at the same time.
IPC-2221 and IPC-2222 give generic and organic-board design frameworks, and the final spacing also reflects your placement accuracy, feeder clearance and inspection optics.
On SMT, component-to-component spacing should let the nozzle approach without disturbing neighbours and leave room for the inspection camera.
Test points are the first DFT failure because they are added late.

A test point should be a dedicated pad with controlled size, plating and solder mask opening, not a random via or a component lead. For in-circuit test, probe access needs enough diameter and spacing to prevent probe interference.
For functional test, the pad should survive repeated probing and should not sit under a component or inside a panel rail.
Fiducials turn a placement program into a repeatable coordinate system.

Global fiducials go near the panel corners, and local fiducials close to fine-pitch or high-accuracy components. The fiducial needs high contrast, a clean circular or cross shape, and a clear zone free of copper, silkscreen and nearby pads.
Check the size and the clear zone against the placement camera field of view, because a fiducial the camera cannot resolve is decoration.
Panelisation affects handling, deformation, breakaway quality, and where fiducials and test points can sit.

The panel fits the conveyor, placement, reflow, wave and in-circuit equipment, and it should not force the board to flex during depaneling. Rails, V-scores, mouse bites and routed breakaways each carry trade-offs.
Fiducials belong on the panel or rails where the camera sees them, and test points must stay reachable after depaneling.

theory.h: Hole and lead specs decide THT quality
p: Hole and lead specifications are often the difference between a sound joint and a weak or bridged one.

Drill size, plating, annular ring and hole-to-lead clearance decide wetting and fill. IPC-2221 and IPC-2222 give the frameworks, and the final hole size is checked against drill tolerance, plating thickness and lead diameter variation.
For wave or selective solder, the hole and annular ring should give a fill that meets the acceptance criteria without a dwell long enough to damage the board.

theory.h: Write the rule as a change request with proof
p: The conversion from limitation to rule is a change request with a measurable target.

If SPI shows paste collapse on a fine-pitch QFN, the rule reduces thermal-pad aperture area, adds sub-aperture gaps and sets an SPI height window. If wave soldering shows insufficient fill at a through-hole connector, the rule increases the annular ring or adjusts the hole size. If probes miss test points, the rule adds dedicated pads of the right diameter and spacing.
Each rule arrives with the measurement that will show it worked.

calc.task: A 0.4 mm pitch QFN has a 4.0 mm x 4.0 mm thermal pad. SPI shows paste height near 0.16 mm with a 0.12 mm stencil, and the line sees paste bleed between peripheral pads. Convert this limitation into a specific, testable design rule change for the thermal-pad paste aperture.
calc.solution: Pad area calculation: 4.0 mm x 4.0 mm = 16.0 mm2. Target aperture area: 60% of pad area, so 0.60 x 16.0 mm2 = 9.6 mm2. Aperture pattern: use 4 square sub-apertures with a 0.10 mm gap between adjacent sub-apertures. If each sub-aperture is 1.55 mm x 1.55 mm, total aperture area is 4 x 1.55 mm x 1.55 mm = 9.61 mm2, which is 60.1% of the pad area. Layout envelope check: 2 sub-apertures plus the gap span 2 x 1.55 mm + 0.10 mm = 3.20 mm, leaving 0.40 mm of outer margin on each side inside the 4.0 mm pad. Nominal paste volume: 9.61 mm2 x 0.12 mm = 1.153 mm3. Acceptance window: SPI paste height 0.10 mm to 0.13 mm, no bridging at 0.4 mm pitch, and package seating confirmed by X-ray or cross-section per IPC-A-610. Design rule to release: thermal-pad aperture area shall be 58% to 62% of pad area, implemented as 4 sub-apertures of 1.55 mm +/- 0.05 mm with 0.10 mm +/- 0.05 mm gaps, verified on a pilot panel by SPI and X-ray.

defect.symptom: After reflow, 0.4 mm pitch QFN packages show lifted corners and voided center pads, while SPI shows high paste height on the thermal pad.
defect.cause: Full-area thermal-pad aperture plus a 0.12 mm stencil produced excess paste volume; the package floated on paste and trapped flux.
defect.action: Reduce thermal-pad aperture to 58% to 62% area, split into 4 sub-apertures with 0.10 mm gaps, re-run SPI with height window 0.10 mm to 0.13 mm, and verify seating by X-ray per IPC-A-610.

takeaways: Convert the limitation into a dimension, because a rule the designer can draw is a rule the line can verify.
Give paste relief a measured window, since a stencil change without an SPI limit is an experiment.
Place the test point and the fiducial early, because both are cheap at layout and expensive afterwards.

mistakes.mistake: Asking for more spacing without a reason
mistakes.instead: Tie the number to placement and inspection, because ungrounded requests lose.

mistakes.mistake: Adding test points on existing vias
mistakes.instead: Use dedicated pads, because a via under mask cannot be probed reliably.

mistakes.mistake: Changing the stencil without an SPI limit
mistakes.instead: Set the window first, since the change will drift back.

terms.def: A reduction or splitting of paste aperture area to control volume and voiding.
A high-contrast mark used by the placement machine to establish coordinates.
A breakaway tab with drilled perforations used to separate a board from its panel.
An area kept clear of components or copper for a process reason.
